children.tldr: Becoming a public company will raise legal, accounting and compliance costs, strain management with limited public company experience, and may invite litigation and stockholder activism.
children.summary: As a public company, Anthropic will be subject to the [[Exchange Act, Sarbanes-Oxley Act, Dodd-Frank Act|p562]], SEC rules and Nasdaq Global Select Market listing standards, which will raise costs and may make director and officer insurance more expensive. It expects significant spending on [[Section 404 auditor attestation|p563]] and will need to hire more accounting staff, and it may face [[stockholder activism|p563]]. Greater visibility from public filings may lead to [[threatened or actual litigation|p564]], including by competitors. Many managers have [[limited experience managing a publicly traded company|p565]], and the new obligations could pull their attention from running the business.

children.title: Our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected by war, terrorism, natural disasters, public health crises, political crises, or other unexpected events.
children.tldr: War, terrorism, natural disasters, pandemics and other crises could disrupt Anthropic's operations and data centers, and its San Francisco Bay Area headquarters faces earthquake and fire risk.
children.summary: Anthropic warns that war, terrorism, natural disasters, power outages and public health or political crises could disrupt its operations, the internet, [[data centers|p566]] and its partners, with climate change possibly raising these risks. Its headquarters sit in the [[San Francisco Bay Area|p566]], an area prone to earthquakes and fires. Armed conflict could damage data centers or cut power, cooling or connectivity, leading to outages, delays and security incidents. Its [[disaster recovery plans|p566]] may prove inadequate and its [[insurance may be insufficient|p566]] to cover losses.

children.title: If we are unable to ensure that our models, platform, and applications interoperate with a variety of software applications that are developed by others, including our integration partners, we may become less competitive and our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.
children.tldr: Anthropic depends on third-party APIs, operating systems and app stores like Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store, and changes by those providers or competitors could hurt its business.
children.summary: Anthropic's products must integrate with many hardware and software platforms, and it relies on other providers, including competitors, to give it [[access to their APIs|p567]] under terms they can change. Its business would suffer if a provider [[limits access|p568]], changes its terms or fees, or [[favors its own competing offerings|p572]]. The company also relies on [[iOS and Android and their app stores|p573]] to drive downloads of the Claude app, so changes to availability, cost, functionality or search rankings could slow user growth. Competitors could also [[disrupt compatibility|p574]] or give preference to rival products.

children.title: Many of the risks we face are interconnected and may compound or trigger cascading adverse effects across our business, which could amplify their overall impact.
children.tldr: Anthropic's risks are interconnected, so one event, such as a compute shortage or copyright loss, could trigger others, including defaults and cross-defaults under its A&R Credit Agreement.
children.summary: Anthropic says many of its risks are linked, so one event can trigger others and the [[combined effect may be materially greater|p575]] than any single risk. For example, adverse [[copyright or other litigation|p575]] could force it to retrain or limit its models, hurting demand and revenue. [[Constraints on compute|p575]] could delay launches and slow growth. Weak revenue without new capital could lead to covenant breaches under the [[A&R Credit Agreement|p575]] and commercial agreements, which could set off [[cross-defaults|p575]] and faster repayment, further limiting operations.

children.title: Risks Related to Privacy, Cybersecurity, and Intellectual Property
children.tldr: Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle the Bartz copyright suit and faces unsettled fair use law, nation-state attacks on its model weights, and evolving privacy rules.
children.summary: Courts have not settled whether training AI on copyrighted data is [[fair use|s85]], and adverse rulings could force license fees or retraining. Anthropic agreed to pay [[$1.5 billion to settle the Bartz|s91]] copyright class action and still faces suits from music publishers and Reddit, plus patent claims and uncapped indemnities. [[Reddit alleges improper access|s89]] to its posts through Anthropic's web data collection. The company has experienced security incidents and is a target for [[nation-state attackers seeking model weights|s88]], including Mythos. It is subject to fragmented [[privacy laws such as the GDPR|s86]], and its AI safety work requires processing sensitive personal data. Other risks include gaps in protecting its own intellectual property, [[open-source license obligations|s93]] that AI-generated code could trigger, dependence on licensed technology, disputes with replaced vendors, and [[trade secret claims from hiring|s96]] at rival AI companies.

children.title: The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of opensource licenses to modern AI model training are uncertain.
children.tldr: Courts have not settled whether training AI models on copyrighted data is fair use, and an adverse ruling against Anthropic or a rival could force costly licensing or retraining.
children.summary: Anthropic believes its use of training data is [[fair use|p576]] under copyright law, but U.S. and non-U.S. courts have not authoritatively resolved the question, and some countries do not recognize fair use at all. A court could disagree, for example by adopting the reasoning in [[Bartz|p576]]. Rulings against [[other AI developers|p576]] could set industry-wide precedent even if Anthropic's own practices differ. Possible outcomes include [[significant license fees|p576]], injunctions limiting use of affected models, or having to [[retrain affected models from scratch|p576]] at substantial cost.

children.title: We are subject to complex and evolving laws, regulations, and other legal obligations related to privacy and data protection, and any actual or perceived failure to comply with such obligations could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic faces fragmented, evolving privacy laws such as the GDPR, and actual or perceived noncompliance could bring investigations, fines, lawsuits and forced product changes.
children.summary: Anthropic is subject to privacy and data protection rules in the EU, the United States and elsewhere, including the [[GDPR|p577]], that are not harmonized and are being applied to AI in new ways. Plaintiffs and state Attorneys General are [[pursuing claims against AI companies|p577]] over data handling. Exposure varies with how customers access the products and the type of data involved, and Anthropic has [[faced operational errors or claims|p578]] that its data use broke its obligations. Data security failures can trigger [[notification obligations|p579]], and any compliance failure could lead to [[investigations, fines and reputational harm|p580]].

children.title: We process personal and sensitive data for AI safety, and any actual or perceived failure to comply with the legal and regulatory obligations applicable to such processing could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic's AI safety work requires processing personal and sensitive data, which raises legal, security and litigation risks under unsettled and evolving rules.
children.summary: Anthropic's commitment to AI safety sometimes requires it to [[collect and process personal and sensitive data|p581]], which increases the harm and litigation risk if that data is exposed. Laws not written for AI safety are being [[applied in inconsistent or novel ways|p581]], and failures could bring investigations, fines, required practice changes and reputational damage.

children.title: Any security breaches or other incidents, including those that affect our networks, systems, or data, or the networks, systems, or data of our service providers, suppliers, or customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic has suffered security incidents and is a priority target for nation-state attackers seeking its model weights, including Mythos, with gaps in defenses and limited insurance.
children.summary: Anthropic has experienced [[security breaches and unauthorized access|p582]] and faces cyberattacks from nation-states, which see model weights as high-value targets; Mythos may be [[specifically targeted|p583]]. The company has operated with [[known gaps in its defenses|p584]], and stolen weights could be deployed outside its safety controls. Other risks include [[insider threats|p585]], such as applicants with false identities and foreign laws compelling cooperation with intelligence agencies, supply chain attacks, AI-specific threats like prompt injection, and new [[agentic attack surfaces|p588]] where agents take real-world actions. Post-deployment defects and customer misconfigurations add exposure. Anthropic faces strict [[EU incident reporting rules|p594]] under the GDPR, NIS2 and the EU AI Act, and U.S. laws such as the [[RAISE Act and California's frontier AI law|p595]]. Its [[insurance may not cover|p596]] all losses.

children.title: We employ automated data collection across the web and use other methods to collect data for training our AI models, and such activities may subject us to liability or limit our ability to use the collected data, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, or results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic's web scraping and other data collection for training could create privacy and IP liability, and Reddit is suing over alleged improper access to its posts.
children.summary: Anthropic trains models on [[public internet data, licensed datasets and synthetic data|p597]], gathered through web crawling, book scanning and other methods. It tries to respect robots.txt and paywalls but may not always succeed or know whether data is protected, and weak provenance records could create legal exposure. [[Reddit, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC|p598]] alleges improper access to Reddit posts; Anthropic removed it to federal court on July 3, 2025, and it was remanded to state court on March 30, 2026. Defending such suits is [[costly regardless of merit|p599]], and settlements or judgments could [[bar certain techniques|p600]] or require [[substantial payments|p601]].

children.title: We collect, integrate, and analyze data via agreements from multiple sources, including data provided by our customers and users and data sourced from third parties under contractual arrangements, and such activities may subject us to liability or limit our ability to use the collected data, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, or results of operations.
children.tldr: If Anthropic or its data sources lack rights to use customer, user or third-party data, it could face claims requiring it to limit features, segregate data or retrain models.
children.summary: Insufficient rights to use data from customers, users or third parties, including for model training, could bring [[legal claims or contractual liability|p602]] and force Anthropic to limit functionality or retrain models. Such claims are costly, may be broad, and are [[likely in the ordinary course of business|p603]].

children.title: We have been, are currently defending against, and may in the future be, subject to intellectual property rights claims by third parties, which are extremely costly to defend, may require us to pay significant damages and may limit our ability to use certain technologies, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle the Bartz copyright class action and still faces music publisher, Reddit and patent suits, plus uncapped indemnities.
children.summary: As Anthropic's profile grows, [[intellectual property claims|p604]] may increase. In September 2025 it agreed to settle the [[Bartz copyright class action for $1.5 billion|p605]], approved by the district court in July 2026. It is defending suits from music publishers including Concord, BMG, Round Hill and Sony over song lyrics, along with the Reddit case, and statutory damages add risk. It also faces [[patent claims|p606]] from competitors with larger portfolios. Settlements could require [[licenses that may be unavailable|p608]]. Some agreements require Anthropic to [[indemnify counterparties without a cap|p610]] against claims that its models or outputs infringe, including agreements with external evaluators.

children.title: If we fail to adequately protect our intellectual property rights, our competitive position may be impaired, and we may lose valuable assets, generate reduced revenue, and incur costly litigation to protect our rights, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic's patents, trade secrets, confidentiality agreements and trademarks may fail to stop insiders or rivals from misappropriating its model weights, technology or brand.
children.summary: Anthropic relies on trademark, copyright, patent and trade secret law plus contracts, but [[insiders with access to model weights|p611]] could misappropriate them. Enforcement litigation is [[costly and may invite counterclaims|p612]] challenging its rights. Patent applications [[may not be granted|p613]] or may be too narrow, and unpublished applications by others create [[priority and infringement risks|p614]]. Confidentiality agreements may not protect [[unpatented technology|p615]], and successful [[trademark challenges|p616]] could force a rebrand.

children.title: We incorporate open-source software in our models, platform, and applications, which may subject us to litigation or other requirements, each of which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Open-source software in Anthropic's products could bring license claims, forced release of proprietary code, and security flaws, risks heightened by AI-generated code from tools like Claude Code.
children.summary: Anthropic uses [[open-source software|p617]] in its models, platform, and applications and could face claims of ownership or license non-compliance. Some licenses require releasing proprietary code at no cost. The company says its own [[AI tools, including Claude Code|p617]], could reproduce open-source code without its knowledge, triggering copyleft obligations, and similar worries could lead [[enterprise customers to limit their use|p617]] of its products. Most license types have [[never been tested in court|p617]]. A successful claim could mean legal costs, re-engineering, damages, sales injunctions, or public release of source code. Open-source code also comes with [[no warranties|p618]] and may contain [[security vulnerabilities, defects, or errors|p618]] that take time to fix.

children.title: We currently, and may in the future, license technology from third parties for use in our models, platform, and applications, and our inability to maintain those licenses could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations, and our use of such third-party technology could subject us to litigation.
children.tldr: Anthropic depends on licensed third-party technology; losing those licenses or facing infringement claims against licensors could limit its products and raise costs.
children.summary: Anthropic incorporates [[technology licensed from third parties|p619]] into its products. If it cannot keep these licenses on reasonable terms, or the technology fails, it may not find timely alternatives. The company has [[less visibility into how licensed technology is developed|p619]], raising infringement and security risks, and some licenses [[may be terminated or have a limited term|p619]]. Replacing them could require [[lower quality alternatives|p620]] and higher costs, and third-party software may be [[unsupported or contain unresolved errors|p620]].

children.title: Our development of solutions that replace or reduce reliance on third-party vendors may expose us to litigation and other disputes.
children.tldr: Building tools that replace third-party vendors could prompt those vendors to sue Anthropic for breach of contract, infringement, or unfair competition.
children.summary: As Anthropic builds solutions that [[replace or reduce reliance on vendors|p621]], those vendors may bring claims such as breach of contract, intellectual property infringement, tortious interference, or unfair competition. Such claims could lead to [[costly litigation, settlements, or injunctions|p622]] and distract management, regardless of merit.

children.title: We may be subject to claims that we or our employees have misappropriated the intellectual property of other companies, particularly as we hire employees from other AI and technology companies.
children.tldr: Hiring from other AI companies exposes Anthropic to claims that it or its employees misappropriated trade secrets, even without intentional misconduct.
children.summary: Intense [[competition for AI talent|p623]] means Anthropic hires people from competitors and loses staff to them. Despite confidentiality requirements, the company could face claims of [[misappropriating trade secrets|p624]], even without merit or intentional misconduct. Such disputes could bring damages, injunctions, [[limits on employees' roles|p625]], and reputational harm.

children.title: Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
children.tldr: Anthropic faces legal, antitrust, anti-corruption, export control, international, ESG and payment processing risks, including a September 2026 Sherman Act class action and June 2026 export restrictions on two models.
children.summary: This group of risk factors covers Anthropic's legal and regulatory exposure. The company faces [[lawsuits, investigations and government orders|s98]], including novel liability theories for agentic AI and an antitrust class action over the pace of AI development. It must comply with [[anti-corruption and anti-money laundering laws|s99]] and with [[export controls and sanctions|s100]], which in June 2026 forced it to disable two models worldwide. [[International expansion|s101]] brings data, tax, staffing and geopolitical risks, especially around China. The company also faces conflicting [[ESG expectations and anti-ESG pressure|s102]], and fraud and chargeback risks in [[payment processing|s103]].

children.title: We are subject to claims, lawsuits, investigations, executive and administrative orders and directives, other regulatory actions, and various actions and proceedings, and face potential liability, expenses for legal claims, and harm to our business.
children.tldr: A September 2026 putative class action accuses Anthropic and other frontier AI developers of agreeing to slow model development in violation of the Sherman Act, seeking treble damages.
children.summary: Anthropic faces many types of legal and regulatory proceedings, and agentic AI and healthcare offerings may expose it to [[novel, untested liability theories|p626]] and health regulation. Its AI safety advocacy and industry collaboration carry antitrust risk: in September 2026 a [[putative class action|p627]] in the Northern District of California alleged that Anthropic and other developers agreed to slow model development, seeking treble damages and injunctive relief for paid consumer subscribers. Anthropic disputes the claims. Its proposal for a [[narrow antitrust safe harbor|p628]] for safety collaboration has drawn political opposition, and these risks may lead it to limit its advocacy. Proceedings could hurt revenue and customer relationships, and the company may [[settle even meritorious cases|p630]], as in Bartz, where insurance did not fully cover the claim.

children.title: We are subject to anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering laws, and similar laws.
children.tldr: Anthropic could be held liable for bribery or money laundering by its employees or third-party agents, a risk that grows as non-U.S. sales increase.
children.summary: Anthropic must comply with the [[FCPA, the UK Bribery Act 2010|p631]] and similar laws. It uses intermediaries and agents that interact with government officials and could be [[liable for third parties' conduct|p632]] even without authorizing it, and its [[compliance policies may not be effective|p633]]. Violations could bring [[criminal or civil sanctions|p634]], debarment from U.S. government contracts, and significant fines.

children.title: Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets.
children.tldr: In June 2026 the Commerce Department imposed worldwide export restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, forcing Anthropic to disable them until safeguards were updated and restrictions lifted.
children.summary: Anthropic's models fall under U.S. export controls, including the EAR and in some cases ITAR, and their [[classification is uncertain|p635]] as capabilities and rules change. In June 2026 the Department of Commerce [[imposed worldwide restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5|p637]]; Anthropic disabled both for all customers and redeployed them after updating safeguards and the restrictions were lifted. Similar controls could recur, last longer or cover more models. Sanctions and rules on [[adversary-linked supply chains|p638]] could also affect data center suppliers. Anthropic uses geo-blocking and party screening, but its controls [[have not always been fully effective|p639]] and it has voluntarily disclosed past noncompliance. Violations could cost it [[government sales|p643]] and bring penalties.

children.title: To continue to grow our business, we will need to continue to expand internationally, and our non-U.S. operations and sales to customers outside of the United States expose us to risks inherent in international expansion, sales, and operations.
children.tldr: Anthropic's growth depends partly on international expansion, which brings data rules, staffing, tax, investment review and U.S.-China tension risks.
children.summary: Anthropic has operations in the [[UK, EU, Canada and Asia-Pacific|p645]] and expects growth to depend partly on further expansion. Risks include data localization and conflicting privacy rules, a [[Justice Department rule effective April 2025|p649]] limiting data transfers linked to China, and fast-changing laws such as the [[EU AI Act and UK Online Safety Act 2023|p651]]. Other risks include staffing through employer-of-record arrangements, currency declines and tax changes. [[Foreign direct investment reviews|p671]] may limit investments and acquisitions abroad, and growing [[U.S. scrutiny of exposure to Chinese state actors|p672]] could restrict whom Anthropic serves and shrink its addressable market.

children.title: Increasing scrutiny and changing expectations from global regulations, our investors, customers, and employees with respect to ESG may result in additional compliance risk and costs and may impact our reputation and business.
children.tldr: Anthropic faces rising ESG disclosure rules and concern about AI's energy and water use, while anti-ESG policies create opposing litigation and reputational risks.
children.summary: Concerns about AI's [[power and water use and reliance on critical minerals|p674]] may lead some investors to avoid Anthropic if its ESG practices seem inadequate. Complying with [[California climate disclosure rules and EU and UK reporting regimes|p675]] will take significant resources, while anti-ESG policies could expose its practices to litigation and antitrust challenges. The company may also face [[backlash and activism|p676]] from stakeholders who disagree with its positions or lack of positions.

children.title: If we or our payment processing partners fail to manage the risks related to our payment processing activities, we could be subject to fines, regulatory scrutiny, disruptions to our business, or reputational harm.
children.tldr: Anthropic has experienced subscription payment fraud using false identities and stolen cards, and excessive chargebacks could raise fees or cut off card acceptance.
children.summary: Anthropic has seen [[fraud using false identities and stolen credentials|p677]], causing processing fees, chargeback fees and fines, and it does not verify cardholders' physical identities. [[Excessive chargebacks|p678]] could bring higher fees or suspension of card payments. Failure to meet [[changing payment network rules|p679]] could disrupt its ability to process payments.

children.title: Risks Related to Tax and Accounting Matters
children.tldr: Tax law changes, sales tax collection demands, limits on using past losses, transfer pricing disputes, accounting misjudgments, weak internal controls, and interest and currency swings could all hurt Anthropic's results.
children.summary: This group of risks covers taxes and accounting. New or reinterpreted tax rules could raise costs or [[increase the global tax rate|s105]], and jurisdictions could demand [[sales or digital services tax collection|s106]]. The company's [[net operating losses may be limited|s107]] after ownership changes, and tax authorities could challenge its [[transfer pricing and intercompany arrangements|s108]]. Wrong [[accounting judgments or estimates|s109]] could hurt reported results, and [[ineffective internal controls|s110]] could lead to restatements or a Nasdaq delisting. Finally, the company faces [[interest rate and currency exchange risk|s111]].

children.title: Changes in tax laws or regulations could be enacted, or existing tax laws or regulations could be applied to us or our customers in a manner that could increase the costs of our models, platform, and applications and adversely affect our business.
children.tldr: New or reinterpreted tax laws, possibly retroactive, including the OECD's 15% global minimum tax, could raise Anthropic's taxes and costs as its non-U.S. operations grow.
children.summary: Tax laws in the U.S. and abroad could be enacted or reinterpreted, possibly with retroactive effect, in ways that [[fall heavily on internet-delivered services|p680]]. If Anthropic fails to collect taxes owed by customers, [[it would be liable for those costs|p680]]. Hiring abroad, employer-of-record providers, and overseas data center work may create [[permanent establishments or other taxable presence|p681]]. Anthropic signs some international infrastructure agreements through [[interim contracting arrangements|p681]] before local entities exist, which could bring material non-recoverable indirect taxes. The company has paid [[only immaterial income taxes to date|p681]], but this could rise sharply. The OECD's [[15% global minimum tax|p681]] has been adopted in some jurisdictions, and on January 5, 2026 the OECD announced a [[side-by-side elective safe harbor|p681]] for U.S.-parented groups.

children.title: Our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected if we are required to collect sales or other related taxes for subscriptions to our models, platform, and applications in jurisdictions where we have not historically done so.
children.tldr: Jurisdictions could force Anthropic to collect additional sales, value added, or digital services taxes, possibly retroactively, raising costs and discouraging customers.
children.summary: Anthropic [[collects sales tax in a number of jurisdictions|p682]], but states or countries could claim it should collect more, which could mean large tax payments, administrative burden, and fewer customers. Some jurisdictions have also enacted a [[digital services tax on gross revenue|p682]], and others are considering one.

children.title: Our ability to use our net operating loss carryforwards and certain other tax attributes may be limited.
children.tldr: Ownership changes, including from this offering, could limit Anthropic's use of its substantial net operating losses, and federal losses after 2017 offset only 80% of taxable income.
children.summary: Anthropic has [[substantial net operating losses|p683]]. Under Sections 382 and 383 of the Code, an [[ownership change of more than 50 percentage points|p683]] over three years limits their yearly use. The company has [[experienced ownership changes in the past|p683]] and may again, including from this offering. States such as [[California have suspended or limited NOL use|p683]], and federal NOLs from years after 2017 can offset [[only 80% of taxable income|p683]]. Even if profitable, the company may be unable to use a material portion of these losses.

children.title: Our corporate structure and intercompany arrangements are subject to the tax laws of multiple jurisdictions, and we could be required to pay additional taxes, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Tax authorities could challenge Anthropic's transfer pricing and intercompany arrangements, leading to extra taxes, penalties beyond reserves, and possible double taxation.
children.summary: As non-U.S. operations grow, Anthropic must report income in more places, and its tax position faces [[higher rates and new or retroactive laws|p684]]. Countries apply [[divergent transfer pricing rules|p685]], and a successful challenge could force income reallocation, extra taxes, and [[double taxation|p685]]. Infrastructure agreements signed by U.S. entities before local subsidiaries exist may create [[material non-recoverable indirect taxes|p685]]. Although Anthropic believes its positions are reasonable, authorities could impose [[taxes and penalties exceeding its reserves|p686]].

children.title: If our judgments or estimates relating to our critical accounting policies prove to be incorrect, our results of operations may be adversely affected.
children.tldr: If management's accounting judgments and estimates, on items such as revenue recognition and stock-based compensation, prove wrong, reported results and the stock price could suffer.
children.summary: GAAP requires management to make estimates covering areas including [[revenue recognition, stock-based compensation, and SAFEs|p687]]. The company also enters [[complex and novel transactions|p687]] that may require consolidating assets or entities, which could make results volatile and push them below analyst expectations.

children.title: If we fail to maintain an effective system of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, our ability to produce timely and accurate financial statements or comply with applicable regulations may be impaired, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Weak disclosure controls or internal control over financial reporting could cause restatements, investor distrust, or loss of the Nasdaq listing; formal Section 404 reporting begins with the second 10-K.
children.summary: As a public company Anthropic must maintain effective controls under the Exchange Act and Sarbanes-Oxley, and it is still [[developing and refining these controls|p688]] at significant cost. Controls may become inadequate, and failures could lead to a [[restatement of prior financial statements|p689]]. The company also [[relies on distribution partners and other third parties|p689]] for financial data, with limited ability to audit them. Ineffective controls could hurt investor confidence or [[threaten its Nasdaq listing|p690]]. Management's annual control report will begin with its [[second annual report on Form 10-K|p690]].

children.title: We are exposed to fluctuations in interest rates and currency exchange rates, which could negatively affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Falling interest rates could cut investment income on Anthropic's large cash holdings, and a stronger dollar could raise costs for non-U.S. customers paying in euros or pounds.
children.summary: Much of Anthropic's cash and investments earn [[variable or market-based interest rates|p691]], so lower rates would reduce income and volatility could affect portfolio value. Sales are in [[U.S. dollars, euros, and the pound sterling|p692]], so a stronger dollar could reduce non-U.S. demand, and growing foreign operating expenses add exchange rate exposure.

children.title: Risks Related to our Governance Structure
children.tldr: Anthropic's governance gives the LTBT and the Founder LLC control over the board and stockholder votes, so Class A holders will have little practical say.
children.summary: This group of risks covers how Anthropic's structure limits Class A holders. The [[novel multi-class structure|s113]] lets the LTBT and the Founder LLC elect the whole board. Their [[voting power is not tied to economic stakes|s114]]. The structure may [[deter some institutional investors|s115]] and index funds. Anthropic is a Nasdaq [["controlled company"|s116]]. As a public benefit corporation, it [[cannot guarantee it will achieve its Company Purpose|s117]] and may [[put its purpose ahead of financial returns|s118]]. It also faces [[balancing litigation risk|s119]], [[exclusive Delaware and federal forums|s120]] for lawsuits, and [[anti-takeover provisions|s121]].

children.title: Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control.
children.tldr: The LTBT elects a board majority and the Founder LLC holds 50.1% of general voting power, so Class A holders generally cannot affect stockholder votes or director elections.
children.summary: Anthropic is a Delaware PBC with a [[structure that has no direct public company precedent|p693]]. Through Class T stock, the LTBT, five financially disinterested Trustees, elects directors who make up a board majority. A single Class F share held by the Founder LLC carries [[50.1% of total voting power|p693]] on general matters. Class E stock for employees votes only on limited matters. Class A holders generally [[cannot affect the outcome of any vote|p693]] unless a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree, in which case Class F votes in proportion to Class A. The structure makes [[unsolicited takeovers and proxy contests less likely|p694]]. Because there is [[no judicial precedent|p695]], governance litigation is unpredictable.

children.title: Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the LTBT and the Founder LLC for the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in our company.
children.tldr: The LTBT and the Founder LLC will hold voting control that does not track their economic stakes and will not be diluted by new share issuances.
children.summary: Class T stock [[stays outstanding indefinitely|p696]] unless it is amended, terminated or redeemed with the required approvals. It can also be transferred with those same approvals. Trustee pay is a reasonable cash amount not tied to company profits, and Trustees may not hold Anthropic securities. Class F stock lasts until the [[Class F Sunset Time|p697]]. That time comes after a transition period that begins once there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders for 90 consecutive days, or when no Class F stock remains outstanding. This voting power is [[not proportionate to economic interests|p698]] and will not be diluted by new issuances. These holders may [[favor the Company Purpose over stockholders' financial interests|p698]].

children.title: Our governance structure and the adoption of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation may negatively affect the decision by certain institutional investors to purchase or hold shares of our Class A common stock.
children.tldr: The multi-class structure may keep some institutional investors and index funds from buying the stock, which could depress its valuation.
children.summary: Some institutional investors may be [[barred or discouraged by their investment policies|p699]] from investing. The structure may also make Anthropic [[ineligible for stock indices|p700]], so funds that passively track those indices would not buy the stock. That could lower Anthropic's valuation compared with similar companies.

children.title: We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, and, as a result, we qualify for, and currently rely on, exemptions from certain corporate governance requirements.
children.tldr: Because the LTBT can elect a board majority, Anthropic is a Nasdaq controlled company and will rely on an exemption for its nominating and governance committee only.
children.summary: As a [[controlled company|p701]], Anthropic may skip Nasdaq rules requiring [[a majority independent board|p702]] and [[fully independent nominating|p703]] and [[compensation committees|p704]]. Anthropic expects to [[use the exemption only for its NGC|p705]], which will not be fully independent. Its board currently has a majority of independent directors, and its audit and compensation committees are fully independent.

children.title: We operate as a Delaware public benefit corporation. As a public benefit corporation, we cannot provide any assurance that we will achieve our Company Purpose.
children.tldr: As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic cannot assure it will achieve its Company Purpose, and a late or poorly received biennial benefit report could hurt its reputation.
children.summary: Anthropic [[cannot assure it will achieve its Company Purpose|p706]] or deliver the expected benefits of being a PBC. Under [[Section 366 of the DGCL|p706]], it must report to stockholders at least every two years on its public benefit performance. A late report, or one viewed unfavorably by stakeholders, could hurt its reputation.

children.title: Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock.
children.tldr: Anthropic's directors must weigh its public benefit purpose alongside stockholder returns, and it has already given up revenue by banning autonomous weapons and mass surveillance uses.
children.summary: Anthropic may make [[decisions that hurt financial performance|p707]], such as slowing model development for safety reasons. Its usage policy [[bans fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance|p708]] despite the revenue those uses could bring. It released Mythos only as a [[gated research preview through Project Glasswing|p708]] and chose not to build image and video generation models. It [[may forgo revenue and growth|p709]] that a profit-focused company would pursue. Directors are [[obligated to weigh other stakeholders|p710]] and need only make informed, disinterested and rational decisions, and court precedent is limited. PBC status makes [[hostile bids easier to reject|p711]]. Spending on [[public benefit initiatives|p712]], including the Public Benefit Issuances, may be substantial and reduce results.

children.title: As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and our Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
children.tldr: Holders of at least 2% of shares or $2,000,000 in market value can sue to enforce the PBC balancing duty, a litigation risk traditional corporations do not face.
children.summary: Under [[Section 367 of the DGCL|p713]], stockholders owning the lesser of [[two percent of shares or $2,000,000 in market value|p713]] may sue to enforce the board's balancing duty. Traditional corporations do not face this kind of claim. Such suits could be costly and distract management, and [[limited judicial precedent|p713]] makes the outcome uncertain.

children.title: Our amended and restated bylaws will designate a state or federal court located within the State of Delaware as the exclusive forum for substantially all disputes between us and our stockholders, and also provide that the federal district courts will be the exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause of action arising under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, each of which may limit our stockholders’ ability to choose the judicial forum for disputes with us or our directors, officers, stockholders, or employees.
children.tldr: Anthropic's bylaws make Delaware courts the exclusive forum for most stockholder disputes and federal courts the exclusive forum for Securities Act claims.
children.summary: The [[Delaware Court of Chancery|p714]] will be the exclusive forum for derivative suits, fiduciary duty claims, DGCL claims, and internal affairs claims. [[Federal district courts|p715]] will be the exclusive forum for Securities Act claims. The District of Delaware will hear derivative suits brought under the Exchange Act. Buyers of Anthropic securities are [[deemed to consent|p716]] to these rules, which may discourage lawsuits but do not waive compliance with securities laws.

children.title: Provisions in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and amended and restated bylaws could make a merger, tender offer, proxy contest, or other significant corporate transaction difficult, potentially depressing the market price of our Class A common stock.
children.tldr: Charter and bylaw provisions, including multi-class control and 80% board approval thresholds, could deter takeovers and lower the Class A share price.
children.summary: Anti-takeover provisions include the [[multi-class structure giving the Founder LLC control of stockholder votes|p718]]. Before the Class T Sunset Time, changing the board's size requires [[80% board approval|p720]]. Special meetings and written consents are restricted ([[special meetings|p721]], [[written consents|p722]]). After the Class F Sunset Time, the board becomes a [[classified board with staggered three-year terms|p724]], and certain amendments need [[66 2/3% of Class A voting power|p725]]. The board can also issue [[undesignated preferred stock|p727]] with 80% board approval and, before the Class F Sunset Time, the Founder LLC's consent. Together these provisions could [[deter a premium sale|p728]].

children.title: Risks Related to Ownership of our Class A Common Stock
children.tldr: Buyers of Class A stock face a new and possibly volatile market, dilution from Class N and other issuances, large future share sales, no dividends, and no voting dilution of founders.
children.summary: This group of risk factors covers owning Anthropic's Class A common stock. There has been [[no prior public market|s123]], and the price [[may be volatile|s124]], so investors could lose all or part of their investment. Issuing more stock for financings, notes, equity plans or public benefit initiatives will [[dilute Class A holders|s125]], and the large amount of [[Class N stock held by Amazon and Google|s126]] dilutes economic interests now and voting power on conversion. New issuances [[will not dilute Class F voting power|s127]], which stays fixed at 50.1%. Sales after [[lock-ups expire|s128]] could push the price down. The company [[does not expect to pay cash dividends|s129]], and [[analyst coverage|s130]] could affect the price and trading volume.

children.title: There has been no prior public trading market for our Class A common stock, and an active trading market may not develop or be sustained following this offering.
children.tldr: Class A stock has never traded publicly, and an active market for it on Nasdaq under the symbol "ANT" may never develop or last.
children.summary: Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the [[Nasdaq Global Select Market under "ANT"|p729]], but no public market existed before the offering, and an active one may not develop or be sustained. The offering price is [[set by negotiation|p729]] among the company, selling stockholders and underwriters, and may not match later trading prices.

children.title: The market price of our Class A common stock may be volatile, and you may lose all or part of your investment.
children.tldr: The Class A stock price may swing widely for reasons outside Anthropic's control, investors could lose some or all of their money, and volatility could invite securities class actions.
children.summary: The offering price comes from negotiation and may not reflect later trading, and the market price [[may fluctuate substantially|p730]] for reasons often unrelated to operating results. The filing lists many causes, including [[swings in technology stocks|p732]], [[compute supply constraints and tariffs|p733]], [[sales by stockholders and expected lock-up releases|p735]], [[new model announcements by Anthropic or competitors|p741]], [[conversions of Class N stock|p748]] and [[departures of founders or key personnel|p756]]. A broad loss of investor confidence or events at peer companies could also lower the price, so liquidity and sale prices are [[not assured|p758]]. Volatility could also bring [[securities class action lawsuits|p759]], which would be costly and distracting.

children.title: The issuance of additional stock in connection with financings, acquisitions, investments, our equity incentive plans, the conversion of our outstanding convertible promissory notes, the conversion of our outstanding Class N common stock, our public benefit initiatives, or otherwise will dilute the interests of the holders of our Class A common stock.
children.tldr: Anthropic may issue shares from a very large authorization, including 300 billion Class A shares, for financings, notes, equity plans and public benefit grants, diluting Class A holders.
children.summary: The new charter authorizes [[300,000,000,000 Class A shares|p760]], 100,000,000,000 Class N shares, one Class T share, one Class F share, 30,000,000,000 Class E shares and 30,000,000,000 preferred shares. The company may issue stock for financings, acquisitions, equity plans, [[conversion of convertible notes and Class N stock|p760]], and [[public benefit initiatives|p760]] such as grants to nonprofits and research institutions. Such issuances could substantially dilute Class A holders and lower the price. [[Registration rights|p761]] held by counterparties to certain note purchase agreements could also enable large block sales that depress or unsettle the price.

children.title: A substantial number of shares of our Class N common stock will be outstanding upon the completion of this offering, which will dilute the voting power of the holders of our Class A common stock upon conversion.
children.tldr: Amazon and Google will each own more than five percent through non-voting Class N stock, which dilutes Class A economics now and voting power once converted on transfer.
children.summary: After the Preferred Stock Conversion and Convertible Notes Conversion, [[Amazon and Google will each hold more than five percent|p762]] of outstanding capital stock, mostly as Class N common stock. More Class N shares will be issuable on conversion of [[remaining notes held by Amazon|p762]] that could not convert without exceeding an ownership cap, and through Public Benefit Issuances and future note drawdowns. Class N stock has no vote but [[shares equally in dividends and liquidation proceeds|p763]], so it dilutes the economic interests of Class A holders. It [[converts automatically into Class A|p764]] on a registered offering, open market sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party, and the new Class A shares then carry one vote each, diluting voting power.

children.title: Future issuances of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock will not dilute the voting power of our Class F common stock.
children.tldr: Class F common stock always holds a fixed 50.1% of total voting power, so new Class A or Class N issuances never dilute it.
children.summary: Class F common stock is entitled to a [[fixed 50.1% of total voting power|p765]] on general stockholder matters, so issuing more Class A or Class N stock does not reduce it. For example, issuing 1,000,000 new Class A shares would give Class F about [[1,004,008 additional votes|p765]]. Future issuances generally [[need no stockholder approval|p765]] except where Nasdaq listing standards require it.

children.title: Future sales of our Class A common stock in the public market could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline.
children.tldr: Large share sales after lock-ups end, in 180 or 365 days or earlier around earnings releases, plus co-founders' 80% philanthropy pledge, could push the Class A price down.
children.summary: Sales of many shares, or the expectation of them, could lower the price. Insiders and nearly all holders have [[lock-up or market standoff agreements|p766]]: co-founders and holders of more than 0.5% are restricted until the earlier of shortly after results for the quarter ending September 30, 2027 or 365 days, and other holders until the earlier of shortly after results for the quarter ending March 31, 2027 or 180 days. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley can release holders early. Some shares become saleable [[from the first trading day|p767]], and holders have [[demand registration rights|p768]] under the investors' rights agreement dated May 28, 2026. The co-founders have each made a voluntary, revocable [[pledge of 80% of their equity to philanthropy|p769]], and donated shares could be sold. Their voting control through the Founder LLC would not change. Such sales could also [[make future equity raises harder|p770]].

children.title: Because we do not anticipate paying any cash dividends on our capital stock in the foreseeable future, capital appreciation, if any, will be your sole source of gain.
children.tldr: Anthropic does not expect to pay cash dividends in the foreseeable future, so any gain must come from selling shares at a higher price.
children.summary: Anthropic plans to [[keep future earnings to fund growth|p771]] and does not expect to pay cash dividends. The [[A&R Credit Agreement limits dividends|p771]], and any future payout is up to the board, so investors can only gain through share price appreciation.

children.title: If securities or industry analysts do not publish research or publish inaccurate or unfavorable research about us, our business or our market, or if they change their recommendation regarding our Class A common stock adversely, the market price and trading volume of our Class A common stock could decline.
children.tldr: If analysts give little coverage, drop coverage, or publish negative or inaccurate research, the Class A stock price and trading volume could fall.
children.summary: The stock's price and trading volume depend partly on [[analyst research and reports|p772]], whose estimates may differ from the company's. [[Downgrades or unfavorable research|p772]] would likely lower the price, and [[thin or lapsed coverage|p772]] could reduce visibility and demand for the stock.

children.title: Special Note Regarding Forward-looking Statements
children.tldr: Many statements in the prospectus about future results, compute spending, profitability, safety commitments and the offering are forward-looking, may prove wrong, and should not be relied on unduly.
children.summary: Anthropic warns that any statement in the prospectus that is not historical fact is forward-looking. These are often signaled by words like "may," "expect" or "believe." The [[list of topics|p773]] includes [[future revenue, expenses and profitability|p774]], [[compute and infrastructure commitments|p776]] and the ability to turn them into revenue, [[conflicts with cloud and chip partners|p780]], [[AI safety commitments|p785]], and risks from its [[public benefit corporation status and the LTBT|p790]]. These statements rest on current expectations and face risks such as those in "Risk Factors." [[Actual results could differ materially|p801]]. The company [[will not update them|p802]] except as the law requires. It also notes that its [["we believe" statements|p803]] may rest on limited or incomplete information.

children.title: Industry, Market, and Other Data
children.tldr: Market and industry figures come from third parties such as IDC, IQVIA, the BLS and the World Bank, plus internal estimates that Anthropic has not independently verified.
children.summary: Market size and industry data in the prospectus come from [[third-party reports and internal estimates|p804]] that Anthropic believes are reliable but has not independently verified. The sources include [[IDC reports from 2025 and 2026|p806]], [[IQVIA's Global Medicine Use Trends 2026|p809]], [[U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data|p810]] and [[World Bank GDP data|p811]]. The company built its own [[estimate of global knowledge workers' wages|p813]]. It started with U.S. knowledge worker wages for 2025. It then scaled that figure up using the ratio of total U.S. wages to estimated global wages, which it derived from International Labor Organization data and 2025 global GDP.

children.title: Use of Proceeds
children.tldr: Anthropic plans to use its offering proceeds for general purposes, including compute and infrastructure, hiring, and RSU Settlement tax withholding, and will have broad discretion over how to spend them.
children.summary: The filing leaves blank both the [[estimated net proceeds|p814]] and the assumed share price. Anthropic will receive nothing from shares sold by selling stockholders. The [[offering's main purposes|p816]] are to add capital and flexibility, create a public market for the Class A common stock, and let selling stockholders sell shares in an orderly way. Anthropic intends to use the money for [[general corporate purposes|p817]], including investments in compute and infrastructure and hiring skilled staff. It may also make acquisitions, though it has no material deals agreed. Part of the proceeds will cover [[tax withholding for the RSU Settlement|p818]]. The company will have [[broad discretion|p819]] over the proceeds and may hold them in short-term investment grade instruments in the meantime.

children.title: Dividend Policy
children.tldr: Anthropic has never paid cash dividends, does not expect to in the foreseeable future, and its A&R Credit Agreement limits any dividends it could pay.
children.summary: Anthropic has [[never declared or paid cash dividends|p820]]. It plans to keep its earnings to fund the business. Any future dividend is up to the board and is [[limited by the A&R Credit Agreement|p820]], even though nothing is currently outstanding under that facility.

children.title: Capitalization
children.tldr: This section shows capitalization as of September 30, 2026 on actual, pro forma and pro forma as adjusted bases; most dollar figures and share counts are still blank.
children.summary: The table presents cash and capitalization as of September 30, 2026 [[on an actual basis|p822]], [[on a pro forma basis|p823]] and [[on a pro forma as adjusted basis|p824]]. The pro forma column reflects the Preferred Stock Conversion, the Convertible Notes Conversion, the Class F Stock Issuance and a new certificate of incorporation. The as adjusted column adds the offering and the RSU Settlement tax payments. Dollar amounts are blank. [[The table|p826]] shows that 1,040,440,652 preferred shares are outstanding today and none afterward. It also shows that authorized Class A shares rise from 10,906,111,730 to 300,000,000,000, and authorized Class N shares rise from 7,128,888,270 to 100,000,000,000. The share counts [[exclude options, unvested RSUs and plan reserves|p829]], among them the [[2026 Plan and ESPP|p835]]. Both plans [[grow automatically each year|p838]].

children.title: Dilution
children.tldr: New Class A investors will face immediate dilution in net tangible book value per share. The amounts are still blank, and future option exercises and RSU settlements will dilute further.
children.summary: Dilution is the [[gap between the IPO price and net tangible book value per share|p839]] after the offering. It is measured across Class A and Class N shares. Classes T, F and E have [[no economic rights|p840]] and are excluded. The filing shows [[an immediate increase for existing holders and dilution for new investors|p841]], but all figures are blank. A [[second table|p846]] compares the shares and consideration of existing stockholders and new investors. [[Sales by selling stockholders|p847]] would shift ownership further toward new investors. Share counts [[exclude options, unvested RSUs and plan reserves|p850]], and [[further dilution|p860]] will follow as options are exercised, RSUs settle or new awards are granted.

children.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
children.tldr: Revenue grew from $1.2 billion to $16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026, and Adjusted Operating Income reached $1.6 billion, though fair value charges drove an $80.7 billion net loss.
children.summary: Anthropic, founded in 2021 as a safety-focused research lab, says Claude has grown from no revenue at its 2023 launch to [[$16,286 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026|s171]], up 1,300% from $1,163 million a year earlier. Results rest on four drivers: adoption, compute efficiency, operating efficiency and compute investment, and margins may [[fluctuate as new compute comes online|s139]]. Customers paying $100,000 or more a year rose to [[more than 11,900|s140]] as of September 30, 2026. Consumption-based pay-per-token sales made up [[80% of revenue|s144]] in the first half of 2026. Adjusted Operating Income was [[$1,618 million|s206]], and the company posted [[$974 million of operating income|s209]] in the second quarter of 2026. Net loss was still $80,748 million, mostly from fair value charges on convertible notes. As of June 30, 2026, Anthropic held [[$112.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents|s227]] and expects compute spending to [[use significant cash|s143]] for the foreseeable future.

children.title: Overview
children.tldr: Anthropic, founded in 2021 as a research lab focused on safe AI, sells its Claude AI and says it has seen the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history.
children.summary: Anthropic was [[founded in 2021|p862]] and describes itself as first and foremost a research lab whose mission is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. It delivers [[Claude through its models, platform, and applications|p862]], and says revenue has grown from [[$0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023|p862]]. The figure for the three months ended September 30, 2026 is left blank in the filing.

children.title: Our Financial Model
children.tldr: Four drivers shape results: Claude adoption, compute efficiency, operating efficiency and compute investment; margins expanded in 2026 but may compress as new compute comes online ahead of revenue.
children.summary: Anthropic's financial model rests on [[four drivers|p863]]: adoption of Claude, [[compute efficiency|p865]], [[operating efficiency|p866]], and continued [[compute investments|p867]]. Compute is committed in advance and expensed as it comes online, so there is a [[lag between investment and full revenue|p868]]. Operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin [[expanded significantly year over year|p869]] for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, but may compress when large amounts of new compute arrive, causing margins to fluctuate. Most compute is bought under multi-year deals [[12 to 18 months in advance|p870]], and the company expects more costly short-term compute use in the near term to compress margins.

children.title: Adoption of Claude
children.tldr: Customers paying $100,000 or more a year grew from over 950 to over 11,900 in the year to September 30, 2026, with Net Revenue Retention near 900%.
children.summary: Anthropic says Claude's frontier capabilities drive adoption, supported by direct sales, Applied AI teams, and [[availability on AWS, GCP, and Azure|p871]]. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, [[over 50% of customers|p872]] with $100,000 or more of trailing twelve month revenue used both Claude Platform and a first-party application, up from about 30% in the quarter ended December 31, 2025. Such customers rose to [[more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026|p873]] from more than 950 a year earlier, with more than 1,900 at $1 million or more and about 250 at $10 million or more. [[Net Revenue Retention was approximately 900%|p874]]. The company believes adoption across the economy [[remains nascent|p875]].

children.title: Compute Efficiency
children.tldr: Revenue grew 1,368% year over year in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 300%, reflecting large compute efficiency gains.
children.summary: Compute is Anthropic's [[largest operating cost|p876]], and the company measures efficiency as intelligence and revenue produced per dollar of compute. Three pillars drive it: [[training efficiency|p878]], where Claude increasingly helps build its successors; [[inference efficiency|p879]] in a business that has consistently been compute constrained; and a [[multi-chip approach|p880]] across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. For the three months ended June 30, 2026, [[revenue grew 1,368%|p881]] year over year while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 300%, even as the company released new models and products such as Claude Cowork and Claude Design.

children.title: Operating Efficiency
children.tldr: Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026, and Adjusted Operating Income was $1.6 billion, versus a $1.8 billion adjusted loss a year earlier.
children.summary: Anthropic credits its operating efficiency to talent density, efficient sales, and heavy internal use of Claude, which wrote [[over 90% of codebase contributions|p882]] in September 2026. From September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026, trailing twelve month revenue rose about 1,200% while headcount rose about 170%, lifting [[revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million|p883]]. Revenue was [[$16.3 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026|p885]], up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. The operating loss narrowed to $693 million from $2.1 billion, and [[Adjusted Operating Income was $1.6 billion|p885]], compared with an Adjusted Operating Loss of $1.8 billion. The company expects margins to fluctuate as new compute arrives.

children.title: Compute Investments
children.tldr: Anthropic plans aggressive compute spending, increasingly through its own leased chips and facilities called Anthropic Direct, with commitments running through 2045 that will heavily use cash.
children.summary: Anthropic says investing in compute is a [[prerequisite for long-term growth|p886]], and that building its own infrastructure will change its cash flow profile and use significant cash for the foreseeable future. It is adding [[Anthropic Direct|p887]], a model of leasing chips and hosting them in dedicated facilities, which lets it secure data center capacity early while deferring larger chip commitments. Its purchase and lease commitments [[extend from now to 2045|p888]], with a significant portion tied to Anthropic Direct; the dollar amounts are blank in the filing. The company plans to [[fund these investments|p889]] with revenue, cash, a credit facility, note purchase agreements and equity commitments from strategic partners, and the offering proceeds.

children.title: How We Generate Revenue
children.tldr: Consumption-based, pay-per-token revenue was $13.1 billion, or 80% of revenue, in the six months ended June 30, 2026, with subscriptions making up the remaining 20%.
children.summary: Anthropic offers [[four model classes|p890]]: Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Its main model is [[pay-for-intelligence|p891]], where customers pay for tokens used at a price set by model; it also sells [[subscriptions of generally 12 months or less|p892]]. Consumption revenue grew from $288 million (75%) in 2024 to $3.8 billion (83%) in 2025 to [[$13.1 billion (80%) in the six months ended June 30, 2026|p895]], while subscription revenue grew from $98 million to $789 million to $3.2 billion. Revenue in 2023 was $41 million. The company [[expects its growth rate to decline|p896]], possibly significantly.

children.title: Our Customers and Approach to Claude Diffusion
children.tldr: Anthropic serves organizations of all sizes worldwide and spreads Claude through product-led adoption, direct and Applied AI teams, cloud and ecosystem partners, at 19% of revenue in sales costs.
children.summary: This section covers [[who Anthropic's customers are|s146]], from large enterprises to startups and prosumers, with software developers as key early adopters. It also describes [[how Claude spreads|s147]]: individual users championing it inside organizations, direct sales and Applied AI teams, the three major cloud platforms, systems integrators, and the new Ode with Anthropic venture, with sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses at 19% of revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2026.

children.title: Our Customers
children.tldr: Claude serves enterprises of all sizes worldwide, with developers as core early adopters and prosumers acting as an entry point into enterprise sales.
children.summary: Customers range from the largest enterprises to startups and nonprofits, gaining value through [[more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence|p897]]. [[Software developers|p898]] are central, and Claude Code adoption often starts with individual engineers. [[Prosumers|p899]] serve as a top-of-funnel engine who champion Claude at work, and single use cases often [[expand into broader adoption|p900]] across coding, legal, finance, and other knowledge work.

children.title: Our Approach to Claude Diffusion
children.tldr: Claude spreads through user-led adoption, direct and Applied AI teams, cloud and ecosystem partners, with sales, marketing, and partnerships costing 19% of revenue in the first half of 2026.
children.summary: Anthropic sees Claude's intelligence as the core driver of adoption, with [[individual users becoming internal champions|p902]]. Direct teams then build enterprise-wide adoption, and [[Applied AI teams|p904]] build custom solutions for select customers. Claude is sold through AWS, GCP, and Azure under a [[joint go-to-market approach|p905]] in which Anthropic contracts directly with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee. Systems integrators and data platforms extend reach, and [[Ode with Anthropic|p907]], a new services company formed with private equity firms, targets mid-sized companies. Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses were [[19% of revenue|p908]] for the six months ended June 30, 2026.

children.title: Key Factors Affecting Our Performance
children.tldr: Performance depends on staying at the AI frontier, securing compute and capital, keeping talent, spreading Claude in enterprises, usage patterns, and public benefit spending.
children.summary: Anthropic lists the factors that most affect its results: [[staying at the frontier|s149]], [[securing and using compute well|s150]], keeping technical talent, [[access to capital|s152]], and [[spreading Claude across enterprises|s153]]. Revenue also varies with [[model releases and seasonality|s157]], and the company expects its [[public benefit commitments|s158]], including large share contributions to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, to affect results.

children.title: Remaining at the Frontier of AI
children.tldr: Revenue growth depends on releasing ever more capable models, since most customers move to each new version and expand their spending.
children.summary: Anthropic believes enterprises choose the [[most capable and trustworthy AI|p909]]. With each release, [[most customers use the latest version|p910]] and expand into new use cases. Staying ahead requires [[continued investment in research, compute, talent, and capital|p911]].

children.title: Securing Sufficient Compute and Optimizing its Utilization
children.tldr: Anthropic has long been compute constrained, and its access to compute faces supplier, power, export control, and partner conflict risks, partly offset by using multiple chip vendors.
children.summary: Using a [[range of chip partners|p912]] helps Anthropic secure compute, but supply depends on concentrated chip makers, power, data center capacity, and export controls, and demand has historically exceeded supply. Some cloud providers it relies on are also [[investors, customers, and competitors|p912]], which could create conflicts. It is adding [[Anthropic Direct|p913]], leasing chips for dedicated facilities. It also aims to [[direct compute to its highest-value use|p914]] across research, customers, and internal work.

children.title: Attracting and Retaining Technical Talent
children.tldr: All seven of Anthropic's co-founders remain with the company, and retaining top technical talent is a key driver of innovation and results.
children.summary: Anthropic says advancing the frontier requires top technical talent, starting with its [[seven co-founders, all still at the company|p915]], and believes its culture and mission help it hire and retain staff.

children.title: Our Continued Access to Capital
children.tldr: Large compute commitments must be paid regardless of revenue, so Anthropic depends on continued access to capital and a credible path to profitability.
children.summary: Compute requires [[large upfront commitments|p916]] that grow with the business, tying compute to capital access. Investors must see capital [[converted into model performance and adoption|p917]]. Commitments [[generally must be paid regardless of revenue or utilization|p918]], and some build-out has been funded or supported by cloud providers and chip partners, a reliance the company hopes to reduce by borrowing on its own credit.

children.title: Our Ability to Diffuse Claude in the Enterprise
children.tldr: Anthropic says enterprise adoption is still early, and growth depends on shipping products, expanding distribution, and winning and expanding customers.
children.summary: Anthropic believes [[enterprise adoption remains nascent|p919]] and that growth depends on three things: [[turning model gains into products|s154]], including safety-related release delays; [[expanding distribution|s155]], including internationally; and [[landing and expanding customers|s156]], which grew to more than 11,900 at $100,000 or more of trailing twelve month revenue by September 30, 2026.

children.title: First, our ability to translate model improvements into accessible products and platform capabilities.
children.tldr: Anthropic launched 250 models, features and applications in nine months of 2026, but safety reviews have delayed or restricted releases such as Mythos and Fable 5.
children.summary: In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, Anthropic launched [[250 new model versions, platform features, and applications|p920]]. It has [[delayed or limited releases for safety|p920]], such as releasing Mythos first through Project Glasswing and Fable 5 with safety restrictions, and may do so again when evaluations are inconclusive. These steps and future regulation could slow adoption, though the company believes safety builds customer trust.

children.title: Second, our ability to expand and diversify distribution.
children.tldr: Growth has been mostly self-service so far, and Anthropic is now investing in direct sales, partners, and international offices to reach regulated industries and global customers.
children.summary: Much growth has been [[self-service and organic|p921]], but Anthropic is investing in direct sales, Applied AI, and partners, and expects [[international expansion|p921]] to be a meaningful growth driver.

children.title: Third, our ability to land new customers and expand within existing accounts.
children.tldr: Customers paying $100,000 or more grew from about 20 in 2023 to over 11,900 by September 2026, yet Fortune 500 customers spend under 0.1% of expenses on Anthropic.
children.summary: Customers with $100,000 or more of trailing twelve month revenue grew from [[about 20 at December 31, 2023 to more than 11,900 at September 30, 2026|p922]], and their revenue rose from about $37 million in 2023 to $220 million in 2024 and $3.5 billion in 2025. About 40 million smaller customers make up the rest. [[Over 50% of the Fortune 500|p923]] are such customers, but they spent on average under 0.1% of total expenses with Anthropic in the third quarter of 2026, while the [[top 10 Fortune 500 customers|p924]] spent under 1%. No customer exceeded [[10% of revenue|p926]] for the nine months, and about 79% of third quarter revenue came from outside the top five customers, up from about 64% in the first quarter.

children.title: Customer Usage Patterns
children.tldr: Revenue swings with new model releases and holidays: recent models made over 80% of third quarter 2026 revenue, and spending fell about 20% over the 2025 year-end holidays.
children.summary: Model versions released in the six months ended September 30, 2026 accounted for [[over 80% of revenue|p927]] in that quarter. Usage is seasonal, and total customer spend fell [[about 20% in the two weeks ended January 2, 2026|p928]] versus the prior two weeks. As growth slows, the company expects [[seasonal effects to become more visible|p929]] and results harder to forecast.

children.title: Our Commitment to Public Benefit
children.tldr: Anthropic gave 5% of its fully diluted shares to its Public Benefit Fund and may add up to 2% more each time its share price rises 50%.
children.summary: Anthropic contributed [[846,840,960 Class N shares|p931]], 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026, to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. The board may issue up to [[an additional 2% of outstanding shares|p931]] each time the share price rises 50% above the prior milestone, starting from the IPO price, subject to trading tests and board discretion. The fund's [[initial managers|p933]] are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark, and Dr. Neil "Buddy" Shah. The company matches employee equity donations with shares, and the co-founders have pledged [[80% of their personal equity|p934]] to philanthropy. Donation matching expenses were [[$541 million in 2025|p935]], about 4% of operating expenses, and public benefit spending is expected to grow and may lower margins and add dilution.

children.title: Components of Results of Operations
children.tldr: Anthropic's results are built from token and subscription revenue, five operating expense lines led by compute, interest income, large fair value swings on convertible notes, other items and taxes.
children.summary: This section explains what goes into each line of Anthropic's statement of operations. [[Revenue|s160]] comes from customers using Claude. Operating expenses are split into [[compute and infrastructure, personnel, the Bartz settlement, sales and partnerships, and other costs|s161]]. Below operating loss sit [[interest income|s167]], the [[change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs|s168]], [[other income (expense), net|s169]], and the [[provision for income taxes|s170]].

children.title: Revenue
children.tldr: Revenue is recognized as customers consume tokens or ratably over subscriptions, and an estimated 5% to 7% of nine-month 2026 revenue came from customers violating usage terms.
children.summary: Anthropic earns revenue as customers use Claude through its platform and applications, buying directly or through [[CSP marketplaces|p936]]. Customers pay per use, by subscription, or both, and more enterprises sign [[annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments|p937]]. Usage revenue is recognized [[based on tokens consumed|p938]], while prepaid subscriptions are recognized ratably over periods generally of 12 months or less. The company [[expects its revenue growth rate to decline|p939]] over time and to fluctuate. It estimates that customers later found to violate its usage policy or commercial terms made up [[approximately 5% to 7% of revenue|p940]] for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and expects that share to fall after stronger enforcement in August and September 2026.

children.title: Operating Expenses
children.tldr: Anthropic expects compute and infrastructure to remain its largest expense, with personnel, sales and partnerships, and administrative costs all rising in absolute dollars.
children.summary: Operating expenses fall into five groups. [[Compute and infrastructure|s162]] covers the cost of running models for research and customers and is expected to stay the largest expense. [[Personnel|s163]] is mostly stock-based and cash compensation. The [[Bartz settlement|s164]] is a one-time 2025 legal charge. [[Sales, marketing, and partnerships|s165]] is mainly channel partner fees and advertising, and [[other operating and administrative|s166]] costs include donation matching, vendors, software and public company costs.

children.title: Compute and Infrastructure
children.tldr: Compute and infrastructure, mostly CSP fees contracted 12 to 18 months ahead, will remain the largest expense, and its share of revenue depends on revenue growth against that fixed base.
children.summary: This expense covers running Anthropic's technology for research, model development, serving customers and internal use, mainly [[compute fees paid to CSPs|p941]], plus data center and, from 2026, lease and depreciation costs. Anthropic views compute as tied to revenue because model development and customer serving [[each inform the other|p942]] in an iterative cycle. Most compute is under multi-year commitments [[procured 12 to 18 months in advance|p943]], recognized when it becomes available, and treated as one shared resource. As a result, the expense as a share of revenue depends mainly on how revenue scales against the committed cost base.
