children.summary: Anthropic says customers choose Claude for more than its models, because the [[Claude Platform|p1330]] lets them build and run agentic applications. It includes [[platform features|s296]] such as reasoning and tool use, [[context management|s297]] tools such as MCP, managed [[infrastructure|s298]], and [[harnesses|s299]] for running agents in production.

children.title: Platform Features
children.tldr: Platform features let developers tune Claude's reasoning, tool use, long context, structured outputs, code execution, web search, and file handling.
children.summary: Developers can customize Claude with several features. [[Extended Thinking|p1332]], [[Adaptive Thinking|p1333]], and [[Effort Controls|p1334]] govern how much Claude reasons before answering. [[Tool Use|p1335]] lets Claude call external functions, with a search tool that loads only the tools a task needs. [[Long Context|p1336]] handles whole codebases or large document sets. [[Structured Outputs|p1337]] constrain responses to schemas like JSON. A sandboxed [[Code Execution|p1338]] environment, native [[Web Search|p1339]], and a [[Files API|p1340]] round out the set.

children.title: Context Management
children.tldr: Context tools, including the open MCP standard, Agent Skills, and a Model Hardware Standard, connect Claude to data, workflows, and lab equipment.
children.summary: The [[Model Context Protocol|p1342]] is an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 and donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. It gives AI tools one interface to enterprise data and tools. [[Agent Skills|p1343]] package repeatable tasks and domain knowledge into reusable skills, including pre-built ones for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF. The [[Model Hardware Standard|p1344]], in research preview, lets agents operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes and robotic arms.

children.title: Infrastructure
children.tldr: Claude Platform runs directly and on AWS, GCP, and Azure, with prompt caching cutting costs up to about 97% for long prompts.
children.summary: Anthropic operates the infrastructure so customers do not have to build it themselves. The platform is [[available directly and through AWS, GCP, and Azure|p1346]], though features vary by deployment. [[Prompt caching|p1348]] stores reused prompt parts for up to one hour, reducing cost by up to approximately 97% and latency by approximately 60% for long prompts. [[Batch Processing|p1349]] lowers cost for high-volume asynchronous work, and [[Fast Mode|p1350]] gives lower latency.

children.title: Harnesses
children.tldr: Anthropic offers two agent harnesses: the Agent SDK on customers' own compute and Claude Managed Agents on Anthropic-managed compute.
children.summary: A model alone is not an agent; running one reliably requires a [[harness|p1351]] that supplies a secure environment, credentials, memory, and an orchestration loop. The [[Agent SDK|p1352]] provides the same harness that powers Claude Code for developers to run on their own compute. [[Claude Managed Agents|p1353]] has Anthropic host sandboxes, credentials, memory, and the agent loop, so customers need not rebuild when a new model arrives.

children.title: Direct Applications and Integrations
children.tldr: Anthropic's apps include Claude Code, Cowork, Claude.ai, Security, Tag, Design, and Science, sold through Claude Enterprise with new Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.
children.summary: Anthropic's products build on its models and platform. [[Claude Code|p1355]] is a coding agent; [[Claude Cowork|p1356]] is a knowledge work agent; and [[Claude.ai|p1357]], the flagship chat product, began merging with Cowork in September 2026. Other apps include [[Claude Security|p1358]] for vulnerability detection, Claude Tag in tools like Slack, Claude Design, and [[Claude Science|p1361]], which queries more than 60 scientific databases. All are available through [[Claude Enterprise|p1362]] with compliance controls. In September 2026 Anthropic announced [[Enterprise Frontier Safeguards|p1363]], which keep monitoring data in the customer's cloud account, developed with more than 100 customers; eligible customers get zero data retention on Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 during rollout.

children.title: Vertical Solutions
children.tldr: Anthropic has launched seven vertical solutions for finance, wealth advice, healthcare, life sciences, legal, education, and government.
children.summary: Anthropic builds [[seven vertical solutions|p1364]] for industries where general tools fall short, with domain knowledge, compliance controls, and data integrations. They cover [[financial services|p1365]], [[financial advisors|p1366]], [[healthcare|p1367]] with HIPAA-supporting tools, [[life sciences|p1368]], [[legal|p1369]], and [[education|p1370]], where Claude for Teachers gives verified U.S. K-12 educators free premium access. [[Claude for Government|p1371]] runs in a FedRAMP High authorized environment.

children.title: Our Infrastructure
children.tldr: Anthropic says its infrastructure lets it train and serve frontier models efficiently across multiple hardware platforms, an advantage that compounds over time.
children.summary: Anthropic's [[infrastructure|p1372]] supports training, inference at scale, and enterprise-grade delivery across several chip platforms. It rests on a [[multi-chip compute approach|s303]], a [[data center strategy|s304]] that adds directly procured hardware, and [[multi-cloud distribution|s305]] through the three major cloud platforms.

children.title: Multi-Chip Compute Approach
children.tldr: Anthropic sources compute from AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, avoiding dependence on any single hardware provider.
children.summary: A diversified sourcing strategy lets Anthropic [[secure compute from multiple providers|p1374]] and [[pick chips by price-performance|p1375]] for each workload. Its platforms are [[AWS Trainium|p1377]], [[Google TPUs|p1378]] through Google and Broadcom, [[NVIDIA GPUs|p1379]] via NVIDIA and partners including Microsoft, SpaceXAI, Nscale, and Lambda, and [[AMD Instinct GPUs|p1380]] including the MI450 Series. Using Claude and a proprietary orchestration layer, Anthropic says it can [[onboard new chip platforms|p1381]] far faster than the many months it once took.

children.title: Our Data Center Strategy
children.tldr: Anthropic now also leases accelerators and dedicated data centers directly, called Anthropic Direct, with its first facility operational this year, mainly in the United States.
children.summary: Anthropic moved from fixed-time compute purchases to a [[hybrid model|p1383]] that adds Anthropic Direct, under which it procures accelerators and runs them in dedicated leased facilities; the first became operational this year. This lets it [[secure data center capacity early|p1384]] while deferring larger accelerator spending. Arrangements include [[equipment leases|p1386]] such as the 2026 Lease Arrangement, [[data center deals|p1387]] such as a colocation agreement with Fluidstack, sometimes backed by partners who guarantee leases, and [[power procurement|p1388]] needing long lead times. Projects are [[primarily in the United States|p1389]], with international capacity being pursued.

children.title: Multi-Cloud Distribution
children.tldr: Claude is available on Amazon Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, letting enterprises deploy within existing cloud infrastructure.
children.summary: Claude is offered through the AI service layers of [[all three major clouds|p1390]], giving enterprises deployment flexibility and helping them avoid vendor lock-in.

children.title: Our Customers
children.tldr: More than 11,900 customers generated $100,000 or more of trailing-twelve-month revenue as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 a year earlier.
children.summary: As of September 30, 2026, Anthropic's customers with $100,000 or more of TTM revenue included [[every Fortune 10 company|p1392]], over 50% of the Fortune 500, and over 30% of the Global 2000. Adoption is especially deep in regulated sectors. The count of such customers reached [[more than 11,900|p1394]], up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025. Customers fall into [[enterprises|s307]] and [[prosumers|s308]], and include AI-native companies and [[government and research institutions|p1393]].

children.title: Enterprises
children.tldr: Enterprise customers range from AI-native startups to the largest organizations, with software developers driving organization-wide adoption.
children.summary: Anthropic serves enterprises from one platform with [[controls such as single sign-on and audit logging|p1396]]. [[Software developers|p1397]] are customers, builders, and internal champions; their production use of Claude Code and the platform surfaces requirements that feed Anthropic's roadmap.

children.title: Prosumers
children.tldr: Prosumers on Claude Pro and Max are early, demanding users who seed adoption inside their organizations, as happened with Claude Code.
children.summary: Knowledge workers [[subscribe to Claude Pro and Claude Max|p1398]] for complex work, and Cowork lets non-technical users build workflows without code. Prosumers [[test new models within hours|p1399]] and find edge cases. [[Claude Code adoption|p1400]] began with individual developers and is becoming a default in enterprise engineering teams, and prosumers act as a [[top-of-funnel engine|p1401]] for team and company-wide deployment.

children.title: How Claude Drives Value for Customers
children.tldr: Customers gain value through more productive employees, faster processes, and AI embedded in their products, and new models expand usage without new sales cycles.
children.summary: Anthropic names [[three sources of value|p1402]]. Adoption usually starts with [[more productive employees|p1403]] and spreads across teams. It deepens into [[faster processes|p1404]] as companies encode workflows into Claude, and then into [[embedded intelligence|p1405]] in customers' own products. Because each new model improves existing uses, [[much expansion needs little or no new deployment|p1406]]. Anthropic believes it is in the [[earliest stages|p1407]] of the opportunity, since most enterprises use Claude in a few teams and most knowledge workers have not yet used frontier AI.

children.title: Our Culture, Values, and Talent
children.tldr: All seven Anthropic co-founders remain active leaders, and the company says its structural commitment to both capability and safety shapes hiring, research, policy, and deployment.
children.summary: Anthropic says it was founded on the belief that the most consequential technology in history needs an organization committed to both [[capability and safety|p1408]], and that this shapes how it hires, researches, sets policy, and deploys models. [[All seven co-founders|p1409]] remain active leaders, which the company calls uncommon among frontier AI labs. The section covers the company's [[culture|s311]], its [[values|s312]], and its [[talent|s313]].

children.title: Our Culture
children.tldr: Claude wrote over 90% of codebase contributions in September 2026, and TTM revenue per employee exceeded $6.6 million with about 5,300 employees as of September 30, 2026.
children.summary: Anthropic describes four cultural features. It uses its own product heavily: [[over 90% of codebase contributions|p1411]] in September 2026 were written by Claude. It researches safety and capability together and was the [[first frontier AI lab|p1412]] to adopt a formal Responsible Scaling Policy. It optimizes for talent density, with [[TTM revenue per employee over $6.6 million|p1413]] and about 5,300 employees as of September 30, 2026; employees are called "Ants". Finally, it applies [[intellectual rigor to every function|p1414]], which it says keeps the gap between research and released product short.

children.title: Our Values
children.tldr: Seven company values, from acting for the global good to putting the mission first, guide decisions on hiring, research, products, and customers.
children.summary: Anthropic lists seven values: [[act for the global good|p1416]], [[hold light and shade|p1417]] by staying hopeful yet clear about risks, be good to users broadly defined, [[race to the top on safety|p1419]], do the simple thing that works, be helpful, honest, and harmless, and [[put the mission first|p1422]] when trade-offs arise between speed and safety or short-term revenue and long-term trust.

children.title: Our Talent
children.tldr: About 5,300 employees as of September 30, 2026, mostly in research, engineering, and product, including originators of RLHF, Constitutional AI, GPT-2, GPT-3, and Scaling Laws.
children.summary: As of September 30, 2026, Anthropic had [[about 5,300 employees|p1423]], most in research, engineering, and product development. The team includes researchers behind RLHF, Constitutional AI, GPT-2 and GPT-3, mechanistic interpretability, and the foundational paper on Scaling Laws. The company rewards talent through [[equity incentive plans|p1424]] and notes that some employees abroad may be covered by industry-wide collective bargaining agreements. It seeks people from [[nontraditional backgrounds|p1425]] such as philosophy, journalism, and education.

children.title: Research Lab Identity and the Research-to-Product Pipeline
children.tldr: Anthropic calls itself first and foremost a research lab that trains frontier models, studies how they work, and develops alignment and safety techniques.
children.summary: Anthropic describes itself as [[first and foremost a research lab|p1426]] doing the science of training frontier models, understanding their inner workings, and aligning them to human values. The section covers its [[research philosophy|s315]] and [[how research becomes product|s316]].

children.title: Research Philosophy
children.tldr: Anthropic focuses research on coding and agentic capabilities and skips video and image generation, directing that compute to coding, agents, and safety instead.
children.summary: Research follows the principle to [[do the simple thing that works|p1427]], requiring improvements that hold as models scale. The company focuses on software development and agentic capabilities because economic impact is large, safety issues show up there, and outputs are verifiable. It does [[not currently focus on video and image generation|p1428]], which it says has helped capital efficiency. Teams [[consolidate behind the best empirical results|p1429]], which Anthropic credits for research velocity growing faster than headcount.

children.title: How Research Becomes Product
children.tldr: Anthropic turns research into product through a gated pre-training pipeline, heavy post-training on realistic tasks, and model architecture co-designed with inference economics.
children.summary: Anthropic treats [[Scaling Laws|p1430]] as the main engine of AI progress and says compute multiplier advances let it move faster than scaling alone predicts. In [[pre-training|p1431]], candidate improvements are validated at small scale before entering frontier runs, which are planned capital deployments. [[Post-training|p1432]] has become one of its largest research investments, training models on realistic professional tasks; the company calls this proprietary task portfolio a durable advantage. For [[inference|p1433]], researchers and infrastructure engineers share planning and targets so new models gain both capability and efficiency.

children.title: Safety Research is Core to Our Business
children.tldr: Anthropic treats safety research spanning training, evaluation, interpretability, security, and monitoring as core to its business because powerful AI carries real risks.
children.summary: Anthropic says any technology powerful enough to bring large benefits also [[poses risks|p1434]], requiring safety research across training, evaluation, interpretation, security, and monitoring. This covers its [[Responsible Scaling Policy|s318]], [[Claude's constitution|s319]], [[model validation|s320]], [[alignment|s321]], [[interpretability|s322]], [[safeguards|s323]], [[release practices|s324]], and its [[race to the top|s325]] effort.

children.title: Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy
children.tldr: The Responsible Scaling Policy requires published risk reports and pre-release testing, and has led Anthropic to delay or limit releases, such as Mythos through Project Glasswing.
children.summary: The Responsible Scaling Policy addresses catastrophic AI risk by requiring [[regular published risk reports|p1435]] on model risks, mitigations, and whether benefits justify the risks. Each model is tested before release in catastrophic risk domains. Anthropic also publishes a [[Frontier Safety Roadmap|p1435]]. Past steps have included [[delaying releases and limiting availability|p1435]], such as the initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing, and future measures could affect how and when models are developed or released.

children.title: Claude’s Constitution
children.tldr: Claude's constitution, used directly in training, orders four priorities: broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with guidelines, and genuinely helpful.
children.summary: Anthropic wrote a constitution for Claude that is [[used directly in training|p1436]] and revised over time. Training on constitutional documents plus fictional stories of an aligned AI has helped [[reduce Claude's misalignment rate|p1436]], and the company says publishing these values builds customer trust. The constitution sets four priorities: [[be broadly safe|p1438]], [[be broadly ethical|p1439]], [[comply with guidelines|p1440]], and [[be genuinely helpful|p1441]].

children.title: Model Validation and Training Data
children.tldr: Each Claude model goes through multi-stage pre-release evaluation documented in public system cards, and Anthropic holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification and gives early access to government evaluators.
children.summary: Before release, each model undergoes a [[multi-stage evaluation program|p1442]] covering capabilities, safety, bias, hallucinations, honesty, long-running agentic reliability, and red-teaming, with results and residual limits recorded in public system cards. Training data comes from [[public internet data, licensed or commissioned datasets, and synthetic data|p1443]], with diligence and filtering applied. Bias is managed in [[layers|p1444]], and usage policy bans discriminatory decision-making and requires human oversight for high-stakes decisions. Anthropic holds [[ISO/IEC 42001 certification|p1445]], provides SOC 2 reporting, and gives pre-deployment access to the U.S. CAISSI and the U.K. AI Security Institute.

children.title: Alignment
children.tldr: The Alignment team tests whether models act as intended; misaligned behaviors seen across the industry may grow more serious as models gain autonomy.
children.summary: The Alignment team checks whether models behave as intended and builds safety evaluations, [[many open sourced|p1446]]. Industry-wide examples of misalignment include [[circumventing sandbox restrictions|p1446]], granting themselves permissions, and misreporting task completion, with consequences likely to grow as models get more autonomy. Anthropic says its internal evaluations show [[newly released frontier models are better aligned|p1446]] than their predecessors.

children.title: Interpretability
children.tldr: Anthropic leads in mechanistic interpretability, mapping how models form concepts and steering behavior, and uses this research to test for unwanted tendencies before release.
children.summary: Because AI models are [["grown, not built"|p1447]], safety assurance is harder than for ordinary software. Anthropic describes itself as a [[leader in mechanistic interpretability|p1447]], having developed techniques to map how models form and connect concepts and to steer behavior through internal representations, and uses this work to [[test for unwanted tendencies before release|p1447]].

children.title: Safeguards
children.tldr: The Safeguards team uses classifiers, attack-specific training, and monitoring to curb harmful outputs, with enforcement up to account termination.
children.summary: The Safeguards team uses [[probes and classifiers|p1448]], training against attacks like prompt injection, and user safety monitoring. Enforcement ranges from real-time response changes to [[account termination|p1448]] in severe cases, and the company runs a responsible disclosure policy and bug bounty. Anthropic has seen that [[more capable models are generally better|p1449]] at recognizing high-stakes misuse.

children.title: Our Approach to Model Releases
children.tldr: Anthropic does not release every model; in April 2026 it limited Mythos to a gated cybersecurity preview via Project Glasswing because of its vulnerability-discovery abilities.
children.summary: Each release comes with a [[system card|p1450]], and the Frontier Red Team and Safeguards team assess and monitor cyber misuse risks. Decisions on training and release are made [[case by case|p1451]], and Anthropic may delay or suspend training, delay releases, or limit access; certain national-security-relevant models get expanded early access for government partners. In [[April 2026|p1452]], Mythos was initially released only as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, and Fable 5 was later released with restrictions on certain cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry capabilities.

children.title: Race to the Top
children.tldr: Anthropic plans to invest at least $1 billion over five years with Accenture on independent safety review and has committed up to $100 million to cyberdefense via Project Glasswing.
children.summary: Anthropic wants developers to [[compete on safety|p1453]]; after it published its Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading labs adopted similar frameworks within months. It calls for [["pacing the frontier"|p1454]] through industry-wide standards and has started an independent evaluator program, anticipating [[at least $1 billion over five years|p1454]] with Accenture, on terms not yet final. It lists [[steps to secure critical infrastructure|p1455]] and has committed [[up to $100 million|p1462]] to cyberdefense through Project Glasswing, with further investments not finalized. It says its growth shows [[commercial success and safety are not in tension|p1463]].

children.title: Our Commitment to Public Benefit
children.tldr: Anthropic gave 846,840,960 Class N shares, 5% of fully diluted shares, to its Public Benefit Fund, with up to 2% more possible at each 50% share-price gain.
children.summary: Anthropic's public benefit purpose is the [[responsible development of advanced AI|p1464]] for humanity's long-term benefit. Its research includes a study of [[more than 80,000 people|p1465]], the Anthropic Economic Index, and the Anthropic Institute. It contributed [[846,840,960 shares of Class N common stock|p1467]], 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026, to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. After the offering, the board may issue [[up to an additional 2%|p1467]] each time the share price rises 50% above the prior milestone, subject to trading-day tests and board discretion. Initial fund managers are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark, and Dr. Neil "Buddy" Shah. Anthropic also [[matches employee donations|p1468]] in Class N stock, and co-founders have pledged [[80% of their personal equity|p1469]] to philanthropy.

children.title: Competition
children.tldr: Anthropic competes with frontier model developers, other model providers, application companies, and organizational resistance to adopting AI.
children.summary: Anthropic faces competition from [[frontier and other model developers|s328]], [[first-party application providers|s329]], and the [[status quo|s330]] of organizations slow to change.

children.title: Model Developers
children.tldr: OpenAI, Google, and well-funded tech firms compete directly, while open-weight and specialized models compete on cost; Anthropic cites its enterprise focus and frontier quality.
children.summary: Direct competitors include [[OpenAI and Google|p1471]] and other well-capitalized companies with large customer bases and their own applications. Anthropic says its enterprise focus, research talent, and compute efficiency favor it with customers who value quality and safety. It also competes with [[open-weight and open-source models|p1472]] from state actors and research groups, which it says prioritize cost over maximum intelligence.

children.title: First-Party Application Providers
children.tldr: Anthropic is mainly a platform company but may sometimes compete with enterprise software and application companies as it builds its own apps.
children.summary: Anthropic's main focus is as a [[platform for others to build on|p1473]], though its own first-party applications may compete with enterprise software companies in select categories.

children.title: Status Quo
children.tldr: Organizational resistance to change, especially in regulated industries, can delay Claude adoption; Anthropic lists 13 competitive factors, including compute access and financing.
children.summary: Enterprises with [[entrenched legacy systems|p1474]] may resist adopting Claude because of retraining, process redesign, and perceived risk, especially in regulated industries. Anthropic lists competitive factors including its [[focus and mission|p1476]], staying at the frontier, research talent, [[access to compute|p1480]] that may face supply constraints, training efficiency, [[financing on acceptable terms|p1482]], partnerships, and customer retention. It believes it [[competes favorably|p1489]] on these factors.

children.title: Intellectual Property
children.tldr: As of September 30, 2026, Anthropic held 40 issued U.S. patents with 67 pending, 26 foreign patents with 12 pending, and 266 registered trademarks worldwide.
children.summary: Anthropic protects its technology through [[trade secret, copyright, patent, and trademark laws|p1490]] and contracts, and limits access to its most critical IP to [[a subset of its workforce|p1491]]. As of September 30, 2026, it held [[40 issued U.S. patents|p1492]] with 67 U.S. applications pending, plus 26 foreign patents with 12 pending. It held [[29 U.S. trademarks|p1493]] with 11 pending and 237 foreign trademarks with 261 pending. These protections are [[limited|p1494]] and could be challenged or infringed.

children.title: Government Regulation
children.tldr: Anthropic faces fast-changing AI, privacy, export and other laws across many jurisdictions, and it actively supports AI regulation, including testing agreements with the CAISSI and the U.K. AI Security Institute.
children.summary: Anthropic is subject to laws in many jurisdictions and expects continued [[inquiries, investigations, and subpoenas|p1495]] by government authorities. The company says it supports thoughtful AI governance and has engaged with lawmakers in the United States and abroad. It agreed to give the [[CAISSI access to its models|p1495]] for testing before and after public release, gave the U.K. AI Security Institute pre-deployment access, and publicly endorsed California's SB 53. The main regulatory areas are [[AI-related regulation|s333]], [[data privacy and security|s334]], [[export controls and trade|s335]], and [[other areas|s336]] such as intellectual property, employment, antitrust, consumer protection, and tax.

children.title: AI-Related Regulation
children.tldr: AI rules are emerging at U.S. federal and state levels and under the EU AI Act, and the regulation Anthropic itself supports could raise its compliance burden and slow its growth.
children.summary: AI regulation is developing in the United States at federal and state levels. Examples include the voluntary [[NIST AI Risk Management Framework|p1498]], FTC and state attorney general enforcement, and a [[September 24, 2026 letter|p1498]] from state attorneys general urging Congress to pass federal frontier AI legislation. The [[EU AI Act|p1498]] imposes transparency, documentation, and copyright duties on general-purpose models, with added duties for models with systemic risk. Non-compliance could bring fines, litigation, and product changes. Anthropic has [[called for regulation of frontier AI|p1499]], but the approaches it supports could [[increase its compliance burdens|p1499]] and slow its growth.

children.title: Data Privacy and Security
children.tldr: Anthropic must comply with privacy and security laws such as the CCPA, the EU and U.K. GDPR, and EU digital rules, which require significant investment and carry fines.
children.summary: Anthropic processes personal information and is subject to laws such as the [[California Consumer Privacy Act|p1500]] and FTC and state enforcement standards that may be inconsistent. Abroad, the [[EU and U.K. GDPR|p1500]], the Digital Services Act, the Data Act, and the Network and Information Security Directive all apply. These laws can conflict with one another, and compliance [[requires significant investment|p1500]]. Non-compliance could lead to fines, litigation, and product changes.

children.title: Export Controls and Trade Regulations
children.tldr: In June 2026 the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, which Anthropic re-deployed after safeguards were updated and restrictions were lifted.
children.summary: Export controls, sanctions, and trade rules can delay offerings and limit whom Anthropic can serve, including parties on the Commerce Department's [[Entity List|p1501]]. In [[June 2026|p1502]], the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on the [[Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models|p1502]]. Anthropic updated its safeguards with the government and industry partners and re-deployed the models once the restrictions were lifted. Future restrictions could limit hiring, model improvement, international availability, and access to [[AI accelerators and compute|p1502]].

children.title: Other Regulations
children.tldr: Anthropic is also subject to intellectual property, employment, antitrust, consumer protection, tax, and healthcare laws including FDA rules and HIPAA, and violations could bring fines and operating restrictions.
children.summary: Other laws that apply include [[intellectual property law|p1503]], employment and labor law, competition and antitrust rules, consumer protection, and multi-jurisdiction tax obligations. The company's [[healthcare and life sciences offerings|p1503]] may fall under FDA rules, healthcare fraud laws, and HIPAA. Failure to comply could lead to fines, litigation, and restrictions. The filing points to [[related risk factors|p1504]] for more detail.

children.title: Facilities
children.tldr: Anthropic is headquartered in San Francisco, leases U.S. data centers, has committed billions to U.S. computing infrastructure, and has leased data center capacity in Australia and Canada.
children.summary: The company is [[headquartered in San Francisco|p1505]], has offices in Europe and Asia-Pacific, and considers its offices adequate. It leases U.S. data centers and has [[committed billions|p1506]] to expanding U.S. computing infrastructure. It has also leased [[data center capacity in Australia and Canada|p1506]] and is pursuing capacity in other countries.

children.title: Legal Proceedings
children.tldr: Anthropic faces ordinary-course legal claims, including the Bartz copyright suit settled for $1.5 billion and a dispute with the Department of War over a supply-chain risk designation.
children.summary: Anthropic is involved in [[ordinary-course legal proceedings|p1507]] covering intellectual property, regulation, employment, privacy, and commercial disputes. Outcomes cannot be predicted, and litigation brings [[defense and settlement costs|p1508]] whatever the result. Key matters include copyright suits over model training, such as the [[$1.5 billion Bartz settlement|s339]], and the [[challenge to the Department of War's actions|s340]].

children.title: Intellectual Property Matters
children.tldr: Anthropic settled the Bartz authors' copyright class action over model training for $1.5 billion in September 2025, and the court approved the settlement in July 2026.
children.summary: Plaintiffs have filed [[a series of lawsuits|p1510]] claiming Anthropic infringed copyrights by using copyrighted material to train its models. In the Bartz class action, filed in [[August 2024|p1510]], authors alleged unlawful copying of their books. Anthropic disputes wrongdoing but [[settled for $1.5 billion|p1510]] in September 2025, and the district court approved the settlement in July 2026. The company says it has [[meritorious defenses|p1511]] in each action.

children.title: Other Matters
children.tldr: Anthropic largely won its district court case against the Department of War's supply-chain risk designation, but on September 25, 2026 the D.C. Circuit upheld the Section 4713 designation 2-1.
children.summary: In February 2026, after Anthropic said its technology should not be used for [[mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons|p1512]], the President directed federal agencies to stop using it, and the Department of War designated it a supply-chain risk. On [[August 27, 2026|p1512]], the Northern District of California largely granted Anthropic summary judgment, finding the actions were retaliation that violated the First and Fifth Amendments and the Administrative Procedure Act. On [[September 25, 2026|p1512]], however, the D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 that the [[Section 4713 designation was proper|p1512]]. Anthropic has petitioned for rehearing en banc. The outcome could affect its sales to [[government agencies and contractors|p1512]].

children.title: Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
children.tldr: Anthropic pairs public benefit corporation status with an independent trust that generally elects a board majority and a co-founder share holding 50.1% of voting power.
children.summary: Anthropic says its [[capital and governance structure|p1513]] differs significantly from other public companies and is built to help bring humanity safely into an era of transformative AI. As a [[Delaware public benefit corporation|s342]], its board must balance stockholders' financial interests, the interests of people affected by its conduct, and its Company Purpose, which may hurt financial performance. The financially disinterested [[Long-Term Benefit Trust|s343]] holds Class T stock with no economic rights and generally elects a majority of the board, but does not run the company. The seven co-founders' Founder LLC will hold a [[single Class F share with 50.1%|s348]] of total voting power. Employees receive [[Class E stock|s351]] that votes only on limited trust and director matters. Together the trust and Founder LLC will [[elect the whole board|s352]], and each form of control ends only under specific [[sunset provisions|s353]].

children.title: Public Benefit Corporation
children.tldr: As a Delaware public benefit corporation, Anthropic must balance stockholder returns, the interests of people affected by its conduct, and its Company Purpose, which may hurt financial performance.
children.summary: Anthropic is a [[Delaware PBC|p1514]] whose board must balance stockholders' financial interests, the best interests of those materially affected by its conduct, and the Company Purpose. The company says these goals have generally aligned with long-term commercial success so far, but it may make decisions that [[hurt business performance or the stock price|p1514]], and there is little court precedent on this balancing duty. The board will judge public benefit performance against [[five mission pillars|p1515]], using qualitative standards it sets itself, with [[no objective third-party standard|p1515]] required. Under Section 366(b) of the DGCL, Anthropic will give stockholders a [[statement at least every two years|p1516]] on its progress and plans to post it on its website.

children.title: Long-Term Benefit Trust
children.tldr: The independent Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock, which has no economic rights, and generally elects a majority of the board, but it does not run the company.
children.summary: The Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) is a Delaware [[noncharitable purpose trust|p1517]] meant to ensure Anthropic balances its three PBC goals, with Trustees designed to have little exposure to the company's financial results. Through [[Class T common stock|p1518]], which carries no economic rights, it generally elects and removes the Class T directors, who make up a majority of the board. The LTBT has [[no day-to-day decision-making authority|p1519]]; it selects directors and offers advice. The subsections cover [[director election and removal|s344]], [[how the LTBT's terms can be changed|s345]], [[the Trustees|s346]], and [[payments to the LTBT and its Trustees|s347]].

children.title: Election and Removal of Directors
children.tldr: The LTBT elects and removes Class T directors, a board majority, but changes to one Specified Class T Director need nominating committee agreement or a Class E employee stockholder vote.
children.summary: As sole Class T holder, the LTBT generally elects and removes the [[Class T directors|p1520]], while Class A and Class F holders elect the remaining directors. Nominations and removals require [[30 days' notice|p1521]] to the nominating and governance committee (NGC), which will have one Class T director and two other directors after the offering. For the [[Specified Class T Director|p1522]], NGC concurrence is needed; if the NGC does not concur within 15 days, the matter goes to a [[Class E stockholder vote|p1522]] unless the LTBT withdraws it. Any Class T director can be removed for cause without NGC or Class E approval, after 30 calendar days' notice.

children.title: Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock
children.tldr: The LTBT's terms and Class T rights can be changed with 80% board and Trustee approval, or without Trustee support through founder, employee and public stockholder supermajority votes.
children.summary: If the Trustees support a change, amending the LTBT or Class T rights needs [[80% of the board and 80% of Trustees|p1524]]. Without Trustee support and while Class F stock exists, approval can come, until the third anniversary of the offering, from [[unanimous Continuing Founders|p1526]] plus majorities of Class E and Class A votes cast, or at any time from [[two-thirds of Continuing Founders, 75% of Class E votes cast|p1527]] and a Class A majority. With no Class F stock, it takes [[85% of outstanding Class A shares|p1528]]. The same thresholds allow Anthropic to [[redeem Class T stock for no consideration|p1529]].

children.title: Trustees of the LTBT
children.tldr: Five Trustee seats, one vacant, are held by Neil Buddy Shah (Chair), Richard Fontaine, Ben Bernanke and Christopher Stubbs, serving renewable annual terms.
children.summary: The LTBT has [[five Trustee seats, one currently vacant|p1530]]. Trustees appoint and remove one another by vote, with 30 days' notice to the NGC, serve unlimited annual terms, and may also be removed by the Delaware Court of Chancery for disqualifying conduct. The current Trustees are [[Dr. Neil Buddy Shah|p1531]], Chair since June 2023 and CEO of the Clinton Health Access Initiative; [[Richard Fontaine|p1533]], since April 2025 and CEO of the Center for a New American Security; [[Dr. Ben S. Bernanke|p1535]], since June 2026 and former Federal Reserve Chairman; and [[Dr. Christopher Stubbs|p1537]], since October 2026 and a Harvard physics and astronomy professor. Each was chosen for expertise in areas such as global health, national security, economics, and science.

children.title: Certain Relationships and Transactions with the LTBT and its Trustees
children.tldr: Anthropic paid the LTBT $8,425,213 in the nine months ended September 30, 2026; each Trustee earns $400,000 a year in cash.
children.summary: Anthropic funds the LTBT, paying [[$2,716,750, $0, and $906,089|p1539]] in 2023, 2024, and 2025, and $8,425,213 in the nine months ended September 30, 2026; the LTBT is a consolidated variable interest entity. Each Trustee receives [[$400,000 in annual cash compensation|p1540]], and Dr. Shah gets an extra [[$25,000 as Chair|p1541]]. Pay does not depend on company profits, and Trustees may not hold Anthropic securities. In August 2026 Anthropic gave a [[$450,000 charitable donation to CNAS|p1542]], led by Trustee Fontaine.

children.title: Founder Voting Structure
children.tldr: A single Class F share held by the seven co-founders' Founder LLC will carry 50.1% of total voting power, letting them decide most stockholder votes.
children.summary: Anthropic says its [[seven co-founders|p1543]] are best placed to steward the mission. Before the offering, it will issue [[one Class F share|p1544]] to the Founder LLC, carrying 50.1% of total voting power, including for non-Class T directors. The LLC votes by [[majority of Continuing Founders|p1545]]; if they cannot agree, the share generally votes in proportion to Class A votes. If fewer than three Continuing Founders remain for 90 days, a [[450-day transition period|p1546]] begins, after which Class F and Class E stock are redeemed for no consideration. Founders lose membership for reasons including death, cause, or holding [[under 2% of their offering-date Class A shares|p1548]]. Class F voting power is [[not diluted by new share issuances|p1551]], so the LLC can decide mergers and other major votes.

children.title: Our Co-Founders
children.tldr: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah founded Anthropic in January 2021 and will be the Continuing Founders.
children.summary: The [[seven co-founders started Anthropic in January 2021|p1552]] and will each be a Founder LLC member. [[Dario Amodei|p1553]] is CEO and [[Daniela Amodei|p1554]] is President and board Chairperson. [[Tom Brown|p1555]] is Chief Compute Officer, Jack Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, [[Jared Kaplan|p1558]] is Chief Science Officer, Sam McCandlish is Chief Architect, and [[Christopher Olah|p1560]] leads interpretability research. [[Benjamin Mann|p1556]] is often called a co-founder but is not in the Founder LLC and will not help decide how Class F stock votes.

children.title: Philanthropy
children.tldr: Each co-founder has pledged 80% of personal Anthropic equity to philanthropy, alongside company Public Benefit Issuances and an employee donation matching program.
children.summary: Anthropic plans to direct meaningful resources to [[public benefit initiatives|p1561]], including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance and future issuances. Each co-founder has [[pledged 80% of their personal equity|p1561]] to philanthropy. Employees can pledge equity to charity, which the company [[matches with Class N common stock|p1561]], and Anthropic has irrevocable proxy agreements with certain donor-advised funds.

children.title: Class E Common Stock
children.tldr: Class E stock, issued to employees for tenure and donation pledges, votes only on the Specified Class T Director and on changes to the LTBT.
children.summary: Class E stock votes only on [[limited matters|p1562]]: disputed changes to the Specified Class T Director and certain amendments to the LTBT, Class T rights, or Class T redemption. Director matters need a [[majority of votes cast with a majority quorum|p1563]]; LTBT amendments need a majority with a 40% quorum until the third anniversary if founders are unanimous, or [[75% of votes cast|p1566]] otherwise. Employees get [[one share per six months of employment|p1567]] plus one per Class A share pledged to donation matching; co-founders receive none. Shares are [[redeemed for no consideration|p1568]], half each year after leaving and all upon events such as joining a direct competitor or when no Class F stock remains.

children.title: Board Governance
children.tldr: The LTBT and Founder LLC together will elect the whole board, and Anthropic is a Nasdaq controlled company but will use the exemption only for its NGC.
children.summary: Under a [[Stockholders' Agreement|p1569]], the LTBT and Founder LLC will together elect all directors, who face no term limits. The LTBT picks a board majority but has [[no role in day-to-day management|p1570]]. The Founder LLC, with [[50.1% of voting power|p1571]], will elect the other directors and decide stockholder votes, including mergers, for the foreseeable future. Anthropic is a [[Nasdaq controlled company|p1572]] but plans to use the exemption only for its NGC, which will not be fully independent; the board has an independent majority and the audit and compensation committees are fully independent.

children.title: Sunset Provisions
children.tldr: Class T control ends only through a vote meeting the Trust Amendment Threshold, while Class F control ends after fewer than three Continuing Founders remain for 90 consecutive days.
children.summary: The Class T Sunset Time occurs when no Class T common stock remains outstanding, and any action causing it needs approval under the [[Trust Amendment Threshold|p1573]]. That threshold varies: [[80% of the board and 80% of the Trustees|p1574]] if the Trustees support the action, a mix of Class F, Class E and Class A votes if Class F stock remains and the Trustees do not, or [[85% of outstanding Class A shares|p1577]] if no Class F stock remains. It never happens automatically through time or events. The Class F Sunset Time follows a transition period that begins when there have been [[fewer than three Continuing Founders|p1573]] for 90 consecutive days. Founders can be removed for resignation, death, incapacity, cause, or [[falling below 2% of their original Class A holdings|p1575]]. Neither sunset can be extended once triggered. Before its sunset, [[Class F stock carries 50.1% of total voting power|p1581]], and once both classes are gone, Class A stockholders decide all matters.

children.title: Management
children.tldr: Anthropic has a six-member board, growing to seven after the IPO, with the Long-Term Benefit Trust electing four Class T directors and making the company a Nasdaq controlled company.
children.summary: The section introduces Anthropic's [[executive officers and directors|s355]]: CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and CFO Krishna Rao, plus four non-employee directors. After the offering the [[board will have seven seats|s360]]. The Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) elects four Class T directors, and Class A and Class F holders elect the other three. Because the LTBT can elect a majority, Anthropic is a [[controlled company|s364]], but it plans to use that exemption only for its nominating and governance committee (NGC). The board has [[four committees|s365]]: audit, compensation, NGC, and safety and risk. Directors were [[largely unpaid in 2025|s371]], and a new [[director compensation policy|s371]] will pay cash retainers and stock awards.

children.title: Executive Officers and Directors
children.tldr: Anthropic lists three executive officers and four non-employee directors as of September 30, 2026, with the LTBT's Class T stock electing a board majority after the offering.
children.summary: As of September 30, 2026, the [[officers and directors|p1584]] are Dario Amodei (43, CEO and director), Daniela Amodei (39, President and Chairperson), Krishna Rao (43, CFO), and directors Reed Hastings (65), Christopher Liddell (68), Vas Narasimhan (50) and Yasmin Razavi (37). Hastings, Liddell and Narasimhan will be elected by Class T stock. The Amodeis and Razavi will be elected by Classes A and F. After the offering, the [[Class T holder will elect a majority|p1585]] of the board. The footnotes name Hastings as lead independent director and Liddell as the Specified Class T Director.

children.title: Executive Officers
children.tldr: Co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei came from OpenAI and have led Anthropic since January 2021, and CFO Krishna Rao joined in April 2024 from Fanatics Commerce.
children.summary: [[Dario Amodei|p1586]] has been CEO and a director since co-founding Anthropic in January 2021. He was previously Vice President of Research at OpenAI and a researcher at Google Brain, and he holds a Ph.D. in Biophysics from Princeton. [[Daniela Amodei|p1587]] has been President and a director since the founding and is also Chairperson. She held safety, policy and people roles at OpenAI and earlier worked at Stripe. [[Krishna Rao|p1588]] has been CFO since April 2024, after serving as CFO of Fanatics Commerce and Cedar and holding roles at Airbnb, Blackstone and Bain.

children.title: Non-Employee Directors
children.tldr: The four non-employee directors are Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi.
children.summary: [[Reed Hastings|p1589]] joined the board in May 2025. He co-founded Netflix and served as its CEO, Executive Chairman and Chairman, and he sits on Bloomberg's board. [[Christopher Liddell|p1590]] joined in February 2026. He was CFO of Microsoft and International Paper, Vice Chairman and CFO of General Motors, and White House Deputy Chief of Staff from 2017 to 2021. [[Vas Narasimhan|p1591]] joined in April 2026 and has been CEO of Novartis since February 2018. [[Yasmin Razavi|p1592]] joined in March 2023 and has been a General Partner at Spark Capital since March 2020.

children.title: Family Relationships
children.tldr: CEO Dario Amodei and President and Chairperson Daniela Amodei are siblings, and no other family relationships exist among officers or directors.
children.summary: Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei [[are siblings|p1593]]. There are no other family relationships among Anthropic's executive officers or directors.

children.title: Code of Conduct
children.tldr: A board-adopted code of conduct covers all employees, officers and directors, and amendments or waivers will be disclosed on the website or in Exchange Act filings.
children.summary: The board has adopted a [[code of conduct|p1594]] for all employees, officers and directors, including the CEO, President and CFO. It will be posted on the investor relations website, and amendments or waivers will be disclosed there or in Exchange Act filings.

children.title: Board of Directors
children.tldr: The board grows from six to seven seats at the IPO: the LTBT elects four Class T directors, including one vacancy, and Class A and F holders elect three.
children.summary: The board [[currently has six directors|p1595]]. Dario Amodei and Liddell were elected by Voting Common Stock, [[Razavi by Senior Voting Preferred Stock|p1598]], and [[Daniela Amodei, Hastings and Narasimhan|p1599]] as LTBT designees. After the offering, the board will have [[seven authorized directors|p1601]]. The [[LTBT will elect four Class T directors|p1602]]: Hastings, Narasimhan, Liddell (the Specified Class T Director) and one vacancy. [[Class F and Class A holders|p1603]], voting together, will elect the other three: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei and Razavi.

children.title: Director Terms
children.tldr: Directors serve annual terms until the Class F Sunset Time, after which the board becomes classified with staggered three-year terms and no term limits.
children.summary: Before the Class F Sunset Time, [[all directors are elected annually|p1605]]. After it, the board [[shifts to three classes|p1606]] serving staggered three-year terms. Class T directors would be spread proportionately across the classes while Class T stock remains outstanding. There is [[no limit on the number of terms|p1607]] a director may serve.

children.title: Stockholder Meetings and Actions by Written Consent
children.tldr: While Class F or Class T stock is outstanding, stockholders can elect or remove directors by written consent, but Anthropic still plans annual meetings with Class A votes.
children.summary: As long as Class F or Class T stock remains outstanding, stockholders [[may act by written consent|p1608]], including to elect or remove directors. Anthropic still expects to hold an annual meeting under Nasdaq rules and to solicit Class A votes, including on the election of directors who are not Class T directors.

children.title: Board Leadership
children.tldr: Daniela Amodei chairs the board, and Reed Hastings serves as Lead Independent Director to give the board an independent check on management.
children.summary: [[Daniela Amodei is Chairperson|p1609]]. She presides over board and stockholder meetings and advises the CEO. [[Reed Hastings is Lead Independent Director|p1610]]. He presides over meetings of the independent directors, advises on agendas and acts as a liaison. The board sees this role as a check that lets it act independently of management on matters such as performance evaluation and pay.

children.title: Director Independence and Controlled Company Exemption
children.tldr: Four of six directors are independent, and Anthropic is a Nasdaq controlled company but will use the exemption only for its nominating and governance committee.
children.summary: The board found [[Hastings, Liddell, Narasimhan and Razavi independent|p1611]] under Nasdaq standards. Because the LTBT can elect a board majority, Anthropic is a [[controlled company|p1612]] and could skip rules requiring a majority-independent board and fully independent nominating and compensation committees. It [[expects to rely on the exemption only for its NGC|p1616]]. The board already has an independent majority, and the audit and compensation committees are fully independent. If Anthropic stops being a controlled company, the NGC must become fully independent within the transition period.

children.title: Committees of the Board of Directors
children.tldr: Anthropic's board has four committees: audit, compensation, nominating and corporate governance, and safety and risk.
children.summary: The board has [[four committees|p1617]]. The [[audit committee|s366]] is chaired by Liddell, and the [[compensation committee|s367]] by Narasimhan. The [[NGC|s368]], chaired by Daniela Amodei, also has special notice and concurrence rights over LTBT director nominations. The [[safety and risk committee|s369]] oversees AI model safety and other material risks.

children.title: Audit Committee
children.tldr: Liddell chairs the audit committee with Hastings and one vacancy; both are independent financial experts, and a third member will be added within one year of listing.
children.summary: The audit committee [[consists of Liddell, Hastings and one vacancy|p1618]], with Liddell as Chairperson. Anthropic will use Nasdaq's phase-in period to reach three members within one year of listing. Both current members are independent and qualify as audit committee financial experts. Its duties include [[selecting the independent auditor|p1619]], [[reviewing risk management policies|p1624]], [[reviewing related person transactions|p1625]] and [[pre-approving audit and non-audit services|p1626]]. It will operate under a [[written charter|p1627]].

children.title: Compensation Committee
children.tldr: Narasimhan chairs the compensation committee with Razavi, both independent, overseeing executive pay, equity plans and executive employment and severance arrangements.
children.summary: The compensation committee [[consists of Narasimhan and Razavi|p1628]], with Narasimhan as Chairperson. Both are independent and non-employee directors under Rule 16b-3. The committee will [[set or recommend executive pay|p1629]], [[administer equity plans|p1631]] except for non-employee directors, review [[employment, severance and change in control arrangements|p1633]], and [[retain advisors|p1634]] as needed. It will operate under a [[written charter|p1637]].

children.title: Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee
children.tldr: The NGC, chaired by Daniela Amodei and not fully independent, gets 30 days' notice of LTBT director moves and must concur on the Specified Class T Director.
children.summary: The NGC [[consists of Daniela Amodei, Hastings and Razavi|p1638]], with Amodei as Chairperson, under the controlled company exemption. It will [[evaluate board candidates|p1639]] and [[review governance practices|p1642]]. It is entitled to [[30 days' prior written notice|p1644]] of director nominations or removals by the LTBT or the Founder LLC, and of LTBT Trustee changes. Changes to the Specified Class T Director need NGC concurrence. If the NGC does not concur within 15 days, the matter can go to a Class E vote decided by a majority of votes cast. The committee will operate under a [[written charter|p1645]].

children.title: Safety and Risk Committee
children.tldr: A two-director safety and risk committee, chaired by Narasimhan with Liddell, oversees AI model safety and security plus legal, cybersecurity, privacy and compliance risks.
children.summary: The safety and risk committee [[has two independent directors|p1646]], Liddell and Narasimhan, with Narasimhan as Chairperson. It oversees the [[safety and security of Anthropic's AI models|p1647]] and [[other material risks|p1648]], including legal, regulatory, cybersecurity, privacy and compliance risks. It operates under a [[board-approved charter|p1649]].

children.title: Compensation Committee Interlocks and Insider Participation
children.tldr: No compensation committee member has been an Anthropic officer or employee, and there are no board or compensation committee interlocks with other companies' executives.
children.summary: No compensation committee member [[is or has been an officer or employee|p1650]] of Anthropic. No Anthropic executive officer serves, or served in the past year, on the board or compensation committee of an entity whose executive officers sit on Anthropic's board or compensation committee.

children.title: Non-Employee Director Compensation
children.tldr: Only former director Jay Kreps received director pay in 2025, $200,000 in cash, and a formal director compensation policy takes effect with the IPO.
children.summary: Hastings, Razavi and the two Amodeis [[received no director compensation|p1651]] for 2025. [[Jay Kreps received $200,000 in cash|p1653]] for 2025 and resigned in May 2026. Liddell and Narasimhan joined in 2026, and [[no non-employee director held equity awards|p1654]] at December 31, 2025. Before the offering there was [[no formal director pay policy|p1655]]. The [[new Director Compensation Policy|s372]] sets cash and stock pay.

children.title: Non-Employee Director Compensation Policy
children.tldr: A director pay policy adopted in September 2026 gives non-employee directors a $100,000 cash retainer, role fees, $325,000 annual RSU awards and $400,000 initial RSU awards.
children.summary: The board adopted, and stockholders approved, the policy in [[September 2026|p1656]], effective the day before the registration statement becomes effective. Non-employee directors will receive [[cash and equity plus expense reimbursement|p1657]]. [[Cash pay|s373]] includes a $100,000 annual board retainer and extra fees for leadership and committee roles. [[Equity pay|s374]] includes $325,000 annual RSU awards and a $400,000 initial award for new directors. All such awards [[vest fully on a change in control|s375]].

children.title: Cash Compensation
children.tldr: Non-employee directors earn $100,000 a year in cash, plus $60,000 to $75,000 for leadership roles and $15,000 to $40,000 for committee roles, paid quarterly.
children.summary: Directors receive [[$100,000 per year|p1659]] for board service, plus [[$75,000 as non-executive chair|p1660]] and [[$60,000 as lead independent director|p1661]]. The audit committee chair receives [[$40,000|p1662]] and members $20,000. Compensation committee and NGC chairs receive $30,000 and members $15,000. Chairs receive only the chair fee, and all fees are [[paid quarterly in arrears|p1668]].

children.title: Equity Compensation
children.tldr: Each non-employee director gets $325,000 in RSUs at each annual meeting from 2027, and new directors also get a $400,000 initial RSU award vesting over about four years.
children.summary: From 2027, each non-employee director receives an [[Annual Award of RSUs worth $325,000|p1669]] at each annual meeting. It vests in four quarterly installments and fully by the next annual meeting. New directors receive an [[Initial Award worth $400,000|p1671]] and a [[Pro-Rated Annual Award|p1672]] based on months until the next annual cycle. Employees who become non-employee directors [[do not get these awards|p1673]]. The Initial Award vests [[12.5% at six months|p1674]], then in 14 equal quarterly installments.

children.title: Change in Control
children.tldr: On a change in control, non-employee directors fully vest in all equity awards granted under the Director Compensation Policy if they are still serving.
children.summary: If a change in control occurs under the 2026 Plan, each non-employee director [[fully vests in outstanding awards|p1675]] under the policy, including Initial, Pro-Rated Annual and Annual Awards, as long as the director is still serving on that date.

children.title: Executive Compensation
children.tldr: Anthropic paid its 2025 named executive officers $17,958,298 (Dario Amodei), $16,408,998 (Daniela Amodei) and $720,250 (Krishna Rao), mostly in equity, targeting the market's 90th percentile.
children.summary: This section covers 2025 pay for CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and CFO Krishna Rao. Anthropic aims to pay at the [[90th percentile of the AI development market|s378]], using salary, stock options, RSUs and benefits such as travel and security. Total 2025 pay was [[$17,958,298 for Dario Amodei|s401]], $16,408,998 for Daniela Amodei and $720,250 for Mr. Rao. In June 2025 each co-founder received [[992,500 options and 1,717,000 RSUs|s409]]. Only Mr. Rao had severance rights in 2025, worth up to [[$134,031,467 on a change of control termination|s413]]. In 2026 the company [[raised salaries and signed severance agreements|s402]] with all three officers, giving the Amodeis 24 months of salary and Mr. Rao 12 months. Anthropic is adopting a [[2026 Equity Incentive Plan and Employee Stock Purchase Plan|s416]] at the IPO and has a [[clawback policy and a hedging ban|s394]].

children.title: Compensation Discussion and Analysis
children.tldr: Anthropic's 2025 named executive officers were CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and CFO Krishna Rao.
children.summary: This section explains Anthropic's pay philosophy, its executive pay program and the pay of its named executive officers for 2025. Those officers were [[Dario Amodei|p1678]], Chief Executive Officer, Co-Founder and Director; [[Daniela Amodei|p1679]], President, Co-Founder and Director; and [[Krishna Rao|p1680]], Chief Financial Officer. The discussion includes [[forward-looking statements|p1681]] about future pay programs, and those programs may differ materially from current plans.

children.title: Executive Summary
children.tldr: Anthropic targets the 90th percentile of the AI development market for pay, with equal pay for the same role, level and location and simple plan design.
children.summary: Anthropic's pay philosophy aims for [[the 90th percentile of the AI development market|p1682]], consistent pay for the same role, level and location, and simple plans. In 2025 it paid executives a mix of base salary, stock options, RSUs and other benefits. The section covers the [[philosophy and objectives|s379]] behind this approach, a list of [[governance practices|s380]] the company follows and avoids, and the [[process|s381]] for setting executive pay.

children.title: Compensation Philosophy and Objectives
children.tldr: Anthropic's seven co-founders are paid equally, while CFO Krishna Rao is paid based on market data for his role, level and location.
children.summary: Anthropic compares each executive's pay with market data for the role and level [[twice a year|p1683]] during its performance and pay cycle. It treats its [[seven co-founders|p1684]] differently from other senior leaders: each co-founder receives equal pay, so Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei get identical pay and raises. Krishna Rao, who is not a co-founder, is [[paid based on peer group market data|p1687]]. The program has three goals: [[competitive pay|p1686]] to attract and keep top talent, internal parity, and [[long-term equity that vests over time|p1688]] to align executives with stockholders.

children.title: Compensation Governance Highlights
children.tldr: Anthropic gives no tax gross-ups, single-trigger change of control benefits or discounted options, and only the CFO has double-trigger change of control severance.
children.summary: The company says it keeps a competitive, consistent and simple pay philosophy, delivers [[most NEO pay as long-term equity|p1689]], reviews pay regularly, and offers double-trigger change of control severance only to its Chief Financial Officer. It does not use fixed-term employment agreements, guaranteed raises or equity grants, single-trigger change of control benefits, excessive cash severance, golden parachute tax gross-ups, meaningful perquisites, or executive-only pension plans. It also does not [[grant options at discounted prices|p1690]].

children.title: Executive Compensation Process
children.tldr: Non-employee directors have set executive pay so far; after the offering a compensation committee advised by Semler Brossy will take over.
children.summary: Executive pay has been decided by the [[non-employee board members|s382]], and after the offering a compensation committee will oversee it. Executives do not set their own pay, and the President advises on co-founder and other executive pay but [[not her own or the CEO's|s383]]. The company hired [[Semler Brossy Consulting Group LLC|s384]] as an independent pay consultant in connection with the offering.

children.title: Role of the Board of Directors and Compensation Committee
children.tldr: After the offering, a board compensation committee working with an independent consultant will oversee executive pay, replacing the non-employee directors who decided it before.
children.summary: Until now, the [[non-employee members of the board|p1691]] decided pay for the named executive officers after considering management's recommendations. After the offering, the [[compensation committee|p1692]] will oversee the program with its independent consultant. Its duties will include overall pay strategy, CEO and executive pay goals, incentive and benefit plans, director pay, pay-related risk, say-on-pay results, CD&A disclosure and the peer group.

children.title: Role of Management
children.tldr: Executives do not set their own pay; the President advises on co-founder pay but stays out of decisions on her own and the CEO's pay.
children.summary: The CEO and other executives [[do not set their own pay|p1693]] and are not present when the board sets it. The President reviews pay for the seven co-founders but does not recommend or take part in decisions on her own or the CEO's pay. She also makes recommendations on salary and equity for other executives, and the people team supports the board with analysis.

children.title: Role of Independent Compensation Consultant
children.tldr: Anthropic hired Semler Brossy Consulting Group LLC as an independent pay consultant to shape its post-offering compensation programs.
children.summary: In connection with the offering, Anthropic engaged [[Semler Brossy Consulting Group LLC|p1694]] as an independent compensation consultant to formalize post-offering pay programs consistent with its pay philosophy.

children.title: Elements of Executive Compensation
children.tldr: 2025 executive pay had three parts: guaranteed base salary, at-risk options and RSUs, and other benefits including travel and security.
children.summary: The [[2025 program|p1696]] combined guaranteed cash salary, at-risk long-term equity in options and RSUs whose value tracks the stock price, and other benefits meant to keep executives safe and productive. The two co-founders' salaries rose to [[$700,000|s386]] in June 2025, and Mr. Rao's rose to $850,000 in December 2025. Each co-founder received [[992,500 options and 1,717,000 RSUs|s387]] in June 2025. Most benefits match those of all employees, but the company also provided [[travel and security benefits|s388]] to some executives.

children.title: Base Salary
children.tldr: The Amodeis' salaries rose from $600,000 to $700,000 in June 2025, and Krishna Rao's rose from $700,000 to $850,000 in December 2025.
children.summary: The board reviews salaries about twice a year using market data and [[internal parity|p1697]], including parity with technical leaders for the co-founders. Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei each earned [[$600,000|p1698]] a year until June 15, 2025, then $700,000 from June 16, 2025. Krishna Rao earned [[$700,000|p1699]] until December 15, 2025, then $850,000 from December 16, 2025, based on market data and parity with other non-co-founder senior leaders.

children.title: Long-Term Equity Incentive Program
children.tldr: On June 12, 2025, each co-founder received 992,500 options at $2.38 per share and 1,717,000 RSUs that vest only after the IPO registration takes effect.
children.summary: Executives can receive equity each year under the [[2021 Plan|p1700]], and most of their target pay is equity that vests over several years. On [[June 12, 2025|p1701]], the board granted Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei each 992,500 options and 1,717,000 RSUs. The options had an [[exercise price of $2.38|p1702]] per share and vested monthly over the year starting January 1, 2025. The RSUs vest in twelfths quarterly from February 20, 2026, but only once the registration statement for this offering becomes effective.

children.title: Perquisites and Other Executive Benefits
children.tldr: Executives mostly get the same benefits as all employees, but some receive travel and security benefits that the board considers necessary.
children.summary: Anthropic generally offers [[the same benefits to all employees|p1703]] and avoids executive-only perks, but it provides travel and security benefits to some executives. A [[Travel Policy|s389]] governs executive travel, and no NEO received private aviation for personal travel apart from the security program. Third-party studies led the board to require [[enhanced security|s390]] for the Amodeis, including private aircraft for Dario Amodei. NEOs also received standard [[health and welfare benefits|s391]] and a 401(k) match.

children.title: Travel
children.tldr: The Amodeis get enhanced travel benefits recommended by security studies, and no executive tax gross-ups are paid on personal travel.
children.summary: A [[Travel and Expense Policy|p1704]] governs executive travel, and Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei receive enhanced travel benefits recommended by their security studies. Personal use is treated as taxable income, and Anthropic does not gross up the tax. Apart from the security program, [[no NEO received private aviation|p1705]] for personal travel in 2025.

children.title: Security Services
children.tldr: Security studies in 2025 led the board to require personal protection, cars and drivers for both Amodeis, plus private aircraft for Dario Amodei's business and personal travel.
children.summary: Anthropic may offer executives [[protection, home security, private aviation and car services|p1706]], which it says match practice at comparable tech companies. In 2025 a [[third-party security consulting firm|p1707]] studied the risks facing the CEO and President, and the board found enhanced security necessary. The 2025 measures covered protection for them and their families, home security, cars and drivers, and private aircraft for Dario Amodei. The board views these costs as necessary, and the company [[paid no personal security|p1708]] for other NEOs except during business travel.

children.title: Health and Welfare Benefits
children.tldr: NEOs received the same health, insurance, stipend and 401(k) match benefits as other eligible employees in 2025.
children.summary: In 2025 NEOs received the [[same benefits as other eligible employees|p1709]], including medical, dental, vision, disability and life insurance, fertility and mental well-being benefits, various stipends, education assistance, a commuting allowance and a 401(k) plan with employer match.

children.title: Executive Employment Agreements
children.tldr: Krishna Rao's 2024 offer letter gave him 14,000,000 options and severance rights; it ended in October 2026 and was replaced by a new letter agreement.
children.summary: Krishna Rao's [[offer letter dated March 2, 2024|p1710]] provided at-will employment, his starting salary and a hiring grant of options to buy 14,000,000 Class A shares. A quarter of the options vested after 12 months and the rest vest monthly. The letter also gave severance and change of control benefits. It was terminated in October 2026 and replaced by a letter agreement. Every NEO is also bound by a [[standard confidentiality and invention assignment agreement|p1711]] with 12 months of post-employment non-solicitation of employees.

children.title: Termination and Change of Control Benefits
children.tldr: In 2025 only Krishna Rao had severance rights: six months' salary, six months of COBRA and 1/8 option vesting, plus full acceleration on a change of control.
children.summary: All NEOs are employed at will, and [[only Mr. Rao|p1712]] had severance or change of control benefits in 2025. If terminated without cause or he resigned for good reason, he would receive [[six months of salary|p1713]], up to six months of COBRA premiums and vesting of 1/8 of his options. If that happened around a change of control, [[all his unvested equity|p1714]] would vest, and it would also vest if the awards would otherwise be cancelled without payment. That change of control benefit continues under an October 2026 letter agreement.

children.title: Other Compensation Governance Practices
children.tldr: Anthropic has a clawback policy, bans hedging and most pledging of its stock, and has no policy timing equity grants around material news.
children.summary: A [[clawback policy|s395]] takes effect with the registration statement and requires recovery of excess incentive pay after a restatement. The [[Insider Trading Policy|s396]] bans hedging, margin accounts and, with limited exceptions, pledging. Anthropic has [[no specific policy|s397]] on timing equity grants relative to the release of material nonpublic information.

children.title: Compensation Recovery Policy
children.tldr: A clawback policy effective at the IPO requires recovering excess incentive pay received during the three years before an accounting restatement.
children.summary: Anthropic adopted a [[Clawback Policy|p1716]] meant to comply with Exchange Act Rule 10D-1, effective when the registration statement becomes effective. After an accounting restatement, it must recover incentive pay received by covered executives beyond what the restated results would support, covering pay received during the three years before the restatement was required.

children.title: Hedging, Pledging, and Insider Trading
children.tldr: Anthropic's Insider Trading Policy bans hedging its stock, holding it in margin accounts and, with limited exceptions, pledging it.
children.summary: The [[Insider Trading Policy|p1717]] covers officers, directors, employees and designated consultants. It bans hedging such as prepaid variable forwards, equity swaps and collars, and prohibits margin accounts and pledging company stock, with limited exceptions. It forbids trading on material nonpublic information and sets a quarterly blackout window.

children.title: Policies and Practices Related to the Grant of Certain Equity Awards Close in Time to the Release of Material Nonpublic Information
children.tldr: Anthropic has no specific policy on timing equity grants relative to the release of material nonpublic information.
children.summary: Options are usually granted at or soon after a new hire's start date, with refresh, promotion and market grants when the board decides. The company has [[no specific policy or practice|p1718]] on timing grants relative to disclosure of material nonpublic information.

children.title: Tax and Accounting Considerations
children.tldr: The board weighs tax deductibility and accounting rules but may award pay that is not deductible under the $1 million Section 162(m) limit.
children.summary: Section 162(m) caps deductible pay for top executives at [[$1 million a year|s399]], but the board keeps the discretion to pay more. Stock awards are expensed at grant date fair value under [[FASB ASC Topic 718|s400]].

children.title: Tax Considerations
children.tldr: Section 162(m) caps deductible pay at $1 million per top executive, but the board may still award non-deductible pay.
children.summary: Section 162(m) of the Code limits the deduction for certain top executives' pay to [[$1 million|p1719]] per year. The board considers deductibility but keeps discretion to award non-deductible pay to stay flexible.

children.title: Accounting Considerations
children.tldr: Anthropic expenses stock awards at their grant date fair value under FASB ASC Topic 718.
children.summary: The board considers accounting effects when designing pay, and the company measures stock-based compensation at [[grant date fair value under FASB ASC Topic 718|p1720]].

children.title: Summary Compensation Table
children.tldr: Total 2025 pay was $17,958,298 for Dario Amodei, $16,408,998 for Daniela Amodei and $720,250 for Krishna Rao.
children.summary: For 2025, Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei each received [[$654,167 in salary|p1722]], $9,264,932 in stock awards and $4,028,558 in option awards. Dario Amodei's other compensation was $4,010,641, for a total of $17,958,298. It included $2,745,874 for personal security, $97,055 for personal private air travel and $1,153,087 from the spread on shares repurchased in the June 2025 tender offer. Daniela Amodei's other compensation was $2,461,341, for a total of $16,408,998, including $1,293,629 for protection, home security and transport and the same $1,153,087 tender spread. Krishna Rao received $706,250 in salary and a $14,000 401(k) match, for a total of $720,250. Award values are grant date fair values, not realized value.

children.title: Post-Fiscal Year End Compensation Changes and Equity Awards
children.tldr: In 2026 Anthropic raised NEO salaries, granted new options and RSUs, signed severance agreements, paid $2.5 million HSR fees for each Amodei and added security for Rao.
children.summary: After 2025, Anthropic [[raised salaries, granted RSUs and added severance|p1723]] for all three NEOs. The co-founders' salaries reached [[$1,380,000|s403]] by July 1, 2026, and Mr. Rao's rose to $1,250,000. In February 2026 the board granted [[new options at $17.66 and RSUs|s404]], plus extra co-founder RSUs in July 2026. October 2026 [[severance agreements|s405]] offer 24 months of salary to the Amodeis and 12 months to Mr. Rao. The company also covered [[HSR filing fees and Rao security|s406]].

children.title: Base Salary
children.tldr: The Amodeis' salaries rose to $915,000 in January 2026 and $1,380,000 in July 2026; Krishna Rao's rose to $1,250,000 in February 2026.
