children.summary: The shares are [[not registered with the Financial Supervisory Commission|p2138]] and may not be publicly offered in Taiwan. No person in Taiwan is [[authorized to intermediate|p2138]] the offering.

children.title: Thailand
children.tldr: There is no public offering in Thailand; shares may be offered there only under exemptions from approval and filing requirements.
children.summary: The prospectus is [[not a public offering|p2139]] in Thailand. Shares may be offered only under exemptions or in circumstances that require no approval under the [[Securities and Exchange Act of 1992|p2139]].

children.title: United Arab Emirates
children.tldr: There is no public offer in the UAE, and no UAE regulator, including the Dubai Financial Services Authority, has approved or received the prospectus.
children.summary: The shares are [[not publicly offered|p2140]] in the UAE, including the Dubai International Financial Centre, except in compliance with local law. The prospectus has not been approved by or filed with the [[Central Bank, the Securities and Commodities Authority|p2140]], the Financial Services Regulatory Authority or the DFSA.

children.title: United Kingdom
children.tldr: No UK prospectus will be published, the shares will not trade on a UK regulated market, and the offering targets only professional and high net worth Relevant Persons.
children.summary: The offering relies on exceptions under the [[Public Offers and Admissions to Trading Regulations 2024|p2141]], so no UK prospectus will be published, and the shares will not be admitted to a UK regulated market. Underwriters agree to make UK offers only under [[Schedule 1 exceptions|p2142]] and to communicate investment inducements only where [[section 21 of FSMA|p2144]] does not apply. The section defines an [[offer to the public|p2143]]. The prospectus is directed only at [[Relevant Persons|p2145]], such as investment professionals and high net worth entities.

children.title: Legal Matters
children.tldr: Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati will pass on the validity of the shares, and Freshfields US LLP represents the underwriters.
children.summary: [[Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati|p2146]] will pass on the validity of the Class A shares, and its members own less than 0.01% of Anthropic's capital stock. [[Freshfields US LLP|p2146]] advises the underwriters. Orrick advised on executive compensation, John Morley and Cleary Gottlieb advised the [[Long-Term Benefit Trust|p2146]], and Cravath advised the co-founders on governance matters.

children.title: Change in Independent Accountant
children.tldr: On October 30, 2025, Anthropic replaced Grant Thornton LLP with Ernst & Young LLP as its auditor, with no disagreements or reportable events.
children.summary: On [[October 30, 2025|p2147]], Anthropic engaged Ernst & Young LLP to audit 2025 results and dismissed Grant Thornton LLP. Grant Thornton's reports for 2023 and 2024 were [[unqualified|p2148]]. There were [[no disagreements|p2150]] and [[no reportable events|p2151]]. Grant Thornton's [[letter dated October 26, 2026|p2152]] is filed as Exhibit 16.1.

children.title: Experts
children.tldr: Grant Thornton LLP audited the 2023 and 2024 financial statements and Ernst & Young LLP audited the 2025 statements.
children.summary: The statements as of December 31, 2024 and for 2023 and 2024 rely on [[Grant Thornton LLP|p2154]]. The statements as of and for the year ended December 31, 2025 were audited by [[Ernst & Young LLP|p2155]].

children.title: Where You Can Find Additional Information
children.tldr: The full registration statement and exhibits are on the SEC website, and Anthropic will file periodic reports after the offering, available at www.anthropic.com.
children.summary: The prospectus omits some information found in the [[registration statement and its exhibits|p2156]], available at www.sec.gov. After the offering, Anthropic will file [[periodic reports and proxy statements|p2157]] and make them free at www.anthropic.com.

children.title: Anthropic, PBC
children.tldr: This section begins the index to Anthropic's consolidated financial statements.
children.summary: This heading introduces the [[index to consolidated financial statements|p2158]].

children.title: Financial Statements and Notes
children.tldr: Revenue reached $16,286 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026, but the net loss was $80,748 million, driven by a $72,388 million fair value charge on convertible notes.
children.summary: Grant Thornton [[audited the 2023 and 2024 statements|p2175]], and Ernst & Young [[audited 2025|s532]]. Revenue grew from $41 million in 2023 to $4,585 million in 2025, then to [[$16,286 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026|p2187]]. The operating loss narrowed to $693 million in that period. The net loss was $80,748 million, mostly from a $72,388 million loss on the change in fair value of convertible notes and related instruments. At June 30, 2026, total assets were $147,358 million, including [[$112,389 million of cash and cash equivalents|p2183]], against convertible notes payable of $108,566 million. Operating cash flow turned [[positive at $3,929 million|p2204]] in the first half of 2026, and financing brought in $110,774 million. The notes also cover [[about $265.6 billion of purchase commitments|s633]] and [[major copyright litigation|s633]], plus [[later fundraising and a supply-chain risk designation|s643]].

children.title: Opinion on the Financial Statements
children.tldr: Ernst & Young found that Anthropic's consolidated financial statements fairly present its financial position at December 31, 2025 and its 2025 results under U.S. GAAP.
children.summary: Ernst & Young audited Anthropic's [[consolidated balance sheet as of December 31, 2025|p2160]] and the related statements of operations, comprehensive loss, preferred stock and stockholders' deficit, and cash flows for that year. In its opinion, these statements [[present fairly, in all material respects|p2160]] the company's financial position, results and cash flows in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles.

children.title: Basis for Opinion
children.tldr: Ernst & Young audited Anthropic under PCAOB standards for reasonable assurance against material misstatement, but did not audit or give an opinion on internal control over financial reporting.
children.summary: Anthropic's management is [[responsible for the financial statements|p2161]], and the auditor, a PCAOB-registered firm required to be independent, is responsible for its opinion. The audit followed PCAOB standards to obtain [[reasonable assurance|p2162]] that the statements are free of material misstatement from error or fraud. The company was [[not required to have an audit of internal control|p2162]] over financial reporting, so the auditor gives no opinion on it. The work included [[testing evidence and evaluating estimates|p2163]] and the overall presentation.

children.title: Critical Audit Matters
children.tldr: The auditor flagged two critical audit matters: legal loss contingencies, and the $41.7 billion fair value of convertible notes, which produced a $34.5 billion loss in 2025.
children.summary: Ernst & Young identified two critical audit matters. The first is [[loss contingencies|p2165]] from legal claims and regulatory proceedings, some for substantial or indeterminate damages. Judging their likelihood and size took significant judgment, so the auditor [[read board minutes and obtained legal counsel letters|p2166]]. The second is the fair value of convertible promissory notes, estimated at [[$41.7 billion as of December 31, 2025|p2167]], with a $34.5 billion loss from the change in fair value for 2025. The value is [[particularly sensitive to the weighting|p2168]] between the contingent claims and common stock equivalent methods. The auditor brought in valuation specialists and [[inspected the company's IPO plans|p2169]] and secondary market transactions. Ernst & Young has been the [[auditor since 2025|p2171]]. It signed the report in San Jose on [[June 1, 2026|p2172]], with the stock split note dated September 30, 2026.

children.title: 1. Description of Business and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
children.tldr: Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation formed in January 2021, and its key policies include expenses grouped by nature, token-based revenue, and heavy reliance on CSP marketplaces.
children.summary: Anthropic is a [[Delaware public benefit corporation|p2208]] founded in January 2021 and based in San Francisco, with a purpose of developing advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. In 2025 it [[switched to grouping expenses by nature|s537]], such as compute and infrastructure and personnel, without changing totals. Sales through CSP marketplaces made up [[about 48% of revenue|s541]] in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Revenue is [[recognized as tokens are consumed|s559]] or ratably over subscriptions, and CSP sales are booked gross. Accounts receivable reached [[$5.8 billion at June 30, 2026|s551]], up from $909 million at December 31, 2025. Stock-based compensation was [[$1.2 billion in 2025|s566]] and $2.2 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026. On September 17, 2026, the company carried out a [[10-for-1 stock split|s539]] of Class A and Class N common stock.

children.title: Basis of Presentation
children.tldr: The financial statements follow U.S. GAAP and consolidate wholly owned subsidiaries and variable interest entities where Anthropic is the primary beneficiary.
children.summary: Anthropic prepares its consolidated statements under [[U.S. GAAP|p2209]]. It consolidates [[wholly owned subsidiaries|p2209]] and [[variable interest entities|p2209]] where it is the primary beneficiary, and eliminates all intercompany balances and transactions.

children.title: Change in Presentation and Reclassification of Prior Periods
children.tldr: In 2025 Anthropic switched from functional expense lines to expenses grouped by nature, recasting prior periods without changing losses, totals or cash flows.
children.summary: During 2025, Anthropic dropped its functional expense lines, including [[cost of revenue and gross profit|p2210]], research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative. It now groups expenses by nature: [[compute and infrastructure|p2211]], personnel, sales, marketing, and partnerships, the Bartz settlement, and other operating and administrative. It also combined some balance sheet and cash flow captions and recast all prior periods. The changes [[affect presentation only|p2211]] and leave total assets, liabilities, equity, operating loss, net loss and cash flows unchanged.

children.title: Unaudited Interim Consolidated Financial Information
children.tldr: Figures as of June 30, 2026 and for the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026 are unaudited and may not predict full-year results.
children.summary: The interim balance sheet as of June 30, 2026 and the statements for the [[six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026|p2212]] are unaudited and follow SEC interim rules, so they omit some annual disclosures. Management says they are prepared on the [[same basis as the annual statements|p2212]] and include all normal recurring adjustments. Results for the six months ended June 30, 2026 are [[not necessarily indicative|p2212]] of full-year results.

children.title: Stock Split
children.tldr: On September 17, 2026, Anthropic split Class A and Class N common stock 10-for-1 and reverse split Class T stock 1-for-1,000, restating all periods.
children.summary: On [[September 17, 2026|p2213]], Anthropic carried out a [[10-for-1 stock split|p2213]] of its Class A and Class N common stock and adjusted the preferred stock conversion rate to match. On the same date it carried out a [[1-for-1,000 reverse split|p2213]] of Class T common stock. All share and per share figures are restated for every period presented.

children.title: Use of Estimates
children.tldr: Management relies on estimates for items such as common stock fair value, SAFE and convertible note valuations, goodwill, stock compensation and taxes, and actual results could differ materially.
children.summary: Preparing GAAP statements requires management to make estimates, and [[actual results could differ materially|p2215]]. Key estimates cover the [[fair value of common stock|p2215]], deferred tax assets and uncertain tax positions, [[SAFEs and convertible notes|p2215]], goodwill, stock-based compensation, useful lives of assets, contingencies, financial instruments, and lease borrowing rates.

children.title: Concentrations of Risk
children.tldr: Anthropic depends heavily on a few customers, a limited number of cloud providers, and CSP marketplaces, which drove about 48% of revenue in the six months ended June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Credit risk sits mainly in cash, receivables and investments, and bank deposits exceed [[FDIC limits|s542]] without any losses. A few customers each made up 10% or more of revenue or receivables, such as [[Customer C at 43% of 2023 revenue|s543]]. The company relies on a [[limited number of cloud providers|s544]] for compute. Sales through [[CSP marketplaces|s544]] made up about 48% of revenue in the six months ended June 30, 2026.

children.title: Concentration of Credit Risk
children.tldr: Cash deposits exceed FDIC insured limits, but Anthropic has had no losses and holds investment-grade, diversified short-term investments.
children.summary: Credit risk comes mainly from cash, restricted cash, receivables and short-term investments. Deposits sit with high-quality banks [[above FDIC insured limits|p2216]], with no losses to date. Short-term investments are mostly [[investment-grade fixed-income securities|p2216]] spread across industries and issuers.

children.title: Significant Customers
children.tldr: Single customers have made up large shares of revenue, including Customer C at 43% in 2023 and Customer B at 18% in the six months ended June 30, 2025.
children.summary: Customer A held [[13% of accounts receivable|p2218]] at both December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026, and Customer C held 10% at June 30, 2026. In revenue, [[Customer C made up 43%|p2221]] in 2023 and 11% in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Customer D made up 11% in 2023. Customers A and B each made up 12% in 2025, and [[Customer B made up 18%|p2221]] in the six months ended June 30, 2025.

children.title: Other Concentrations
children.tldr: Anthropic gets most compute from a few providers, and CSP marketplace sales grew from about 11% of revenue in 2023 to 48% in the six months ended June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Before 2026, Anthropic got almost all its compute from [[three cloud service providers|p2223]], and in the six months ended June 30, 2026 it relied on a limited number of providers and suppliers, so disruptions could hurt operations. It is adding providers and leased infrastructure. Sales through [[CSP marketplaces|p2224]] were about 11%, 32% and 47% of revenue in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and 44% and 48% in the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026. These sales made up [[58% of net accounts receivable|p2224]] at June 30, 2026. Some CSPs also [[hold preferred stock and convertible notes|p2225]].

children.title: Cash and Cash Equivalents
children.tldr: Cash equivalents include bank balances, money market funds and liquid investments maturing within three months of purchase.
children.summary: Cash and cash equivalents include checking and interest-bearing accounts, [[money market funds|p2226]], and liquid investments with [[original maturities of three months or less|p2226]].

children.title: Restricted Cash
children.tldr: Restricted cash is noncurrent collateral pledged for leases and other contractual obligations.
children.summary: Restricted cash is [[pledged as collateral|p2227]] for leases and other obligations. It is classified as noncurrent and is [[released or applied|p2227]] as the related conditions are met.

children.title: Short-Term Investments
children.tldr: Short-term investments are available-for-sale debt securities carried at fair value, all classified as current even if they mature beyond 12 months.
children.summary: Short-term investments are mainly [[Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt and commercial paper|p2228]]. They are classified as [[available-for-sale|p2228]] and shown as current assets, even with maturities beyond 12 months, because they may be sold at any time. Credit-related impairments are [[recorded as losses|p2230]] in other income (expense), while non-credit unrealized losses and gains go to accumulated other comprehensive income until realized.

children.title: Variable Interest Entities
children.tldr: Anthropic consolidates VIEs it controls, including entities financing compute capacity and its Long-Term Benefit Trust.
children.summary: Anthropic consolidates a VIE when it is the [[primary beneficiary|p2232]], meaning it directs the key activities and bears significant gains or losses. It consolidates certain [[VIEs that finance compute and infrastructure capacity|p2232]]. It also consolidates the [[Long-Term Benefit Trust|s549]], whose assets and liabilities are not material.

children.title: Long-Term Benefit Trust
children.tldr: The Long-Term Benefit Trust, set up in 2023, holds Class T stock that lets it elect certain directors, and Anthropic consolidates it as a VIE.
children.summary: In [[2023|p2233]], Anthropic created the Long-Term Benefit Trust, a body of financially disinterested trustees. The trust exclusively holds [[Class T common stock|p2233]], which lets it elect and remove certain directors. Because it relies on Anthropic for funding, the trust is a [[consolidated VIE|p2234]]. Its total assets and liabilities were [[not material|p2234]] at December 31, 2024 and 2025 and June 30, 2026.

children.title: Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
children.tldr: Anthropic measures fair value using a three-level hierarchy, and short-term items like cash and receivables are carried near fair value.
children.summary: Fair value follows the [[three-level hierarchy|p2235]] of ASC 820, from quoted prices to [[unobservable inputs|p2238]]. Financial instruments include receivables, investments, [[convertible notes, SAFE liabilities and derivatives|p2239]]. Cash, receivables and payables are carried at amounts close to fair value because they are short term.

children.title: Accounts Receivable and Allowances
children.tldr: Accounts receivable rose from $909 million at December 31, 2025 to $5.8 billion at June 30, 2026, with a $71 million credit loss allowance.
children.summary: Receivables include amounts owed by customers and amounts collected by channel partners not yet passed on. They were [[$10 million, $95 million and $909 million|p2241]] at December 31, 2023, 2024 and 2025, and $5.8 billion at June 30, 2026. Management sets the [[allowance for credit losses|p2242]] using history, aging and market conditions. The allowance stood at [[$5 million, $17 million and $71 million|p2244]] at December 31, 2024, December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026.

children.title: Property and Equipment, Net
children.tldr: Property and equipment is depreciated straight line over three to five years, with leasehold improvements limited by lease term.
children.summary: Property and equipment is carried at cost and depreciated straight line over [[three to five years|p2245]]. Useful lives are [[reviewed periodically|p2246]], and routine repairs are expensed as incurred.

children.title: Software Development Costs
children.tldr: AI model development costs are generally expensed as incurred, and capitalized software costs were not significant.
children.summary: Model development costs are [[generally expensed as incurred|p2249]] because of high development uncertainty. Software costs are capitalized only once a project is funded and likely to be completed, and capitalized amounts were [[not significant|p2250]] for the years presented.

children.title: Evaluation of Long-Lived Assets for Impairment
children.tldr: Long-lived assets are tested for impairment when events suggest their carrying amount may not be recovered from future cash flows.
children.summary: Property, ROU assets and finite-lived intangibles are tested when [[events suggest a possible impairment|p2252]]. If carrying value exceeds undiscounted cash flows, the company records a charge for the [[excess over fair value|p2252]].

children.title: Intangible Assets, Net
children.tldr: Amortizable intangible assets are amortized straight line over one to six years.
children.summary: Intangible assets are amortized straight line over [[one to six years|p2253]] and tested for impairment under the long-lived asset model.

children.title: Goodwill
children.tldr: Goodwill is tested yearly for impairment in one reporting unit, and no impairment was recorded in 2025 or the six months ended June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Goodwill is not amortized but is tested [[annually in the fourth quarter|p2254]] or when warning signs arise. The test uses a [[single reporting unit|p2255]], starting with a qualitative review. No goodwill was recognized in 2023 or 2024, and [[no impairment losses|p2255]] were recorded in 2025 or the six months ended June 30, 2026.

children.title: Acquisitions
children.tldr: Business acquisitions are recorded at fair value under ASC 805, with any excess purchase price booked as goodwill.
children.summary: Acquired assets and liabilities are recorded at [[fair value under ASC 805|p2256]], and any excess price becomes goodwill. Adjustments may be made during a [[measurement period of up to one year|p2256]].

children.title: Leases
children.tldr: Leases over 12 months are booked as operating or finance leases using an incremental borrowing rate, while shorter leases are expensed as incurred.
children.summary: Anthropic leases facilities and equipment and classifies leases over 12 months as [[operating or finance|p2257]] under ASC 842. Lease liabilities use an [[incremental borrowing rate|p2259]] based on its estimated unsecured rate. Operating lease cost is recognized straight line. Finance lease assets sit within [[property and equipment, net|p2261]]. Leases of [[12 months or less|p2263]] are expensed as incurred, and ROU assets are tested for impairment like other long-lived assets.

children.title: Revenue Recognition
children.tldr: Revenue is recognized as customers consume tokens or ratably over subscriptions, and CSP marketplace sales are booked gross because Anthropic acts as principal.
children.summary: Anthropic earns revenue from its [[Claude-based intelligence service|p2266]], measured in tokens and offered through its own interfaces, APIs and CSP marketplaces, but not for on-premise hosting. Consumption revenue is recognized [[as tokens are consumed|p2268]], and subscription revenue is recognized ratably over terms that are generally 12 months or less. Payment terms are generally under 60 days. For CSP marketplace sales, Anthropic is the [[principal and records revenue gross|p2270]] because it holds the customer relationship, delivers the service and sets prices.

children.title: Deferred Revenue
children.tldr: Deferred revenue is mainly prepaid subscriptions recognized ratably over terms that are generally 12 months or less.
children.summary: Deferred revenue covers amounts [[billed or received in advance|p2271]], mostly subscriptions recognized [[ratably over 12 months or less|p2271]].

children.title: Compute and Infrastructure
children.tldr: Compute and infrastructure expenses are mainly cloud compute fees to CSPs plus data center leases, power and related costs for research, training and serving customers.
children.summary: This expense covers infrastructure for [[research, model development, serving customers and internal use|p2272]]. It consists mainly of [[cloud compute fees paid to CSPs|p2272]], partner channel serving costs, colocation, equipment leases, committed power and related software.

children.title: Personnel
children.tldr: Personnel expenses consist of stock-based compensation, salaries and bonuses, benefits, and payroll taxes.
children.summary: Personnel expenses include [[stock-based compensation|p2273]], [[salaries and bonuses|p2273]], employee benefits and employer payroll taxes.

children.title: Bartz Settlement
children.tldr: This line is the charge recorded in 2025 to settle the Bartz copyright infringement lawsuit.
children.summary: This line holds the charge recorded [[in 2025|p2274]] to settle the [[Bartz copyright infringement suit|p2274]], described further in Note 13.

children.title: Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships
children.tldr: Advertising expense rose from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million in 2025, within sales, marketing, and partnerships costs.
children.summary: This category covers [[channel partner costs and marketing|p2275]]. Advertising expense was [[$33 million in 2024 and $147 million in 2025|p2276]], and was not material in 2023.

children.title: Other Operating and Administrative
children.tldr: Other operating and administrative costs include donation matching, data quality vendors, IT and software, payment fees, facilities, taxes, professional services and bad debt.
children.summary: This category includes [[charitable donation matching|p2277]], data quality and evaluation vendors, IT and cloud software, payment fees, facilities, non-income taxes, professional services, [[bad debt expense|p2277]], and depreciation of non-data center assets.

children.title: Stock-Based Compensation
children.tldr: Stock-based compensation rose from $29 million in 2023 to $1.2 billion in 2025 and reached $2.2 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Awards are measured at grant-date fair value and recognized over the service period. Stock-based compensation was [[$29 million, $192 million and $1.2 billion|p2279]] in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and [[$286 million and $2.2 billion|p2279]] in the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026. Options are valued with [[Black-Scholes-Merton|s567]]. No expense has been recognized for [[RSUs with IPO or change-in-control conditions|s568]].

children.title: Stock Options
children.tldr: Stock options are valued with the Black-Scholes-Merton model, using a board-estimated common stock value, peer volatility and a zero dividend yield.
children.summary: Option expense is recognized straight line over the vesting period, with fair value from the [[Black-Scholes-Merton model|p2280]]. Until public trading, the [[board estimates common stock value|p2281]] using third-party valuations and other factors. Volatility comes from [[comparable public companies|p2282]], and the expected term averages vesting and contractual terms. The risk-free rate uses Treasury yields, and the [[dividend yield is zero|p2285]].

children.title: Restricted Stock Units
children.tldr: RSUs vest only after service and an IPO or change in control within seven years, so no RSU expense had been recognized as of June 30, 2026.
children.summary: RSUs have a service condition, generally over [[four years|p2286]], and a performance condition met by a change in control or public listing [[within seven years of grant|p2286]], or they are forfeited. Expense will use accelerated attribution once the condition becomes probable, which happens at an IPO or change in control. As of December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026, [[no RSU expense had been recognized|p2287]].

children.title: Redeemable Convertible Preferred Stock
children.tldr: Redeemable convertible preferred stock is recorded outside permanent equity and is not adjusted to its liquidation preference because a deemed liquidation is not probable.
children.summary: Preferred stock is recorded at fair value net of issuance costs and kept [[outside permanent equity|p2288]] because redemption depends on events outside the company's control. It is [[not adjusted to liquidation preferences|p2288]] because such an event is not considered probable.

children.title: Foreign Currency
children.tldr: Foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses go to other income (expense), and translation adjustments go to accumulated other comprehensive income.
children.summary: Foreign subsidiaries use local currency or the U.S. dollar. Remeasurement gains and losses are recorded in [[other income (expense), net|p2289]], and translation adjustments go to [[accumulated other comprehensive income (loss)|p2289]].

children.title: Loss Contingencies
children.tldr: Anthropic records legal liabilities when losses are probable and estimable, and adverse outcomes beyond expectations could materially hurt results.
children.summary: A liability is recorded when a loss is [[probable and reasonably estimable|p2290]], and reasonably possible losses are disclosed. Estimates require significant judgment, and outcomes beyond management's expectations could [[materially adversely affect|p2291]] results and financial condition.

children.title: Share Repurchase
children.tldr: Share repurchases are recorded on the trade date, and retired shares reduce common stock with any excess charged to accumulated deficit.
children.summary: Repurchases are recorded on the [[trade date|p2292]]. For shares retired right away, value above par is [[recorded to accumulated deficit|p2292]].

children.title: Income Taxes
children.tldr: Income taxes use the asset and liability method, with valuation allowances against deferred tax assets not more likely than not to be realized.
children.summary: Anthropic uses the [[asset and liability method|p2294]], recording deferred taxes for book and tax differences and loss carryforwards. It sets [[valuation allowances|p2294]] when realization is not more likely than not, and treats Net CFC Tested Income as a period cost. Uncertain tax positions are recognized only if [[more likely than not to be sustained|p2295]], with related interest and penalties in the tax provision.

children.title: Net Loss per Share
children.tldr: Anthropic uses the two-class method for net loss per share, but losses are not allocated to preferred stock, and diluted loss per share equals basic loss per share.
children.summary: Anthropic calculates net loss per share under the [[two-class method|p2296]] because all series of its [[redeemable convertible preferred stock are participating securities|p2297]] that share in distributions to common stockholders. The preferred holders are not required to absorb losses, so [[net losses were not allocated|p2298]] to them. Basic net loss per share divides the net loss attributable to common stockholders by weighted-average common shares outstanding, less shares subject to repurchase. Because the company reports net losses, [[diluted net loss per share is the same as basic|p2299]], since all potentially dilutive securities would be anti-dilutive.

children.title: Recently Adopted Accounting Pronouncements
children.tldr: Anthropic adopted four new accounting standards on segments, income taxes, credit losses and internal-use software, and two of them had no significant financial statement impact.
children.summary: Anthropic adopted [[ASU 2023-07 on segment reporting|p2301]] effective January 1, 2024, applied retrospectively, which adds segment expense disclosures. It adopted [[ASU 2023-09 on income tax disclosures|p2302]] effective January 1, 2025, applied prospectively. It early adopted [[ASU 2025-05 on credit losses|p2303]] effective January 1, 2025, electing the practical expedient that assumes current conditions at the balance sheet date do not change. It also early adopted [[ASU 2025-06 on internal-use software|p2304]] effective January 1, 2025, which allows capitalizing costs once a funded project is probable to be completed. Neither of the two early-adopted standards had a significant impact on the consolidated financial statements.

children.title: Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements Not Yet Adopted
children.tldr: Anthropic is still evaluating ASU 2024-03 on expense disaggregation, effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2026, and expects no material impact from other new standards.
children.summary: Anthropic is still evaluating [[ASU 2024-03|p2305]], as clarified by ASU 2025-01, which requires more detailed disclosure of certain costs and expenses. It takes effect for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2026 and interim periods within annual periods beginning after December 15, 2027. The company does not expect [[other new FASB pronouncements|p2306]] to have a material impact on its financial statements or disclosures.

children.title: 2. Revenue
children.tldr: Revenue grew from $1,163 million in the six months ended June 30, 2025 to $16,286 million in the same 2026 period, after $4,585 million for all of 2025.
children.summary: Anthropic's revenue was $41 million in 2023, $386 million in 2024 and [[$4,585 million in 2025|p2309]]. It reached $16,286 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026, up from $1,163 million a year earlier. In that 2026 period, [[$11,763 million came from the United States|p2309]] and $4,523 million came from international customers, based on billing address. [[Consumption-based revenue was $13,064 million|p2311]] and subscription-based revenue was $3,222 million. [[Deferred revenue rose to $1,650 million|s578]] at June 30, 2026. Remaining performance obligations totaled [[$10.8 billion|s579]].

children.title: Deferred Revenue
children.tldr: Deferred revenue rose from $269 million at December 31, 2025 to $1,650 million at June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Deferred revenue was $7 million at the end of 2023, $28 million at the end of 2024 and [[$269 million at the end of 2025|p2313]]. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, the company recognized $196 million from the opening balance and added [[$1,577 million of advance billings|p2313]], bringing the balance to $1,650 million.

children.title: Remaining Performance Obligations
children.tldr: Anthropic had $10.8 billion of remaining performance obligations at June 30, 2026, about 75% of which it expects to recognize as revenue within 12 months.
children.summary: Remaining performance obligations, meaning deferred revenue plus future revenue under non-cancelable commitments, were [[$10.8 billion as of June 30, 2026|p2314]]. The company expects to recognize [[about 75% over the next 12 months|p2314]]. The timing depends on customer usage and contract terms.

children.title: 3. Investments
children.tldr: At June 30, 2026, Anthropic held $108.9 billion of cash equivalents and $19.3 billion of short-term investments, mostly money market funds and U.S. Treasury securities.
children.summary: Anthropic's [[cash equivalents and short-term investments|s581]] grew sharply. At June 30, 2026 it held $108,897 million of cash equivalents, mostly money market funds, and $19,262 million of short-term investments at fair value. Its [[equity method investments|s582]] had an immaterial carrying value, with $265 million of a $325 million funding commitment still unfunded.

children.title: Cash Equivalents and Short-Term Investments
children.tldr: Cash equivalents rose from $16,459 million at December 31, 2025 to $108,897 million at June 30, 2026, and short-term investments rose from $2,889 million to $19,262 million.
children.summary: At December 31, 2024, Anthropic held only [[$3,029 million of money market funds|p2317]]. By December 31, 2025, it had [[$16,459 million of cash equivalents|p2318]] and $2,889 million of short-term investments at fair value. At June 30, 2026, cash equivalents were [[$108,897 million|p2319]], including $108,603 million in money market funds. Short-term investments were $19,262 million at fair value, mainly $14,785 million of U.S. Treasury and agency securities. Of the June 2026 total, [[$120,654 million at fair value matures within one year|p2323]]. Investments with unrealized losses totaled [[$18,159 million with $44 million of losses|p2327]], all held for less than 12 months. The company [[does not intend to sell them|p2329]] before recovery and recorded [[no credit loss allowance or impairment|p2325]].

children.title: Equity Method Investments
children.tldr: Anthropic's equity method investments were not material at June 30, 2026, but it had committed up to $325 million, of which $265 million was unfunded.
children.summary: Anthropic holds some investments where it has significant influence but not control. Their [[carrying value was not material|p2332]] at June 30, 2026, and it had [[$265 million unfunded of $325 million committed|p2332]].

children.title: 4. Fair Value Measurements
children.tldr: Convertible notes carried at fair value rose to $108,566 million at June 30, 2026, from $41,677 million at December 31, 2025, using hard-to-verify Level 3 estimates.
children.summary: Anthropic's largest fair value item is its convertible notes, which are Level 3 liabilities. They were [[$14,116 million at December 31, 2024|p2335]] and [[$41,677 million at December 31, 2025|p2336]]. At June 30, 2026 they were [[$108,566 million|p2337]], when total fair value assets were $131,633 million. The six-month increase reflects a [[$72,388 million change in fair value|p2350]] less $5,499 million of conversions. The notes are valued with a [[blend of contingent claims and common stock equivalent methods|p2347]]. Note purchase agreements with [[Google and Amazon|p2343]] to sell Series G-2 preferred stock at $259.1364 per share are marked to market each period. Level 3 values [[could change significantly|p2351]] if assumptions change.

children.title: 5. Goodwill and Intangible Assets
children.tldr: Goodwill grew to $576 million and net intangible assets to $109 million at June 30, 2026, driven by acquisitions.
children.summary: Anthropic's [[goodwill rose from $154 million|s585]] at December 31, 2025 to $576 million at June 30, 2026 after acquisitions. [[Net intangible assets reached $109 million|s586]], mostly technology-related.

children.title: Goodwill
children.tldr: Goodwill went from zero at the end of 2024 to $154 million at the end of 2025 and $576 million at June 30, 2026.
children.summary: An acquisition in 2025 added [[$154 million of goodwill|p2353]]. Acquisitions and other items in the six months ended June 30, 2026 added [[$422 million|p2353]], for a balance of $576 million.

children.title: Intangible Assets
children.tldr: Net intangible assets grew from $20 million at December 31, 2025 to $109 million at June 30, 2026, with $27 million of amortization in the first half of 2026.
children.summary: Net intangible assets were [[$5 million at the end of 2024|p2356]] and [[$20 million at the end of 2025|p2358]]. At June 30, 2026 they were [[$109 million|p2359]], from a gross $138 million less $29 million of accumulated amortization, mostly technology-related. Amortization expense was [[$13 million in 2025|p2360]] and $27 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026. As of December 31, 2025, the company expected [[$15 million of amortization in 2026|p2362]] out of $20 million in total.

children.title: 6. Property and Equipment, Net

The June 2026 balance included $618 million of servers, networking and infrastructure equipment and $536 million of construction in progress. [[Depreciation expense was $35 million|p2365]] in the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $10 million for all of 2025.

children.title: 7. Leases
children.tldr: Total lease cost was $89 million in the first half of 2026, and leases not yet commenced, mainly for compute, total about $321.4 billion.
children.summary: Anthropic leases offices and infrastructure equipment with [[terms up to 20 years|p2366]] and options to extend up to 14 years. [[Total lease cost was $89 million|p2368]] in the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $22 million in all of 2025. At June 30, 2026, the [[present value of lease liabilities|p2379]] was $1,079 million for operating leases and $443 million for finance leases. Leases signed but [[not yet commenced total about $321.4 billion|s589]]. Some compute leases are held through [[consolidated variable interest entities|s590]].

children.title: Leases Not Yet Commenced
children.tldr: Anthropic had about $321.4 billion of signed but not yet commenced lease obligations, mainly compute, at June 30, 2026, up from $50.2 billion at December 31, 2025.
children.summary: Future undiscounted obligations under compute and infrastructure leases not yet commenced were [[about $50.2 billion at December 31, 2025 and $321.4 billion at June 30, 2026|p2381]]. Some depend on contractual conditions being met. They [[start between 2026 and 2028|p2381]], with terms from under one year to 20 years. The company may pay part of these obligations with convertible promissory notes.

children.title: Leases Held Through a Consolidated Variable Interest Entity
children.tldr: Consolidated VIEs that finance compute capacity held $296 million of ring-fenced assets and $328 million of liabilities at June 30, 2026, and Anthropic guarantees some of their obligations.
children.summary: Anthropic consolidates entities formed to finance and deploy compute capacity. At June 30, 2026, they held [[$296 million of assets|p2382]] generally available only for their own obligations. Because Anthropic [[guarantees certain VIE obligations|p2383]], some creditors can reach its general credit. VIE liabilities were $328 million, including $310 million of lease liabilities. Anthropic may pay some rent with convertible notes, but [[none had been issued|p2384]] as of June 30, 2026.

children.title: 8. Supplemental Financial Information
children.tldr: Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash reached $114,918 million at June 30, 2026, while first-half 2026 operating expenses were $16,979 million.
children.summary: Anthropic's [[cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash|s592]] totaled $114,918 million at June 30, 2026. [[Accrued legal expenses|s595]] rose to $1,309 million. Other expense, net, was [[$8,757 million|s596]] in the six months ended June 30, 2026, driven by note purchase agreements. [[Noncash financing activity|s597]] included large note conversions. [[Operating expenses|s598]] were $16,979 million in the period, including $9,741 million of research and development.

children.title: Cash, Cash Equivalents, and Restricted Cash
children.tldr: Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled $114,918 million at June 30, 2026, up from $17,401 million at December 31, 2025.

The company [[may have to restrict up to an additional $10.0 billion|p2387]] under certain arrangements, though no such requirement was in effect.

children.title: Prepaid Expenses and Other Current Assets
children.tldr: Prepaid expenses and other current assets fell to $496 million at June 30, 2026, from $2,560 million at December 31, 2025.

children.title: Other Assets, Noncurrent
children.tldr: Noncurrent other assets rose to $3,929 million at June 30, 2026, mostly from other items of $3,707 million.
children.summary: Noncurrent other assets were [[$2,373 million at the end of 2024|p2391]], mostly prepaid expenses, and $476 million at the end of 2025. They rose to $3,929 million at June 30, 2026, of which $3,707 million was other assets and $222 million was prepaid expenses.

children.title: Accounts Payable, Accrued Expenses, and Other Current Liabilities
children.tldr: Current payables and accrued liabilities rose to $5,422 million at June 30, 2026, including $2,810 million owed to cloud providers and $1,309 million of accrued legal expenses.
children.summary: This balance was $333 million at the end of 2024, $2,511 million at the end of 2025 and [[$5,422 million at June 30, 2026|p2393]]. The June 2026 total included $2,810 million of cloud service provider payables and [[$1,309 million of accrued legal expenses|p2393]], up from $775 million. The $541 million donation matching liability at the end of 2025 was gone by June 2026. [[Accounts payable alone was $766 million|p2394]] at June 30, 2026.

children.title: Other Income (Expense), Net
children.tldr: Other expense, net, was $8,757 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026, driven by a $9,405 million loss on note purchase agreements.
children.summary: Other income and expense was small through 2025, with [[a net expense of $8 million|p2396]] that year. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, the company recorded a [[$9,405 million loss on note purchase agreements|p2396]], partly offset by a $724 million gain on warrant rights, for a net expense of $8,757 million.

children.tldr: In the first half of 2026, noncash activity included $11,810 million of note purchase agreements converted into Series G-2 preferred stock and $5,499 million of notes converted into Series G-3 and G-4.

In the first half of 2026, [[$5,499 million of notes converted|p2400]] into Series G-3 and G-4 preferred stock. The company also issued $667 million of Class N common stock to settle the donation matching program.
