The 2025 total included a $1,500 million Bartz settlement. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, expenses were $16,979 million: [[cost of revenue $2,380 million|p2402]], research and development $9,741 million, sales and marketing $3,808 million, and general and administrative $1,050 million. [[Cost of revenue is mostly compute and infrastructure|p2403]] for serving customers, and research and development is largely compute for model development.

children.title: 9. Convertible Notes, Revolving Credit Agreement and SAFEs
children.tldr: Anthropic raises money through note purchase agreements for convertible notes, and treats commitments to issue future notes as derivative liabilities until the notes are issued.
children.summary: Under [[note purchase agreements|s600]], Anthropic can issue one or more convertible notes. Commitments to issue notes in the future are carried as derivative liabilities until the notes are issued.

children.title: Convertible Notes
children.tldr: Obligations under note purchase agreements to issue convertible notes in the future are recorded as derivative liabilities until the notes are issued.
children.summary: Anthropic's note purchase agreements allow it to issue convertible notes. Any [[obligation to issue notes in the future|p2404]] is carried as a derivative liability on the balance sheet until the note is issued.

children.title: Google
children.tldr: Google's earlier convertible notes, up to $2.0 billion in 2023 and about $1.3 billion in 2024, have fully converted, and a new 2026 agreement allows up to $20.0 billion more.
children.summary: Under the [[Google 2023 note purchase agreement|s602]], Anthropic issued $2.0 billion of notes, all converted into preferred stock by January 2026. The [[Google 2024 agreement|s603]]'s note of about $1.3 billion converted in 2025. The [[Google 2026 agreement|s604]] allows up to $30.0 billion through 2030, reduced to $20.0 billion after Google's $10.0 billion Series H investment.

children.title: Google 2023 Note Purchase Agreement
children.tldr: Google bought $2.0 billion of 10.0% convertible notes in three tranches from 2023 to 2025, all converted into non-voting preferred stock by January 2026.
children.summary: Under the September 2023 agreement, Anthropic issued notes to Google of [[$500 million in 2023, $750 million in 2024 and $750 million in 2025|p2405]]. They carried [[10.0% annual interest|p2406]] and matured 48 months after issuance. In 2025, the first two tranches [[converted into Series E-3 and E-4 non-voting preferred stock|p2407]] at discounts to the $56.0865 Series E-1 price. In January 2026, the third tranche [[converted into 3.3 million Series G-4 shares|p2409]] at $233.2228 per share, leaving nothing outstanding.

children.title: Google 2024 Note Purchase Agreement
children.tldr: Google's roughly $1.3 billion 8.5% convertible note from August 2024 converted in 2025 into 24.2 million Series E-5 non-voting preferred shares.
children.summary: In August 2024, Anthropic issued Google a [[convertible note of about $1.3 billion|p2410]] at 8.5% annual interest, due August 2030. In 2025 it [[converted into 24.2 million Series E-5 shares|p2411]] at $53.2822 per share. Nothing remains outstanding.

children.title: Google 2026 Note Purchase Agreement (Unaudited)
children.tldr: A March 2026 agreement lets Anthropic issue Google up to $30.0 billion of convertible notes or non-voting stock through 2030, cut to $20.0 billion after a $10.0 billion Series H investment.
children.summary: Under the March 2026 agreement, Anthropic may issue [[up to $30.0 billion of convertible notes or non-voting common stock|p2412]] to Google through December 31, 2030, subject to conditions. Notes would carry 9.0% annual interest and mature after six years. Stock would be priced at the 30-day trailing volume-weighted average. In May 2026, Google [[invested $10.0 billion in Series H preferred stock|p2413]], reducing availability to $20.0 billion. Nothing had been issued under the agreement as of June 30, 2026.

children.title: Amazon
children.tldr: Amazon holds about $6.2 billion of Anthropic convertible notes as of June 30, 2026, and signed a further agreement for up to $20.0 billion in April 2026.
children.summary: Anthropic has raised money from Amazon through convertible notes under [[2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements|s606]], each for up to $4.0 billion. Part of these notes has converted into preferred stock, and Amazon's ownership cap has kept the rest from converting. As of June 30, 2026, about $2.2 billion of the 2023 notes and $4.0 billion of the 2024 notes remained outstanding. Under an [[April 2026 agreement|s607]], the company may issue Amazon up to $20.0 billion of non-voting common stock or notes. Amazon's $5.0 billion Series H investment reduced that amount to $15.0 billion.

children.title: Amazon 2023 and 2024 Note Purchase Agreements
children.tldr: Amazon's two $4.0 billion note agreements have partly converted into preferred stock; about $2.2 billion and $4.0 billion remained outstanding at June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Under the [[Amazon 2023 NPA|p2414]], Anthropic issued $1.2 billion of notes in September 2023 and $3.4 billion in March 2024, receiving $2.8 billion in proceeds for the second tranche. Under the [[Amazon 2024 NPA|p2415]], it issued $1.3 billion in November 2024, $1.3 billion in May 2025 and $1.4 billion in November 2025. The 2023 notes bear [[8.0% interest|p2416]] and the first 2024 tranche bears 8.5%. The later tranches carry no interest. In an [[initial public offering|p2419]], the notes convert automatically into Class N common stock at the lower of $2.0928 per share (2023 notes) or $5.0478 per share (2024 notes) and the public offering price. All conversions are subject to Amazon's [[ownership cap|p2420]], and any amount that cannot convert is reissued as a rollover note. Conversions produced 95.3 million Series E-2, [[20.7 million Series F-2|p2422]] and [[20.6 million Series G-3|p2425]] shares. As of June 30, 2026, about [[$2.2 billion and $4.0 billion|p2426]] remained outstanding under the two agreements.

children.title: Amazon 2026 Note Purchase Agreement (Unaudited)
children.tldr: In April 2026 Anthropic agreed it may issue Amazon up to $20.0 billion of stock or notes, later reduced to $15.0 billion after Amazon's $5.0 billion Series H investment.
children.summary: The [[Amazon 2026 NPA|p2427]] lets Anthropic issue up to $20.0 billion of non-voting common stock, priced at the 30-day volume-weighted average price, or notes bearing 8.0% interest that mature in ten years. Amazon's [[$5.0 billion Series H investment|p2428]] in May 2026 cut the available amount to $15.0 billion. Nothing had been issued under this agreement as of June 30, 2026.

children.title: Other Note Purchase Agreements
children.tldr: Anthropic has two undrawn note agreements, for up to $10.0 billion and $42.0 billion, that can be used only to finance rent on compute and infrastructure leases.
children.summary: Under a [[2025 agreement|s609]], Anthropic may issue up to $10.0 billion of convertible notes to fund compute lease rent. That ability ends at an initial public offering. A [[2026 agreement|s610]] allows up to $42.0 billion of notes bearing 9.0% interest paid in kind. Nothing was outstanding under either agreement as of June 30, 2026.

children.tldr: An August 2025 agreement allows up to $10.0 billion of convertible notes for compute lease rent, ending at an IPO; nothing was outstanding.
children.summary: In August 2025 Anthropic entered a [[note purchase agreement|p2429]] that lets it issue up to $10.0 billion of convertible notes solely to pay rent under a compute and infrastructure equipment lease. Its ability to issue these notes ends at an initial public offering. No amounts were outstanding as of December 31, 2025 or June 30, 2026.

children.title: 2026 (Unaudited)
children.tldr: A March 2026 agreement allows up to $42.0 billion of 9.0% paid-in-kind convertible notes for compute rent; none were outstanding at June 30, 2026.
children.summary: In March 2026 Anthropic signed a [[second note purchase agreement|p2430]] allowing up to $42.0 billion of convertible notes, used only to pay rent under a compute and infrastructure agreement. The notes would bear 9.0% interest paid in kind. Issuance is possible for five years after the draw period begins, and the draw period had not yet started. No amounts were outstanding as of June 30, 2026. [[Issuance costs|p2431]] for convertible notes are expensed as incurred.

children.title: SAFEs
children.tldr: Anthropic issued $122 million of SAFEs in 2023, and all of them converted into preferred stock by 2024; none remain outstanding.
children.summary: In 2023 Anthropic issued [[$122 million of SAFEs|p2432]]. Of that amount, $1 million converted into Series C-1 preferred stock in 2023 and $121 million converted into Series D-1 and D-2 preferred stock in 2024. Because they would settle for a fixed amount through a variable number of shares, the SAFEs were [[classified as liabilities|p2434]] measured at market value under ASC 480. The company had [[no outstanding SAFEs|p2435]] as of December 31, 2024 and 2025 or June 30, 2026.

children.title: Fair Value Option
children.tldr: Anthropic carries its convertible notes and SAFEs at fair value, estimated with probability-weighted scenarios, and reports the changes in its statement of operations.
children.summary: The company elected the [[fair value option|p2436]] under ASC 825 for its SAFEs and convertible notes. This avoids accounting separately for their debt and equity parts. Fair value is estimated with a [[scenario-based analysis|p2437]] that weighs possible outcomes, including conversion into preferred stock or Class N common stock and repayment at maturity. No fair value changes [[attributable to credit risk|p2438]] were recognized through June 30, 2026.

children.title: Derivative Liability
children.tldr: A derivative liability for Amazon's rights to later 2024 note tranches existed at the end of 2024 and was fully settled in 2025 when those tranches were issued.
children.summary: As of December 31, 2024, Anthropic recorded a [[derivative liability|p2439]] for Amazon's rights to buy later tranches under the Amazon 2024 NPA. The liability was settled and removed in full when the second and third closings took place in 2025. No tranche rights remained at December 31, 2025.

children.title: Revolving Credit Agreement
children.tldr: Anthropic's secured revolving credit facility grew to $3.3 billion with nothing drawn; it had $78 million of letters of credit outstanding at June 30, 2026.
children.summary: On May 14, 2025 Anthropic entered a [[$2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility|p2440]] with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit, maturing May 14, 2030, with Morgan Stanley Senior Funding as agent. The facility is secured by substantially all company assets and requires [[liquidity of at least $500 million|p2442]] at each quarter end. Commitments rose to [[$2.8 billion|p2443]] in September 2025 and [[$3.3 billion|p2444]] in November 2025. The letter of credit sublimit rose to [[$1.0 billion|p2445]] in February 2026. The company had [[no borrowings|p2446]] at December 31, 2025 or June 30, 2026, with $4 million and $78 million of standby letters of credit outstanding on those dates, and it was in compliance with all covenants.

children.title: 10. Redeemable Convertible Preferred Stock, Common Stock and Stockholders’ Deficit
children.tldr: As of June 30, 2026, Anthropic had 853.4 million preferred shares outstanding carried at $157.5 billion, alongside large stock option, RSU and donation matching share reserves.
children.summary: This note covers Anthropic's capital structure and equity awards. [[Redeemable convertible preferred stock|s616]] runs from Series A through Series H and reached a carrying value of $157.5 billion by June 30, 2026. The company has [[Class A, Class N and Class T common stock|s623]], and equity awards are granted under the [[2021 Stock Plan|s624]]. The note details [[stock options|s625]], [[restricted stock units|s626]] whose expense depends on an IPO or change in control, and [[restricted stock awards|s627]]. It also covers a 2025 [[share repurchase and a 2026 tender offer|s628]] and the [[Donation Matching Plan|s629]], which lets employees have donations matched in Class N shares or cash.

children.title: Redeemable Convertible Preferred Stock
children.tldr: Preferred stock grew from $2.9 billion carrying value at December 31, 2024 to $157.5 billion at June 30, 2026, with $136.3 billion of liquidation preference.
children.summary: The preferred stock is [[carried at issuance price, net of issuance costs|p2447]] and spans Series A through Series H-4. At December 31, 2024 there were [[220.2 million shares outstanding with a $2,874 million carrying value|p2450]]. By December 31, 2025, Series E and F had been added, bringing the total to [[544.3 million shares, $29,769 million carrying value and $24,646 million liquidation preference|p2452]]. At June 30, 2026, after the Series G and H rounds, there were [[853.4 million shares with a $157,510 million carrying value and $136,286 million liquidation preference|p2454]]. The largest single series was [[Series H-1 at $589.01 per share|p2454]], carried at $45,728 million. Subsections cover the [[Series G and H financings|s617]], [[dividend rights|s618]], [[liquidation preference|s619]], [[conversion|s620]], [[voting|s621]] and [[redemption|s622]].

children.title: Series G and Series H Financings (Unaudited)
children.tldr: In the first half of 2026, Anthropic raised $30.2 billion and $15.0 billion in Series G at $259.1364 per share and $65.2 billion in Series H at $589.0095.
children.summary: In the first quarter of 2026 Anthropic sold [[90.5 million Series G-1 and 26.0 million Series G-2 shares at $259.1364 each for $30.2 billion gross|p2455]]. In the second quarter it sold [[another 57.9 million Series G-2 shares for $15.0 billion|p2456]]. Also in the second quarter it sold [[77.6 million Series H-1 and 33.1 million Series H-2 shares at $589.0095 each for $65.2 billion gross|p2457]].

children.title: Dividend Rights
children.tldr: Preferred holders get non-cumulative dividends of 6% of the original issue price only if the Board declares them, and none have been declared through June 30, 2026.
children.summary: Preferred holders are entitled to [[dividends at 6% per year of the original issue price|p2458]], ahead of common stock, but only when declared by the Board. These dividends are [[not cumulative and none have been declared or paid|p2459]] through December 31, 2025 or June 30, 2026.

children.title: Liquidation Preference
children.tldr: In a liquidation or deemed liquidation, preferred holders receive their original issue price plus declared unpaid dividends before common holders, or their as-converted amount if larger.
children.summary: In a [[Liquidation Transaction|p2460]], preferred holders are paid the original issue price per share plus declared but unpaid dividends before common holders receive anything. If assets fall short, they share ratably by preferential amount, and they are treated as converted if converting would give them more.

children.title: Conversion
children.tldr: Preferred shares convert 10:1 into common, except Series D (about 10.4 to 10.6:1), and convert automatically in an IPO raising at least $100 million.
children.summary: Voting series convert into [[Class A common stock and non-voting series into Class N|p2461]]. Holders may convert at any time; the [[conversion ratio was 10:1 for all series|p2462]] except Series D-1, D-2 and D-3, which were about 10.6:1, 10.4:1 and 10.6:1 at June 30, 2026 after antidilution adjustments triggered by the Series E-2 issuance at $20.9280. Conversion is [[mandatory on an underwritten IPO raising at least $100 million|p2463]], on certain SPAC transactions, or on [[a vote by specified majorities of preferred holders|p2464]].

children.title: Voting
children.tldr: Series A, C-1, D-1, D-2, E-1, F-1, G-1 and H-1 vote with Class A common on an as-converted basis; all other series have no voting rights.
children.summary: Holders of the [[voting series vote with Class A common stock as one class|p2465]], with votes equal to their as-converted Class A shares. Holders of the [[non-voting series have no voting rights|p2466]], including in Board elections, except as required by law or the charter.

children.title: Redemption
children.tldr: Preferred stock has no voluntary redemption right but sits outside permanent equity because a deemed liquidation event outside the company's control could trigger redemption.
children.summary: Holders [[cannot voluntarily redeem shares|p2467]], but because a deemed liquidation event could force redemption outside the company's control, the stock is presented outside permanent equity. Carrying values [[have not been accreted to redemption values|p2468]] because a liquidation event is not considered probable.

children.title: Common Stock
children.tldr: Anthropic had 12.9 billion common shares reserved for future issuance on an as-converted basis at June 30, 2026, up from 9.3 billion at December 31, 2025.
children.summary: The company has [[Class A common stock with one vote per share, non-voting Class N common stock, and one share of Class T common stock|p2470]]. The May 27, 2026 charter authorizes 10,991.0 million Class A shares and 7,044.0 million Class N shares. Participating common stock ranks below preferred stock, and Class T carries no dividend or liquidation rights. [[Total shares reserved for issuance|p2473]] were 4.9 billion at December 31, 2024, 9.3 billion at December 31, 2025 and 12.9 billion at June 30, 2026, including 2.8 billion for options and RSUs.

children.title: Equity Compensation Plan
children.tldr: The 2021 Stock Plan had 3,864.8 million shares reserved at June 30, 2026, with 569.1 million available, and vesting moved to faster schedules starting January 2026.
children.summary: The [[2021 Stock Plan|p2474]] allows options, restricted stock and RSUs. It had 3,112.4 million shares reserved at December 31, 2025 and 3,864.8 million at June 30, 2026, with 287.6 million and 569.1 million available. Options last up to ten years. From January 2026, four-year grants vest 12.5% after six months instead of 25% after one year.

children.title: Stock Options
children.tldr: At June 30, 2026, 1.8 billion options were outstanding with $98.2 billion of intrinsic value, and options exercised in the first half of 2026 had $6.8 billion of intrinsic value.
children.summary: Options outstanding were [[1,797.1 million at June 30, 2026, with a $2.89 weighted-average exercise price and $98,205 million of intrinsic value|p2477]]; 902.7 million were vested. Intrinsic value of [[options exercised was $1.1 billion in 2025 and $6.8 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026|p2478]]. Grant-date fair value rose to [[$19.90 per share in 2026|p2479]]. Unrecognized cost was [[$2.8 billion, to be recognized over 1.2 years|p2480]]. Estimated [[common stock fair value ranged from $21.56 to $57.14|p2482]] in the 2026 period.

children.title: Restricted Stock Units
children.tldr: Anthropic has recognized no expense on 1.05 billion RSUs because an IPO or sale is not deemed probable; it would have recognized $2.9 billion by June 30, 2026.
children.summary: RSUs vest only after service and an [[initial event, such as a listing or change in control, within seven years|p2483]]. No expense has been recognized because the event was not judged probable. Had it been, the company would have recorded [[$2.9 billion of cumulative expense, with $23.7 billion unrecognized, at June 30, 2026|p2484]]. RSUs outstanding were [[1,049.6 million at a $25.34 weighted-average grant-date fair value|p2486]], and [[none have vested|p2487]].

children.title: Restricted Stock Awards (“RSAs”)
children.tldr: Anthropic granted 10.4 million restricted shares in 2026 acquisitions, leaving $325 million of unrecognized cost to be expensed over 2.7 years.
children.summary: In early 2021 the company granted [[1,731.3 million RSAs to founders and early employees|p2488]], which vested over time. All remaining founder era RSAs [[vested by the end of 2025|p2489]]. In the six months ended June 30, 2026 it [[granted 10.4 million RSAs in connection with acquisitions|p2490]], with [[about $325 million of unrecognized cost over 2.7 years|p2491]].

children.title: Share Repurchases
children.tldr: Anthropic repurchased 27.9 million shares at $5.61 in 2025, and a third-party tender offer at $25.9136 bought 179.9 million shares in April 2026.
children.summary: In 2025 the company [[repurchased and retired 27.9 million shares at $5.61 per share|p2492]], above fair value, recording $149 million against accumulated deficit and $7 million of stock-based compensation. It made [[no repurchases in the first half of 2026|p2493]]. A [[third-party tender offer at $25.9136 per share|p2494]] closed in April 2026 with 179.9 million shares sold at fair value, so no compensation expense was recorded.

children.title: Donation Matching Plan
children.tldr: Anthropic issued 30.6 million Class N shares in early 2026 to settle employee donation matches, after accruing $541 million for the obligation at December 31, 2025.
children.summary: Under the [[Donation Matching Plan|p2495]], adopted in November 2021, the company matches eligible employee donations in Class N stock or cash. Reserved shares fell from 964.3 million to 933.7 million at June 30, 2026. The company recorded a $126 million fair value change in the six months ended June 30, 2026, issued 30.6 million Class N shares in the first quarter of 2026, and had accrued $541 million at December 31, 2025 and zero at June 30, 2026.

children.title: 11. Income Taxes
children.tldr: Anthropic lost $41.9 billion before taxes in 2025 but paid only a $20 million provision, holding a full $3.4 billion valuation allowance and $8.2 billion of federal NOLs.
children.summary: Loss before taxes was [[$41,945 million in 2025|p2497]], almost all domestic, and the [[tax provision was $20 million|p2499]], mostly foreign. Mark to market items were the main gap between the 21% statutory rate and the near zero effective rate ([[$7,192 million of tax effect|p2502]]). Because of cumulative losses, a [[full valuation allowance|p2507]] reached [[$3,422 million|p2509]]. At year end there were [[$8.2 billion of federal and $4.2 billion of state NOL carryforwards|p2510]], plus $656 million federal R&D credits. Section 382 ownership changes in 2024 and 2025 [[may limit their use|p2513]]. Unrecognized tax benefits rose to [[$293 million|p2515]]. The [[OBBB Act|p2522]] did not materially affect results. A subsection covers the [[first half of 2026|s631]].

children.title: For the Six Months Ended June 30, 2025 and 2026 (Unaudited)
children.tldr: In the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic recorded a $21 million tax provision on an $80.7 billion pre-tax loss, an effective rate of about zero.
children.summary: For the six months ended June 30, 2026, the [[provision was $21 million on a loss before taxes of $80,727 million|p2524]], versus $7 million on $12,962 million a year earlier. The provision is [[mostly US state and foreign taxes|p2525]], and a full valuation allowance remains.

children.title: 12. Net Loss per Share
children.tldr: Net loss per share was $(39.88) in the six months ended June 30, 2026, on an $80.7 billion net loss, versus $(23.04) for full year 2025.
children.summary: Class A and Class N share identical economic rights, so [[loss per share is shown on a combined basis|p2526]]. Net loss per share was [[$(1.42) in 2023, $(5.43) in 2024, $(23.04) in 2025, and $(39.88) in the six months ended June 30, 2026|p2528]], when the net loss was $80,748 million. Basic and diluted figures are equal because [[potential shares would be anti-dilutive|p2529]]; [[12.2 billion such securities|p2532]] were excluded at June 30, 2026, and [[1,049.6 million performance-based RSUs|p2533]] were also left out.

children.title: 13. Commitments and Contingencies
children.tldr: Anthropic had $54.6 billion of non-cancelable purchase commitments at December 31, 2025, rising to about $265.6 billion by June 30, 2026, alongside major copyright litigation.
children.summary: This note covers Anthropic's contractual obligations and legal exposure. [[Purchase commitments|s634]], mainly for cloud hosting and infrastructure, totaled $54,559 million at December 31, 2025 and about $265.6 billion by June 30, 2026. The company also has [[guaranty arrangements|s635]] with data center developers of up to $0.8 billion. Its [[legal matters|s636]] include the $1.5 billion Bartz copyright settlement and many pending suits from music publishers, Canadian authors and news publishers, Reddit, and opt-out authors. Anthropic also gives [[uncapped intellectual property indemnities|s637]] in some cases, and its [[401(k) matching contributions|s638]] were $15 million in 2025.

children.title: Purchase Commitments
children.tldr: Non-cancelable purchase commitments totaled $54,559 million at December 31, 2025 and about $265.6 billion by June 30, 2026, mostly for cloud and infrastructure services.
children.summary: Anthropic's non-cancelable commitments [[primarily relate to CSP hosting|p2534]] and other third-party infrastructure. At December 31, 2025, future minimum payments were [[$54,559 million in total|p2536]], including $7,059 million due in 2026 and $11,128 million in 2027. By June 30, 2026, fixed or minimum commitments reached [[about $265.6 billion|p2537]] with terms of one to 20 years. Some compute agreements [[have no fixed minimum|p2538]] and are excluded from these figures, though the company expects those payments to be significant.

children.title: Guaranty (unaudited)
children.tldr: In 2026 Anthropic guaranteed data center developers' costs, with maximum potential payments of up to $0.8 billion as of June 30, 2026.
children.summary: In 2026, Anthropic entered into [[guaranty and cost reimbursement arrangements|p2540]] with developers building data center capacity. If certain trigger events occur, it could owe [[up to $0.8 billion|p2540]] as of June 30, 2026. Amounts accrued were not material.

children.title: Legal Matters
children.tldr: Anthropic settled the Bartz authors' class action for $1.5 billion but still faces many copyright suits from music publishers, Canadian plaintiffs, Reddit, and opt-out authors.
children.summary: The largest matter is [[the Bartz settlement|p2542]] of $1.5 billion plus interest, approved in July 2026. Anthropic paid $300 million in 2025 and had $1.2 billion accrued at June 30, 2026. Music publishers are suing in [[Concord I|p2543]], where summary judgment was heard on October 21, 2026, and in newer [[Music Publisher Matters|p2546]] filed during 2026. Other cases include [[four Canadian copyright actions|p2544]], a [[Reddit suit|p2545]] narrowed to contract and unfair competition claims, [[authors who opted out|p2549]] of Bartz, and [[class actions over subscription advertising|p2548]]. The company also faces [[government inquiries|p2551]], including from the FTC. Anthropic disputes the claims and warns that [[outcomes could be material|p2552]] to its results.

children.title: Indemnification Agreements
children.tldr: Anthropic gives customers intellectual property indemnities that are sometimes uncapped and generally perpetual, but it has not incurred costs under them.
children.summary: Anthropic indemnifies parties against [[third-party intellectual property claims|p2553]] related to its technology. These obligations are [[not capped in certain instances|p2554]] and generally last indefinitely. The maximum exposure cannot be determined, and the company has not yet incurred defense or settlement costs under them.

children.title: Employee Benefit Plan
children.tldr: Anthropic's 401(k) matching contributions rose from $2 million in 2023 to $15 million in 2025, and reached $20 million in the first half of 2026.
children.summary: Anthropic matches employee 401(k) contributions [[up to a fixed dollar cap|p2555]]. Matching contributions were [[$2 million, $7 million, and $15 million|p2555]] in 2023, 2024, and 2025. They were $7 million and $20 million in the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026.

children.title: 14. Segment and Geographical Information
children.tldr: Anthropic reports one segment judged on consolidated net loss; stock-based compensation reached $2.2 billion in the first half of 2026 and 95% of long-lived assets are U.S.-based.
children.summary: Anthropic's chief operating decision maker is [[the CEO and President|p2556]], and the company has a single reportable segment. Management measures performance using [[consolidated net loss|p2557]]. Stock-based compensation is reported to them separately: it was $1.2 billion in 2025 and [[$2.2 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026|p2557]]. About [[95% of long-lived assets|p2558]] were in the United States at June 30, 2026.

children.title: 15. Business Combinations
children.tldr: Anthropic bought Stainless Software for $306 million in May 2026 and Bun for about $171 million in December 2025, both mainly paid in stock.
children.summary: In [[2026 acquisitions|s641]], Anthropic bought Stainless Software for $306 million and made other purchases totaling $260 million. In [[its 2025 acquisition|s642]], it bought Bun for about $171 million, most of it in equity, and recorded $154 million of goodwill. Pro forma results were not presented because the effects were not material.

children.title: 2026 Acquisition Activity (Unaudited)
children.tldr: Anthropic acquired Stainless Software on May 18, 2026 for $306 million, mostly in stock, recording $253 million of goodwill.
children.summary: Stainless Software was acquired [[for $306 million|p2559]], funded mainly by Class A stock worth $295 million. The price included $65 million of intangible assets and [[$253 million of goodwill|p2559]]. Other first-half 2026 acquisitions totaled [[$260 million|p2560]].

children.title: 2025 Acquisition Activity
children.tldr: On December 2, 2025 Anthropic bought Bun for about $171 million, mostly in stock, with $154 million recorded as goodwill.
children.summary: Anthropic acquired [[100% of Bun|p2561]] mainly to add developer ecosystem talent. The [[$171 million consideration|p2562]] included $136 million of equity, a $25 million share holdback liability, and $10 million in cash. The holdback covers [[1.6 million shares|p2564]] held for 18 months. Anthropic recorded [[$154 million of goodwill|p2566]], and pro forma results were [[not presented as immaterial|p2567]].

children.title: 16. Subsequent Events
children.tldr: After 2025, Anthropic raised over $100 billion in equity, signed about $417 billion of new compute commitments, and was labeled a supply-chain risk by the Department of War.
children.summary: These events were evaluated [[through June 1, 2026|p2568]]. On [[equity and financing|s644]], the company raised $30.2 billion in Series G and $60.8 billion in Series H, and got investment and financing commitments from Google and Amazon. On [[compute and infrastructure|s645]], it signed new agreements with about $417 billion of minimum obligations. [[Strategic deals|s646]] included buying Coefficient Bio and Stainless Software. Under [[other matters|s647]], the U.S. government ordered a halt to use of its models and designated Anthropic a Supply-Chain Risk, which the company has challenged in court with mixed results.

children.title: Equity and Financing Transactions
children.tldr: In early 2026 Anthropic raised $30.2 billion in Series G and $60.8 billion in Series H, plus $10 billion from Google and $5 billion from Amazon.
children.summary: In January and February 2026, Anthropic sold Series G preferred stock at $259.1364 per share for [[$30.2 billion|p2569]]. In May 2026, it sold Series H at $589.0095 per share for [[$60.8 billion|p2575]]. Google bought [[about $10.0 billion|p2572]] of Series G-2 stock and will provide [[up to $30.0 billion|p2573]] of further financing through 2030. Amazon bought [[about $5.0 billion|p2574]] and committed up to $20.0 billion more. A secondary sale of [[179.9 million shares|p2570]] closed in April 2026. Settling the donation match with Class N stock added [[$126 million of expense|p2571]].

children.title: Compute and Infrastructure Transactions
children.tldr: After December 31, 2025 Anthropic signed compute and infrastructure agreements with about $417 billion of minimum payments, plus an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion more.
children.summary: New and amended leases and commercial agreements carry [[about $417 billion|p2580]] of future minimum payments, with terms of up to 20 years. Expanded agreements for capacity delivered between 2028 and 2031 are estimated at [[$125 billion to $150 billion|p2580]]. Anthropic may issue [[up to $42.0 billion of convertible notes|p2577]] solely to pay rent on a compute lease. It also [[guaranteed up to $500 million|p2578]] of a provider's power contract, [[deposited $2.5 billion|p2579]] in escrow, and signed a [[20-year data center lease|p2576]] expected to start in 2027.

children.title: Strategic Transactions and Partnerships
children.tldr: In April and May 2026 Anthropic bought Coefficient Bio and Stainless Software for stock and agreed to invest $325 million in a new entity.
children.summary: Anthropic acquired [[Coefficient Bio|p2581]], which builds AI models for biological research, for 15.4 million Class A shares. It also acquired [[Stainless Software|p2582]] for 11.6 million shares. In May 2026 it agreed to [[invest $325 million|p2584]] in a new entity meant to speed AI adoption at mid-sized companies.

children.title: Other Matters
children.tldr: In February 2026 the U.S. government ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic's models and labeled it a supply-chain risk; a district court sided with Anthropic, but the D.C. Circuit did not.
children.summary: On February 27, 2026, the President ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic's models, and the Department of War issued a [[Supply-Chain Risk designation|p2587]]. Anthropic warned of possible material revenue losses. A [[district court largely ruled for Anthropic|p2587]], finding retaliation and violations of the First and Fifth Amendments and the Administrative Procedure Act. However, the [[D.C. Circuit denied review 2-1|p2587]], and Anthropic is evaluating its next steps. Separately, a new [[San Francisco office lease|p2585]] added a $200 million right-of-use asset, and [[stock option cliffs were shortened|p2586]] to six months.

children.title: 17. Subsequent Events (Unaudited)
children.tldr: After June 2026 Anthropic granted $5.8 billion of RSUs, expanded its credit line to $15.0 billion, split its stock 10-for-1, and added about $245 billion of compute commitments.
children.summary: These events were evaluated [[through October 26, 2026|p2588]]. On [[equity and financing|s649]], Anthropic granted RSUs worth $5.8 billion, raised its revolving credit to $15.0 billion, carried out a 10-for-1 stock split, and adopted new equity plans. On [[compute and infrastructure|s650]], it signed a hardware deal with AMD and new agreements with about $245 billion of minimum payments.

children.title: Equity and Financing Transactions
children.tldr: After June 30, 2026 Anthropic granted about 91 million RSUs worth $5.8 billion, raised its revolver to $15.0 billion, did a 10-for-1 split, and booked $2.0 billion for donation matching.
children.summary: The board granted [[about 91 million RSUs|p2589]] worth $5.8 billion, which vest partly upon the IPO registration becoming effective. The credit agreement's revolving commitments rose [[from $3.3 billion to $15.0 billion|p2590]], with maturity extended to September 2031. Anthropic carried out a [[10-for-1 stock split|p2592]] in September 2026 and recorded [[$2.0 billion of expense|p2593]] for donation matching. Stockholders approved up to [[846.8 million Class N shares|p2595]] for a subsidiary serving the public benefit purpose. New equity plans reserve [[2,950.0 million and 160.0 million shares|p2596]].

children.title: Compute and Infrastructure Transactions
children.tldr: After June 30, 2026 Anthropic signed an AMD hardware deal and new compute agreements with about $245 billion of minimum payments, plus about $21 billion short-term.
children.summary: Under a [[Hardware Supply Agreement with AMD|p2597]] for Helios systems with MI450 GPUs, AMD may buy up to $5.0 billion of Class N stock if certain conditions are met. Anthropic also entered agreements with [[about $245 billion|p2598]] of minimum payments, starting between 2026 and 2036, plus short-term contracts with [[about $21 billion|p2598]] of non-cancelable payments.

children.title: Part II
children.tldr: Part II holds regulatory material not required in the prospectus: offering expenses, director and officer indemnification, recent unregistered securities sales, exhibits, and formal undertakings.
children.summary: Part II covers [[information not required in the prospectus|p2599]]. It lists the [[expenses of the offering|s652]], explains how the company will [[indemnify its directors and officers|s653]], and records [[securities sold without registration|s654]] since November 2023. It also points to the [[exhibits and financial statement schedules|s659]] and sets out the company's [[undertakings to the SEC|s662]].

children.title: Other Expenses of Issuance and Distribution. Item 13.
children.tldr: The estimated costs of the offering, other than underwriting discounts, have not yet been disclosed and will be filed by amendment.
children.summary: Anthropic will pay [[all offering expenses other than underwriting discounts and commissions|p2600]], including SEC, FINRA and exchange listing fees, printing, legal, accounting and transfer agent costs. Every amount in the table is [[to be filed by amendment|p2602]].

children.title: Indemnification of Directors and Officers. Item 14.
children.tldr: Anthropic will limit director and officer liability as far as Delaware law allows, indemnify them and advance their legal costs, and carry insurance, which may discourage stockholder suits.
children.summary: The new certificate of incorporation will [[limit director and officer liability for monetary damages|p2604]] to the fullest extent Delaware law allows, with exceptions such as breaches of the duty of loyalty and bad faith acts. The new bylaws will require the company to [[indemnify directors and officers and advance their expenses|p2611]], and the company has or will sign [[indemnification agreements|p2612]] that may go further than Delaware law. The filing warns these protections [[may discourage lawsuits against directors and officers|p2613]], and notes that failing to meet its public benefit corporation balancing duties will not by itself count as bad faith or disloyalty absent a conflict of interest. The company also holds [[directors and officers insurance|p2614]], and the [[underwriters will indemnify the company|p2616]] for certain Securities Act liabilities.

children.title: Recent Sales of Unregistered Securities. Item 15.
children.tldr: Since November 1, 2023, Anthropic issued large amounts of unregistered stock, notes and equity awards, including preferred stock rounds, $10.2 billion of convertible notes, and acquisition shares.
children.summary: This section lists securities Anthropic issued without registration [[from November 1, 2023 through the filing date|p2617]]. They include [[preferred stock sold in funding rounds|s655]] from Series D through Series H, [[$10.2 billion of convertible promissory notes|s656]], [[options, RSUs and RSAs|s657]] granted to employees and other service providers, and [[shares and options issued in acquisitions|s658]].

children.title: Preferred Stock Issuances
children.tldr: Anthropic raised money through preferred stock rounds rising from $30.0045 per share in early 2024 to $589.0095 in mid 2026, including about $65.2 billion in Series H.
children.summary: From January to May 2024, Anthropic sold Series D shares for about [[$1.2 billion at $30.0045 per share|p2618]]. In early 2025 it sold Series E-1 shares for about [[$3.6 billion at $56.0865 per share|p2619]] and issued Series E-2 through E-5 shares on conversion of notes. In August and September 2025 it sold Series F-1 shares to 202 investors for about [[$13.0 billion at $140.9676 per share|p2620]]. In October 2025 it bought back [[4,453,900 Series B shares from the U.S. government|p2621]] and resold them for about $627 million, keeping no net proceeds. In 2026 it sold Series G-1 and G-2 shares for about [[$23.5 billion and $21.7 billion at $259.1364 per share|p2622]]. From May to June 2026 it sold Series H-1 shares to 305 investors for about [[$45.7 billion and Series H-2 shares for about $19.5 billion|p2623]], both at $589.0095 per share.

children.title: Convertible Note Issuances
children.tldr: Since November 2023, Anthropic issued $10.2 billion of convertible promissory notes to two accredited investors.
children.summary: From November 2023 through the filing date, Anthropic issued convertible promissory notes with an [[aggregate principal amount of $10.2 billion to two accredited investors|p2624]].

children.title: Option, RSU, and RSA Issuances
children.tldr: Since November 2023, Anthropic granted options on about 2.07 billion Class A shares and about 1.17 billion RSUs to employees and other service providers.
children.summary: From November 2023 through the filing date, Anthropic granted [[options on 2,066,876,470 Class A shares|p2625]] at exercise prices from about $0.6420 to $57.5360 per share. It issued [[409,116,603 Class A shares on option exercises|p2626]] at a weighted average exercise price of $1.2043. It also granted [[1,171,364,280 RSUs|p2627]] and [[RSAs covering 214,960 Class A shares|p2628]].

children.title: Securities Issued in Connection with Acquisitions
children.tldr: Anthropic issued 37,215,830 Class A shares, 848,882 Class N shares, and options on 376,320 shares in acquisitions, all claimed exempt from registration as private or compensatory issuances.
children.summary: Since November 2023, Anthropic issued [[37,215,830 Class A shares, 848,882 Class N shares and options on 376,320 Class A shares|p2629]] in connection with acquisitions of companies or their assets. None of the unregistered issuances in this item involved underwriters or a public offering, and the company relies on [[Section 4(a)(2) and Rule 701 exemptions|p2630]] from registration.

children.summary: Financial statement schedules are [[omitted|p2632]] because the information is not required or is shown in the consolidated financial statements or their notes.

children.title: Undertakings. Item 17.
children.tldr: Anthropic acknowledges the SEC views indemnification for Securities Act liabilities as unenforceable and makes standard undertakings about prospectus information and post-effective amendments.
children.summary: The company notes the SEC considers [[indemnification for Securities Act liabilities against public policy|p2633]], and agrees to let a court decide any such claim unless settled precedent applies. p14: This is an initial public offering of shares of Class A common stock of Anthropic, PBC. We are selling shares of Class A common stock and the selling stockholders identified in this prospectus are selling an additional shares of Class A common stock. We will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares of our Class A common stock by any of the selling stockholders. Prior to this offering, there has been no public market for our Class A common stock. It is currently estimated that the initial public offering price per share will be between $ and $ . We have applied to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure. We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation under Delaware law, a structure consistent with our commitment to artificial intelligence (“AI”) safety and responsibility. As a public benefit corporation, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that Anthropic, PBC is managed in a manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company organized by our co-founders (the “Founder LLC”). Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of our board of directors, together with our five other co-founders, will initially be the sole members of the Founder LLC. Our Class F common stock, which will be held by the Founder LLC, will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. Upon the completion of this offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. In addition, we have authorized Class A common stock and Class N common stock. The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock are identical, except with respect to voting and conversion. Each share of Class A common stock is entitled to one vote per share and shares of Class N common stock have no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law. The holders of our Class N common stock are primarily strategic business partners, and shares of Class N common stock will generally convert to Class A common stock upon a sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party. Our Class A common stock is not convertible. See the sections titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure,” “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for more information. We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. See the sections titled “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for additional information. See the section titled “Risk Factors” beginning on page 26 to read about factors you should consider before buying shares of our Class A common stock.

p20: The following are abbreviations, acronyms, and definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus:
p21: “agent loop” refers to the iterative cycle in which an AI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic AI behavior.
p22: “agentic AI” refers to AI systems that, with varying degrees of autonomy, can plan, determine, and sequence actions and execute them to accomplish defined objectives, including through interaction with external tools, services, datasets, and environments on behalf of a user.
p23: “AI” refers to artificial intelligence, a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments.
p24: “AI accelerators” refer to processors purpose-built or adapted for the large-scale computations required to pre-train, post-train, refine, and run AI models. These processors are significantly more efficient and faster than general-purpose processors for AI workloads.
p25: “API” refers to application programming interface, a standardized interface that allows external software to access a system’s capabilities programmatically. AI model providers may offer APIs that allow software developers to send inputs to an AI model and receive outputs, enabling integration into the software developers’ products and workflows.
p26: “Applied AI” refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding AI capabilities directly into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to a customer’s own systems and processes.
p27: “closing the loop” refers to a development cycle in which successive versions of an AI model assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time.
p28: “compute” refers to the computational processing resources used to train and run AI models, including, without limitation, specialized AI accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments.
p29: “compute multipliers” refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that increase the effective output of a given amount of compute.
p30: “computer use” refers to an AI capability that allows a model to observe and interact with a graphical user interface, such as clicking, typing, and navigating applications, similar to how a human operator would.
p31: “Constitutional AI” refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we refer to as Claude’s constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique, and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers.
p32: “context window” refers to the maximum amount of text, code, or other content, measured in tokens, that an AI model can process in a given request, encompassing instructions, prior conversation history, user input, and the model’s output.
p33: “CSP” refers to a cloud services provider, a technology company that owns and operates large-scale cloud computing infrastructure and provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking. CSPs may also serve as distribution channels through which AI products and services are made available to customers. The largest CSPs, sometimes referred to as hyperscalers, operate at global scale with significant infrastructure and market concentration.
p34: “customer” refers to a prosumer or an organization that uses our models, platform, or applications.
p35: “customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” “customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” and “customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis” each refer to customers contributing revenue equal to or greater than the applicable dollar amount during the trailing twelve-month (“TTM”) period ending on the measurement date. For purposes of this metric, we define a customer as a distinct organization, identified by aggregating the accounts that we determine belong to the same organization based on internal records and available data. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.”
p36: “frontier AI” refers to AI systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks.
p37: “hallucinations” refer to outputs in which an AI model generates factually incorrect or fabricated information with apparent confidence.
p38: “inference” refers to the process by which a trained AI model processes an input and generates an output. Inference occurs each time a user or agent interacts with an AI system.
p39: “interleaved thinking” refers to a capability whereby an AI model interposes discrete reasoning steps between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning phase at the outset.
p40: “interpretability” refers to research into how and why AI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications.
p41: “knowledge work” refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining, producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses, synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows.
p42: “LLMs” refer to large language models, or AI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code.
p43: “mechanistic interpretability” refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverseengineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing.
p44: “model weights” refer to the numerical parameters encoding a trained AI model’s behavior, which are the primary intellectual asset of a frontier AI developer, representing the accumulated investment in compute, data, and research.
p45: “multi-agent orchestration” refers to an architecture in which multiple AI agents collaborate on a shared task, with one coordinating while others execute subtasks in parallel, enabling more complex, long-horizon work than a single agent can complete alone.
p46: “Net Revenue Retention” reflects customer expansion, contraction, and churn as of a measurement date. We calculate Net Revenue Retention by dividing the Qualified Customers’ Current Period revenue by their Base Period revenue. A Qualified Customer is a customer with at least $1 of revenue during the Base Period, excluding subscribers to our Claude Pro and Max plans, whose fixed-price subscriptions do not reflect the expansion and contraction behavior this metric is intended to capture. The Base Period is the three months ending a year prior to the measurement date. The Current Period is the three months ending as of the measurement date.
p47: “open-weight” refers to an AI model whose trained model weights, or the numerical parameters encoding the model’s learned behavior, are publicly released, allowing third parties to download, run, and modify the model, subject to the terms of the model’s license, without necessarily providing access to the underlying training data or code.
p48: “pay-for-intelligence” or “consumption” refers to our revenue model under which customers pay for their usage of our intelligence service, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected.
p49: “persistent,” in the context of AI applications, refers to denoting data, state, or context that is continuously retained beyond the boundary of a single operation, session, or interaction, remaining accessible for reuse across subsequent steps, sessions, or workflows without requiring reinitialization.
p50: “post-training” refers to the collection of techniques applied to a pre-trained model to refine its behavior, including reinforcement learning, supervised refinement methods, and other alignment methods. Post-training is the stage in which much of the work to make a frontier model helpful, accurate, and safe is performed, including the application of safety and alignment techniques.
p51: “pre-training” refers to the initial stage of training an AI model, in which the model learns general patterns and representations from large-scale datasets of text, code, and other data, typically by predicting the next token in a sequence. The output of pre-training is a base model with broad capabilities that has not yet been adapted for any specific deployment context.
p52: “primitives” refer to the foundational, modular building blocks of a software system from which more complex applications and workflows are constructed.
p53: “prompt injection” refers to an adversarial technique in which malicious instructions are embedded in content an AI model is asked to process, such as websites, documents, or tool outputs, with the aim of overriding or manipulating the model’s intended behavior, typically without the user’s knowledge.
p54: “prosumers” refer to individual users who subscribe to AI tools to perform knowledge work.
p55: “reinforcement learning” refers to a machine learning approach in which a model learns to perform a task by taking actions, receiving feedback signals called rewards, and adjusting its behavior to maximize the rewards it accrues over time. In contemporary AI development, reinforcement learning is widely used to refine model behavior after pre-training, including to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines.
p56: “RLHF” refers to reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide training.
p57: “Run-Rate Revenue” is an operating metric that refers to the estimated annualized value of our revenuegenerating activity as of a measurement date, calculated as the sum of (i) our consumption-based fees during the trailing 28-day period ended on the measurement date, multiplied by 13, and (ii) our aggregate monthly subscription fees as of the measurement date, multiplied by 12. For purposes of calculating Run-Rate Revenue, consumption-based fees and subscription-based fees are derived from customer usage and active subscriptions.
p58: “SIs” refer to systems integrators, or third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build, and deploy integrated solutions for customers by combining products and services from multiple technology vendors into unified systems tailored to customer needs.
p59: “tokens” refer to numeric units into which an AI model converts the data it processes, including text, images, audio, and video, the number of which varies by the model and tokenizer applied. Tokens are the smallest individual units of a language model and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes. A tokenizer is the component of a model that converts customer inputs into the sequence of tokens the model processes and then converts the processed tokens into the outputs provided to customers.

This summary does not contain all of the information you should consider before investing in our Class A common stock. p61: For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. AI that truly delivers on its potential—with the risks well managed—could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.
p62: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $ for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research in frontier AI.
p63: Mission & Focus. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
p64: Talent & Culture. Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier AI capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
p65: Frontier & Safety Research. We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is required to build the most capable and safest AI systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that are more reliable, steerable, and well-suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity, and have consistently released better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.
p66: Our Approach to Compute. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance the frontier of AI capabilities through research and model development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude. We have achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of Claude, we continue to invest at scale. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of more than $ , substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $ expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $ of these commitments are due in the next 12 months. See the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” for more information.
p67: Enterprise Strategy. Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement loops from customer feedback are richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus and makes Claude more capable over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our AI reach people and organizations at scale.
p68: We believe that Powerful AI, a highly capable and impactful form of frontier AI characterized by the following key attributes, will become widely available within a few years:
p69: • cognitive capabilities matching or exceeding those of top human experts across most professional and scientific disciplines;
p70: • the ability to navigate all interfaces available to a human working virtually, including text, audio, video, and direct computer control;
p71: • the ability to reason through complex tasks autonomously over extended periods—lasting hours, days, or weeks—and seek clarification and feedback when needed;
p72: • the ability to coordinate across multiple instances and collaborate with both humans and other AI systems; and
p73: • the ability to interface with the physical world by digitally controlling laboratory equipment, robotic systems, and other machines through digital connections.
p74: If Powerful AI is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the potential is extraordinary. The possibilities include compressing decades of scientific progress into years; accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy; providing individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice; advancing power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability; and extending to the developing world capabilities that took wealthy nations generations to build.
p75: Frontier AI is transforming cognitive work—the application of knowledge, reasoning, and judgment to produce economic value. We believe it will make humans far more capable and expand the world’s overall capacity for that work, including accelerating scientific discovery and helping businesses grow. Knowledge workers are the leading edge of this opportunity. As frontier AI advances, more capable models can unlock entirely new use cases while also efficiently serving a wide range of cognitive work at scale across the capability-cost-speed curve. We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic 1 value globally in 2025, and with frontier AI’s potential to make them meaningfully more productive, our nearterm opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth. While it is still early to forecast frontier AI’s full impact across the economy, International Data Corporation (“IDC”) estimates that investment 2 in AI solutions and services will yield a cumulative global economic impact of $22.5 trillion by 2031. We believe the impact could be even greater.
p76: We believe frontier AI represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle, and Claude is already demonstrating this potential. Claude can now execute complex projects autonomously and turn open-ended tasks into finished, high-quality deliverables. These capabilities enable it to transform the largest sectors of the economy, driving meaningful gains in productivity and output. Frontier AI’s capabilities may extend beyond current markets to open entirely new ones, reaching domains such as robotics, advanced manufacturing, and logistics, and accelerating progress in scientific research, including drug discovery and materials science. For example, in the life sciences sector, where annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion 3 in 2026, Claude is used in drug discovery and development by our customers, our biotechnology partners, and our own researchers. We are also extending Claude into robotics, where our Model Hardware Standard enables AI agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes, liquid handlers, and off-the-shelf robotic arms. Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth. As frontier AI makes workers and organizations more productive, becomes embedded in the products and services they deliver, and unlocks new business models, it creates economic output that did not previously exist. We believe our opportunity is to capture a share not only of today’s economic activity but also of that newly created output as the global economy expands.
p77: While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decisionmaking or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators. We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner for mission-critical workloads.
p78: We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them, which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual

p80: Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending 4 them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028.
p81: Claude Code. The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. Claude Code shifted the market’s understanding of what an AI system could do in collaboration with software developers: the model suggests the next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that results in production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point for measuring the progress of frontier AI. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants. What makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.
p82: Software developers are powerful advocates for Claude—they understand how systems work, have credibility evaluating technical tools, and often serve as internal champions for adopting new technologies. Winning their trust creates a foundation for broader diffusion of Virtual Collaborators across enterprise workforces. We are already seeing this pattern play out with non-technical teams increasingly adopting Claude Code and Claude Cowork to manage their own workflows.
p83: Claude Cowork. All digital work is ultimately an expression of code, and Claude’s mastery of it powers Virtual Collaborators capable of handling complex work far beyond software development. Claude Cowork extends the same agentic architecture of Claude Code to knowledge workers broadly by translating a user’s intent into completed work, autonomously reading files, navigating applications, and executing multi-step workflows on a user’s desktop while the underlying code is abstracted away. By extending beyond Claude Code with applications purpose-built for specific professions and industry verticals, we accelerate Claude’s diffusion into new categories of knowledge work and deepen our presence across the enterprise. As of September 30, 2026, adoption of Claude Cowork, which we made available as a research preview in January 2026, outpaced the adoption Claude Code achieved at the equivalent point following its research preview release in February 2025. In September 2026, we began merging Claude Cowork and Claude.ai, bringing agentic and conversational work into a unified application. Users can now move from a simple question to complex, multi-step tasks in the same conversation.
p84: Extending Virtual Collaborators. We believe the trajectory for Virtual Collaborators is clear and accelerating. Each generation of Claude models has expanded along multiple dimensions: the depth and rigor of their reasoning, the duration and autonomy of the work they can sustain, the complexity of tasks they can complete, and the volume of useful output they can produce. Capability evaluations and benchmarking have shown substantial improvements across Claude model versions in the duration and complexity of tasks that can be completed reliably, with more recent model versions demonstrating particularly significant advances.
p85: We are building towards a world where Claude can be given open-ended tasks lasting hours, days, or weeks, and then execute them autonomously with the judgment and initiative of a brilliant colleague. Ultimately, millions of Virtual Collaborators can run in parallel, each working independently on unrelated problems or collaborating seamlessly to achieve a shared objective. The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a data center, available to every organization and sector of the economy.
