If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our brand, reputation, and ability to compete could be adversely affected.
p336: Resource Allocation and Scaling. Safety-focused development is resource-intensive. We must allocate limited resources, capital, and talent between safety-focused workloads and other initiatives, often without clear returns on our safety-focused investments. For example, our investments in interpretability research and techniques designed to ensure our models’ behavior remains consistent with intended goals, values, and safety objectives may not yield actual or perceived commercial returns. Additionally, as we develop our models, platform, and applications, safety testing may become more expensive and resource intensive. Limited-access programs such as Project Glasswing may also require us to design, operate, and continually maintain bespoke vetting, contracting, monitoring, and offboarding processes that differ materially from our standard commercial release processes, including coordination among participating organizations, transition planning to successor models, and enhanced internal controls commensurate with the heightened sensitivity of the underlying capabilities. These activities impose ongoing operational, legal, and security costs that may recur as future frontier models with similar capability profiles are released. If we fail to successfully manage resource allocation or develop more efficient methods with respect to our safety initiatives, our safety outcomes, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p337: As our product portfolio and employee and customer base expand globally, applying safety principles consistently across our rapidly expanding organization, models, platform, applications, use cases, and jurisdictions and regulatory regimes has become increasingly challenging. For more information, see the section titled “—To continue to grow our business, we will need to continue to expand internationally, and our non-U.S. operations and sales to customers outside of the United States expose us to risks inherent in international expansion, sales, and operations.”
p338: If we are unable to successfully manage the foregoing risks related to our focus and commitment to AI safety, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p339: We believe that maintaining and enhancing our brand identity and reputation is critical to our relationships with, and to our ability to attract and retain, customers, partners, and employees. Our brand and reputation are influenced not only by our actions, but also by the actions of our partners, our customers, and other third parties with whom we do business, and by broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct. The successful promotion of our brand depends on a number of factors, including our ability to continue to develop and deliver reliable, high-quality, and responsible models, platforms, and applications that meet the needs of our customers; our sales and marketing efforts, including our effectiveness at developing a strong brand name and positive presence within the AI industry through participation in industry events and key media coverage; the perceptions and experiences of both our enterprise and individual customers, including through testimonials, use cases, and word-of-mouth; our ability to maintain security and reliability of our models, platform, and applications; the actions of our management; and our ability to differentiate our models, platform, and applications from those of our competitors, including through product design choices, safeguards, business models, and policies, including our approach to monetization strategies that differ from those of certain competitors. In addition, our brand is subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts of AI technologies, and a single perceived failure could result in outsized reputational harm. For example, as AI systems become more capable or prevalent, public perception that our models, platform, and applications contribute to job displacement or economic disruption could generate significant negative media coverage, customer or employee backlash, or organized opposition, regardless of the actual impact of our models, platform, and applications on employment. Our ability to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation also depends on the effectiveness and scalability of our internal communications and reputation-management capabilities, including our ability to support global operations, and limitations in these areas could adversely affect our brand as we grow. Our crisis response and reputation-management capabilities may be limited or underdeveloped, particularly as we scale, which could impair our ability to respond effectively to adverse events and mitigate reputational harm.
p340: The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive. We have in the past, and may in the future, face challenges in building broader brand awareness and may fall behind competitors with more established or widely recognized brands. Our brand promotion activities may not be successful or generate the awareness or increased revenue we expect, and even if they do, any increase in revenue may not offset the significant expenses we incur in the efforts to build our brand.
p341: If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers or fail to attract potential customers or we could fail to hire and retain employees, all of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p342: We currently derive substantially all of our revenue from a limited number of products and applications, primarily our Claude models and portfolio of applications that sit on top of the Claude Platform. This dependence on a narrower set of offerings subjects us to various risks that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p343: Our concentration in a limited number of products and applications, as well as our focused development strategy within specific areas of the broader AI landscape, reduces our ability to mitigate business risks through diversification. While this focused approach may enable us to allocate resources efficiently and compete effectively in our prioritized areas, it also creates the risk that significant market opportunities or the largest addressable markets may emerge in areas outside our current strategic focus. Many of our competitors offer diverse product portfolios across multiple business lines or pursue broader development across AI modalities, enabling them to offset weaknesses in a particular area. In contrast, any decline in demand for our core offerings, whether due to competition, technological changes, pricing pressure, changes in customer demand, or other factors, would have a direct and disproportionate impact on our revenue and ability to achieve and sustain profitability. Our concentration also reflects a strategy that prioritizes model capability as a principal source of differentiation and relies substantially on organic adoption rather than a large direct sales organization. The risks of that strategy, including the risks that differentiation among advanced models narrows, that customers select providers based on factors other than capability, or that competitors capture the individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, are described in the sections titled “—We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected” and “—We have a limited history under our current go-tomarket strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful.”
p344: The AI industry is rapidly evolving, and it is difficult to predict which modalities or applications will capture the most durable commercial value or how the competitive landscape will shift. If the market for AI models, platforms, and applications develops in ways that do not align with our chosen areas of focus, or if competitors are better positioned to address the areas where the market opportunity ultimately proves largest, our ability to sustain revenue growth and compete effectively could be adversely affected. If we experience a decline in demand for our core offerings, we may not be able to successfully expand our product and application portfolio, and even if we do, our new products and applications may not achieve market acceptance or generate sufficient revenue to offset any decline in our existing business. Further, technical issues, security incidents, regulatory restrictions, or reputational harm affecting our models, platform, and applications could have an immediate and disproportionate impact on our business due to our product concentration where alternative revenue streams may not be available to offset such impact.
p345: The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is evolving quickly, and customer requirements and expectations are changing rapidly. Customers may increasingly demand specialized solutions or specialized integration and tooling that we do not currently offer and may not plan to offer, or may seek AI solutions embedded more deeply into enterprise workflows. Enterprises may prefer to develop their own AI capabilities internally or choose competitors that offer more comprehensive product suites. Moreover, because substantially all of our models and applications are built on top of our frontier models, any defect, vulnerability, safety issue, or performance degradation in an underlying frontier model could simultaneously affect multiple products and applications and customer deployments, amplifying the impact of any such issue across our business. If we fail to anticipate or respond effectively to these evolving customer needs, we may lose customers to competitors or fail to acquire new customers.
p346: In addition, we currently compete, and may increasingly compete, with some of our own customers. As we expand our product portfolio or introduce new capabilities, our offerings may overlap with or directly compete with the models, platforms, and applications that our customers provide. This risk is particularly acute with software-as-a-service and other software companies, whose offerings may incorporate AI functionality similar to, or dependent on, the capabilities we provide. These customers may view our product expansion as a competitive threat to their business models and may reduce their purchases from us, limit their adoption of new offerings, terminate their relationships with us, seek alternative providers, restrict our access to the compute we obtain from them, initiate intellectual property or other litigation against us, or accelerate efforts to develop competing solutions internally in order to avoid relying on a direct competitor. This dynamic could result in customer attrition, reduced expansion within our existing customer base, pricing pressure, or reputational challenges, any of which could adversely affect our revenue growth and business prospects.
p347: Expanding our product portfolio requires substantial time and investment. We must make significant investments in research and development, compute infrastructure, engineering talent, sales and marketing, and go-to-market capabilities to develop new models, platforms, and applications and enable continued adoption. We may seek to expand into new products and markets, including areas outside of our current core competencies or where we have limited experience, and we may not successfully develop, commercialize, or support such offerings. Development timelines for AI models, platforms, and applications are uncertain, and new capabilities, even when continuously improved and released into our models, platform, and applications, may take significant time to achieve commercial scale. We may invest significant resources in products or services that fail to gain market traction, experience technical difficulties, face unexpected competition, lead to unexpected harm or societal impacts that do not align with our values, or generate insufficient returns to justify the investment. Additionally, we face other constraints on our ability to expand our offerings, including the ability to hire, retain, and motivate qualified AI researchers, engineers, and technical personnel; the capital intensity of developing and operating AI models, platforms, and applications which require substantial compute and infrastructure investment; and our limited portfolio may make it difficult to provide the comprehensive, integrated solutions that customers may expect.
p348: If we are unable to successfully expand our product and service portfolio, if we fail to compete effectively with our current offerings, or if customer preferences shift away from our models, platform, and applications, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p349: A substantial portion of our revenue is driven by a limited number of customers. While no single customer represented more than 10% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our top five customers represented approximately 25% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Many of our top customers are not subject to long-term contracts with us or have contracts with near-term expiration dates and are able to reduce or in some cases cease spending at any time and for any reason. Further, we have agreements with certain large customers which provide flexibility around financial commitments, termination rights, indemnification, and security obligations. Our top customers may vary spend levels period to period, and there can be no assurances that our large customers will continue to spend at levels similar to prior periods.
p350: We anticipate that we will continue to derive a significant portion of our revenue from a limited number of customers for the foreseeable future, and in some cases, the portion of our revenue attributable to certain customers may increase in the future. The composition of our customer base, including our top customers, may fluctuate from period to period given that our customer composition has evolved and is expected to continue to evolve significantly as our business continues to evolve and scale and as the use cases for AI continue to develop.
p351: In addition, a significant portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is associated with transactions conducted with a limited number of CSPs that act as distribution and billing channels for our models. During the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025 and the six months ended June 30, 2026, revenue generated from sales to customers through CSP marketplaces represented approximately 11%, 32%, 47%, and 48%, respectively, of total revenue. As of December 31, 2024 and 2025 and June 30, 2026, net accounts receivable from sales through CSP marketplaces to customers represented 42%, 60%, and 58%, respectively, of our net accounts receivable. These platforms bill end customers, collect payments on our behalf, and remit such amounts to us, net of applicable platform and other fees. Any change to, or termination of, one of our significant distribution relationships could adversely affect our business by disrupting customer access to our models, reducing usage, or increasing customer acquisition, onboarding, and migration costs. In these third-party arrangements, we generally maintain separate contractual arrangements with end customers governing access to, and pricing for, our models, independent of the applicable platform, and changes in, or termination of, a particular distribution relationship would not independently eliminate those contractual relationships. However, customers may be unwilling or unable to transition to alternative access points on commercially acceptable terms or timelines, or at all, following a disruption, which could result in revenue loss, increased costs, or adverse impacts to our growth, margins, and results of operations. In addition, any delay, dispute, or operational issue affecting a platform’s collection or remittance of customer payments could adversely affect our cash flows and working capital.

p360: In order to operate and grow our business, including to fund our substantial compute commitments, we have incurred a substantial amount of debt, which requires significant interest and principal payments. As of June 30, 2026, our total indebtedness was $6.2 billion, reflecting the aggregate principal amount outstanding under the convertible promissory notes issued to Amazon (through Amazon Web Services, Inc.) pursuant to the Convertible Note Purchase Agreement, dated as of September 19, 2023, by and between us and Amazon (the “Amazon 2023 NPA”) and the New Convertible Note Purchase Agreement, dated as of November 22, 2024, by and between us and Amazon (the “Amazon 2024 NPA”) (all such notes issued thereunder, collectively, the “Amazon Notes”). We may also incur additional indebtedness to meet our future financing needs. We have guaranteed the obligations of certain of our subsidiaries that are party to AI infrastructure arrangements, as well as pursuant to agreements we entered into in connection with an equipment lease with a third-party partner, Broadcom Inc. (“Broadcom”) in March 2026 to procure specialized AI accelerators and associated components (under which Broadcom intends to assign to a designated financial partner) (the “2026 Lease Arrangement”). In addition, we have the ability to issue, if needed, up to $42.0 billion in aggregate principal amount of convertible promissory notes to Broadcom or, subject to our consent (not to be unreasonably withheld), a designated financial partner pursuant to a note purchase agreement that we entered into with Broadcom in March 2026 (the “Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA”) to finance obligations under the 2026 Lease Arrangement. We may be required to use a substantial portion of our cash flows from operations to pay interest, principal, or other required payments on our indebtedness.

p362: Our ability to make scheduled payments in respect of, to pay interest on, or to refinance our indebtedness, including the A&R Credit Agreement and our outstanding convertible promissory notes, depends on our future performance, which is subject to economic, financial, competitive, and other factors beyond our control. Such payments will reduce the funds available to us for working capital, capital expenditures, and other corporate purposes and may limit our ability to obtain additional financing for working capital, capital expenditures, expansion plans, and other investments. Our business may not be able to generate cash flows from operations in the future that are sufficient to service our debt and make necessary capital expenditures. If we are unable to generate such cash flows, we may be required to adopt one or more alternatives, such as selling assets or obtaining additional debt financing or equity capital on terms that may be onerous or highly dilutive. Our ability to refinance our indebtedness will depend on the capital markets and our financial condition at such time. We may not be able to engage in any of these activities or engage in these activities on desirable terms, which could result in a default on our debt obligations and adversely affect our financial condition. p363: We are also subject to variable interest rate risk because the interest rate under the A&R Credit Agreement varies based on a margin over an indexed rate or an adjusted base rate. If interest rates associated with our floating rate debt increase, our debt service obligations in connection with the A&R Credit Agreement would increase even though the amount borrowed remained the same, and our available cash would correspondingly decrease. Our substantial amount of debt, combined with variable interest rates, could limit our flexibility in planning for, or reacting to, changes in our business and the markets in which we operate, including limiting our future investments or our ability to enter into acquisitions and strategic partnerships, and obtain financing for such transactions.

p371: A failure by us to comply with the covenants, including those tied, in part, to operational and performancebased metrics, or payment obligations under the A&R Credit Agreement or our outstanding convertible promissory notes, as applicable, whether as a result of financial constraints, operational challenges, inexperience managing complex infrastructure and large-scale capital commitments, or otherwise, could result in an event of default under these instruments. p374: We have in the past changed, and we expect that in the future we may change, our pricing models, including as a result of competition, macroeconomic conditions, compliance with increased regulatory hurdles, the maturation of the market for AI models, platforms, and applications, or changes in how our models, platform, and applications are broadly consumed. As a result, we may be required to reduce our prices, offer shorter contract durations or offer alternative pricing models, such as outcome or task-based pricing, any of which could adversely affect our business. In addition, our agentic offerings are structurally more compute-intensive than our non-agentic offerings. If we are unable to implement pricing models that adequately reflect the higher compute intensity of these agentic workloads, or if competitive dynamics constrain our ability to price these products at levels sufficient to cover their costs, our compute efficiency could deteriorate as agentic usage grows, which could adversely affect our ability to achieve or sustain profitability.
p375: Additionally, as we continue to target selling our models, platform, and applications to our enterprise customers, these customers may demand different pricing structures, price concessions, or additional functionality at the same price levels. If we are unable to modify or develop effective pricing models and strategies that are attractive to existing and prospective customers, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.
p376: Our performance and ability to grow our business depend on the talents and efforts of highly skilled individuals, and our future success depends on our continuing ability to identify, hire, develop, motivate, and retain highly skilled personnel for all areas of our organization. Our business is particularly dependent on a limited pool of researchers, engineers, and technical personnel with specialized experience in designing, training, deploying, and operating frontier models and the underlying infrastructure that supports them. We have from time to time experienced, and we expect to continue to experience, difficulty in hiring and retaining highly skilled employees with appropriate qualifications at the pace that our operations require. Competition in our industry relating to hiring and retaining employees with appropriate qualifications and on competitive economic terms is exceptionally intense and has escalated significantly in recent periods, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, where our headquarters is located and where we have a substantial presence and need for highly skilled personnel. A small number of well-capitalized AI labs, large technology companies, and new market entrants compete aggressively for a relatively fixed supply of individuals with the requisite expertise. Certain of our competitors have directly solicited, and continue to directly solicit, our employees. Our former employees are also generally able to join or found competing companies immediately following their departure, and, subject to their confidentiality and other legal obligations, use the general skills, know-how, and experience they developed while employed by us. In addition, we have in the past, and may in the future, be subject to claims or disputes relating to the solicitation or hiring of employees, including allegations that such hires violated non-compete, non-solicitation, intellectual property, confidentiality, or other employmentrelated obligations.
p377: As our company continues to grow and our industry evolves, the incentives to attract, retain, and motivate employees provided by our cash and equity awards or by future arrangements may not be as effective as in the past. Many of the companies with which we compete for highly qualified personnel have greater resources than we have and may be willing to offer more attractive compensation packages. We may need to invest significant amounts of cash and equity to attract and retain employees, resulting in substantial additional share-based compensation expense and dilution to the ownership of our existing stockholders, and we may never realize returns on these investments that are commensurate with the level of our expenditures. If the perceived value of our compensatory package declines or is subject to significant value fluctuations, it may adversely affect our ability to attract and retain highly skilled employees. In addition, we have a number of current employees, including our co-founders, who hold equity in our company or whose equity awards are or will become substantially vested upon the completion of this offering. This may be particularly true for certain of our longertenured and early employees, whose equity holdings may represent a significant portion of their personal wealth. As a result, it may be difficult for us to continue to retain and motivate these employees, and the value of their holdings could affect their decisions about whether or not they continue to work for us.
p378: Historically, our ability to successfully attract, retain, and motivate our personnel has in large part been due to our company culture and commitment to safety and responsible scaling and development. If we are unable to maintain our culture, if we make decisions as a company that our employees do not believe align with our values, or if events take place, regardless of fault, that call into question whether we have operated in accordance with our values, our ability to attract, retain, and motivate our personnel may be adversely affected. Rapid growth has also created workforce-planning and execution challenges, including limitations in our ability to accurately forecast headcount needs, periods of accelerated hiring followed by corrective actions that may disrupt operations or reduce morale, and increased reliance on managers operating at greater scale than in their prior experience, which introduces additional operational, legal, reputational, and execution risk as the organization continues to expand. If we move into new geographies, we will need to attract and recruit skilled personnel in those geographic areas, but it may be challenging for us to compete with traditional local employers in these regions for talent. If we fail to attract new personnel or fail to retain and motivate our current personnel who are capable of meeting our growing technical, operational, and managerial requirements, our business may be adversely affected.
p379: In addition, heightened public attention on AI has increased physical and informational security risks, and we have experienced threats to employee safety and attempts to obtain confidential information through physical or digital means, which, despite the security measures we have implemented at certain facilities, may be exacerbated by our global and flexible working arrangements and could adversely affect employee morale, productivity, and our ability to attract, retain, and motivate highly skilled personnel. Addressing these risks also requires us to attract and retain additional specialized security personnel, and difficulties in recruiting qualified security engineers could further exacerbate these challenges.
p380: Further, changes to immigration policies that restrain the flow of professional and technical talent, including but not limited to U.S. immigration policies, may inhibit our ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p381: We were founded in 2021 and launched our first commercial product, Claude, publicly in the first quarter of 2023. During this time, our business has grown rapidly. Our limited operating history and our evolving and nascent business and industry make it difficult to evaluate our future prospects and the risks and challenges we may encounter. p396: We have grown rapidly over the last several years, and therefore our recent revenue growth and financial performance should not be considered indicative of our future performance. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, our revenue was $41 million, $386 million, and $4.6 billion, respectively, representing year-over-year growth rates of 841% and 1,088%, respectively. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, our revenue was $16.3 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,300%. We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all. Our recent growth may reflect early-stage adoption dynamics, the nascency of the AI market, and rapid initial customer expansion that may not be sustainable over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of the other factors described below. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time. In addition, because the AI industry is very nascent, we have struggled to accurately forecast our revenue in the past and may struggle to do so in the future.
p397: We may experience declines in our revenue growth rate as a result of a number of factors, including:
p398: • the slowing or shifting demand for our models, platform, and applications or the market as a whole;
p399: • our inability to secure sufficient compute and direct it efficiently across our organization;
p400: • insufficient growth in the number of users and paying customers of our models, platform, and applications or the failure to increase sales of our models, platform, and applications to existing customers;
p401: • failures, errors, or performance limitations in our models, including unexpected behavior, degraded outputs, outages, or inability to meet customer expectations or use-case requirements;
p402: • increasing competition among existing competitors and new market entrants;
p403: • the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models, including any resulting delays in model development or release, or the adoption of laws, regulations, or standards that affect how and when frontier AI models may be developed or released;
p404: • our failure to continue to capitalize on growth opportunities;
p405: • our ability to collect amounts owed to us from customers, including as a result of customer credit risk, billing disputes, or delays in payment;

p410: Since 2021, we have experienced rapid growth in our employee headcount, number of customers, geographic reach, and our operations, and we expect this growth to continue. p411: Our ability to successfully manage this growth depends on our ability to scale and integrate our operations, workforce, technologies, models, platform, and applications, and any future acquisitions while preserving the beneficial aspects of our company culture. Continued growth may strain our ability to develop and enhance our operational, compliance, technical, financial, and management controls, improve our reporting systems and procedures, recruit, train, and retain highly skilled personnel, and maintain customer satisfaction. p412: As we expand, we must also manage an increasing number of relationships with strategic partners, customers, vendors, and other third parties that are critical to our business, including those that provide compute, data center infrastructure, networking, software tools, and other services necessary to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. In addition, our ability to manage our growth depends in part on our ability to accurately plan for and efficiently manage the compute required to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. Any material underinvestment or overinvestment in such resources could result in service limitations, increased costs, operational inefficiencies, or delays in model development, any of which could adversely affect our business.
p413: If we fail to effectively manage the growth of our business and operations, we may be unable to maintain effective internal controls, reporting systems, and compliance processes, may face increased regulatory scrutiny, and may suffer harm to our brand and our ability to attract and retain customers. p429: Our results of operations have historically varied from period to period, and we expect that our results of operations will continue to vary significantly from quarter to quarter and from year to year in the future, such that the results of any one period should not be relied upon as an indication of future performance. In particular, our financial performance may be significantly influenced by strategic decisions we make regarding the allocation of resources and the amount and timing of operating expenses and capital expenditures that we may incur to maintain and expand our business and operations and to remain competitive. We may make significant and, at times, discrete investments in areas such as research and development, compute and related infrastructure, product development, safety and security initiatives, and go-to-market expansion, which may be uneven in size and timing. These investments may materially increase our expenses in a given period and cause our results of operations to fluctuate significantly or vary meaningfully from period to period, and may result in periods of reduced margins or increased losses even if our underlying business trends remain unchanged or continue to improve. As a result, our financial performance may not follow any consistent pattern, and prior or interim periods of improved results of operations should not be viewed as indicative of our future performance.
p430: Our revenue in any period has also included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, and we cannot assure you that we will identify such usage, or restrict or terminate a customer’s access, on a timely basis or at all. Customers may evade our controls, and customers whose access is restricted or terminated may re-register under new accounts. As a result, revenue from such customers may continue or recur notwithstanding our enforcement efforts. Our continued detection and enforcement efforts, and in particular, the enhancement of such efforts in August and September 2026, and the timing of any resulting restrictions or terminations, are expected to reduce the percentage of revenue from customers using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and may reduce our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods and contribute to variability in our results from period to period.
p431: Our results of operations are also affected by seasonal variations in the usage of our models, platform, and applications. Because our revenue is primarily consumption-based, we have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, lower usage around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when certain customer workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. Our results of operations may also vary with the timing and cadence of our model and product releases, which are uneven from period to period and may cause usage, and therefore revenue, to increase or decline between periods. Our historical growth rates may have masked the impact of seasonal trends on our results. As our growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-toperiod results. In addition, other seasonal trends may develop, and the seasonal trends that we currently experience may become more pronounced, as we continue to scale.
p432: Our results of operations may also fluctuate due to a variety of additional factors, many of which are outside of our control and difficult to predict, including, but not limited to:

p434: • our ability to forecast required compute and to obtain additional compute as needed, and any increase in costs thereof;

p457: Any one or more of the factors above, or other factors in this “Risk Factors” section, may result in significant fluctuations in our results of operations or other key metrics, which may cause such results to fall below our financial guidance or other projections or the expectations of analysts or investors, and cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline.
p458: Certain of our operating metrics, such as Run-Rate Revenue, Net Revenue Retention, customer counts, and Claude’s success rate, are based on numerous assumptions and limitations, are calculated using data from internal systems and tools, have not been independently verified by third parties, are subject to inherent limitations in measurement, and may not accurately reflect actual results or provide an accurate indication of future or expected results.
p459: Run-Rate Revenue is not a substitute for revenue prepared in accordance with GAAP or a forecast of revenue. Because Run-Rate Revenue annualizes our consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and our subscription-based fees for a single month, it assumes that activity during those measurement periods has continued at the same rate for a full year. Because it annualizes a short measurement period, Run-Rate Revenue measured during a period of seasonally higher or lower usage, such as the reduced usage we have typically experienced around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, may differ significantly from RunRate Revenue measured at other times, and in each case may not correspond to the revenue we ultimately recognize over any quarter or fiscal year. Our actual historical revenue and future revenue may differ materially from this measure. Both our consumption-based and subscription-based revenue may fluctuate from period to period, and in particular, our consumption-based revenue may fluctuate significantly or decline if customers reduce, limit, or do not expand their usage or spend, or shift usage to lower-priced models, including in response to competitive offerings, pricing changes, changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities regarding AI investment, seasonality, or general economic conditions. In addition, sustaining and growing this revenue depends on our ability to continue to offer models at the frontier of AI capability, which we may not be able to do. Our ability or decision to remain at the frontier may also be affected by the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models. Our recent Run-Rate Revenue growth has also been driven in part by rapid initial customer adoption and expansion often characteristic of an early-adoption period and the nascency of the AI market that may not be sustainable, and we expect our Run-Rate Revenue growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of other factors. In addition, our Run-Rate Revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms. When we identify such usage, we seek to restrict or terminate the customer’s access; however, because our detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date includes amounts from customers that have not yet been restricted or terminated and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access. Our continued enforcement efforts may reduce our revenue, Run-Rate Revenue, and growth rates in future periods. See “—Our results of operations may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as a result of strategic investment decisions and substantial compute-related expenditures, which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline.” Accordingly, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date is not indicative of historical revenue and may not be indicative of our revenue for any future period.
p460: The determination of the number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis is based on our internal records and involves judgment, including in determining which accounts should be aggregated and treated as belonging to the same organization. We apply our most current customer records in calculating this metric, and our determination of which accounts belong to a single organization may change over time, including as a result of acquisitions and account consolidations. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.” As a result, this measure may not precisely correspond to the population of organizations that would otherwise be characterized as enterprises, and may over- or understate that population.
p461: Certain success rates and similar AI performance metrics with respect to Claude referenced in this prospectus are measured using internal benchmarks developed and maintained by us. These benchmarks reflect our proprietary testing methodology and are based on tasks, data sets, and evaluation criteria selected by us. Performance results derived from these internal benchmarks may not be replicable by customers, researchers, or other third parties who evaluate our models using different tasks, data sets, evaluation criteria, or computing environments. Accordingly, such metrics may differ materially from performance outcomes experienced by any particular customer or user in their specific deployment environment or use case, and should not be relied upon as indicative of the results any customer or user will achieve. Because AI performance benchmarking methodologies vary significantly across developers, such performance metrics as we measure them may also not be comparable to similarly titled or analogous metrics reported by other AI developers, and direct comparison of such metrics across companies may be misleading.
p462: Investors should consider these metrics in light of the assumptions and processes used in calculating such metrics and the limitations as a result thereof. In addition, our internal systems and tools have a number of limitations, which could result in unexpected changes to our metrics, including the metrics we publicly disclose. Further, certain of our operating metrics are based in part on data reported to us by our third-party partners. If the internal systems and tools we use to track these metrics or if the data reported to us by our third-party partners undercount or overcount performance, or contain algorithmic or other technical errors, the data we report may not be accurate. While our operating metrics are based on what we believe to be reasonable estimates for the applicable period of measurement, there are inherent challenges in these measurements. We may also refine or change our methodology for tracking certain operating metrics from time to time, to the extent practicable, including to improve overall accuracy and alignment with management’s view of business and operating performance and as a result of acquisitions. Any of these updates may result in changes in certain business and operating trends and may impact comparability of these metrics across periods. Investors should not place undue reliance on these metrics as an indicator of our future or expected results. Moreover, these metrics may differ from similarly titled metrics presented by other companies and may not be comparable to such other metrics. See the sections titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” and “Business” for more information regarding our operating metrics.
p463: The development, deployment, and use of AI technologies are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. Governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and in other countries in which we operate or distribute our models, platform, and applications have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage and privacy, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, the EU AI Regulation 2024/1689 (“EU AI Act”), which came into force in August 2024 and will become fully applicable following a transitional period, imposes a range of obligations on AI systems and general-purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the EU, including transparency, risk management, and governance requirements, and provides for significant penalties for non-compliance. In the United States, the regulatory framework for AI remains fragmented and uncertain, with evolving federal policy initiatives, continued debate regarding the scope and durability of executive actions, and a growing number of state-level laws and proposals addressing the development and use of AI. For example, several U.S. states, including New York and California, have passed AI safety laws. More generally, proposed legislation in the United States contemplates more expansive governmental oversight of AI, including potential nationalization, mandatory shutdown or discontinuation requirements for frontier AI systems or other strategic measures to prevent or manage the development of artificial superintelligence. Further, in June 2026, the U.S. federal government issued an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for developers of frontier AI models to engage with the government prior to the deployment of such AI technologies, directing federal agencies to strengthen cyber defenses, and prioritizing enforcement against criminal misuse of AI; although that framework is voluntary and does not establish a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development or deployment of AI models, it reflects increasing federal attention to the national security implications of frontier AI and the order may be followed by further executive or legislative action. If executive or legislative action of this nature were enacted to regulate AI technologies, it could constrain how we operate our business.
p464: We have also advocated, and expect to continue to advocate, for regulation and oversight of frontier AI, including industry-wide standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them, and we have proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier AI developers to establish safety standards. Regulatory or other measures of the kind we advocate, if adopted, would apply to us and could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth. The effect that any such measures would have on the rate at which AI capabilities advance, and on our business, is uncertain and would depend on the specific requirements adopted and on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. There is no assurance that policymakers will adopt the approaches we support, and our advocacy has in the past drawn, and may continue to draw, criticism, heightened scrutiny, or other challenges.
p465: Regulatory approaches to AI also vary significantly by geography and may be influenced by local political, economic, social, or environmental considerations. In some jurisdictions, public concern regarding the potential displacement of labor by AI systems, the perceived societal impacts of automation, or the environmental footprint associated with AI development and deployment, has led, or could lead, to restrictive legislation or other governmental actions. In particular, to the extent the rate of job displacement rapidly increases due to the adoption of AI or for related reasons, whether actual or perceived, governments or other regulatory authorities may intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems. Even in the absence of any legal or regulatory requirements, we may from time to time voluntarily elect to take actions intended to ameliorate the impact of such displacement. Any such actions would represent additional costs and expenditures for which we may not receive a corresponding commercial benefit, and there can be no assurance that any such actions would be effective in reducing displacement-related harms or in mitigating the associated reputational, regulatory, or political risks.
p466: Increasingly restrictive AI regulation in the United States and other western jurisdictions could enable competitors operating in less regulated environments to innovate, scale, and deploy AI technologies more rapidly, potentially allowing such competitors to become more advanced and pose greater competitive or strategic threats over time. In particular, increasing strategic competition between the United States and China in AI development may lead to divergent regulatory approaches, with the potential for the United States to impose restrictions on AI companies’ interactions with Chinese entities or markets, and for China to impose reciprocal measures that limit access to or demand for U.S.-origin AI models, platforms, and applications.
p467: As a result of these and other regulatory developments, our business could be subject to a wide range of regulatory limitations, obligations, or restrictions, including, among other things:
p468: • limitations, conditions, or prohibitions on certain AI use cases, applications, or deployment contexts;
p469: • requirements to modify, restrict, delay, or withdraw specific models, features, or functionalities in particular markets or for specific customers; for example, in early 2026, the U.S. Department of War suggested it could invoke the Defense Production Act to compel us to remove the limitations we have placed on the use of our models for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance;
p470: • heightened transparency, documentation, auditing, governance, or human-oversight obligations;
p471: • restrictions on the collection, use, transfer, localization, or retention of data used to train or operate AI systems, based on intellectual property, privacy, or other frameworks;
p472: • mandated safety, risk-management, or evaluation frameworks, certifications, or approvals, including requirements for independent, third-party review or approval prior to model development, training, or release; for example, in September 2026, a state attorney general asked a court, in pending litigation alleging harm to minors, to enjoin an AI company from developing new AI models without independent, third-party guardrails and approval;
p473: • restrictions on data center development or expansion, including permitting, zoning, or limits on energy or water usage;
p474: • heightened energy efficiency, sustainability, or environmental compliance requirements;
p475: • limitations on cross-border deployment, access, or commercialization of AI models, including through export controls, national security determinations, or other governmental measures that could restrict our ability to sell our models, platform, and applications in certain markets or to certain customers; for example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which were subsequently lifted after we updated our safeguards, and other models may be subject to these or similar export restrictions in the future; for more information, see the section titled “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets.”;
p476: • AI-specific taxes, fees, reporting obligations, or other financial burdens; or
p477: • outright bans or moratoria on activities material to our business or the businesses of our customers and partners.
p478: Because AI regulation is developing rapidly and in a fragmented manner, including as a result of political considerations, public sentiment, and geopolitical dynamics, we will not be able to fully anticipate how existing laws will be interpreted or enforced, how new legal frameworks will evolve, or whether regulatory regimes across jurisdictions will converge or diverge over time. Compliance with new or changing requirements may require substantial investment in research and development, compliance systems, operational processes, or localized offerings, and we may need to adjust or limit our activities in certain jurisdictions to address conflicting or inconsistent legal obligations. In addition, regulatory actions affecting our customers or partners, including restrictions on their ability to develop, deploy, or commercialize AI-enabled models, platforms, or applications, could indirectly reduce demand for our models, platform, and applications. Any failure, or perceived failure, to comply with applicable laws and regulations, or any significant increase in the cost or complexity of compliance, could result in litigation, enforcement actions, penalties, reputational harm, delayed or reduced adoption of our offerings, or other adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p479: Additionally, as AI systems become more sophisticated, emerging debates regarding whether AI systems possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status may lead to regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts that could constrain how we develop, train, deploy, or modify our models, increase our costs, or affect our reputation, regardless of the ultimate resolution of these philosophical and scientific questions. In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

p495: Any such event or activity, among others, could cause governments and government agencies to delay, pause, or cancel contracts or seek to modify their contracts, or refrain from entering into contracts with us or purchasing our models, platform, and applications in the future, undermine our ability to pursue future contracts, damage our relationships with partners and customers who also sell models, platforms, or applications to governments, or reduce the size or timing of payment with respect to our services to or purchases from existing or new government customers. p496: For example, in February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the Secretary of War directed the Department of War to designate us as a “supply-chain risk to national security” and stated that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent us two letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (“FASCSA”)—asserting that our models, platform, and applications present a supply-chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged these Challenged Actions in Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (N.D. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied our petition for review, ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain risk designation was proper, and that our rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a petition for rehearing en banc asking the full D.C. Circuit to review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the ultimate outcome of these lawsuits. While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p497: Further, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which we disabled for all customers until those restrictions were lifted, as described in the section titled “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets.” Similar restrictions could be imposed again in the future.
p498: Each of the foregoing may result in significant reputational harm, including adverse media coverage, public scrutiny, and negative perceptions among existing and prospective customers, partners, employees, and investors, regardless of the ultimate outcome of the litigation.
