Further, these developments may create uncertainty in the broader market regarding our long-term ability to operate in certain sectors, which could result in increased volatility in demand for our models, platform, and applications, reduced willingness of counterparties to enter into longterm or strategic arrangements with us, and fluctuations in investor sentiment, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p499: The bidding process for government contracts can be highly competitive, expensive, and time-consuming, often requiring significant upfront time and expense without any assurance that these efforts will generate revenue. Government agencies often undertake a significant evaluation process that results in a lengthy sales cycle. Some contracts with government agencies are structured in phases or include options, where each phase is subject to satisfaction of certain conditions and where the exercise of options is discretionary. As a result, the actual scope of work performed pursuant to any such contracts, in addition to related contract revenue, could be less than total contract value. In addition, product purchases by such organizations are frequently subject to budget constraints, multiple approvals, and unanticipated administrative, processing, and other delays. All of these factors can add further risk to business conducted with these customers and could lead to lower revenue results than originally anticipated.
p500: We also must comply with both local and international laws and regulations relating to the formation, administration, and performance of contracts. Contracts with government agencies are subject to extensive, evolving, and sometimes complex regulations which provide public sector customers rights, many of which are not typically found in commercial contracts. For example, government contracts generally include the ability of government agencies to terminate for convenience, which if exercised, would result in a lower contract value and lower than anticipated revenue generated by such arrangement. Any changes to the government regulations applicable to government contracts could affect our ability to enter into, or the profitability of, contracts with government entities.
p501: Our subsidiary, Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC, is required to maintain a facility security clearance to perform on classified contracts for the U.S. federal government and must comply with National Industrial Security Program requirements. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC’s facility clearance being revoked. To the extent Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC, is not able to maintain its facility security clearance, we may not be able to bid on or win new classified contracts, and existing contracts requiring a facility security clearance could be terminated, either of which could have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p502: Contracts with government agencies are also subject to audits and reviews of contractors’ administrative processes and other contract-related compliance obligations. Breaches of government contracts, failure to comply with applicable regulations, failure to obtain and maintain required facility and/or security clearances, or unfavorable findings from government audits or reviews could result in contract terminations, reputational harm, or other adverse consequences, including ineligibility to sell to government agencies in the future, government refusal to continue buying our subscriptions, or fines or civil or criminal liability, which could adversely affect our results of operations.
p503: We rely on a limited number of CSPs—Amazon.com, Inc. (together with its affiliates, “Amazon”), Google, and Microsoft Corporation (“Microsoft”)—and suppliers, such as Broadcom, for compute and critical components of our compute infrastructure. These relationships are governed by contractual arrangements that, while providing us with significant committed compute, also create dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. These CSPs may experience service outages, security incidents, or capacity constraints that affect our operations. The terms of our arrangements, including pricing, compute commitments, and service levels, are subject to negotiation upon renewal, and we may be unable to secure renewals on terms as favorable as our current arrangements. Migrating workloads to alternative providers would be costly, time-consuming, and operationally complex, and may not be feasible within timeframes that would avoid material disruption to our model development roadmap or our ability to serve customers. The engineering investment required to maintain the performance of our unified compute platform across new hardware environments means that any such migration could degrade our compute efficiency, increasing the compute and infrastructure costs required to support a given level of business activity during and following any such migration period.
p504: Our relationships with these CSPs are multifaceted and complex. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, through their respective affiliates, have made significant equity investments in our company. At the same time, they may have made, and may in the future make, equity investments in, provide financing to, or otherwise support companies whose models, platforms, or applications compete with ours. These CSPs are also our customers, purchasing our intelligence service for internal use or for their own products and services. Their purchasing decisions may be influenced by their own competing offerings, which could affect their demand for our intelligence service. Additionally, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are among the largest technology companies in the world, each with substantial AI research and development programs, AI-powered models, platforms, and applications that compete with ours, and strategic interests that may not be fully aligned with our own. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft each offer AI services and develop and deploy competing AI models through their respective cloud platforms. We make certain of our models available through these cloud platforms, and our distribution relationships with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft generate revenue for us, but they also create dependencies, give them visibility into our pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate, and may influence their incentives regarding pricing, compute allocation, service quality, sales prioritization, and compensation structures. To the extent these CSPs promote, integrate, prioritize, or provide customer access to our models, platform, and applications on terms that are less favorable than those applicable to their own competing offerings or to the offerings of other companies, including with respect to pricing, commercial terms, product placement, integration, or access to compute or sales incentives, our competitive position, customer adoption, and business results could be adversely affected.
p505: Our relationships with our strategic partners—whether with these CSPs, who simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors, or with Broadcom, which simultaneously serves as a supplier and lessor—create potential conflicts of interest that are difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate. These CSPs may prioritize their own compute needs or those of their other customers, including competitors in which they have invested, may gain insight into our operations and compute requirements through their roles as providers that could inform their competitive strategies, or may make business decisions regarding their platforms that disadvantage our models, platform, and applications relative to their own offerings or the offerings of other companies they support. Similarly, Broadcom may prioritize the supply of AI accelerators and infrastructure capacity to other customers, alter the terms of our equipment lease or the operation of our dedicated facilities, or make decisions regarding the availability or pricing of hardware that adversely affect our access to the compute infrastructure they provide. Any deterioration in these relationships, or any decision by Amazon, Google, Microsoft, or Broadcom to reduce their support for our models, platform, and applications or limit our access to compute, could adversely affect our business. In addition, such relationships, including any exclusive or preferential arrangements, investment ties, bundling of services, or cooperative initiatives, have attracted and may in the future attract antitrust or competition law scrutiny from regulators and private plaintiffs in the United States or other non-U.S. jurisdictions, and any resulting investigations, enforcement actions, or required modifications to our business arrangements could be costly, distracting, and harmful to our business.
p506: If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p507: To help reduce our dependence on CSPs, address constraints on available compute, and secure access to compute at the scale necessary for frontier model development, we are pursuing initiatives to develop our own dedicated on-premise data center infrastructure. These efforts include long-term leases and partnerships with third-party partners to procure the underlying real estate, power, and data center facilities while we lease capacity in those facilities and contract with specialized third-party operators for ongoing facility management. We also procure certain compute and infrastructure equipment directly and operate them in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification. For example, under the 2026 Lease Arrangement, the rent payments over the five-year equipment lease are equal to an aggregate of approximately $125.2 billion excluding interest, with rent payable in quarterly installments and payment obligations typically commencing upon AI infrastructure equipment becoming “ready for service” at the applicable data center facility. The 2026 Lease Arrangement is non-cancelable by the parties to such agreement during the applicable lease period except in the case of a default. In addition, we deposited cash into a restricted account in April 2026 for the benefit of Broadcom to secure compute capacity, which amount may be released or applied toward obligations under the lease depending on the satisfaction of specified conditions. Under certain circumstances, we may be required to place additional cash into this restricted account for future amounts due under the 2026 Lease Arrangement. Upon the occurrence of certain uncured events of default, such as certain payment or performance failures pursuant to the terms of the 2026 Lease Arrangement, a substantial portion of our obligations under the 2026 Lease Arrangement would be accelerated and, while we have access to multiple sources of capital and are not dependent on the potential financing capacity provided in the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA that we entered into in connection with the 2026 Lease Arrangement, we may not be permitted to elect to issue the convertible promissory notes under the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA to finance such obligations. Furthermore, we may in the future continue to directly procure such data center infrastructure and we may also undertake other efforts to build out our own compute and infrastructure and invest more deeply in the compute supply chain, which could result in significantly higher upfront costs and adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. For more information about such lease arrangements, see the sections titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” and “—If our actual compute requirements differ materially from our projections, we may fail to secure sufficient compute to meet our needs or we may be committed to excess compute that remains underutilized.” We have limited experience in managing such data center infrastructure projects at scale. Successfully executing on these data center infrastructure initiatives requires us to recruit personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multiyear deployment timelines and relationships with developers, contractors, and service providers.
p508: As we continue to build out our own compute and infrastructure and further vertically integrate across the compute supply chain, these multi-party structures will become more prevalent and will expose us to a structural timing and liquidity risk in our payment obligations that differs from our historical compute arrangements. Historically, we have generally obtained compute from a limited number of CSPs under arrangements in which our compute and infrastructure expenses are paid as compute becomes available to us. In the future, we expect we will increasingly enter into separate arrangements with a greater number of different counterparties, each responsible for discrete services or inputs across the compute supply chain. Under many of these arrangements, we may be obligated to pay a counterparty once it performs its discrete obligation, even if delays or failures by others prevent us from assembling those discrete services or inputs into usable compute we can deploy to generate revenue. In addition, counterparties may deliver their services or inputs later than scheduled, or may fail to deliver them at all, and any such delay or non-delivery by a single counterparty could postpone or prevent our deployment of the associated compute. As a result, we could incur significant cash outflows without obtaining usable compute on a timely basis, which could adversely affect our liquidity, financial condition, and results of operations.
p509: Certain of our data center infrastructure arrangements involve complex multi-party structures in which chips are procured from or through our CSPs, leased to us by third-party financing entities, installed in data center facilities procured by or through other third-party partners, and operated by yet another set of third-party service providers. The complexity of these arrangements increases execution risk, as delays or failures by any participant in the chain could affect the availability or performance of the resulting compute.
p510: In addition, to meet the substantial energy demands of large-scale AI workloads, we have entered into, and may in the future enter into, arrangements involving dedicated power generation assets and/or the development, operation, or control of power stations or other energy infrastructure. Such arrangements expose us to new operational, regulatory, and environmental liabilities, and require expertise and capabilities that differ from our core competencies. Successfully executing on these power infrastructure projects requires us to recruit personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multi-year deployment timelines and relationships with developers, contractors, service providers, and regulators, including aligning project completion schedules with the data centers such projects are expected to serve in order to avoid timing delays that constrain our ability to utilize this compute and to generate revenue and recoup costs from such investments.
p511: Deployment of our data center and power infrastructure projects involves execution risks, including delays due to permitting issues, change in law, force majeure, lack of network connectivity between facilities, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, or contractor performance; cost overruns due to equipment pricing changes, design modifications, or unanticipated requirements; and technical risks that facilities may not perform as specified or achieve expected reliability or efficiency levels. Certain of our arrangements are also subject to conditions precedent that must be satisfied before construction can commence, and completion guarantees that may terminate upon a lender foreclosure before construction is complete, leaving us without contractual recourse to compel completion. Certain of these arrangements also depend on the continued performance of credit support provided by a third party that is also a competitor, the loss or impairment of which could jeopardize the underlying arrangements. Such credit support provided to third-party data center developers or hardware providers, from which we derive no direct contractual rights or obligations, may also affect the availability and cost of data center capacity and hardware generally. Additionally, new tariffs or import fees enacted after the effective date of certain arrangements may be passed through to us as additional costs. Any delay in or limitation on the amount of compute delivered to us could adversely affect our business.
p512: The capital-intensive and long-term nature of leasing and equipping data center capacity creates financial risk, as large upfront investments and long-term payment commitments must be made months before facilities become fully operational. If our compute requirements or technology needs change, we may find ourselves with leased or dedicated infrastructure that is poorly suited to our actual needs, and technological changes in AI hardware or training methodologies could render such infrastructure less efficient than newer alternatives. Unlike CSP arrangements where compute can be adjusted relatively dynamically, long-term leases, reserved compute, and dedicated infrastructure investments are much less flexible and create long-term financial obligations regardless of whether the capacity continues to meet our needs. For example, certain of our dedicated power and data center infrastructure arrangements have initial terms of 20 years with annual escalators and include take-or-pay compute payment obligations and uncapped fuel cost pass-throughs that apply for the duration of the term regardless of actual utilization.
p513: Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. Our existing commitments are substantial, and we expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we continue to expand our compute and infrastructure build-out. See the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital Resources” for more information. As a result, we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future, and our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly alter our expected results of operations and cash flows for a given period. If our cash flows from operations and available capital are insufficient to fund these investments, we may be required to raise additional capital on unfavorable terms or to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p514: If we are unable to successfully execute on our data center infrastructure initiatives, experience significant delays or cost overruns, or find that the infrastructure we lease, deploy, or build does not meet our evolving needs, we may not realize the expected benefits of these investments, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p515: We have grown, and will continue to grow, our direct sales force. Whether we are able to increase our sales to existing customers, identify and engage new customers, and enter new U.S. and non-U.S. markets, each with a focus on broadening use of our models, platform, and applications across departments and entire organizations, will depend, among other things, on our ability to successfully test new market segments and customer types, validate product-market fit through early customer engagement, timely and effectively scale our sales motions, and adapt quickly when market conditions change. We have limited experience building, managing, and scaling a direct sales force. We have dedicated and plan to continue to dedicate significant resources to sales and marketing programs and to expand our sales and marketing capabilities to target potential customers and achieve broader market adoption of our models, platform, and applications, but there is no guarantee that we will be successful in attracting and maintaining additional customers. Moreover, identifying, recruiting, training, and managing sales personnel requires significant time, expense, and attention, including from our senior management and other key personnel, as there is significant competition for sales personnel with the skills and technical knowledge that we require, including the ability to understand and communicate complex and evolving AI use cases, regulatory considerations, customer risk sensitivities, and rapidly changing product capabilities. These challenges are particularly acute for international expansion, which requires qualified personnel with international experience, language skills, cultural competencies in the geographic markets which we target, and an aligned mission-oriented culture. If we are unable to successfully manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p516: We periodically make adjustments to our sales and marketing organization in response to market opportunities, product introductions or enhancements, acquisitions, and other internal and external considerations. Any future sales and marketing organization changes may result in a temporary reduction of productivity, which could negatively affect our rate of growth. In addition, any significant change to the way we structure and implement the compensation of our sales and marketing organization may be disruptive or may not be effective and may adversely affect our revenue growth. If we are unable to attract, hire, develop, retain, and motivate qualified sales and marketing personnel, if our new sales personnel are unable to achieve sufficient sales productivity levels in a reasonable period of time or at all, if our marketing programs are not effective, or if we are unable to effectively build, expand, and manage our sales organization and operations, our sales and revenue may grow more slowly than expected or decline, and our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p517: We have a limited history selling consumption-based access and subscriptions to our models, platform, and applications under our current business model, and we are continuing to scale our operations and go-to-market strategy. Our future success depends in part on our ability to continue attracting, onboarding, expanding, and retaining customers under this model, including determining whether, when, and how to target, develop, and deepen relationships with individual customers over time. Scaling our operations, including hiring, training, and retaining additional sales, sales engineering, and customer-facing personnel, and evolving our go-tomarket strategy may take more time and require more effort than anticipated, and the results of these efforts are difficult to predict. Our business and operating models have not been fully proven, and our limited history with our current approach makes it difficult to evaluate our prospects, plan for future growth, and forecast our results of operations.
p518: In addition, our strategy and customer mix expose us to competitive and execution risks as the AI market continues to evolve. We have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, and much of the diffusion of Claude to date has been organic— driven by individual users, including software developers and prosumers, who adopt Claude and often serve as internal champions for its broader adoption within their organizations—rather than by a large direct sales organization. This approach has allowed us to scale with a smaller team relative to other large enterprise technology companies, but it assumes that our applications and distribution will be sufficient to deliver the capabilities of our models to customers and that individual adoption will continue to translate into organizational adoption and expansion. Companies with stronger consumer-facing businesses, larger consumer user bases, more established brands, broader distribution, or deeper customer relationships may choose to increase their focus on enterprise customers or enterprise use cases and could leverage their scale, resources, and market presence to compete more effectively with us. In particular, if such competitors capture the individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, whether through their consumer applications, by integrating AI functionality into products those users already use, or otherwise, our pipeline of enterprise opportunities could be reduced in ways that a direct sales organization of our current scale may not be able to offset. Building a substantially larger sales organization, or shifting investment toward consumer and application-layer products to compete for those users, would require significant time and resources beyond our current plans and would involve the trade-offs described in the section titled “—We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.” Because we have a limited operating history with our current business model and go-tomarket strategy, we have less experience predicting customer adoption, expansion, and retention patterns, and customers may be slower than expected to adopt our models, platform, and applications or expand usage. Any failure to successfully scale our operations or effectively execute on and refine our go-to-market strategy could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p519: We derive a large portion of our revenue from sales to enterprise customers. Our ability to attract, retain, and expand relationships with enterprise customers depends in significant part on our ability to meet their generally heightened operational, technical, security, reliability, and compliance requirements. Enterprises typically expect high levels of system uptime, performance consistency, data security, auditability, internal controls, and scalability, as well as robust support and service levels. These requirements may be heightened for our agentic offerings, where enterprise customers may require detailed logs of each action taken by an autonomous agent within their environment, including the agent’s reasoning, tool invocations, and interactions with external systems. Any inability on our part to provide such logs at the level of granularity customers require could limit adoption of our agentic offerings by enterprises or result in customer attrition. If we are unable to deliver models, platforms, and applications that satisfy these enterprise-grade requirements, or if we experience outages, performance degradation, security incidents, or other operational failures, our ability to retain and expand with enterprise customers could be adversely affected. In particular, as we deploy our Virtual Collaborators, like Claude Code and Claude Cowork, within enterprise environments, these systems will require broad permissions and deep integrations with customers’ internal tools, data, and workflows in order to operate effectively. The scope of access required for extended autonomous operation within enterprise environments increases the potential consequences of any security incident, unauthorized action, or system error, and customers may be reluctant to grant the level of access necessary for these systems to operate as designed if they are unable to satisfy themselves regarding the security, reliability, and controllability of such systems.
p520: Our sales efforts targeted at enterprise customers also involve risks and challenges that may not be present, or that are present to a lesser extent, with sales to individuals or smaller organizations. These customers typically have longer decision-making cycles, require greater security, functionality, and scalability, expect a broader range of services, demand that providers take on a larger share of risks, require higher levels of customer service and support, and expect greater payment flexibility from vendors. We are often required to spend significant time and resources to familiarize potential customers with the value proposition of our models, platform, and applications, and this process can take substantially longer with enterprise customers. Enterprises may also require extensive customization, integration support, and vendor evaluations and demand more features than we currently offer or than we can deliver within their expected timeframes, including enterprise-grade functionality such as audit logs, compliance features, security controls, and monitoring tools, which may require us to make additional investments in product development or services capabilities, before committing to a purchase. As a result of these factors, sales opportunities with enterprises require us to devote greater sales and administrative support and professional services resources to each such enterprise customer, which increases our costs, lengthens our sales cycle, and diverts our sales and customer service resources to a smaller number of enterprise customers. We may spend substantial time, effort, and money in our sales efforts without successfully producing any sales. In addition, many enterprise customers procure and deploy our models, platform, and applications through third-party CSP marketplaces, which can introduce additional complexity into the sales and deployment process, including reliance on the CSPs’ procurement, security, and billing workflows and coordination with multiple counterparties. As a result, our ability to attract, retain, and expand relationships with enterprise customers may also depend in part on factors outside of our direct control, including the policies, priorities, and operational requirements of such CSPs.
p521: A number of factors influence the length and variability of our sales cycle. The need to educate potential customers about the uses and benefits of our models, platform, and applications, the discretionary nature of purchasing and budget cycles, competitive evaluation and purchasing approval processes, procurement requirements, legal review of contract terms, and internal budget authorization procedures all contribute to sales cycle variability. The length of our sales cycle, from identification of the opportunity to deal closure, may vary significantly from customer to customer. Sales to enterprises typically take longer to complete than sales to individuals or smaller organizations.
p522: A meaningful portion of our revenue is attributable to a relatively small number of such enterprise customer relationships, which increases the variability of our financial results. Our revenue in any given quarter could be substantially affected if these customers decide to significantly reduce their spend.
p523: Enterprises may have deep existing relationships with our competitors for models, platforms, and applications we do not offer, or relationships with others in the ecosystem, which may delay our sales process or cause us to not succeed with such enterprises.
p524: Enterprise customers are particularly sensitive to our ability to maintain the uptime of our models, platform, and applications, and any degradation in uptime could adversely affect our ability to retain and expand with our enterprise customers. Sustaining the uptime, performance, and scale that enterprise customers expect can place additional demands on our overall compute, and any failure of our capacity management systems to direct sufficient compute to support such demands could adversely affect our ability to serve all workloads. For more information about the foregoing, see the section titled “—If we fail to manage our technical operations infrastructure, or experience service outages, interruptions, or delays in the deployment of our models, platform, and applications, our results of operations may be adversely affected.”
p525: Our sales strategy for these enterprise customers also depends on our ability to build and maintain an effective sales organization. If we fail to effectively manage these risks associated with sales to enterprises, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. For additional discussion of our personnel related risks, see the section titled “—We may not successfully build, expand, and deploy our sales and marketing organization in a timely manner, or we may not successfully hire, retain, train, and motivate our sales personnel.”
p526: A portion of our users access our models, platform, and applications through free tiers or promotional offerings, and we seek to convert these users into paying customers over time. We may not always be successful in doing so, as free users may be satisfied with the limited functionality available in free tiers, may not have budgets to support paid subscriptions, or may choose to use our free offerings indefinitely without converting to paid plans. The availability of free tiers may cannibalize potential paid subscriptions, as some users who would have otherwise paid for our services may instead rely exclusively on free access. Additionally, providing free access to our models, platform, and applications involves costs, including compute and infrastructure, customer support, and other operational costs. In addition, we offer free access in significant part to build awareness of, familiarity with, and engagement with our products, and as a means of reaching individuals engaged in knowledge work outside of a business or organizational context. However, these benefits are inherently difficult to measure, free usage may not generate the awareness or advocacy we expect, and individual adoption of our products may not translate into organizational adoption or expansion. See the section titled “—We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful.” If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p527: Our customers rely on our customer support services to resolve issues and realize the full benefits that our models, platform, and applications provide. In order to deliver high-quality customer support and engagement, we must successfully assist our customers in deploying and continuing to use our models, platform, and applications, resolve performance issues, discover and deploy our models, platform, and applications in new use cases, provide hands-on technical implementation, customization and solution engineering support, provide training and guidance to help customers effectively adopt and scale their use of our models, platform, and applications, address interoperability challenges, and respond to security threats and cyberattacks and performance and reliability problems that may arise from time to time. The importance of our support function will increase as we expand our business and pursue new customers. Many enterprises have complex internal systems and require high levels of focused support to fully realize the benefits of our models, platform, and applications. If we do not help our customers quickly resolve issues and provide effective ongoing support and enablement, or a market perception develops that we do not maintain high-quality customer support and experience, our ability to maintain and expand our subscriptions to existing and new customers could suffer, particularly with respect to our enterprise customers.
p528: In addition, our growth model depends significantly on driving deeper adoption and expanded use cases within our existing customer base. If we are unable to effectively provide support and integration efforts that enable customers to identify, deploy, and scale additional high-value use cases, demonstrate measurable return on investment, or integrate our models, platform, and applications into their core workflows, customers may limit usage, fail to renew at expected levels, or reduce their spend, which could materially slow our revenue growth.
p529: Further, there can be no assurance that we will be able to hire sufficient support personnel as and when needed, particularly if our sales exceed our internal forecasts. We expect to continue to increase our customer base, and that growth may put additional pressure on our customer support teams, which may require additional personnel to respond to customer demand. We may be unable to respond quickly enough to accommodate short-term increases in customer demand for services. To the extent that we are unsuccessful in hiring, training, and retaining adequate support personnel, our ability to provide high-quality and timely support to our customers will be negatively impacted, and our customers’ satisfaction and their use and subscription of our models, platform, and applications could be adversely affected.
p530: In addition, as we continue to grow our operations and reach a larger and increasingly global customer base, we need to be able to provide efficient services that meet our customers’ needs globally at scale, and our customer support teams may face additional challenges, including those associated with delivering support, training, and documentation in languages other than English and providing services across expanded time-zones. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p531: Our product and investment decisions are informed in large part by our commitment to AI safety, expanding our models, platform, and applications securely and responsibly, and providing high quality customer support, all of which, in addition to our status as a PBC, may not necessarily maximize short term financial results. While we generally believe that our product and investment strategy will improve our long-term financial results, we regularly make product and investment decisions that may or may be perceived to negatively impact our shortterm revenue or ability to achieve and sustain profitability. For example, we have in the past delayed the release of new models or features, limited their availability, imposed usage restrictions, or constrained certain functionality until we determined that sufficient safety testing, evaluations, or mitigations were completed, such as with Mythos through Project Glasswing, which may have had a negative impact on our short-term revenue, and we may do so again in the future.
p532: Our focus on AI safety and responsible deployment may also require us to incur significant additional costs, including increased research and development expenses, additional personnel and infrastructure, and foregone or delayed revenue opportunities relative to competitors that may prioritize speed to market, broader access, or more permissive use of their products. These decisions may reduce customer adoption, limit usage by certain customers or use cases, or make our offerings less attractive, particularly when compared to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints.
p533: In addition, as we focus on responsibly growing our customer base and engagement across our models, platform, and applications, we may make product, pricing, or access decisions that lead to less short-term profits or engagement compared to our competitors. Customers, partners, or investors may not agree with or fully understand these decisions and may perceive them as limiting our competitiveness or commercial potential, which could adversely affect our reputation, customer relationships, market adoption, or valuation. We cannot assure you that our long-term strategy will ultimately result in superior financial performance or that the anticipated long-term benefits of these decisions will be realized on the timeline we expect, or at all. Any of the foregoing risks could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p534: We regularly make decisions to invest in new products, technologies, business lines, and strategic initiatives, including in areas outside our current core offerings, and the outcomes of these investments are inherently uncertain. These initiatives often require significant upfront investments of capital, research and development resources, and management attention, and their outcomes may not achieve widespread market adoption, may not generate revenue at anticipated levels, may take longer than expected to mature, or may fail entirely. In addition, reallocating resources from our core offerings to pursue new initiatives could slow growth in existing products, reduce operating efficiency, or weaken our competitive position if those initiatives do not succeed. If our investments in new products or business lines do not produce the long-term benefits we anticipate, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and prospects could be adversely affected.
p535: Certain of these initiatives, including our life sciences research program, which involves operating laboratory facilities, and our research in robotics and physical AI, require us to engage in activities outside our historical experience as a software and research organization, such as handling biological and chemical materials, operating laboratory and robotic equipment, and complying with biosafety, occupational health and safety, environmental, hazardous materials, and, potentially, preclinical and clinical research regulations. These activities expose us to categories of liability, including for workplace injury and environmental contamination, that differ from those associated with our core business, and any drug candidates or other discoveries resulting from these efforts would face the lengthy, costly, and uncertain development and regulatory pathways characteristic of the life sciences industry, and may never generate revenue.
p536: Our systems and operations are subject to disruptions resulting from changes to our technology infrastructure. We have experienced, and may continue to experience, service interruptions or degraded performance due to software deployments, configuration changes, system updates, and new model introductions. These disruptions may adversely affect our ability to service customers and could result in lost revenue, customer attrition, or reputational harm. Further, our mitigation efforts and processes may be insufficient to prevent or minimize the impact of system changes on service availability, and we may lack adequate testing, rollback procedures, or monitoring capabilities to detect and remediate issues arising from system changes in a timely manner. For example, in March 2026, we experienced a service outage and periods of degraded performance resulting from a combination of factors, including a significant and rapid increase in usage demand, compute constraints in certain components of our infrastructure, and other factors. Although we have taken and continue to take steps to address these issues, including migrating to more scalable infrastructure and enhancing our operational processes, similar incidents may occur in the future.
p537: In addition, continued growth in our customer base could place additional demands on our models, platform, and applications and could cause or exacerbate slowdowns or interrupt the availability of our models, platform, and applications. If there is a substantial increase in the volume of usage of our models, platform, and applications, we will be required to further expand and upgrade our technology and infrastructure. Any substantial increase in usage will also require increased compute. Because our compute is procured well in advance based on projected demand across all workloads, a significant acceleration in customer demand could cause aggregate capacity to fall short of the levels required to support all of our workloads concurrently at the scale we intend. If our committed compute proves insufficient, or the composition of our committed compute portfolio differs materially from our demand forecasts, we may experience service disruptions, degraded response times, or limitations on customer and user access to our models, platform, and applications, while also experiencing constraints on the compute available to support ongoing model development. There can be no assurance that we will be able to accurately project the rate or timing of increases, if any, in the use of our models, platform, and applications or expand and upgrade our systems and infrastructure to accommodate such increases on a timely basis. If our users are not able to access our models, platform, and applications or encounter slowdowns, we may lose customers or partners. In order to remain competitive, we must continue to enhance and improve the responsiveness, functionality, and features of our models, platform, and applications and the underlying compute infrastructure supporting them. Our disaster recovery plan may not be sufficient to address all aspects or any unanticipated consequence or incidents, and our insurance may not be sufficient to compensate us for the losses that could occur.
p538: Moreover, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft provide substantial portions of the compute infrastructure that we use to host our models, platform, and applications and many of the internal tools we use to operate our business. Any significant disruption of, limitation of our access to, or other interference with this infrastructure would negatively impact our operations, degrade the availability and performance of our models, platform, and applications, and could cause us to lose customers who are unable to access or experience difficulties accessing our models, platform, and applications. Even absent a full disruption, the level of service provided by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft could affect the availability or speed of our models, platform, and applications, which may also impact the usage of, and our customers’ satisfaction with, our models, platform, and applications and could seriously harm our business and reputation.
p539: Any transition of the services and infrastructure currently provided by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft to another CSP would require significant time and expense and could further disrupt or degrade delivery of our models, platform, and applications. Such a transition could require us to re-architect portions of our infrastructure, retrain or migrate models and large datasets, incur data transfer and duplication costs, and adapt our systems to new tools and configurations, which could result in operational delays and reduced performance during the transition period. If Amazon, Google, or Microsoft increases pricing terms, terminates or seeks to terminate our contractual relationship, whether for competitive reasons or otherwise, establishes more favorable relationships with our competitors, or changes or interprets its terms of service or policies in a manner that is unfavorable with respect to us, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p540: In addition, an increasing portion of our compute is hosted in dedicated data center facilities that are leased and operated on our behalf by third parties rather than by our CSPs, and we expect this portion to grow. Certain of these operators have a limited operating history, and these facilities may have less geographic redundancy, failover capacity, or operational tooling than those of large-scale cloud environments, such that an equipment failure, cooling or network disruption, or operator error at a single facility could affect a meaningful portion of our available capacity. Moreover, the continuous availability of our models, platform, and applications depends on the reliable supply of electrical power and water to the facilities that host our infrastructure, whether operated by our CSPs or on our behalf. Utility outages, shortages, price increases, or required curtailment of power during periods of peak demand, whether in connection with or outside of natural disasters or other catastrophic events, could interrupt or degrade the provision of our services in the ordinary course of our business. p541: As part of our business strategy, we will continue to consider a wide array of potential strategic transactions, including acquisitions of businesses, new technologies, services, and other assets and strategic investments that complement our business. In addition, we may overpay for acquisition targets or make investments at valuations that do not ultimately prove justified by the targets’ performance, strategic value, or market conditions, which could adversely affect our financial condition.
p542: We may be unable to identify or complete prospective and attractive strategic transactions for many reasons, including competition from other potential acquirers, the effects of consolidation in our industry, and potentially high valuations of acquisition candidates. p560: If we fail to address the foregoing risks or other problems encountered in connection with past or future acquisitions of businesses, new technologies, services, and other assets, strategic investments, and other strategic transactions, or if we otherwise fail to realize the expected benefits of such acquisitions or investments, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p561: As our business has grown and as interest in us and the AI industry overall has increased, we have attracted, and may continue to attract, significant media coverage, public commentary, and scrutiny from time to time. This coverage and commentary have included, and we expect will continue to include, recurring narratives concerning the potential adverse societal impacts of AI, including that AI may displace or eliminate jobs, may be misused or otherwise cause harm, and may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. We have been, and may continue to be, a particular focus of such narratives, and unfavorable coverage of the AI industry generally may be attributed to us, in each case regardless of whether the underlying concerns are well-founded or specifically applicable to our models, platform, or applications. Unfavorable publicity regarding us, our partners, or the AI industry more broadly could adversely affect our reputation and brand, as described in the section titled “—If we are unable to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.” Negative media coverage, including public figures making negative or threatening statements about our company, whether accurate or not, could also adversely affect our brand and reputation and may reduce market acceptance of our models, platform, and applications or impair our ability to attract and retain customers. As public awareness of our brand increases, any issues that draw media attention may have an amplified adverse effect on our reputation. If unfavorable media coverage or adverse public perceptions persist or intensify, the demand for our models, platform, and applications could decline and our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p562: As a public company, we will incur greater legal, accounting, and other expenses than we incurred as a private company. For example, we are subject to the reporting requirements of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (“Exchange Act”), the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (“Sarbanes-Oxley Act”), the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, the rules and regulations of the SEC, and the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The Exchange Act requires, among other things, that we file annual, quarterly, and current reports with respect to our business and results of operations. Compliance with these requirements will increase our legal, accounting, and financial compliance costs, and increase demand on our systems, making some activities more time-consuming and costly. In addition, changing laws, regulations, and standards relating to reporting obligations and corporate governance disclosure are creating uncertainty for public companies, which could result in continued uncertainty regarding compliance matters and higher costs. We expect these rules and regulations to make it more expensive for us to obtain director and officer liability insurance, and we may be required to accept reduced policy limits and coverage or incur substantially higher costs to maintain the same or similar coverage. As a result, it may be more difficult for us to attract and retain qualified individuals to serve on our board of directors or as our executive officers.
p563: As a public company, we expect to incur significant expenses and devote substantial management effort toward ensuring compliance with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. In that regard, we will need to hire additional accounting and financial staff with appropriate public company experience and technical accounting knowledge. In addition, as a public company, we may be subject to stockholder activism, which can lead to substantial costs, distract management, and impact the manner in which we operate our business in ways we cannot currently anticipate.
p564: As a result of disclosure of information in this prospectus and in our public filings with the SEC as required of a public company, our business and financial condition will become more visible, which we believe may result in threatened or actual litigation, including by competitors and other third parties. If such claims are successful, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected, and even if the claims do not result in litigation or are resolved in our favor, these claims, and the time and resources necessary to resolve them, may divert the resources of our management and our board of directors, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p565: Further, many members of our management team have limited experience managing a publicly traded company, interacting with public company investors, and complying with the increasingly complex laws and regulations pertaining to public companies. Our management team may not successfully or efficiently manage our transition to being a public company subject to significant regulatory oversight and reporting obligations under the federal securities laws and the continuous scrutiny of securities analysts and investors. These new obligations and constituents will require significant attention from our management and may divert their attention away from the day-to-day management of our business, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p566: War, terrorist attacks, and other acts of political violence, or any significant natural disaster, such as an earthquake, fire, hurricane, tornado, flood, or significant power outage, may disrupt our operations, mobile networks, the internet, data centers, or the operations of our partners or third-party service providers, and the impact of climate change may increase these risks. In particular, our corporate headquarters are located in the San Francisco Bay Area, a region known for seismic activity and increasingly for the threat of fires. In addition, any public health crises, pandemics, political crises, terrorist attacks, war and other political or social instability, other geopolitical developments, or other catastrophic events, whether in the United States or in non-U.S. geographies, may adversely affect our operations or macroeconomic conditions. For example, an act of terrorism, armed conflict, or escalation of geopolitical tensions could result in physical damage to or destruction of data centers and other critical infrastructure, whether owned or operated by us or our third-party providers, as well as disruptions to power, cooling, or network connectivity necessary to operate such facilities. The impact of any of the foregoing or other disruption to us, our partners, or other third parties may result in system interruptions and degradation, reputational harm, delays in our product development, lengthy interruptions in our services, data breaches, malware, and other security or hacking incidents, all of which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. All of the aforementioned risks may be further increased if our disaster recovery plans prove to be inadequate. Further, the insurance we maintain may be insufficient to cover our losses resulting from such business interruptions, and any incidents may result in loss of, or increased costs of, such insurance.
p567: Our models, platform, and applications must integrate with a variety of hardware and software platforms, and we need to continuously modify and enhance our models, platform, and applications to adapt to changes in hardware, software, and browser technologies. In particular, we have developed our models, platform, and applications to be able to easily integrate with third-party applications, including the applications of software providers that compete with us as well as our partners, through the interaction of APIs. In general, we rely on the providers of such software systems to allow us access to their APIs to enable these integrations. We are typically subject to standard terms and conditions of such providers, which govern the distribution, operation, and fees of such software systems, and which are subject to change by such providers from time to time. Our business will be harmed if any provider of such software systems:
p568: • discontinues or limits our access to its software or APIs;
p569: • modifies its terms of service or other policies, including fees charged to, or other restrictions on us, or other software developers;
p570: • changes how information is accessed by us or our customers;
p571: • establishes more favorable relationships with one or more of our competitors; or
p572: • develops or otherwise favors its own competitive offerings over our models, platform, and applications.
p573: Further, we depend in part on operating systems, including mobile operating systems such as iOS and Android, and their respective application stores, such as Apple’s App Store and Google’s Play Store, to drive downloads of our Claude app. If such operating systems or application stores limit the availability of our app, make changes that degrade the functionality of our app, increase the cost of using our app, impose terms of use unsatisfactory to us, or modify their search or ratings algorithms in ways that are detrimental to us, or if our competitors’ placement in such mobile operating systems’ application store is more prominent than the placement of our app, our user growth could be adversely affected. Any changes in such operating systems and application stores that degrade the functionality of our app or give preferential treatment to our competitors’ apps could adversely affect our platform’s usage across devices. Some marketplaces have explored changing their policies regarding what content is acceptable within an application. If we are unable to adapt to such changes, this could adversely affect our platform’s access to and usage within those ecosystems. As new mobile devices and mobile platforms are released, there is no guarantee that certain mobile devices will continue to support our platform or effectively roll out updates to our apps. Additionally, in order to deliver a high-quality app, we need to ensure that our models, platform, and applications are designed to work effectively with a range of mobile technologies, systems, networks, and standards. We may not be successful in developing or maintaining relationships with key participants in the mobile industry that enhance users’ experience. If users encounter any difficulty accessing or using our apps on their mobile devices or if we are unable to adapt to changes in popular mobile operating systems, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p574: Third-party models, platforms, and applications are constantly evolving, and we may not be able to modify our models, platform, and applications to assure their compatibility with that of other third parties. In addition, some of our competitors may be able to disrupt the operations or compatibility of our models, platform, and applications with their models, platforms, or applications, or exert strong business influence on our ability to, and terms on which we operate our models, platform, and applications. Should any of our competitors modify their products or standards in a manner that degrades the functionality of our models, platform, and applications or gives preferential treatment to competitive models, platforms, or applications, whether to enhance their competitive position or for any other reason, the interoperability of our models, platform, and applications with these products could decrease and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected. Further, if we are not permitted or able to integrate with these and other thirdparty applications in the future, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p575: Our business and operations are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, as described in this “Risk Factors” section, many of which are interrelated, such that the occurrence of one risk event may exacerbate or trigger additional risk events, and the combined effect may be materially greater than the impact of any individual risk event in isolation. For example, unfavorable developments in intellectual property laws or adverse outcomes in copyright or other litigation could require us to modify, retrain, or limit the capabilities of our models, increasing costs and reducing the performance or competitiveness of our models, platform, and applications, which could in turn harm customer demand, revenue, and our reputation and brand. In addition, constraints on the availability or cost of compute could similarly limit our ability to develop and deploy advanced models, delay product launches, reduce service reliability, and adversely affect our revenue growth, while also affecting customer trust and perception of our offerings. If our revenue growth is limited and we do not have sufficient additional sources of capital, we may be unable to acquire necessary compute or invest in our talent to remain at the technological frontier or to support our customers, or we may face breaches of covenants or defaults under the A&R Credit Agreement and certain of our commercial agreements. If we were to breach covenants or default under the A&R Credit Agreement or certain of our commercial agreements, such an event could trigger cross-defaults, accelerate repayment obligations, restrict our access to capital, and further constrain our operations and growth, potentially magnifying other financial, operational, and reputational risks. Because these and other risks may interact in complex and unpredictable ways, particularly in a fast-moving industry characterized by technological change, evolving regulation, and emerging business models, we may not be able to foresee or effectively manage all potential consequences. If one risk triggers or intensifies others, or if multiple adverse events occur concurrently or in close succession, our prospects, reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p576: The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of open-source licenses to modern AI model training has not been authoritatively resolved by U.S. and non-U.S. courts as of this date. We have a good faith belief that we own or possess all sufficient legal rights and/or defenses to the training data used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications, which is based in part on our belief that our use or acquisition of the training data used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications constitutes “fair use” of such training data under copyright law doctrine. In addition, copyright laws in some jurisdictions outside the United States generally do not recognize fair use, and our reliance on analogous exceptions is subject to evolving conditions and to adverse or unsettled judicial interpretation in those jurisdictions. If a court of law disagrees with our belief that our use or acquisition of such training data constitutes fair use or otherwise concludes that it violates copyright law, for example, by adopting the reasoning in Bartz (as defined below), including without limitation in currently active litigation against us or another company in our industry, our business may be adversely affected. In particular, adverse rulings in litigation involving other AI developers, regardless of the specific facts, data practices, or legal theories at issue in those cases, could establish legal precedents or interpretations of copyright law that apply broadly across the industry and limit our ability to train, develop, or deploy AI models, even if our own data procurement and usage practices differ. Such outcomes could restrict access to certain categories of training data, narrow the scope of available legal defenses, or impose new licensing, compliance, or operational requirements across the AI industry. For example, if we cannot rely on the fair use doctrine to access copyrighted work for training our models, we may be required to pay significant fees to obtain a license to such training data or our ability to further develop our models, platform, and applications and distribute models trained on such data at issue could be adversely affected. In addition, an adverse ruling against us or another company in our industry could result in injunctive relief that restricts our ability to use or distribute models trained on the data at issue or could require us to retrain affected models from scratch at substantial cost. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p577: We are subject to a range of laws and regulations in the EU, the United States, and other jurisdictions, and other legal obligations relating to privacy, data protection, and the collection, use, transfer, storage, and other processing of data. These laws, regulations, and other legal obligations vary across jurisdictions, and include comprehensive frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (“GDPR”), laws that impose sector-specific obligations, and those that impose specific requirements or restrictions on the handling of particular types of data, such as personal data that is considered sensitive. These obligations are not harmonized, continue to evolve in scope, present technical and operational complexities and challenges, and may conflict or impose overlapping or inconsistent obligations. Further, these laws and regulations, as well as other laws and regulations not originally enacted to address privacy or data protection, continue to evolve as they are applied to new technologies, including AI, and may be interpreted or enforced in ways that are inconsistent, unclear, novel, or subject to significant regulatory discretion. Additionally, plaintiffs, class action counsel, state Attorneys’ General, and other claimants continue to pursue claims against artificial intelligence companies relating to data handling, privacy, and cybersecurity; similar disputes could arise against us and they could take the form of privacy, cybersecurity, breach of contract, tort, or other claims. New or evolving laws, regulations, regulatory interpretations, claims, and novel or inconsistent application of existing laws and regulations to us, or our evolving contractual or other legal obligations, including those that arise as we seek to enter into new markets or product offerings, may require us to modify our models, platform, and applications, policies, and practices, delay or limit the development or deployment of certain features, increase compliance and litigation costs, and result in fines or penalties.
p578: Our compliance obligations and expenditures, and our exposure thereunder, may vary depending on both how customers access and use our models, platform, and applications, including through our first-party offerings or third-party distribution channels, and on the nature of data processed in connection with those offerings. For example, our costs and regulatory exposure may vary based on the demands we receive from individuals, regulators, and other parties seeking to exercise rights under privacy or data protection laws. We may be subject to additional obligations, restrictions, or exposure in connection with the processing of data that is considered sensitive under applicable laws. In connection with the development, deployment, and improvement of our services, including model training, improvement, and inference, we have faced, and may face in the future, operational errors or claims or assertions that our use or processing of data, such as personal, sensitive, or confidential data, is inconsistent with our obligations.
p579: Failure to secure data against risks to its confidentiality, integrity, or availability may result in legal obligations, such as notification obligations to individuals, regulators, or customers, which could result in additional legal and reputational risk.
p580: Any actual or perceived failure or inability by us, our personnel, or third parties acting on our behalf to comply with applicable privacy or data protection requirements, our contractual commitments, or our public statements regarding our data practices could result in investigations, litigation, fines, penalties, or other liability; require us to change our models, platform, and applications, policies, or practices; reduce customer demand or harm our reputation; require us to make public disclosures that could expose us to reputational and legal risks; and otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p581: Our commitment to AI safety requires us in some cases to access, collect, and process personal and sensitive data. While our approach and mechanisms relating to handling personal and sensitive data are designed to improve AI safety, they also subject us to compliance with evolving industry practices, laws and regulations, and increased risks related to the processing of sensitive data, such as increased risks of harm or litigation if we experience a security incident or unauthorized access to or processing of data. Further, laws and regulations not originally enacted to address AI safety are being applied to AI safety and may be increasingly interpreted or enforced in ways that are inconsistent, unclear, novel, or subject to significant regulatory discretion. Any actual or perceived failure to comply with AI safety requirements or our processing of personal or sensitive data for AI safety, or any actual or perceived security incident involving such data, could result in investigations, litigation, fines, penalties, or other liability; require us to change our policies or practices; reduce customer demand or harm our reputation; require us to make public disclosures that could expose us to reputational and legal risks; and otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p582: We store, handle, and otherwise process confidential, proprietary, and personal information, and our customers use our models, platform, and applications to process similarly sensitive information. We experience security risks, unintended exposure of or access to data, cyberattacks, and other attempts to gain unauthorized access to our information, sites, networks, systems, models, platform, and applications. These have resulted in, and may in the future result in, breaches of our security measures or those of our third-party service providers; unauthorized access to our sites, networks, systems, and accounts; unauthorized access to, and misappropriation of, personal, confidential, or proprietary information belonging to us, our customers, or others; viruses, worms, spyware, or other malware being served from our models, platform, and applications, networks, or systems; deletion or modification of content; the display of unauthorized content on our models, platform, and applications; interruption, disruption, or malfunction of operations; and other risks.
p583: We have in the past faced and in the future may face risks of phishing schemes and other cyberattacks, including by nation-states and state-sponsored actors, that continue to evolve in sophistication and volume, and may inherently be difficult to detect. Our proprietary model weights, corporate and financial data, and other core intellectual property represent particularly high-value targets for state-sponsored espionage and theft, and security researchers have identified frontier AI companies as priority targets for non-U.S. intelligence services. The efforts of such state-sponsored actors to target us will likely increase over time, especially as we develop models with next-generation capabilities, and they may specifically target models which have not, or have not yet, been released to the general public. For example, in light of its advanced cyber vulnerability discovery capabilities, state-sponsored actors may conduct cyberattacks specifically targeting Mythos.
p584: Our security capabilities continue to evolve, and certain aspects of our security program may not be sufficient to fully address the most sophisticated malicious actors, including well-resourced nation-state or state-sponsored groups, especially as those groups develop or obtain more powerful technology, which may include AI technology with offensive capabilities similar to those displayed by Mythos. While we are actively investing in and enhancing our security infrastructure and controls, we have operated in the past, and may in the future operate, for periods of time with known limitations or gaps in our defenses as we continue to mature our security posture, and no information security program can be expected to prevent all possible incidents. There can be no assurances that we will be able to prevent or adequately detect and defend against all cyberattacks or other cybersecurity incidents affecting our systems, including incidents caused by nation-state and statesponsored actors. An unauthorized exfiltration of our model weights could enable adversaries to bypass significant research investment, eliminate key competitive advantages, and potentially raise national security concerns if such technology is acquired by malicious actors. Further, if our model weights were obtained by unauthorized actors, such actors may be able to deploy such models outside of our usage policies, safety mechanisms, or monitoring frameworks, which could enable harmful or misuse scenarios that our safeguards are designed to prevent and could subject us to regulatory, reputational, or public scrutiny for having developed such capabilities.
p585: We have faced and expect to face insider threat risks and vulnerabilities related to hiring processes, identity verification, remote work environments, and compromised devices that could enable unauthorized access to sensitive systems or information. We have been and expect that we will continue to be targeted by individuals seeking employment under false identities, or with ulterior or malicious motives for seeking employment with us and the third parties on which we rely. We also face the risk that employees, contractors, or other personnel with authorized access to our systems, model weights, or other sensitive information may be compromised after joining us, including due to efforts by state-sponsored actors, competitors, or others to recruit, bribe, coerce, or otherwise induce such personnel, or to compromise their credentials or devices, in order to misappropriate sensitive information, enable unauthorized access, or introduce vulnerabilities into our systems, models, or products. Because personnel with authorized access to our model weights and other core intellectual property are particularly attractive targets, and because our remote and distributed work environment and our reliance on third-party vendors for certain key processes may limit our visibility into such conduct, we may be unable to prevent or timely detect these insider threats. In addition, in certain jurisdictions in which we operate or in which our vendors or the operators of facilities hosting our infrastructure are located, such personnel, vendors, or operators may be legally compelled to cooperate with government authorities, including intelligence and security agencies, in ways contrary to our interests, such as by providing access to our systems, data, or model weights. The laws of those jurisdictions may prohibit the affected parties from notifying us of such demands and may afford us limited or no ability to challenge them, and because such cooperation may be lawful where it occurs and involves personnel acting within their authorized access, our insider-threat and other security controls may not detect it.
p586: We have also seen, and expect to continue to see, industry-wide software supply chain vulnerabilities and attacks, which could affect our or third parties’ systems, or the security of our models, platform, and applications. Geopolitical tensions or armed conflicts around the world may increase these risks. As a result, we may be unable to prevent or timely detect all attempts to access or exfiltrate sensitive information, including by actors with substantial technical, financial, or geopolitical resources.
