p587: As we continue to develop and deploy new features, including those incorporating AI, our systems are exposed to additional or evolving security risks, including those arising from emerging or imperfectly understood AI- specific threat vectors. Such AI-specific threats include prompt injection attacks that manipulate model behavior through malicious inputs, attempts to replicate or reverse engineer our proprietary models through systematic API queries, adversarial inputs designed to cause model failures or misclassifications, malicious corruption of training data that could compromise model integrity, and vulnerabilities in continuous integration and deployment pipelines that could allow insiders or other actors to inject malicious code that is subsequently propagated or amplified through AI-assisted development workflows. Such attacks may be difficult to detect, may not be addressed by traditional cybersecurity defenses, and may require specialized expertise, techniques, and infrastructure to mitigate. Further, features that rely on AI may be particularly susceptible to unanticipated vulnerabilities as both our understanding and the broader market’s understanding of AI-related security risks and mitigation techniques continue to develop. Our efforts to mitigate the foregoing risks may result in false positives and our mistakenly limiting or blocking certain users from accessing our technology, which could result in potential litigation or regulatory action.
p588: In addition, our agentic offerings interact with external tools, APIs, databases, code repositories, and other third-party systems, creating cybersecurity attack surfaces that are distinct from those applicable to traditional AI models. An adversary could manipulate the content of an external data source, API response, document, or web page processed by an agent to cause the agent to take harmful or unauthorized actions based on that manipulated input. An attacker could also attempt to compromise an active agent session and redirect the agent to perform malicious actions using the customer’s authenticated credentials and permissions. Because our agentic offerings are designed to take autonomous actions with real-world consequences, including executing code, modifying files, sending communications, and completing transactions, a successful exploitation of these agentic attack surfaces could result in data exfiltration, unauthorized transactions, code injection, or other adverse effects, potentially across multiple customer deployments simultaneously. Traditional cybersecurity defenses, including firewalls, input validation, and access controls, may not be fully effective against these novel threat vectors, and the security community’s understanding of agentic-specific attack surfaces is still developing.
p589: We have in the past discovered, and may in the future discover, errors, vulnerabilities, or other defects, such as hallucinations, in our models, platform, and applications only after deployment, including in connection with the development of new features, integrations, or capabilities. Such issues have resulted and may in the future result in service disruptions, degraded performance, unintended or harmful outputs, or the unauthorized disclosure of personal or proprietary information, including through security incidents that impact the networks, systems, and data of our customers. In addition, incidents impacting our customers may be caused by customer misconfiguration or misuse, or by inadequate access controls or other security practices by our customers. Such incidents, even if caused by customer misconfigurations or misuse, or by a customer’s lack of adequate security controls, may impact our reputation or the reputation of our models, platform, and applications, and may subject us to liability exposure, disruption of commercial relationships, or other damage.
p590: Cyberattacks, including cyberattacks directed at our networks, our customers’ networks, or the networks of third parties with which we have relationships, have been, and may in the future continue to be, amplified through the use of AI, including our models, platform, and applications. Such capabilities may be used to automate or scale attacks, impersonate employees or members of senior management, or otherwise gain unauthorized access to our systems or those of our customers, partners, or vendors.
p591: Failures in our internal systems or controls, security breaches, failures to comply with our privacy or data protection commitments, or other incidents, whether resulting from malicious activity, human error, or system limitations, could adversely affect our reputation, brand, and business and impair our ability to attract and retain customers. Our offices and the data centers that host our infrastructure, many of which are operated by third parties, are also exposed to physical threats as well as failures by the operators of those facilities. A physical intrusion could damage equipment, interrupt our services, or provide a path to our systems and data, including our model weights, that bypasses our network defenses.
p592: Although we have dedicated significant resources designed to identify and address these security risks, we cannot guarantee that our security measures will be effective or that our recovery protocols, backup, and other systems will be sufficient. Even where we detect an incident, our response may prove inadequate, including if we misjudge its severity, respond too slowly, or fail to fully remediate the underlying cause. In addition, incidents that appear minor when they occur may later prove significant when considered together with other incidents or with information learned afterward, and a series of related incidents, none of which is material on its own, could prove material in the aggregate. We continue to devote significant resources to protect against security breaches and other incidents, and we may need to devote significant resources in the future to mitigate and address problems caused by breaches and other incidents, which may divert resources from the growth and expansion of our business.
p593: Any actual or perceived security breach or other incident experienced by us or third parties with whom we do business, particularly our CSPs, could damage our reputation and brand, cause our business to suffer, require us to expend significant capital and other resources, cause us to incur increasing costs, including costs to deploy additional personnel and protection technologies, train employees, and engage third-party experts and consultants, expose us to litigation or regulatory action, cause us to violate applicable privacy, data protection, security, and other laws and regulations, subject us to adverse publicity and a loss of confidence in our security measures, and cause us to incur significant fines, penalties, and other liability exposure, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We have taken steps to limit our liability for certain incidents, for example through warranty disclaimers and limitations of liability in our terms of service, but those contractual protections may not be upheld, or may not apply to certain claims, or may otherwise be insufficient to limit our liability exposure under applicable law.
p594: In the EU, we face increasingly stringent regulatory reporting obligations for cybersecurity and AI-related incidents. Under the GDPR, we must notify the competent regulators about incidents that involve personal data and are likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. Similarly, the EU Network and Information Security Directive 2022/2555 (“NIS2”) requires us to notify the competent authorities of any significant cybersecurity incident through a staged process. In addition, the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to keep track of, document, and report serious incidents without undue delay to the AI Office and competent authorities. Going forward, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as defined under the EU AI Act, will also have to report serious incidents or malfunctions without undue delay in certain circumstances.
p595: In the United States, companies are increasingly subject to analogous incident reporting obligations, including under federal and state data breach notification laws, such as the New York Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security (SHIELD) Act. In addition, certain U.S. states have adopted incident reporting laws specific to frontier model providers, such as the New York Responsible AI Safety and Education Act (RAISE Act) and the California Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act. These frameworks create heightened compliance and liability exposure in case of delayed, incomplete, or inaccurate incident disclosures.
p596: While we currently maintain insurance that may cover certain costs, liabilities, and other losses in connection with security breaches and other incidents, the insurance market for such losses is continuously evolving, and we may be unable to obtain coverage for certain cybersecurity-related or data-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses. Furthermore, there can be no guarantee that the insurance coverage we do maintain will be adequate to compensate us for the potential losses, or that any insurance claims we submit will be covered, paid in a timely manner, or paid at all by our insurance carrier or carriers.
p597: We collect and use various data sources to train our AI models, including publicly available information from the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and synthetic data generated by our own models. We use such data across the stages of model development, including pre-training and post-training. To collect publicly available information, we utilize web scraping or web crawling techniques, book scanning, and other methods. While we take steps designed to ensure that our activities comply with applicable law, applicable robots.txt notices, and relevant technical measures such as paywalls or logins, our efforts may not always be successful. Further, we may not be able to verify whether information collected using such techniques is protected under privacy, copyright, or other intellectual property laws in certain cases, and our use of any such protected information may subject us to additional liability for intellectual property infringement or privacy violations. More broadly, inadequate documentation of training data sources, provenance, or chain of custody could create legal exposure, complicate our ability to respond to regulatory inquiries or litigation discovery requests, or raise concerns during due diligence by investors, partners, or potential acquirers that could adversely affect our strategic transactions or business relationships.
p598: Our data collection activities have in the past resulted, are presently the subject of, and may in the future result in litigation or other actions filed or instituted against us, alleging that our scraping, web crawling, and other techniques to collect data violate the law. For example, Reddit, Inc. has filed suit against us, captioned Reddit, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC, alleging we improperly accessed posts stored on Reddit, Inc.’s platform in violation of its legal rights. On July 3, 2025, we filed a notice of removal of the case to federal court. The case was remanded to state court on March 30, 2026. The lawsuit is currently pending, and we continue to defend ourselves against the allegations.
p599: The costs of defending against such litigation, regardless of merit, are considerable, and such litigation may divert management and key personnel’s attention and resources, which may seriously harm our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Claims of allegedly illegal scraping and web crawling techniques may be extremely broad, and it may not be possible for us to conduct our business in such a way as to avoid all such claims.
p600: We may be required to settle such litigation on terms that are unfavorable to us. For example, a settlement may require us to discontinue such allegedly illegal practices, preclude us from using certain scraping and web crawling techniques, and/or require us to develop alternative technology or practices. The development of alternative technology or practices would require significant effort and expense or may not be successful.
p601: Similarly, if any litigation to which we may be a party fails to settle and we go to trial, we may be subject to an unfavorable judgment which may not be reversible upon appeal. The terms of a judgment may require us to cease some or all of our operations or require the payment of substantial amounts. Any of these events could cause our business, financial condition, and results of operations to be adversely affected as a result.
p602: If we or the customers, users, or third parties from which we source data lack sufficient rights to collect, use, process, share, or analyze certain third-party data—including for training or improving analytical or AI models —we could be subject to legal claims, regulatory scrutiny, or contractual liability. Such claims could require us to limit functionality, segregate data, or retrain models, and could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p603: The costs of defending against such litigation, regardless of merit, are considerable, and such litigation may divert management and key personnel’s attention and resources, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Claims of misappropriation, misuse, infringement, privacy violations, or other violations of intellectual property or contractual rights, as well as other claims related to using particular data, may be extremely broad, and as such, it is likely we will face certain claims in the ordinary course of business.
p604: There is considerable intellectual property development activity in our industry. Our competitors, as well as a number of other entities, including non-practicing entities and individuals, may own or claim to own intellectual property rights relating to our industry or our technology. As we face increasing competition and our public profile increases, the possibility of intellectual property rights claims against us may also increase.
p605: To train our models, we use material from many sources, some of which may include third-party copyrighted content or trademarks. Regardless of whether the material is copyrighted or the trademarks are registered, parties who own the rights to that content or those trademarks, or distribute that content, may attempt to sue us based on intellectual property infringement or other theories. We also face claims that outputs generated by our models infringe, or facilitate infringement of, third-party works. Lawsuits asserting such claims have been filed, are pending, and may be filed in the future in the United States and internationally. For example, in September 2025, we reached an agreement to settle a copyright infringement class action, captioned Bartz, et al. v. Anthropic PBC (“Bartz”), for $1.5 billion, which was approved by the district court in July 2026. As additional examples, various publishers have filed suit against us alleging copyright infringement of song lyrics and unlawful removal of copyright management information in the cases captioned Concord Music Group, Inc., et al. v. Anthropic PBC, Concord Music Group, Inc., et al. v. Anthropic PBC et al., BMG Rights Management (US) LLC v. Anthropic PBC, Round Hill Music LP, et al. v. Anthropic PBC, Sony Music Publishing (US) LLC v. Anthropic PBC et al., and others. Similarly, a third party alleges we accessed and reproduced posts stored on the third party’s platform in violation of its legal rights and has filed suit against us, captioned Reddit, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC. The possibility of statutory damages under some intellectual property legal frameworks creates additional risk for us. We are vigorously defending ourselves in these pending lawsuits and believe we have meritorious defenses, though these lawsuits address novel issues and areas of law that make the results uncertain.
p606: We also face patent infringement claims, which may seek substantial damages or injunctive relief limiting our ability to use certain technologies, and we expect such claims may increasingly be asserted as our public profile grows. Moreover, certain of our competitors hold substantially larger patent portfolios than we do, which they could assert against us and which may limit our ability to obtain effective cross-licenses or to counter such assertions with our own patent rights.
p607: The costs of defending against such litigation, regardless of merit, are considerable, and such litigation may divert management and key personnel’s attention and resources, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Claims of misappropriation, misuse, infringement, or other violations of intellectual property rights, as well as other claims related to using particular content, may be extremely broad, and as such, it is likely we will face certain claims in the ordinary course of business.
p608: We may be required to settle such litigation on terms that are unfavorable to us. For example, a settlement may require us to obtain a license to continue practices alleged to violate a third party’s rights, which may not be available on reasonable terms and may significantly increase our operating expenses. Such a license may not be available to us at all. As a result, we may be required to develop alternative technology or practices or discontinue such allegedly infringing practices. The development of alternative technology or practices would require significant effort and expense or may not be successful.
p609: Similarly, if any litigation to which we may be a party fails to settle and we go to trial, we may be subject to an unfavorable judgment which may not be reversible upon appeal. The terms of a judgment may require us to cease some or all of our operations or require the payment of substantial amounts. Any of these events could cause our business, financial condition, and results of operations to be adversely affected as a result.
p610: We also offer to indemnify our contract counterparties for certain third-party infringement claims against them, and such indemnification obligations may be excluded from contractual limitation of liability provisions that limit our exposure. In certain cases, our indemnification obligations may be broad or unlimited in scope, which could expose us to significant contingent liabilities, particularly given the unsettled nature of intellectual property law as applied to AI-generated outputs and the potential for claims to arise from a wide range of customer use cases that we cannot predict or control. For example, certain of our agreements require us to defend and indemnify the counterparty, without a cap on our liability, against third-party claims alleging that our models, or outputs generated by our models, infringe third-party intellectual property rights. In addition, as described in the section titled “—We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” certain of our agreements with external evaluators and testing vendors require us to defend and indemnify the evaluator, without a cap on our liability, against certain third-party claims, including claims of intellectual property infringement. Third-party infringement claims may require us to initiate or defend protracted and costly litigation on behalf of our customers and distribution partners, regardless of the merits of these claims. If any of these claims succeed, we may be forced to pay damages on behalf of our customers and reseller partners, may be required to modify our allegedly infringing models, platform, and applications to make them non-infringing, or may be required to obtain licenses under the infringed intellectual property rights. If we cannot obtain all necessary licenses on commercially reasonable terms or are unable to modify our models, platform, and applications or technology so that they are no longer infringing, our customers may be forced to stop using our models, platform, and applications, and our distribution partners may be forced to stop selling our models, platform, and applications. Even if we do not litigate these matters to a judgment, we may be required to settle such litigation on terms that are unfavorable to us.
p611: Our success is dependent, in part, upon protecting our intellectual property rights and proprietary information. We rely and expect to continue to rely on a combination of trademark, copyright, patent, and trade secret protection laws, along with contractual restrictions, to protect our intellectual property rights and proprietary information. However, we cannot guarantee that the steps we take to protect our intellectual property rights and proprietary information will be sufficient, or that we will have adequate remedies for any such failure. In particular, current or former employees, contractors, or other insiders with access to our proprietary model weights, training data, algorithms, research insights, or other proprietary information, could misappropriate such information, whether for personal gain, to benefit competitors, to harm our company, or for other purposes, and our confidentiality agreements and internal security controls may not be sufficient to prevent or detect such malfeasance.
p612: Further, third parties have in the past, and may in the future, knowingly or unknowingly infringe or circumvent our intellectual property rights, and we may not be able to prevent infringement without incurring substantial expense. Litigation brought to protect and enforce our intellectual property rights has been, and would be, costly, time-consuming, and distracting to management and key personnel, and could result in the impairment or loss of portions of our intellectual property rights. Further, our efforts to enforce our intellectual property rights may be met with defenses, counterclaims, and countersuits attacking the validity and enforceability of our intellectual property rights and may result in injunctive relief or monetary damages against us. If the protection of our intellectual property rights is inadequate to prevent use or misappropriation by third parties, the value of our brand and other intangible assets may be diminished and competitors may be able to more effectively mimic our models, platform, and applications and methods of operations. In addition, due to the significant amount of discovery required in connection with intellectual property litigation, our confidential information may be compromised by disclosure during litigation. Any of these events would have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p613: Our future success and competitive position depend in part upon our ability to obtain or maintain certain intellectual property rights used in our models, platform, and applications. While we have issued patents and have patent applications pending, we may be unable to obtain patent protection for the technology covered in our patent applications. In addition, we cannot ensure that any of the patent applications will be granted or that the claims allowed on any issued patents will be sufficiently broad to protect our technology or models, platform, and applications and provide us with competitive advantages. Further, any issued patents may be challenged, invalidated, or circumvented by third parties.
p614: Many patent applications in the United States may not be public for a period of time after they are filed, and since publication of discoveries in the scientific or patent literature tends to lag behind actual discoveries by several months, we cannot be certain that we will be the first creator of inventions covered by any patent application we make or that we will be the first to file patent applications on such inventions. Because some patent applications may not be public for a period of time, there is also a risk that we could adopt a technology without knowledge of a pending patent application, which technology would infringe a third-party patent once that patent is issued.
p615: We also rely on unpatented proprietary technology. It is possible that others will independently develop the same or similar technology or otherwise obtain access to our unpatented technology. To protect our trade secrets and other proprietary information, our policy requires employees, consultants, and independent contractors to enter into confidentiality agreements. We cannot guarantee that these agreements will provide sufficient protection for our trade secrets, know-how, or other proprietary information in the event of any unauthorized use, misappropriation, or disclosure of such trade secrets, know-how, or other proprietary information, or that the employee, consultant or independent contractor will not breach their confidentiality agreements with us. If we are unable to maintain the proprietary nature of our technologies, our business could be adversely affected.
p616: We also rely on our trademarks, trade names, and brand names to distinguish our models, platform, and applications from the products of our competitors and have registered or applied to register many of these trademarks in the United States and certain countries outside the United States. However, occasionally third parties have registered and acquired, and may in the future register or acquire, common law rights in identical or similar marks for products or solutions that also address similar markets to our own and have tried to enforce such rights. As we rely in part on brand names and trademark protection to enforce our intellectual property rights, efforts by third parties to limit use of our brand names or trademarks and barriers to the registration of brand names and trademarks in various countries may restrict our ability to promote and maintain a cohesive brand throughout our key markets. There can also be no assurance that pending or future U.S. or non-U.S. trademark applications will be approved in a timely manner or at all, or that such registrations will effectively protect our brand names and trademarks. Additionally, third parties have opposed, and may in the future oppose, our trademark applications or otherwise challenge our use of the trademarks. In the event that our trademarks are successfully challenged, we could be forced to rebrand our models, platform, and applications, which would result in loss of brand recognition and would require us to devote resources to advertising and marketing new brands. Although we take measures to protect our property, if we are unable to prevent the theft of our intellectual property or its exploitation, the value of our investments may be undermined and our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.
p617: A portion of the technologies we use in our models, platform, and applications incorporates open-source software, and we may incorporate open-source software in our models, platform, and applications in the future. From time to time, companies that use third-party open-source software have faced claims challenging the use of such open-source software and their compliance with the terms of the applicable open-source license. We may be subject to suits by parties claiming ownership of what we believe to be open-source software or claiming non-compliance with the applicable open-source licensing terms. Some open-source licenses require end-users who distribute or make available across a network software that includes open-source software to make available all or part of such software (which may include valuable proprietary code), at no cost, or license such software under the terms of the particular open-source license. While we employ practices designed to help ensure our compliance with the licenses of third-party open-source software and protect our valuable proprietary source code, we may inadvertently use third-party open-source software in a manner that exposes us to claims of non-compliance with the applicable terms of such license, including claims for infringement of intellectual property rights or for breach of contract. These risks may be heightened by our use of our own AI tools, including Claude Code, in our software development processes, as AI-generated code could incorporate or reproduce open-source software such that the associated license obligations, including copyleft requirements to disclose or license proprietary source code, apply to us without our knowledge. Similar concerns regarding AI- generated code could also lead enterprise customers to limit their use of our products. Further, there is an increasing number of open-source software license types, almost none of which have been tested in a court of law, resulting in a dearth of judicial guidance regarding the proper legal interpretation of such license types. If a third party makes a claim against us alleging that we have not complied with the conditions of the applicable open-source license, we could incur significant legal expenses defending against such allegations, expend substantial time and resources to re-engineer some or all of our software, and could be subject to significant damages, enjoined from the sale of our models, platform, and applications that contained the open-source software, and required to comply with the conditions of the open-source license, which may include the public release of certain portions of our proprietary source code, each of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p618: In addition to risks related to license requirements, use of open-source software can lead to greater risks than use of third-party commercial software because open-source licensors generally do not provide warranties or other contractual protections regarding misappropriation, misuse, infringement, ownership, misattribution, or other violations, the quality of the code, or the origin of the open-source software. Many of the risks associated with the use of open-source software cannot be eliminated and may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. For instance, open-source software is developed by programmers beyond our control and may have security vulnerabilities, defects, or errors of which we may not be aware. Even if we become aware of any such vulnerabilities, defects, or errors, it may take a significant amount of time for either us or the relevant programmers to address such vulnerabilities, defects, or errors. Such a delay may negatively impact our models, platform, and applications, including by adversely affecting the market’s perception of our models, platform, and applications, impairing the functionality of our models, platform, and applications, or delaying the launch of new features or functionality on our models, platform, and applications, any of which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p619: We currently incorporate, and may in the future incorporate, technology that we license from third parties into our models, platform, and applications. If we are unable to obtain or continue to use or license these technologies on reasonable terms, or if these technologies become unreliable, unavailable, or fail to operate properly, we may not be able to secure adequate alternatives in a timely manner or at all, and our ability to offer our models, platform, and applications and remain competitive in our market would be harmed. Further, licensing technologies from third parties exposes us to increased risk of being the subject of intellectual property infringement claims and vulnerabilities due to, among other things, our lower level of visibility into the development process with respect to such technology and the care taken to safeguard against risks. We cannot be certain that our licensors do not or will not infringe on the intellectual property rights of third parties or that our licensors have or will have sufficient rights in the licensed technology or related intellectual property rights in all jurisdictions in which we may sell or offer our models, platform, and applications. Some of our agreements with our licensors may be terminated by them or otherwise provide for a limited term. If we are unable to continue to license technology because of intellectual property infringement claims brought by third parties against our licensors or against us, or if we are unable to continue our license agreements or enter into new licenses on commercially reasonable terms, our ability to develop and sell our models, platform, and applications containing or dependent on that technology would be limited, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
p620: Additionally, if we are unable to license technology from third parties, we may be forced to acquire or develop alternative technology, which we may be unable to do in a commercially feasible manner, or at all, and may require us to use alternative technology of lower quality or performance standards. This could limit or delay our ability to offer new or competitive offerings and increase our costs. Third-party software we rely on may be updated infrequently, unsupported, or include errors or vulnerabilities that may not be resolved in a timely manner, any of which may result in errors in our own models, platform, and applications or expose our models, platform, and applications to vulnerabilities. Any impairment of the technologies or of our relationship with these third parties could adversely affect our business, financial condition, or results of operations.
p621: We develop and deploy proprietary and partner-based solutions that replace, deprecate, or reduce our reliance on third-party vendors, including vendors that historically provided software, services, or infrastructure supporting our business. These vendors may perceive our actions as adversely affecting their business interests and may assert claims against us, including claims for breach of contract, intellectual property infringement (including patents, copyrights, or trade secrets), misuse of confidential or proprietary information, tortious interference, or unfair competition.
p622: Such claims may be asserted regardless of their merit and could result in costly litigation, settlements, injunctions, or restrictions on our ability to deploy or expand our models, platform, and applications. Defending against these claims could divert management and key personnel’s attention and resources, require significant legal expenditures, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p623: Our success depends in part on our ability to attract and retain highly skilled employees, including engineers, data scientists, and researchers with experience in AI and machine learning. As competition for AI talent continues to intensify, we have hired and may in the future hire employees who previously worked for or have otherwise been involved with competitors or companies operating in related technology areas, and certain of our employees have left and others may leave to work for such competitors.
p624: These employees may have had access to proprietary or confidential information, including trade secrets, of their former employers. Although we require employees to comply with confidentiality and intellectual property obligations, we may nonetheless be subject to claims that we or our employees have misappropriated or improperly used trade secrets or other intellectual property of competitors or other companies. Such claims may be asserted even if we believe they are without merit and even in the absence of any intentional misconduct.
p625: Defending against these claims could be costly, time-consuming, and disruptive, and could divert management attention and resources away from our business. In addition, such disputes could result in damages, settlements, injunctive relief, restrictions on our ability to use certain technologies, limitations on the roles of certain employees, or reputational harm. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p626: We are subject to claims, lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive and administrative orders and directives, and other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and proceedings, including those involving intellectual property disputes, compliance with regulatory requirements, government approvals and authorizations, labor and employment, anti-discrimination, commercial disputes, competition, privacy, consumer protection, customer complaints, advertising, and other matters relating to our technology, models, platform, and applications, and we may become subject to additional types of claims, lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive and administrative orders and directives, and other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and proceedings as our business grows and as we deploy new technologies, models, platforms, and applications. In particular, as our models, platform, and applications increasingly include agentic AI systems capable of taking autonomous actions with real-world consequences, we may face novel legal theories of liability, including intellectual property infringement, product liability, agency, and negligence claims, that have not been tested in the context of autonomous AI systems and for which the scope of our potential exposure is uncertain. In addition, as we expand our healthcare and life sciences offerings, regulators may conclude that certain of our products, or our customers’ use of them, are subject to healthcare regulation or to other laws governing healthcare and health information, which could require us to obtain authorizations, modify or restrict our offerings, or incur significant compliance costs. Errors or other undesirable outputs from our models in these contexts could contribute to patient harm, compromised research, or regulatory failures by our customers, and could expose us to claims from customers, patients, and other third parties, as well as to regulatory inquiries and enforcement actions.
p627: We are also subject to antitrust and competition law risk arising from our public advocacy regarding AI safety and the responsible pace of AI development and from our participation in industry groups, safety collaborations, and standard-setting initiatives. Communications, advocacy, or collaboration among companies that develop frontier AI models, or conduct alleged to reflect coordination among such companies, may be characterized as concerted action subject to the antitrust and competition laws, including Section 1 of the Sherman Act and analogous state and non-U.S. laws, even where undertaken for safety purposes, conducted publicly, or intended as advocacy for governmental action or industry standards. In September 2026, a putative class action was filed against us and other developers of frontier AI models in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging that we and the other defendants agreed to restrain competition by slowing the pace at which we develop and improve our respective AI models, in purported violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The complaint seeks treble damages, injunctive relief, and other relief on behalf of a purported class of purchasers of the defendants’ paid consumer subscriptions. We disagree with the claims and intend to defend the matter vigorously, but the outcome of this and any similar proceeding is inherently uncertain.
p628: Antitrust litigation can be complex, protracted, disruptive, and expensive, and an adverse outcome could result in treble damages and injunctive relief. We could also become subject to additional private litigation or to investigations or enforcement actions by the U.S. Department of Justice, the FTC, state attorneys general, or non-U.S. competition authorities. We have proposed public efforts to work with the U.S. government and other developers of frontier AI models to establish safety standards, including with respect to the pace of capability development, and have suggested that such collaboration may warrant a narrow exemption or safe harbor from antitrust laws. These proposals have drawn public opposition from political leaders, some of whom have characterized such efforts as anticompetitive regardless of the purpose of such exemption or safe harbor. There is no assurance that any such exemption or safe harbor will be adopted. Our advocacy for such an exemption, and any safety commitments we pursue with other developers of frontier AI in its absence, could subject us to additional regulatory, litigation, and other risks. These risks may cause us to limit or modify our public advocacy, our participation in industry safety and standard-setting initiatives, and our communications with other developers of frontier AI, which could adversely affect our ability to pursue collaborative approaches to AI safety that we believe are important to our mission.
p629: The results of any such claims, lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive and administrative orders and directives, or other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and proceedings cannot be predicted with any degree of certainty. Any claims, lawsuits, investigations, orders, directives, regulatory actions, or proceedings against us, whether meritorious or not, could adversely affect our revenue, cause potential customers to pause sales discussions, cause existing customers to delay, pause or cancel contracts or seek to modify their contracts, undermine our ability to pursue future contracts, damage our relationships with partners and customers, adversely affect our institutional standing, undermine investor confidence, limit our ability to sell our models, platform, and applications in certain industries, result in costly litigation or regulatory or other defense, adversely affect our reputation, require significant management attention, consume significant time, and divert significant resources.
p630: Determining reserves for our pending litigation or other disputes is a complex and fact-intensive process that requires significant subjective judgment and speculation. It is possible that a resolution of one or more such proceedings could result in substantial damages, settlement costs, fines, and penalties that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Because of the potential risks, expenses, and uncertainties of litigation or other dispute resolution processes, we may, from time to time, settle disputes, even where we have meritorious claims or defenses, by agreeing to settlement agreements, as we did, for example, in Bartz. Moreover, as in Bartz, insurance may not fully cover such claims, provide sufficient payments to cover all the costs to resolve one or more such claims, or continue to be available on terms acceptable to us. A claim brought against us that is uninsured or underinsured could result in unanticipated costs. These proceedings could also result in harm to our reputation and brand, sanctions, consent decrees, injunctions, or other orders requiring a change in our business practices. Further, under certain circumstances, we have contractual and other legal obligations to indemnify and to incur legal expenses on behalf of our business and commercial partners and current and former directors and officers. Any of these consequences could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p631: We are required to comply with the United States Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977, the United Kingdom Bribery Act 2010, and other anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering laws, and similar laws in the United States and non-U.S. countries where we have operations and conduct business. Anticorruption and anti-bribery laws, which have been enforced aggressively and are interpreted broadly, prohibit companies and their employees, agents, intermediaries, and other third parties from, among other things, promising, authorizing, making, or offering improper payments or other benefits to government officials and other persons in the public and private sector.
p632: We leverage third parties, including intermediaries and agents, to conduct our business and to sell our models, platform, and applications, and in connection with lobbying and other activities. We and these third parties have in the past and may in the future have direct or indirect interactions with officials and employees of government agencies, including state-owned or state-affiliated entities, and we potentially could be held liable for the corrupt or other illegal activities of third-party business partners and intermediaries, our employees, representatives, contractors, partners, agents, and other third parties, even if we do not explicitly authorize such parties’ activities.
p633: We cannot ensure that our policies and procedures to address compliance with these anti-corruption and antimoney laundering laws will be effective, or that all of our employees, representatives, contractors, partners, agents, intermediaries, or other third parties have not taken, or will not take, actions that violate these laws, for which we may be ultimately held liable.
p634: As we increase our non-U.S. sales and business, our risk of violating these laws may increase. Noncompliance with applicable anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws, anti-money laundering, and similar laws could subject us to criminal or civil sanctions, settlements, prosecution, loss of export privileges, suspension or debarment from U.S. government contracts, other enforcement actions, disgorgement of profits, significant fines, damages, other civil and criminal penalties or injunctions, whistleblower complaints, adverse media coverage, and other consequences. Any investigations, actions, or sanctions could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Responding to any investigation or action could result in a significant diversion of management’s attention and resources and significant defense costs and other professional fees.
p635: Our models, platform, and applications are subject to U.S. export controls, and our current or future models, platform, and applications may be controlled under the Export Administration Regulations administered by the U.S. Department of Commerce or, in more limited circumstances, under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (the “ITAR”) administered by the U.S. Department of State. Because the capabilities of our AI models are currently evolving rapidly through ongoing training and frequent model development, and because the export control treatment of AI technologies under relevant laws is developing, the classification of, and controls related to, our models, platform, applications, and technologies under these regimes is inherently uncertain and is likely to change over time. Certain of our models, platform, and applications, and the underlying technology and source code associated with our models, platform, and applications, may require authorization for export, re-export, or transfer in-country, and for individuals of certain nationalities to access such technology or source code, including within the United States.
p636: In particular, our core models, platform, and applications leverage encryption for data protection, and some of our future models, platform, and applications may be able to produce export-controlled software, which may subject exports, re-exports, and transfer of such models, platform, and applications to export authorization requirements.
p637: Our commercially available models, platform, and applications generally can be exported without an export license. However, some exports may require us to obtain authorization from the cognizant government agency. In certain contexts, the provision of our models, platform, and applications may constitute export of defense articles or defense services subject to the ITAR, which can be exported only if we obtain required export licenses or other government authorizations. Compliance with applicable export controls may delay the introduction or sale of our models, platform, and applications outside the United States, restrict our customers’ ability to deploy our models, platform, and applications globally, inhibit our ability to engage in certain research and development activities, limit the performance of our models, platform, and applications, or prohibit exports to certain jurisdictions altogether. Such restrictions have already affected our offerings directly. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. To ensure compliance, we disabled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all of our customers; access to our other models was not affected. We re-deployed the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models after we updated our safeguards in coordination with the U.S. government and our industry partners and once the U.S. Department of Commerce lifted its restrictions. Similar export controls could recur, could remain in place longer, or could extend to additional models or capabilities. In addition, future updates to our safeguards or other remedial measures may not be sufficient to obtain relief from such restrictions or relief may not be granted on a similar timeline or at all. The restrictions imposed in June 2026 and potential restrictions in the future may also limit our ability to recruit talent, to fully utilize our existing workforce, to continue to improve our models, and to make our products available internationally. Any such restrictions could adversely affect our financial results; impair the research, compute, and development investment our models represent; and cause us to lose customers, partners, and market share, including to competitors not subject to similar restrictions.
p638: Further, our activities are subject to economic, financial, and trade sanctions administered by the United States and other countries. Economic, financial, and trade sanctions restrict or prohibit providing certain services and engaging in certain transactions or other activities or dealings with individuals, entities, organizations, governments, territories, and countries targeted by or the subject of these sanctions. These restrictions, as well as other applicable international trade rules, are subject to change with little to no notice. In addition, U.S. law increasingly authorizes the U.S. government to restrict or review the use of hardware, software, and services originating from, or linked to, countries it designates as adversaries, including such technology incorporated into the supply chains for the data centers and compute infrastructure on which we depend. Such restrictions could narrow our choice of suppliers, delay our infrastructure projects, or increase our costs, and any noncompliance could result in penalties, loss of contracting privileges, or reputational harm.
p639: We take various steps to comply with applicable export controls and sanctions, including: maintaining a global trade policy and a supported regions policy, implementing IP-based geo-blocking controls that restrict access from certain jurisdictions to our models, platform, and applications, conducting restricted party screening of certain customers and vendors, and including sanctions and export compliance provisions in our customer terms of service and vendor agreements. However, we cannot guarantee the compliance measures and internal controls we have adopted will prevent violations of applicable export controls and sanctions. Our compliance measures and internal controls have not always been and may not always be fully effective, and we have in the past voluntarily disclosed, and may in the future voluntarily disclose, instances of noncompliance to the relevant authorities. We cannot guarantee that our measures will prevent future violations or keep pace with the changing substance, application, and interpretation of export controls and sanctions. In addition, third parties have in the past and may in the future take action to circumvent our compliance measures and controls in order to gain access to our products and services.
p640: If we misclassify a product or service, export, re-export, transfer, or provide access to a product, or provide services in violation of applicable export controls or sanctions, or otherwise fail to comply with applicable export controls or sanctions, we could be subject to criminal or civil sanctions, settlements, prosecution, loss of export privileges, suspension or debarment from U.S. government contracts, other enforcement actions, disgorgement of profits, significant fines, damages, other civil and criminal penalties or injunctions, whistleblower complaints, adverse media coverage, and other consequences. Any investigations, actions, or sanctions could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Responding to any investigation or action could result in a significant diversion of management’s attention and resources and significant defense costs and other professional fees.
p641: Decreased use of our models, platform, and applications by customers outside the United States or a limitation on our ability to export, provide access to, or sell our models, platform, and applications to customers and other parties outside the United States may cause our revenue from such unsupported jurisdictions to decline and otherwise adversely affect our business and financial condition.
p642: If we or our business partners or counterparties, including licensors and licensees, prime contractors, subcontractors, sublicensors, vendors, customers, or contractors, violate export controls or sanctions, including by failing to obtain appropriate import, export, or re-export licenses or permits, or if we fail to secure such contractual commitments from such parties, we may also be adversely affected through reputational harm as well as other negative consequences, including government investigations or penalties.
p643: Negative consequences stemming from violations or apparent violations of export controls or sanctions may include the loss of the right to sell our models, platform, and applications or services to the U.S. government, or to other U.S. or non-U.S. public bodies, or a reduction in our ability to compete for such sales opportunities involving government agencies or other public bodies. Further, ensuring that we are complying with applicable export controls and sanctions regulations may be time-consuming and could result in the delay or loss of sales opportunities in connection with particular transactions.
p644: Also, in addition to the United States, various countries regulate the import and export of certain encryption and other technology and have enacted laws that could limit our ability to distribute our models, platform, and applications or could limit our customers’ abilities to implement our models, platform, and applications in those countries. For example, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the United States and other countries imposed financial and trade sanctions and export controls against Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine, and the United States and other countries could impose wider sanctions and export restrictions and take other actions should the conflict further escalate. Any new export restrictions, new legislation, changes in sanctions, or shifting approaches in the enforcement or scope of existing regulations, or in the individuals, entities, governments, territories, countries, or technologies targeted by or subject to such regulations could result in decreased use of our models, platform, and applications by existing customers outside of the United States, reduced adoption of our models, platform, and applications by new customers with non-U.S. operations, limited expansion into new markets, and decreased revenue.
p645: We are a U.S.-headquartered company with extensive U.S. operations, as well as subsidiaries and operations in several other countries and regions, including the UK, the EU, Canada, and Asia-Pacific, and we expect that our future growth will depend in part on expanding our operations, customer base, and market presence in additional jurisdictions. Operating in non-U.S. markets requires significant resources and management attention and subjects us to regulatory, economic, and political risks that are different from those in the United States. As we continue to expand internationally, we have faced and will continue to face risks in doing business internationally that could adversely affect our business, including:
p646: • the need to localize and adapt our models, platform, and applications for specific countries, including translation into foreign languages and associated expenses;
p647: • privacy laws, export controls, sanctions, and other national security regulations that impose different and potentially conflicting obligations with respect to how personal data is processed or require that customer data be stored in a designated territory;
p648: • laws in certain jurisdictions that may compel our personnel, vendors, or facility operators to provide governmental authorities with access to our systems, data, or other information, in some cases without notice to us and with limited means of recourse;
p649: • national security-driven data security regulations. For example, the Department of Justice issued a final rule, effective in April 2025, that places limitations, and in some cases prohibitions, on certain transfers of covered data to partners, service providers, and vendors, employees, and investors located in China or with other specified links to China (and other designated countries). We may be required to re-examine current contracts or engage in new contract negotiations with third parties that aid in processing data on our behalf or otherwise have access to covered data. These rules also may broadly require us to extract promises from other third-party service providers that they will not transfer data we share with them onward to parties linked to countries of concern;
p650: • import regulations, including U.S. and non-U.S. governments’ restrictive trade policies, customs duties and other parallel regulations, tariffs and counter-measures;
p651: • AI, data-related, cybersecurity and digital service laws and regulations (such as the EU AI Act, NIS2, the EU Digital Services Act, the UK Online Safety Act 2023, and the EU Data Act) that are rapidly evolving, require continuous monitoring to ensure constant compliance maturity level, and often provide for substantial penalties in the event of a violation;
p652: • difficulties in staffing and managing non-U.S. operations, including the complexity of engaging in various employer-of-record arrangements that are geographically dispersed, and the risk that these arrangements, or any failure to establish local employing entities on a timely basis, may not comply with local employment, labor, or tax laws, exposing us to fines, penalties, reclassification or backpayment claims;
p653: • difficulties of maintaining our culture across various jurisdictions;
p654: • regulatory and other delays and difficulties in setting up non-U.S. operations, including delays in forming, registering, and obtaining governmental approvals for local subsidiaries, delays in establishing local banking, payroll, and benefits arrangements, and difficulties relating to safety of personnel and information, any of which could delay local hiring efforts;
p655: • the potential need for reviews by the U.S. government or non-U.S. governments of certain transactions with non-U.S. entities;
p656: • different pricing environments, longer sales cycles, longer accounts receivable payment cycles, and collections issues;
p657: • new and different sources of competition;
p658: • weaker protection for, and practical difficulties in enforcing, intellectual property and other legal rights outside of the United States compared to protections available domestically;
p659: • laws and business practices favoring local competitors;
p660: • compliance challenges related to the complexity of multiple, conflicting, and changing governmental laws and regulations, including copyright, employment, tax, privacy, and data protection laws and regulations, export controls, and sanctions;
p661: • parties outside the United States seeking to circumvent sanctions and export controls;
p662: • increased financial accounting and reporting burdens and complexities;
p663: • increased costs in establishing infrastructure across various jurisdictions;
p664: • declines in the values of foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar;
p665: • restrictions on the transfer of funds;
p667: • the cost of and potential outcomes of any claims or litigation;
p668: • future accounting pronouncements and changes in accounting policies;
p669: • changes in tax laws or tax regulations; and
p670: • regional and local economic and political conditions.
p671: Entry into certain transactions with non-U.S. entities or persons may be subject to government regulations and review, including review by U.S. or non-U.S. government entities related to contemplated or past foreign direct investment (“FDI”). In recent years, many countries around the world have adopted FDI regulatory regimes that seek to scrutinize investments into, and acquisitions of, domestic companies by non-domestic parties, granting governments broad discretion to review contemplated and past investment and acquisition transactions. These FDI regimes may restrict our ability to attract investments, invest in or fund partners outside of the United States that build or operate data centers or supply infrastructure for us, or acquire promising new technologies, companies, and talent in countries around the world, potentially limiting our ability to carry out our business strategy.
p672: More broadly, increasing geopolitical tensions, shifting national security priorities, and evolving technologyfocused trade, export control, investment, and data-governance regimes may result in restrictions, heightened scrutiny, or other limitations on our ability to operate, sell products, partner with customers, or deploy our models in certain jurisdictions or with certain counterparties. Governments may adopt or expand policies aimed at protecting domestic technology ecosystems, restricting the cross-border flow of data, or limiting access to AI systems, which could reduce our addressable market, increase compliance costs, or require operational changes. In particular, the U.S. government has increasingly scrutinized AI companies’ exposure to Chinese state actors, and future executive orders, legislation, or regulatory actions could restrict our ability to serve customers or users connected to China, impose new compliance obligations, lead us to implement anti-abuse mechanisms or other technical access restrictions, or limit the deployment of our models in ways that reduce our addressable market. Any escalation of U.S.-China tensions, retaliatory measures by either government, or failure or perceived failure by us to prevent non-U.S. state-actor access to or misuse of our technology could subject us to regulatory action, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p673: As we continue to expand our business globally, our success will depend, in large part, on our ability to anticipate and effectively manage these risks. These factors and others could adversely affect our ability to increase non-U.S. revenue and, consequently, could materially impact our business. The expansion of our existing non-U.S. operations and entry into additional non-U.S. markets will require significant management attention and financial resources. Our failure to successfully manage our non-U.S. operations and the associated risks effectively could limit the future growth of our business.
p674: Companies across many industries are facing increasing scrutiny related to their environmental, social, and governance (“ESG”) practices and reporting, both in the United States and internationally. For example, new U.S. and non-U.S. laws and regulations relating to ESG matters, including environmental sustainability and climate change, are under consideration, being adopted, or being rolled back or revised, which may impact our necessary disclosures and increase compliance costs. Further, there is particular focus on concerns relating to AI and its impact on society and the environment, including the power-intensive nature of the industry, public concern regarding high consumption of water, and reliance on critical minerals and rare elements in the manufacture of chips. Some investors may use these non-financial performance factors to guide their investment strategies and, in some cases, may choose not to invest in us if they believe our policies and actions relating to ESG are inadequate.
p675: Our sustainability initiatives, goals, or commitments could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement. Moreover, compliance with recently adopted and potential upcoming ESG requirements, including California legislation that requires various climate-related disclosures, the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, and the UK’s Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting framework will require the dedication of significant time and resources. At the same time, anti-ESG sentiment has gained momentum across the United States, particularly at the federal level, and the federal and certain state governments have enacted or proposed “anti-ESG” policies or legislation or have issued related legal opinions. Such policies, legislation, initiatives, and scrutiny could expose any sustainability, employment, governance, or other corporate practices we adopt to the risk of litigation, antitrust investigations or challenges by federal or state authorities, and result in injunctions, penalties, and reputational harm.
p676: Additionally, if our competitors’ corporate social responsibility performance is perceived to be better than ours, potential or current investors may elect to invest with our competitors instead. Our business may face increased scrutiny related to these activities and our related disclosures, including from the investment community and the local communities in which we operate, and our failure to achieve progress or manage the dynamic, and at times conflicting, public sentiment and legal landscape in these areas on a timely basis, or at all, could adversely affect our reputation, business, and financial condition. Further, we may experience backlash from customers, government entities, advocacy groups, employees, or other stakeholders who disagree with our actual or perceived positions, or with our lack of position on social, environmental, governance, political, public policy, economic, geopolitical, or other sensitive issues. Any perceived lack of transparency about these matters could adversely affect our brand and reputation, our employees’ engagement and retention, and the willingness of our customers and partners to do business with us. Both advocates and opponents to ESG-related matters are increasingly resorting to a range of activism forms, including media campaigns and litigation, to advance their perspectives. To the extent we are subject to such activism, it may require us to incur costs or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, or results of operations.
p677: A portion of our customers authorize us to bill their credit card accounts through our third-party payment processing partners for our paid subscriptions. We have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, fraudulent activity, including the creation of accounts using false identities and the use of stolen or otherwise unauthorized payment credentials, which has resulted, and may in the future result, in losses, including payment processing fees, chargeback fees, and fines and penalties imposed by our payment processors or card networks, for which we may not be reimbursed. We maintain fraud-detection and identity-verification measures, but these measures have not identified, and may not identify, all such activity. Further, our customers provide us with credit card billing information online, and we do not verify the physical identity of cardholders or conduct additional verification beyond what we collect online, which increases our risk of exposure to fraudulent activity.
p678: We also incur chargebacks when customers or card issuers claim that a transaction was unauthorized or otherwise improper. If the volume of chargebacks were to become excessive, we could be subject to higher processing fees, additional fines, fraud mitigation requirements, or the termination or suspension of our ability to accept certain payment methods, including credit cards, through one or more payment processors.
p679: In addition, payment processors, card networks, and financial institutions periodically revise their rules, standards, and practices, including data protection and documentation standards, required to utilize their services from time to time. Our compliance with these evolving requirements, and the continued compliance of our third-party payment processing partners, may require additional operational resources and expense. Failure by us or our payment processing partners to comply with applicable standards could result in fines, increased scrutiny, disruptions to our business and our ability to process payments for our intelligence service, or reputational harm.
p680: We operate in multiple jurisdictions and are subject to tax laws and regulations of U.S. federal, state, and local and non-U.S. governments. Income, sales, use, or other tax laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances could be enacted or amended at any time (possibly with retroactive effect) and could be applied solely or disproportionately to models, platforms, and applications provided over the internet. These enactments or amendments could reduce our sales activity due to the inherent cost increase the taxes would represent and ultimately harm our results of operations and cash flows. Further, the application of U.S. federal, state, local, and non-U.S. tax laws to services provided electronically is unclear and continuously evolving. Existing tax laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances could be interpreted or applied adversely to us, possibly with retroactive effect, which could require us or our customers to pay additional tax amounts, as well as fines or penalties, and interest for past amounts. If we are unsuccessful in collecting such taxes due from our customers, we would be held liable for such costs, thereby adversely affecting our results of operations and harming our business.
p681: As we expand the scale of our non-U.S. business activities, any changes in the U.S. or non-U.S. taxation of such activities may increase our worldwide effective tax rate and harm our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may be subject to taxation in several jurisdictions around the world with increasingly complex tax laws, the application of which can be uncertain. In addition, our hiring of personnel and engagement of third-party employer-of-record providers in non-U.S. jurisdictions, as well as our data center and other infrastructure activities outside the United States, have created, and may in the future create, permanent establishments or other taxable presence in those jurisdictions, which could subject us to additional income, withholding, and indirect taxes, as well as interest, penalties, and additional compliance obligations. In advance of forming and obtaining approvals for local operating entities, we have entered into, and expect to enter into additional letters of intent, leases, and other agreements relating to our international compute and infrastructure activities through interim contracting arrangements with existing entities, and we may be unable to transfer these arrangements to local entities on a timely basis or at all. Any prolonged reliance on these interim arrangements, or any failure to migrate them to local entities, could increase our exposure to permanent establishment or other taxable-presence determinations and could result in non-recoverable valueadded or similar indirect taxes, which could be material in certain jurisdictions. Although we have not been required to pay income taxes, other than in immaterial amounts in certain jurisdictions to date, the amount of taxes we pay in these jurisdictions could increase substantially as a result of changes in the applicable tax principles, including increased tax rates, new tax laws, or revised interpretations of existing tax laws and precedents, which could adversely affect our liquidity and results of operations. For example, a number of countries and organizations, such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (“OECD”), have proposed changes to existing tax laws or new laws that could impact our tax obligations, including a framework that imposes a 15% global minimum tax, which has been implemented into the domestic laws of some jurisdictions in the EU, among other jurisdictions, and is being considered for implementation by other countries. On January 5, 2026, the OECD announced a “side-by-side” elective safe harbor that exempts electing U.S.-parented multinational entities from certain provisions of the global minimum tax for fiscal years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. In addition, the authorities in these jurisdictions could review our tax returns and impose additional tax, interest, and penalties, and the authorities could claim that various withholding requirements apply to us or our subsidiaries or assert that benefits of tax treaties are not available to us or our subsidiaries, any of which would harm us and our results of operations.
p682: We collect sales tax in a number of jurisdictions. Sales, use, value added, digital service, and similar tax laws and rates vary by jurisdiction. One or more states or countries may seek to impose incremental or new sales, use, or other tax collection obligations on us. A successful assertion by a state, country, or other jurisdiction that we should have been or should be collecting additional sales, use, or other taxes could, among other things, result in substantial tax payments, create significant administrative burdens for us, discourage potential customers from subscribing to our models, platform, and applications due to the incremental cost of any such sales or other related taxes, or otherwise harm our business, financial condition, and results of operations. Further, certain jurisdictions in which we operate have enacted a digital services tax, which is generally a tax on gross revenue generated from users or customers located in those jurisdictions, and other jurisdictions are considering enacting similar laws. Any successful action by taxing authorities to compel us to collect and remit sales, use, value added, digital service, and similar tax laws, either retroactively, prospectively, or both, may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
p683: We have incurred substantial net operating losses (“NOLs”) during our history. In general, under Sections 382 and 383 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), a corporation that undergoes an “ownership change” is subject to annual limitations on its ability to utilize its pre-change U.S. federal NOL carryforwards and certain other tax attributes, including tax credit carryforwards, to offset its future taxable income or tax liabilities. For these purposes, an ownership change generally occurs if the percentage of a corporation’s stock (by value) owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50 percentage points over a rolling three-year period. We have experienced ownership changes in the past, and we may experience ownership changes in the future, including as a result of this offering or subsequent shifts in our stock ownership, some of which may be outside our control. NOLs and other tax attributes of companies we have acquired are, and of companies we may acquire may be, subject to similar limitations. Similar provisions of state tax law and the tax laws of non-U.S. jurisdictions may also limit our ability to utilize state and non-U.S. NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes. In addition, certain states, including California, have suspended or otherwise limited the use of NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes, which could accelerate or permanently increase our state income tax liabilities. Separately, under current law, U.S. federal NOLs arising in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017 may be used to offset only 80% of taxable income in any year, whether or not an ownership change occurs. As a result of the foregoing, even if we attain profitability, we may be unable to use all or a material portion of our NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect our future cash flows and results of operations.
p684: As we continue to expand our non-U.S. operations, we are, and may increasingly be, required to report taxable income in various jurisdictions around the world based on our business activities in those jurisdictions. Our corporate structure and associated transfer pricing policies reflect the functions, risks, and assets of the entities involved in our intercompany transactions. However, our tax position is subject to various risks, including increases in tax rates, new or revised tax laws (which may apply retroactively), and new interpretations of existing tax laws and policies by taxing authorities or courts, any of which could increase our overall tax obligations.
p685: Our intercompany transactions are subject to complex transfer pricing rules administered by tax authorities in the jurisdictions in which we operate, many of which apply divergent, and sometimes conflicting, legal standards. Tax authorities may take inconsistent positions regarding the application of the arm’s-length principle, the characterization or valuation of our intellectual property, or the pricing of intercompany services and other transactions. If a tax authority successfully challenges our transfer pricing or the allocation of income and expenses among jurisdictions, we could be required to reallocate income or pay additional taxes, interest, and penalties.
