p1056: Since inception, we have financed our operations, corporate investments, and capital expenditures primarily through proceeds from the issuance of convertible promissory notes, redeemable convertible preferred stock, cash generated from sales, and SAFEs. To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily under arrangements with our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above and cash generated from operations. As of June 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion, $19.3 billion of short-term investments, and $3.2 billion available under the Credit Facility, as described below. Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase.
p1057: We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of $132.9 billion, which includes $113.2 billion related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including $72.4 billion during the six months ended June 30, 2026. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in 2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We continue to invest in our own data center infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand for our intelligence service. Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of anticipated demand. To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery. These investments help ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI.
p1058: Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out, and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. Our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly affect our cash flows for a given period. In addition, these investments are subject to known trends and uncertainties that could adversely affect our results of operations. The compute and chips necessary for frontier model development are available from a limited number of suppliers and geographies and are subject to intense competition, supply constraints, and evolving export controls, and we have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs and chip partners on which we rely provide us capital or credit support, serve as our infrastructure vendors, and develop and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest that affect our access to compute, its cost, the prioritization of our workloads, or the terms on which such capital or credit support is provided. For a discussion of these and other risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors.”
p1059: We believe our existing available cash and cash equivalents, together with cash generated from sales and amounts available under our A&R Credit Facility (as defined below), will be sufficient to support working capital, operating and finance lease payments, and capital expenditure requirements for at least the next 12 months from the date of this prospectus. However, our future capital requirements will depend on many factors, including our revenue growth, the timing and extent of our investments in compute and infrastructure capacity, including additional or expanded CSP, equipment lease, and data center arrangements, the success and expansion of our sales, marketing, and business development strategies, any potential future investment in complementary businesses, products, technologies, assets, and talent, risks associated with the AI industry, and other factors described under “Key Factors Affecting Our Performance.” As a result of these and other factors, we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate. Even if we determine that additional financing is required, we may not be able to raise it on terms acceptable to us or at all. Any such financing, if completed, may be costly, dilutive, or lead to restrictions on how we operate our business. If we are unable to raise additional capital when required, or if we cannot expand our operations or otherwise capitalize on our business opportunities because we lack sufficient capital, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows would be adversely affected.
p1060: Over the longer term, we expect to have significant cash requirements as we continue to invest in our business, primarily for compute and infrastructure, including our data center infrastructure build-out, as well as for general operating needs. We expect to fund these long-term cash requirements through a combination of cash flows from operations, proceeds from equity financings, including the net proceeds from this offering, proceeds from debt financings and potential future indebtedness, and financing arrangements with our partners, including under our note purchase agreements and our equipment lease and data center arrangements. Our ability to meet these requirements over the long term depends on our ability to grow our revenue and generate cash flows from operations and to access additional capital on acceptable terms. If sufficient funds are not available, we may be required to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, which could adversely affect our business, competitive position, and results of operations.
p1061: In May 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit Agreement (as defined below), the “Credit Agreement”) with certain lenders from time to time party thereto and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion (the Initial Credit Facility, as amended, the “Credit Facility”). As of June 30, 2026, we had no borrowings drawn under the Credit Facility and $78 million of standby letters of credit outstanding. As of June 30, 2026, we were in compliance with all covenants under the Credit Agreement.
p1062: In September 2026, we entered into an Amended and Restated Credit Agreement (the “A&R Credit Agreement”), which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit (the “A&R Credit Facility”). The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than $500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement.
p1063: We may borrow, repay, and reborrow amounts under the A&R Credit Facility from time to time. We are required to pay commitment fees on the unused portion of the A&R Credit Facility and fees in connection with letters of credit. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date (as defined below), such commitment fees will vary depending on our credit ratings, as set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. Our obligations under the A&R Credit Facility are required to be guaranteed by certain of our material subsidiaries and secured by substantially all of our assets and the assets of such subsidiary guarantors, subject to certain exceptions and exclusions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The A&R Credit Agreement further provides that, on and after the date we have obtained an Investment Grade Rating (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement) from at least two out of three of Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch, at our election, all guarantees and security interests securing the obligations under the A&R Credit Facility will be released, discharged, and terminated, subject to certain conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement (such date, the “Guarantee and Collateral Release Date”).
p1064: Borrowings under the A&R Credit Facility bear interest at rates based on either the Alternate Base Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), Term SOFR Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), or other applicable benchmark rates in the case of foreign currencies, plus an applicable margin. From and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, such applicable margin will vary depending on our credit ratings, as more fully set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. In addition, the A&R Credit Agreement includes customary affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to, restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens, asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, the negative covenants limiting asset sales, investments, restricted payments, and affiliate transactions will cease to apply and the negative covenants restricting additional indebtedness and liens will be modified in certain respects, including to permit additional indebtedness, subject to a cap on certain indebtedness that is secured by assets that do not secure the A&R Credit Facility or that is incurred or guaranteed by restricted subsidiaries that are not guarantors under the A&R Credit Facility. The A&R Credit Agreement includes a financial covenant requiring that we maintain liquidity of at least $5.0 billion as of the last day of each fiscal quarter, beginning with the fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2026. The A&R Credit Agreement also includes customary events of default, which, if triggered, could result in the acceleration of amounts due under the A&R Credit Facility and termination of the commitments thereunder.
p1065: In July 2026, we entered into a hardware supply framework agreement (the “Hardware Supply Agreement”) with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (“AMD”) to purchase, lease, or access AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems featuring AMD Instinct™ MI450 series GPUs. Pursuant to the terms of the Hardware Supply Agreement, AMD has provided a commitment to purchase up to $5.0 billion of our Class N common stock, which becomes available for us to draw on in increments following the achievement of specified AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones. Based on the deployment schedule contemplated by the Hardware Supply Agreement, we expect the first of such milestones to be achieved in 2027. Following the completion of this offering, any purchases of our Class N common stock will be made at a price per share equal to the volume-weighted average price of our Class A common stock over the 30 trading days immediately preceding the applicable closing date of such purchase, and we must make any draw request within 12 months following the final delivery and deployment of AMD GPU capacity under the Hardware Supply Agreement.

p1128: We believe that of our significant accounting policies, which are described in Note 1 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus, the following accounting policies involve a greater degree of judgment and complexity. p1129: We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions.
p1130: We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur.
p1131: The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock-based awards. These variables include:
p1132: ▪ Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “— Common Stock Valuations” below.
p1133: ▪ Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options.
p1134: • Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term.
p1135: • Risk-free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options.
p1136: • Expected Dividend Yield. The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any dividends and have no current plans to do so.
p1137: As of June 30, 2026, there was approximately $2.8 billion of total unrecognized compensation cost related to unvested stock options, which is expected to be recognized over a weighted-average period of 1.2 years.
p1138: We have granted RSUs to our employees and non-employee service providers under our 2021 Plan. RSUs outstanding as of June 30, 2026 have both service-based and performance-based vesting conditions. The service-based vesting period for these awards is typically four years. Upon satisfaction of the performance condition, RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition has also been satisfied will vest immediately, and any remaining unvested RSUs will vest ratably over the remaining service period. The performance condition is generally satisfied upon the occurrence of a change in control event or the effective date of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part.
p1139: As of June 30, 2026, no stock-based compensation expense had been recognized for such RSUs because the performance condition was not satisfied. In connection with this offering, we will begin recording stock-based compensation expense based on the grant-date fair value of the RSUs using the accelerated attribution method. As of June 30, 2026, there was approximately $26.6 billion of total unrecognized stock-based compensation expense related to RSUs. Of that amount, $2.9 billion relates to RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition had been satisfied or partially satisfied. Following the completion of this offering, stock-based compensation expense related to our RSUs will result in increases in our expenses in future periods, in particular the quarter in which this offering is completed, as the performance-based vesting condition applicable to a significant portion of our outstanding RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part. Upon the completion of this offering, we will record cumulative stock-based compensation expense of approximately $ related to RSUs outstanding as of the date of this prospectus, for which (i) the service-based vesting condition is fully or partially satisfied as of such date and (ii) the performance-based vesting condition is satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part.
p1140: We have granted RSAs to founders, early employees, advisors, and in connection with acquisitions. The RSAs consist of awards with a service-based vesting condition. RSAs are measured at fair value of the underlying common stock on the date of grant. We record compensation cost for these awards using the straight-line method over the requisite service period.
p1141: Prior to our initial public offering, given the absence of a public trading market of our Class A common stock, and in accordance with the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants Accounting and Valuation Guide, Valuation of Privately-Held Company Equity Securities Issued as Compensation, our board of directors exercised reasonable judgment and considered numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the best estimate of the fair value of our common stock, including:
p1142: • contemporaneous third-party valuations of our common stock;
p1143: • the prices paid for common or redeemable convertible preferred stock sold to third-party investors by us and prices paid in secondary transactions, including any tender offers;
p1144: • the rights, preferences, and privileges of our redeemable convertible preferred stock relative to those of our common stock;
p1145: • actual and forecasted operating and financial performance;
p1148: • the lack of marketability of our common stock;
p1149: • the likelihood of achieving a liquidity event, such as an initial public offering or a sale of our company, given prevailing market conditions;

p1152: Our board of directors determined the fair value of our common stock by first determining the enterprise value of our business and then allocating the value among the various classes of our securities to derive a per share value of our common stock. The enterprise value of our business was primarily estimated by reference to the closest round of equity financing to the date of the valuation.
p1153: In allocating the enterprise value of our business among the various classes of stock prior to this offering, we used a hybrid method based on a contingent claims analysis (“CCA”) and a common stock equivalent (“CSE”) method. The CCA is based on the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model, which models each class of stock as a call option with a unique claim on our assets. The CSE method presumes that all shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock convert into common stock based upon their conversion terms and other differences in the rights and preferences of the shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock are ignored.
p1154: After the allocation of enterprise value to the various classes of stock, a discount for lack of marketability (“DLOM”) is applied to arrive at a fair value of the common stock. A DLOM is meant to account for the lack of opportunity to sell a private company stock that is not traded on public exchanges. In making the final determination of common stock value, consideration is also given to the recent sales and/or expected sales of common stock.
p1155: Application of these approaches involves the use of estimates, judgment, and assumptions that are complex and subjective, such as those regarding our expected future revenue, expenses, and future cash flows, discount rates, market multiples, the selection of comparable companies, and the probability of possible future events. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions or the relationships between those assumptions impact our valuations as of each valuation date and may have a material impact on the valuation of our common stock.
p1156: Following this offering, it will not be necessary to determine the fair value of our common stock, as the shares of our common stock will be traded in the public market.
p1157: We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 825, Financial Instruments. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model.
p1158: In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations.
p1159: The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a scenario-based analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible preferred stock, Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the CCA and CSE framework.
p1160: The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes. In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism— whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is reissued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions, impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized in our consolidated statement of operations.
p1161: The fair value option election described above also applied to the SAFEs that we issued during the year ended December 31, 2023. The SAFEs were measured at estimated fair value using the same scenario-based framework, with the monetary settlement amount fixed at inception and the number of equity shares received upon conversion being variable; consistent with the convertible notes, changes in fair value were recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. All SAFEs were converted into redeemable convertible preferred stock during the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2024, and no SAFEs remained outstanding as of December 31, 2024 or 2025. No SAFEs were outstanding at any point during the six months ended June 30, 2026. Accordingly, the primary ongoing estimation exposure under the fair value option relates to the convertible notes and rollover notes described above.

p1165: We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities for temporary differences between the financial reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities, as well as for net operating loss and credit carryforwards, measured at enacted tax rates applicable in the years of expected reversals. We establish valuation allowances when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts morelikely-than-not expected to be realized, based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence.
p1166: Assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets is an area of significant management judgment. We evaluate our deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable income, reversal patterns of existing temporary differences, and available tax planning strategies. As an AI company operating in a rapidly evolving market with significant ongoing investment in compute and infrastructure, our projections of future taxable income are inherently uncertain. Should our assessment of the recoverability of deferred tax assets change, our income tax provision would be adjusted in that period, which could materially impact our results of operations.
p1167: We account for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC Topic 740, Income Taxes. Tax benefits from uncertain positions are recognized when it is more likely than not that the position will be sustained on examination based on its technical merits, measured at the amount that is more likely than not to be realized upon settlement. These assessments require judgment, particularly with respect to the qualification and documentation of research and development tax credits, where supporting evidence may be subject to differing interpretations. The actual outcome of these matters may differ materially from our current estimates. We recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits within our provision for income taxes.

p1171: For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. AI that truly delivers on its potential—with the risks well managed—could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.
p1172: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $ for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research in frontier AI.
p1173: We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and this process is just beginning. In our view, the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier. Claude’s capabilities have evolved significantly in recent years, and we expect they will continue advancing rapidly. This will lead not only to an expanding addressable market, but also to an expanding scope of impact on the world. We aim to ensure that impact is as positive as possible.
p1174: Mission & Focus. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
p1175: Talent & Culture. Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier AI capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
p1176: Frontier & Safety Research. We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is required to build the most capable and safest AI systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that are more reliable, steerable, and well-suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity, and have consistently released better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI and can greatly accelerate the rate at which capabilities advance. We believe that model capabilities must be advanced together with safety, alignment, and security practices, particularly as the speed of AI development accelerates. We assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release, and take the steps we believe are appropriate to balance model capabilities with safety, alignment, and security, even where doing so may moderate the rate at which we release new capabilities. We view decisions of this kind as deliberate tradeoffs that we make because they serve the Company Purpose, the long-term interests of our mission, and our customers’ demand for safe and aligned models.
p1177: Our Approach to Compute. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance the frontier of AI capabilities through research and model development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude. We have achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of Claude, we continue to invest at scale. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of more than $ , substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $ expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $ of these commitments are due in the next 12 months. p1178: Enterprise Strategy. Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement loops from customer feedback are richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus and makes Claude more capable over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our AI reach people and organizations at scale.
p1179: The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI. Our customer base as of September 30, 2026 includes:
p1180: • More than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis;
p1181: • More than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis; and
p1182: • Approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.
p1183: Unlike a static product that serves a single use case, Claude is frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities. We build at three layers of the stack: the models themselves, the platform for building on those models, and the applications that place Claude directly in the hands of our users. An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025.
p1184: Today, enterprises rely on Claude to reason, plan, and execute across complex workflows with a level of trustworthiness and judgment that we believe was not previously available from earlier generations of AI. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As Claude’s capabilities grow, our customers benefit and often broaden their adoption of Claude in new workflows. This expanding role reflects a broader shift in how Claude is used inside the enterprise, from a tool that responds to discrete prompts to what we call a Virtual Collaborator: an AI system that works alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels.
p1185: We drive the diffusion of Claude primarily by making it accessible across multiple product surfaces. For example:
p1186: • Claude Platform, our comprehensive agentic development environment, provides customers with direct access to the primitives to build, deploy, and scale their own applications that leverage Claude’s capabilities within their own products and workflows.
p1187: • Claude Code, our coding agent, works alongside human software developers on end-to-end software development: writing, planning, editing, testing, debugging, and committing code across productionscale codebases.
p1188: • Claude Cowork, our knowledge work agent, has computer use capability that enables it to work with professionals on end-to-end business tasks: autonomously researching, drafting, analyzing, synthesizing, and executing other knowledge work.
p1189: Much of the diffusion of Claude has been organic. We amplify this with our go-to-market and Applied AI teams, which extend our reach by meeting customers where they are through distribution partnerships that place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks. For example, Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements. Ecosystem partnerships also expand our reach, allowing customers to adopt Claude through SIs, such as Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC, consultants, and data platforms, such as Salesforce and Snowflake. We recently launched Ode with Anthropic, an AI services company, in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to midsized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the long term.
p1190: Building and scaling frontier AI is one of the most important and capital-intensive endeavors in history. Our financial model provides us with the following strengths that allow us to build and scale efficiently:
p1191: • Rapid Revenue Growth. Our enterprise strategy is designed to drive durable customer adoption by embedding Claude directly into business-critical workflows and enabling the development of products built on Claude. We believe that enterprise customers achieve a compelling return on investment from Claude, as agentic workflows can drive both top-line growth and efficiency. This enables us to expand quickly with customers, as demonstrated by our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.
p1192: • Compute Efficiency. Our compute efficiency drives more intelligence from research and model development, and we believe this approach can support more customer and internal usage of Claude for the same amount of compute compared to other approaches. Our compute efficiency is demonstrated by revenue that grew 1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026 compared to compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 300% during the same period.
p1193: • Operating Efficiency. Our operating efficiency, derived from our high talent density, our efficient goto-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work, enables us to scale with a smaller team relative to other large enterprise technology companies. Our operating efficiency is demonstrated by TTM revenue per employee of over $6.6 million as of September 30, 2026, compared to $1.4 million as of September 30, 2025.
p1194: Our financial results reflect continued growth alongside ongoing investment in frontier AI as demonstrated below:
p1195: • Our revenue was $11.6 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026, up from $787 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025.
p1196: • Our operating margin was 8% and operating income was $1.0 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to an operating margin of (152)% and operating loss of $1.2 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2025.

p1198: The demonstrated growth, scale, and efficiency of our financial model help us to continue making significant long-term investments to build frontier AI responsibly. Our business trajectory and financial profile have enabled us to access capital and secure compute from investors and partners. As of June 30, 2026, we had raised an aggregate of $141.1 billion of capital and had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion and shortterm investments of $19.3 billion. Long-term investments come with risks, as we must predict compute needs multiple years into the future. However, we believe our compute efficiency positions us to amplify returns if demand is greater than our forecast and can provide financial resilience if demand is lower or arrives later than we anticipate.
p1199: Our scale and growth create self-reinforcing loops that make Claude better over time and that we believe create durable competitive advantages.
p1200: • Improvement Loop. Enterprise deployments of Claude deepen our understanding of the hard problems, edge cases, and domain-specific challenges that matter most to our customers. We improve our models, platform, and applications based on feedback from customers using our offerings in production across their businesses. These improvements result in wider deployments and adoption that fuel the next cycle of improvement.
p1201: • Investment Loop. Revenue from expanding enterprise adoption helps us to fund the compute, research, and talent needed to improve Claude. Claude’s advancing capabilities expand the range of tasks and workflows customers use Claude for, broadening our addressable market and driving deeper deployment, additional revenue, and continued reinvestment in Claude.
p1202: Claude itself has become one of the most powerful drivers of our progress—each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next. Many aspects of the research, training, and testing of subsequent model generations now involve Claude, including running experiments, generating and processing training data, automating evaluations and safety audits, and writing and reviewing code. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop.” A direct expression of this dynamic is our accelerating pace of producing compute multipliers. More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.
p1203: A clear example of our ability to close the loop is the deployment of Claude Code, our agentic coding product, across our engineering organization. As our models have advanced, we have seen significant improvement in Claude’s capability on more challenging, open-ended engineering problems that lack a clear specification and have historically depended on experienced human judgment. Claude’s success rate on these problems reached approximately 90% in September 2026, up approximately 50 percentage points in nine months, based on our internal benchmarks. Claude Code has progressed from suggesting code to writing and running it directly and working autonomously over long time horizons on complex, multi-step engineering tasks. This has enabled our engineers to increasingly direct and review its work rather than write code line by line. As a result, the average daily volume of code contributed to our codebase per engineer in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was over 45 times the average daily volume in the year ended December 31, 2024. Over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude.
p1204: The impact of Claude extends beyond research and engineering. From December 31, 2024 to September 30, 2026, our headcount grew over five times, while our revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was 86 times our revenue for the three months ended December 31, 2024.
p1205: We believe this operating leverage has been driven by the use of Claude throughout our organization. Across our research, engineering, go-to-market, and operations teams, Claude allows employees to leverage a team of agents in their daily work, enabling a comparatively small team to take on work that would traditionally require a far larger one by multiplying the impact of each person.
p1206: The expansion of our own use of Claude reflects this leverage directly. The value of our own internal Claude usage at list prices has grown by over 250 times from January 2026 to September 2026, and in April 2026, this monthly value first exceeded our monthly personnel expense, excluding stock-based compensation. Because each version of Claude is used to help build the next and because Claude makes our teams more productive across the company, we believe the compute we devote to internal usage compounds these gains, continuously accelerating our pace of development and further strengthening our leadership position.
p1207: Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed “recursive selfimprovement.”
p1208: We believe that Powerful AI, a highly capable and impactful form of frontier AI characterized by the following key attributes, will become widely available within a few years:
p1209: • cognitive capabilities matching or exceeding those of top human experts across most professional and scientific disciplines;
p1210: • the ability to navigate all interfaces available to a human working virtually, including text, audio, video, and direct computer control;
p1211: • the ability to reason through complex tasks autonomously over extended periods—lasting hours, days, or weeks—and seek clarification and feedback when needed;
p1212: • the ability to coordinate across multiple instances and collaborate with both humans and other AI systems; and
p1213: • the ability to interface with the physical world by digitally controlling laboratory equipment, robotic systems, and other machines through digital connections.
p1214: If Powerful AI is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the potential is extraordinary. The possibilities include compressing decades of scientific progress into years; accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy; providing individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice; advancing power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability; and extending to the developing world capabilities that took wealthy nations generations to build.
p1215: The intelligence and capabilities of AI systems have advanced dramatically. Tasks that were beyond the reach of AI systems just a few years ago, such as complex mathematical reasoning, designing scientific experiments, and executing substantial portions of software development, are now routinely performed by AI.
p1216: These advances have followed empirical “Scaling Laws,” the finding that AI model performance improves predictably with increases in model size, training data, and compute. The foundational paper, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, whose lead authors (including Dario Amodei, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Tom Brown) later co-founded Anthropic, was critical in establishing these relationships and helped guide the wave of modern LLMs.
p1217: We expect AI capabilities—across language, reasoning, mathematics, coding, scientific analysis, and an expanding range of agentic tasks and knowledge work—to continue advancing for many years. As a result, we believe this will drive demand for AI that outstrips supply for the foreseeable future, limited principally by the availability of compute. We believe that the majority of this demand will be concentrated at the frontier: our experience has been that enterprises gravitate to our most capable models across a wide variety of workloads, including their highest-value work. In addition, we believe that each successive expansion of the frontier will unlock new categories of work that, in turn, will generate the majority of incremental industry demand. We expect the industry to continue increasing investment in compute, research talent, and engineering resources to advance the frontier of AI. Within this framework, research labs with proprietary training methods, strong data quality, and differentiated research talent are well-positioned to outpace what scale alone would predict.
p1218: Frontier AI is transforming cognitive work—the application of knowledge, reasoning, and judgment to produce economic value. We believe it will make humans far more capable and expand the world’s overall capacity for that work, including accelerating scientific discovery and helping businesses grow. Knowledge workers are the leading edge of this opportunity. As frontier AI advances, more capable models can unlock entirely new use cases while also efficiently serving a wide range of cognitive work at scale across the capability-cost-speed curve. We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic 6 value globally in 2025, and with frontier AI’s potential to make them meaningfully more productive, our nearterm opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth. While it is still early to forecast frontier AI’s full impact across the economy, IDC estimates that investment in AI solutions and services will 7 yield a cumulative global economic impact of $22.5 trillion by 2031. We believe the impact could be even greater.
p1219: History suggests that transformative technologies expand the markets they enter. For example, information technology spend grew from approximately $1.2 trillion in 2006 to $4.3 trillion in 2025, a CAGR of approximately 7%, as cloud computing spend grew from zero to $1.9 trillion over the same period and expanded 8 information technology budgets. We have seen other technologies, including the personal computer, the internet, and the smartphone, grow their markets as well. The companies that built these technologies grew at a far faster rate than the economy as a whole. Global GDP grew from approximately $34 trillion in 2000 to more than $118 trillion in 2025 according to the World Bank, more than tripling. Over that same period, the ten largest publicly traded technology companies by market capitalization as of September 30, 2026 grew their aggregate revenue from $68 billion to more than $2.5 trillion, an increase of approximately 38 times, or approximately 11 times the rate of global GDP growth.
p1220: We believe frontier AI represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle, and Claude is already demonstrating this potential. Claude can now execute complex projects autonomously over hours and days, coordinating thousands of agents in parallel to carry out sophisticated planning, long-form research, and selfcorrecting analysis. Claude also turns open-ended tasks into finished, high-quality deliverables—work that was beyond the reach of frontier AI only a short time ago. These capabilities position Claude to transform the largest sectors of the global economy, including software development, business and professional services, cybersecurity, financial services, and healthcare and life sciences, driving meaningful gains in productivity and output for the organizations that deploy it.
p1221: Cybersecurity represents one of our most important near-term opportunities. As each new generation of AI models grows more capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, we expect that defending enterprise networks and critical infrastructure will increasingly require frontier AI. At the same time, the diffusion of AI is expanding the threat surface, as organizations deploy agents and autonomous capabilities at an accelerating pace. Our leadership in coding has allowed us to advance Claude’s cybersecurity capabilities and build products that help enterprises secure their most critical infrastructure. For example, Claude Security can continuously scan customers’ codebases, triage vulnerabilities, and write fixes. We also recently launched OSS Scanner, which extends some of these capabilities to the open-source projects that enterprise software is built on. p1224: We expect other sectors to follow as Claude’s frontier capabilities extend beyond current markets to open entirely new ones, reaching domains such as robotics, advanced manufacturing, and logistics, and accelerating progress in scientific research, including drug discovery and materials science.

p1226: Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth. As frontier AI makes workers and organizations more productive, becomes embedded in the products and services they deliver, and unlocks new business models, it creates economic output that did not previously exist. We believe our opportunity is to capture a share not only of today’s economic activity but also of that newly created output as the global economy expands.
p1227: While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decisionmaking or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators. We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. p1228: We have five core advantages that define our position at the frontier: our mission and focus, our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy.

p1238: Our approach to research provides key advantages to our business:
p1239: • Our Model Research and Compute Performance Are Co-designed from the Start. Architectural decisions are made with compute efficiency in mind from day one. Our model architecture and inference infrastructure are designed in a single unified process. AI researchers and inference infrastructure engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance targets. This approach enables us to develop model versions that are both more capable and more efficient compared to prior versions.
p1240: • Our Pre-training Process Is Engineered for Capital Efficiency. We focus on a clear pipeline for developing model improvements to architecture, training methodology, and data. These are tested at a smaller scale before they consume significant compute. The bar for inclusion in a frontier training run is high and strictly evidence-based: we require demonstration that a given improvement holds as models increase in size, not merely that it performs well at reduced scale. Frontier training runs are planned, scheduled capital deployments with known inputs and rigorous inclusion criteria. The result is a repeatable process for converting research investment into capability gains, while managing the risks inherent to frontier training runs.
p1241: • Our Post-training Investment Is Purpose-Built for Agentic Capabilities. Post-training has grown from a finishing step into a major research investment, reflecting the market shift from assistants to agents. This is where our models hone their ability to write code, use tools, follow instructions, and operate software on a user’s behalf. We train against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects real professional work.
p1242: • Our Safety Research Is a Commercial Benefit. As models take on agentic roles with access to critical business systems, trust and reliability are paramount. And as capabilities increase, the ability to operate safely becomes one of the key determining factors for commercial viability. Models that are well-aligned are better at following a user’s instructions—for example, they avoid taking potentially destructive actions without fully understanding user intent. They are also more robust against attacks such as prompt injection, where malicious actors attempt to hijack the model by feeding it illicit instructions. Our work on alignment, interpretability research, safeguards, and red-teaming, as well as the use of external reviewers who can assess our safety practices, helps us create safer, more reliable models, and therefore positions us to meet our customers’ rigorous requirements. Safety and capability research are integrated, which enables us to deliver the trust and performance required for enterprise workflows.
p1243: Our approach to compute starts with training models that are designed to be more capable and run more efficiently on any given type of compute.

p1254: We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 10 2028.
p1255: The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants. What makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.

p1330: Customers choose Claude for more than the models. The Claude Platform lets developers and businesses build, manage, and deploy agentic AI applications on infrastructure with high reliability, security, and availability.
p1331: Platform features enable developers to customize their usage of Claude, including:
p1332: • Extended Thinking. Claude can perform additional internal reasoning before producing a final response, working through complex, multi-step problems to improve response quality on tasks like analysis, math, and coding.
p1333: • Adaptive Thinking. Claude automatically calibrates whether a given request calls for extended reasoning and how much reasoning to apply—so developers get the benefits of extended reasoning without configuring reasoning levels request by request.
p1334: • Effort Controls. Developers can specify an effort level on each request to guide how much reasoning Claude applies, allowing them to balance response quality against cost and latency.
p1335: • Tool Use. Claude can natively call external functions and APIs throughout a conversation, with support for parallel execution and interleaved thinking between tool calls. The search tool loads only the tools required for a given task on demand, which can reduce token overhead compared to loading full tool libraries upfront.
p1336: • Long Context. Claude supports large context windows and maintains its strong performance even as inputs grow, meaning that developers can include entire codebases, large document sets, or long agent histories in a single request.
p1337: • Structured Outputs. Developers can constrain Claude’s responses to a specified schema, such as valid JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), so results integrate reliably with downstream systems and application code with less additional parsing or validation.
p1338: • Code Execution. A sandboxed execution environment where Claude can write, run, and iterate on code within an agent loop, which is foundational for data analysis and automation workflows. This environment lets Claude call tools and process large volumes of data more efficiently and run the scripts packaged in Agent Skills.
p1339: • Web Search. A native tool giving Claude access to real-time web information, enabling grounded, citation-aware responses in production applications.
p1340: • Files API. Allows developers to upload documents once and reference them across multiple sessions, simplifying workflows that depend on persistent documents.
p1341: Developers can connect context to Claude for their agents and applications using context primitives.
p1342: • Model Context Protocol. MCP is an open standard we introduced in November 2024 and donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. MCP defines a universal interface through which Claude, as well as other AI tools, can connect to enterprise data sources, tools, and workflows. Claude Platform’s native MCP connector handles connection management, tool discovery, and error handling automatically.
p1343: • Agent Skills. A modular framework that lets organizations encode repeatable tasks, workflows, and domain expertise into reusable packages, or skills, that Claude loads on demand. We provide pre-built skills for common formats like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF, while custom skills can capture anything from engineering standards and regulatory processes to proprietary toolchains. These skills turn institutional knowledge into agent capabilities.

p1351: A model alone is not an agent. Autonomous operation requires a harness, which provides the secure environment, credentials, memory, and orchestration loop a model needs to plan, call tools, verify its work, and complete a task safely on its own. Building and operating that infrastructure is specialized, continuous work that, until recently, each customer had to take on themselves. We offer two ways to run a harness on the Claude Platform:
p1352: • Agent SDK. This solution makes the same production-grade harness that powers Claude Code available to all developers, to run on their own compute. p1353: • Claude Managed Agents. An out-of-the-box solution in which we operate the harness on our customers’ behalf, on Anthropic-managed compute. p1392: As of September 30, 2026, our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis included every company in the Fortune 10, over 50% of the Fortune 500, and over 30% of the Global 2000.
