Claude has achieved particularly deep adoption in highly regulated sectors where the cost of unreliable AI is prohibitive and trust cannot be retrofitted.
p1393: In addition, leading AI-native companies build next-generation coding tools, design platforms, and productivity applications on Claude. Government and research institutions also apply Claude to work that ranges from materials science to energy security; mission-driven organizations use Claude to compress the expected timeline of scientific research, clinical workflows, and the delivery of public benefits.
p1394: Our customer base has grown rapidly in both the number and scale of customer relationships, with organizations expanding from initial use cases into enterprise-wide production deployments. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025.
p1395: Our customers fall into two primary categories: enterprises and prosumers.
p1396: Our enterprise customers include a wide range of organizations deploying AI at scale, from AI-native startups building products to the world’s largest organizations that require enterprise-grade security, governance, and compliance before a single workflow impacts production. We serve this full spectrum from a single composable platform, providing frictionless access to our frontier models as well as the controls customers require, such as single sign-on, audit logging, data retention policies, role-based access controls, and native deployment within their existing cloud infrastructure.
p1397: Software developers remain a critical adoption force within enterprises: they are simultaneously customers, the architects of applications built on our platform, and the internal champions of organization-wide adoption. Software developers use Claude Code and the Claude Platform to write, debug, and ship production-quality code faster—architecting systems, implementing features, building agentic workflows, and resolving complex issues in hours that previously took days. These production deployments surface the governance, reliability, and integration requirements that only emerge under real enterprise load, which creates feedback that flows back into our roadmap and deepens our customer relationships with every release.
p1398: Knowledge workers, including researchers, developers, analysts, and writers, subscribe to Claude Pro and Claude Max to perform complex cognitive work, including drafting analyses, synthesizing research, writing and reviewing code, building financial models, and automating workflows. With Claude Cowork, non-technical prosumers build agentic workflows across their applications without writing code, accomplishing in minutes what previously required hours of manual effort.
p1399: Prosumers are some of our earliest adopters and often among our most discerning users. They test out capabilities within hours of the release of a model, push the latest version of Claude into use cases we may not have anticipated, and discover edge cases and failures that sharpen each successive version of a Claude model.
p1400: The adoption of Claude Code began with individual software developers who noticed the potential of autonomous coding agents before enterprise procurement teams had considered the category; Claude Code is now becoming the default choice inside many enterprise engineering organizations.
p1401: Prosumers serve as a powerful top-of-funnel engine—we have consistently seen that individuals who experience Claude’s value firsthand become advocates within their organizations, seeding adoption that accelerates from individual use to team-wide and ultimately organization-wide deployment.
p1402: Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. These outcomes are different expressions of the same intelligence, each drawing on the same models and primitives.
p1403: More Productive Employees. Adoption most often begins here. An individual experiences the impact that a frontier AI model can have on their own output—for instance, hours of financial analysis or code review completed in minutes—and that conviction spreads from the first user to their team, and from one team to the entire company. This happens for Claude Code in software development; Claude Cowork delivers this for knowledge workers more broadly. Our Claude Enterprise plan provides the governance, security, and administration to support adoption of Claude at organizational scale.
p1404: Faster Processes. As adoption deepens, Claude stops being something employees consult and starts being something the organization runs on. As organizations encode more of their workflows into Claude—their data, systems, conventions, and prior work—the platform becomes more valuable for them. Claude can draw on that accumulated context to suggest the next workflow worth automating, reducing the effort required for each successive deployment.
p1405: Embedded Intelligence. At the deepest level, Claude moves from an operational advantage to a commercial one. Product teams build on the Claude Platform to embed frontier AI into their own products, including customerfacing agents, AI-native features, and entirely new product lines that were not previously viable without AI capabilities. Claude is both a tool the organization uses and an ingredient in the value it delivers to its own customers.
p1406: Across all three dimensions, a significant share of expansion requires minimal to no new deployment at all. Each new version of a Claude model is designed to improve the performance of existing use cases: employees produce higher-quality work, encoded processes run with greater accuracy and reliability, and embedded products deliver more value to end users. As a result, customers can increase usage, utilize higher subscription tiers, and bring additional workflows onto the platform without a new sales cycle or procurement decision.
p1407: Despite the pace of adoption, we believe we are in the earliest stages of penetrating the frontier AI opportunity. Most enterprises that use Claude today have deployed it across a small number of teams and use cases relative to the scope of work Claude can address today, and the scope of work we believe Claude can address in the future. We believe most knowledge workers globally have not yet used frontier AI. As each new version of a Claude model advances in capability, the range of tasks and workflows that become viable on the platform continues to expand. Because we operate the platform and offer applications, model advances reach our customers through several channels simultaneously.
p1408: Anthropic was founded by a team of researchers who believe that the most consequential technology in history demands an organization structurally committed to both capability and safety. That conviction reaches every dimension of the organization: how we hire staff, the research we perform, the policy positions we adopt, and the choices we make about the deployment of our models. As a result, we are able to achieve breakthroughs that we believe would be impossible in a culture where safety, model capability, and commercial success are treated as opposing forces.
p1409: All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders remain active leaders in the organization. It is uncommon to see this level of continuity among the founding team of a technology company, including other major frontier AI labs. The continuity reflects a genuinely mission-driven and high-trust team.
p1410: Several features of our culture are distinctive and difficult for any organization to replicate:
p1411: • We Use What We Build. We are one of the most intensive users of our own technology. Over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude, and Claude is embedded in workflows across all teams at the company. When every team relies on the product daily, the feedback loop between builder and user is compressed: deficiencies can be found rapidly, and improvements are felt company-wide.
p1412: • Researching Both Safety and Capability. At the same time we advance frontier AI, we develop the policies and techniques designed to keep our models safe. We were the first frontier AI lab to adopt a formal Responsible Scaling Policy tying safety evaluations to capability thresholds, which was codeveloped by the same researchers who build our models. Our alignment and mechanistic interpretability research are examples of active scientific fields that help us understand ever-morecapable versions of Claude.
p1413: • We Optimize for Talent Density. As of September 30, 2026, with approximately 5,300 employees, our TTM revenue per employee was over $6.6 million—a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a culture built to compound it. Our employees are known internally as “Ants”—a nickname that captures the collaborative, ego-light culture of the team. Ants include many of the researchers and developers defining the frontier of AI, alongside proven operators across disciplines. Shared purpose paired with low ego translates directly into less organizational friction and greater impact per employee. Claude compounds that impact further: Ants use Claude across every function to take on work that would otherwise require substantially larger teams—allowing us to remain remarkably lean relative to our output.
p1414: • Rigor Applied to Every Function. A majority of our workforce works in research, engineering, and product development. But the culture of intellectual rigor extends to non-technical functions as well: our policy team publishes detailed policy frameworks and proposals; our go-to-market team codevelops deployment architectures alongside customers; and our Applied AI engineers sit at the frontier of what is possible with agentic systems. Our teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title. The result is a company where the distance between a research insight and a released product is unusually short.
p1415: Our values guide daily decisions across the company—from hiring and research prioritization to product development and customer engagement. We chose them because they reflect how we actually work:
p1416: • Act for the Global Good. We strive to make decisions that maximize positive outcomes for humanity over the long run and are willing to take bold action to ensure our technology is a positive force.
p1417: • Hold Light and Shade. We stay hopeful about what AI can achieve while remaining clear-eyed about what could go wrong. Both perspectives are essential, and neither can be sacrificed for the other.
p1418: • Be Good to Our Users. We define “users” broadly: customers, policymakers, our team, and anyone affected by the technology we build or the actions we take. Going above and beyond for each of them— not just meeting their immediate needs but considering downstream consequences and societal effects —is our baseline expectation, not an exception.
p1419: • Race to the Top on Safety. We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it. We work to set the industry bar for AI safety and inspire a dynamic where companies must compete on safety.
p1420: • Do the Simple Thing That Works. We take an empirical approach to problems and solve for the size of our impact. We try to identify the simplest solutions and iterate from there.
p1421: • Be Helpful, Honest, and Harmless. These principles guide Claude’s behavior and reflect how we operate as an organization: a high-trust, low-ego team that communicates kindly and directly, assumes good intentions even in disagreement, and pitches in where needed, regardless of role or team.
p1422: • Put the Mission First. Our mission is the arbiter when trade-offs arise between speed and safety, shortterm revenue and long-term trust, competitive pressure and responsible development. Our mission gives us shared purpose, engenders trust and collaboration, and ensures that no one is a bystander in our success.
p1423: As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately 5,300 employees worldwide, a majority of whom work in research, engineering, and product development functions. Our team includes researchers who originated several foundational advances in AI, including RLHF, Constitutional AI, GPT-2 and GPT-3, and mechanistic interpretability, who developed the first Responsible Scaling Policy to be formally adopted by a frontier AI lab tying safety evaluations to model capability thresholds, and who authored the foundational paper on Scaling Laws. Our team draws from a range of disciplines and includes award-winning computer scientists, physicists, neuroscientists, mathematicians, and policy researchers, as well as seasoned engineering and go-to-market leaders, united by the conviction that the most consequential technology in history requires the most talented team building it. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way.
p1424: We design our human capital programs to attract, retain, and reward top talent through equity incentive plans and other compensation, while supporting employees’ continual growth and reinforcing our culture and values. In certain countries in which we operate, we are subject to, and comply with, local labor law requirements which may automatically make our employees subject to industry-wide collective bargaining agreements.
p1425: We believe that building AI systems that serve all of humanity requires a team that reflects the range of communities we serve. The interdisciplinary nature of our work means we actively seek talent from nontraditional backgrounds for an AI company, such as philosophy, journalism, and education, and we believe this breadth of perspective directly strengthens both the safety and capability of our research. We are committed to fostering an inclusive workplace where employees of all backgrounds can contribute, grow, and thrive.
p1426: We are first and foremost a research lab. We develop the foundational science to train frontier models, perform rigorous research to understand these models’ inner workings, and develop techniques to align these models to human values and make them safe.
p1427: Our research culture is organized around a principle we apply across the company: do the simple thing that works. We pursue continuous, empirically validated improvements to data composition, model architecture, and training methodology, all of which must demonstrate measurable gains that hold as models increase in scale. This is why we currently focus on software development and agentic capabilities: these are areas where economic impact is large; where safety concerns manifest, making them a test bed for safety research; and where outputs are largely verifiable.
p1428: Every research project must ultimately advance our mission. This focus also guides what we choose not to pursue. For example, we do not currently focus on developing video and image generation models, despite their commercial appeal. That compute instead goes to coding, agentic skills, and safety research—a research decision that has also aided the capital efficiency of our models.
p1429: Our research culture is highly collaborative and transparent. When multiple teams pursue parallel approaches, the norm is to consolidate behind the approach with the best empirical results rather than the loudest voice or most senior person in the room. This requires institutional trust we have built since our earliest days, and we believe it is a primary reason our research velocity has scaled significantly faster than headcount.
p1430: Anthropic was founded on the empirical conviction that Scaling Laws are the primary engine of AI progress. We operate with a sustained rigor in how we allocate research resources, including talent and compute, and measure whether each investment translates into scaled model performance. We believe that sustained and focused research can allow us to advance at an accelerated rate beyond what Scaling Laws alone predict through our compute multiplier advancements that have allowed us to push the frontier of model capability with better compute efficiency.
p1431: Pre-training. Our pre-training process operates as a disciplined pipeline. Researchers propose potential improvements to model architecture, training methodology, or data composition, and each candidate is then validated at a smaller scale before we permit it to consume large amounts of compute. We set a high bar for inclusion in a frontier training run; we require evidence that demonstrates a given improvement holds as models increase in size. Frontier training runs are themselves planned capital deployments with defined inputs and strict inclusion criteria. Although not every run performs as our researchers expect, the process is designed to turn research investment into predictable capability gains with greater consistency over time.
p1432: Post-training. Pre-training produces raw model capability. During post-training, that capability is refined into practical utility—the ability to write production-quality code, operate software tools, follow complex multi-step instructions, and act autonomously on a user’s behalf. This phase has evolved from a minor adjustment step into one of the largest areas of our research investment, reflecting evolution in model capability from conversational assistants to autonomous agents that perform tasks independently. Post-training centers on training models against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects the demands of real professional environments. We have made substantial proprietary investments in developing this task portfolio, and its breadth and realism constitute one of our most durable scientific advantages, which we believe is difficult to observe from outside the organization and correspondingly difficult to replicate.
p1433: Inference. Our model architecture and inference infrastructure are co-designed. AI researchers and inference infrastructure engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance targets. Model architecture decisions are made with inference economics as a priority, which is why successive versions of Claude models can deliver both higher capability and greater efficiency than their predecessors.
p1434: Any technology that is powerful enough to produce the enormous benefits that we believe AI will bring also poses risks. Responding to these risks requires a portfolio of safety research that spans how we train, evaluate, interpret, secure, and monitor our models.
p1435: Our Responsible Scaling Policy describes how we approach the catastrophic risks posed by AI. The policy requires us to regularly publish detailed risk reports that reflect our perspectives on the overall level of risk posed by our models and how we are mitigating such risks. Our teams test each model extensively before release, assessing its capabilities in the domains most relevant to catastrophic risk and evaluating the extent to which the model can be misused. Our risk report describes an overall assessment of the results of these evaluations, the mitigations we have implemented to address these risks, and whether, and if so, why, we believe the identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits. As part of the current version of our Responsible Scaling Policy, we publish a Frontier Safety Roadmap, detailing our plans for measurable advances in security, alignment, safeguards, and AI policy. This acts as an internal spur for safety research and development and is externally visible so customers and regulators can use it to gauge our progress. Consistent with this approach, we assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release and we take the steps we believe are appropriate to mitigate those risks. In the past, these steps have included delaying the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include additional measures that affect how and when we develop or release these new models. We believe these practices also serve our customers, since rigorous safeguards and predictable model behavior have become decisive criteria when selecting an AI partner.
p1436: We have developed a constitution for Claude that describes our vision for how an AI model should be and how it should behave, which is used directly in the model training process. We have used Claude’s constitution to meaningfully advance how frontier models are trained, and it is our attempt to grapple with the most difficult questions regarding the development of this new type of artificially intelligent entity. It is a living document that we intend to revise as we develop further models and learn more about how they work. Our researchers have found that training Claude on high-quality constitutional documents combined with fictional stories portraying an aligned AI contributes to reducing Claude’s misalignment rate. We believe Claude’s constitution has also proven commercially valuable: transparently laying out the values we intend Claude to hold increases customer trust.
p1437: This constitution orients Claude around four priorities:
p1438: • Be Broadly Safe. Avoid irreversible actions and support human oversight of AI behavior.
p1439: • Be Broadly Ethical. Maintain honesty and sound moral judgment, and avoid harmful acts.
p1440: • Be Compliant with our Guidelines. Adhere to our operational standards for user interactions and absolute prohibitions on certain categories of harm.
p1441: • Be Genuinely Helpful. Deliver substantive, expert-level assistance that creates real value for users.
p1442: Beyond the assessments performed under our Responsible Scaling Policy, we evaluate each Claude model prior to its release through a structured, multi-stage evaluation program covering model capabilities, safety behaviors, and societal impacts, including bias and discrimination, and we document the results of these predeployment evaluations, and their limitations, in our publicly available model system cards. This testing addresses the reliability and accuracy of model outputs, including through capability and accuracy benchmarking, evaluations focused on factual accuracy and hallucinations, evaluations of whether model outputs are honest and accurately reflect the information on which they are based, reliability testing of agentic performance over long-running tasks, and adversarial red-teaming designed to identify ways in which a model may fail or behave in unintended ways. Where these evaluations identify issues, we address them through additional post-training, adjusted safeguards, and re-evaluation prior to release, and we document residual limitations in the applicable model system card.
p1443: Claude models are trained on data drawn from a broad range of sources, modalities, and languages, including publicly available information from the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and other sources, such as synthetic data generated by our own models. We conduct diligence on third-party data sources to assess their quality, provenance, and suitability for our usage, and in many cases include contractual restrictions intended to discourage the inclusion of personal data in sourced datasets. We apply data curation and filtering processes to sourced data, which are designed to improve data quality, deduplicate content, and reduce potential exposure to harmful content.
p1444: We address bias and fairness risks at multiple stages of model training and deployment. We manage the representativeness and diversity of our training data through a layered approach in which dataset curation, post-training alignment, pre-deployment evaluation, and deployment safeguards each play a part, rather than through dataset composition alone. When deployed, our usage policy prohibits the use of Claude for discriminatory decision-making and requires human oversight for high-stakes automated decisions, such as those affecting employment, housing, or legal issues. Our validation, safeguards, and monitoring practices continue to evolve as model capabilities advance and as new risks and failure modes are identified.
p1445: Further, we have obtained ISO/IEC 42001 certification, an international standard established by the International Organization for Standardization (“ISO”) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (“IEC”), following an independent third-party audit of our AI management system, covering risk identification, assessment, and mitigation processes for the responsible development and deployment of AI. Compliance documentation, including our ISO/IEC 42001 certificate and SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) reporting, is available upon request through the trust center page of our website. We also provide predeployment model access to external evaluators, including government AI evaluation bodies such as the U.S. Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (the “CAISSI”) and the U.K. AI Security Institute, for recent frontier models, as described in our model system cards.
p1446: As AI models grow more capable, ensuring safe and predictable behavior becomes more challenging. Our Alignment team focuses on whether models behave as intended, and do not take unwanted actions of their own accord. The team evaluates models to surface undesirable behaviors and develops comprehensive safety evaluations, many of which we open source. Misaligned behaviors, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed across the industry and include examples of models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified. As models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with internal and external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior may increase. For more information about the risks related to model misalignment, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Our own internal alignment evaluation shows that our newly released frontier models have demonstrated improved alignment compared to their predecessors.
p1447: Unlike traditional software, where unwanted outputs are traceable to specific bugs, the inner workings of LLMs like Claude are more inscrutable. Our researchers describe AI models as “grown, not built”—software developers can set the initial conditions and some constraints, but they cannot fully control any given output or behavior. This makes assurances about safety—and the diagnosis of problems—far more challenging for AI than for standard software. Anthropic is widely recognized as a leader in mechanistic interpretability: the science of how LLMs work. We have developed mathematical techniques to map how models form and connect concepts as they reason through problems; investigated how they reflect constructs analogous to psychological states and thought processes; and tested how their behavior can be steered through direct adjustments to internal representations. We use interpretability research along with other alignment research techniques to test for unwanted behavioral tendencies before a model release.
p1448: Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user’s accounts. Findings from ongoing monitoring, external expert stress-testing, and threat intelligence inform our policies, model training, and detection systems. Identified issues may be addressed through measures such as updates to detection classifiers, reward-model adjustments during training, and changes to the instructions provided to our models that guide their behavior (known as system prompts). We also maintain public reporting channels, including a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty program for testing our safety defenses.
p1449: We have observed that more capable models are generally better at recognizing and preventing high-stakes misuse. We believe that robust safety measures and model utility are not inherently in tension, and that safety can improve alongside the capability of the models themselves.
p1450: Each release is accompanied by a detailed system card covering capability and safety evaluations, external tester reports, and discussion of areas where performance remains limited or where the model shows signs of unwanted behavior. For example, AI poses clear and present risks in the cybersecurity domain as advanced models could assist threat actors in security breaches and exploits. Mitigating these risks is a priority across our research, evaluation, and deployment practices. Before each model release, our Frontier Red Team conducts a detailed analysis to determine whether new models provide meaningful new capabilities to assist potential attackers, and our Safeguards team maintains dedicated classifiers and monitoring systems targeting cyberrelated misuse, including prompts related to malware creation, phishing, and infrastructure attacks.
p1451: We make decisions about model development and deployment, including whether to begin training a new model, on a case-by-case basis. Before releasing a frontier model, we consider a variety of factors, such as the capabilities and behaviors of the specific model at issue and of our models overall, how well our safeguards and security measures work, and how widely the model would be available. We plan to extend our testing to include more assessments at each stage of model training: pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment. Depending on these assessments, we may delay or suspend training or related research, delay releases, or limit access to models until we have confidence they can be developed and deployed safely. Our assessments are also informed by voluntary pre-deployment evaluation of certain models by the CAISSI and the U.K. AI Security Institute. For certain models that materially advance the capability of the frontier in areas relevant to national security, we also provide designated government partners with expanded early access so that they can independently evaluate model capabilities and safeguards before release.
p1452: Based on our analyses, we do not release every model we develop for general use; when the model’s capabilities warrant caution, we may restrict availability or decline to release entirely. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We later released Fable 5 for general use, but with safety restrictions on certain cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry capabilities.
p1453: Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of our Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier AI labs adopted similar frameworks within months.
p1454: Building on this approach, we have publicly called for “pacing the frontier,” by which we mean establishing industry-wide standards primarily related to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them. This call to pace the frontier contemplates frontier AI developers collaborating with governments and does not describe our own model development or release timelines, which continue to be informed by our risk assessments. If standards of this kind are adopted industry-wide through government action or regulation, the rate at which AI capabilities advance could be faster or slower than it is today, depending on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. We believe the first step toward “pacing the frontier” is independent verification of compliance with future regulatory standards, and we have begun implementing a program under which independent evaluators work alongside our own risk and safety teams with broad internal access, subject to legal, confidentiality, and security limits. As part of this program, we currently anticipate investing at least $1 billion over the next five years to build external reviewer capacity with Accenture. The terms of this arrangement have not been finalized and are subject to change. We have also called on other frontier AI developers to adopt comparable practices to demonstrate that safety commitments in our industry can be independently verified. We have further supported regulation and oversight of frontier AI, including measures focused on transparency and independent third-party auditing, and international coordination, so these practices apply across frontier developers rather than depend on voluntary adoption alone.
p1455: We believe frontier AI companies and governments should take action to strengthen the security of critical infrastructure against AI-related and other cyber threats, including by:
p1456: • providing responsible model access, funding, training, and hands-on support, particularly for underresourced critical-infrastructure defenders;
p1458: • working to ensure agentic identities are traceable and accountable;
p1459: • sharing best practices in continuous monitoring;
p1460: • investing in authorized testing, private disclosure, and verified remediation of vulnerabilities; and
p1461: • sharing tools, playbooks, and threat assessments with governments, security partners, and open-source maintainers.
p1462: We believe that by fixing the most dangerous weaknesses, verifying the fixes, and sharing what works, frontier AI companies and governments can turn today’s AI advances into lasting improvements in security that benefit everyone. We have committed up to $100 million in cyberdefense-related initiatives through Project Glasswing, and we expect to devote significant additional resources over time toward strengthening the security of AI systems and the critical infrastructure that depends on them. The scope, timing, and amount of any such future investments have not been finalized and remain subject to change based on business, regulatory, and other considerations, and there can be no assurance that these initiatives will achieve their intended effect.
p1463: Our own trajectory demonstrates that commercial success and a serious commitment to safety are not in tension. We have built one of the fastest-growing businesses in history while maintaining safety as a core priority at every stage.
p1464: We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. Our public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity—a mission in which safety is central to our work. Powerful AI can deliver immense benefits, but only if it is developed and deployed with rigorous attention to its risks. At times, that may require pausing the launch of our own most capable systems if we conclude they cannot yet be deployed safely. It also means actively working to ensure that the benefits of AI reach everyone, that the organizations and communities people depend on are strengthened, and that the hardest problems facing humanity are not left to market forces alone to solve.
p1465: Realizing this mission requires understanding how AI is actually being used and how it is reshaping society. Our Societal Impacts team builds privacy-preserving tools to study real-world, large-scale uses of Claude— examining how students, educators, and workers use the model, how its values surface in everyday conversations, and what users hope and fear about the future of AI. This includes what we believe to be the largest multilingual qualitative study of its kind, in which more than 80,000 people shared in depth how they see AI shaping their lives. Our Economics team extends this work to the labor market, publishing recurring data reports and fully open datasets (the Anthropic Economic Index) on how Claude is used across jobs, industries, and regions, as well as modeling potential future economic scenarios, so that workers, employers, policymakers, and independent researchers can ground their decisions in evidence and rigorous modeling. To deepen and broaden the reach of this work, we have established the Anthropic Institute, an effort to share research and internal data from across Anthropic with external partners and the public, working together to address the biggest questions posed by Powerful AI.
p1466: Our commitment to public benefit also extends to how we deploy our own resources. As part of our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier AI is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed. This might include making contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, or other groups working on problems where AI can have the greatest positive impact, as well as programs that are designed to make Claude accessible to communities, educators, and public institutions that would not otherwise have access. We believe that how we distribute our resources is as much an expression of our mission as the details of how we build our models.
p1467: As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose, which we refer to as the Initial Public Benefit Issuance. As the value we create grows, we intend for the public benefit to share meaningfully in that growth as well. To that end, our board of directors has approved a framework for additional contributions tied to future increases in our share price. Following this offering, our board of directors, in its discretion, may issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price. A share price milestone is reached only when our closing share price has exceeded the applicable threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 consecutive trading days, and our average closing share price over the ten trading days prior to such issuance also exceeds that threshold. Although our board of directors has approved this framework, any future contributions will be made at the discretion of our board of directors. The shares that are contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance, may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction in furtherance of our public benefit initiatives. Our board of directors will determine the allocations and distributions from the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund until it approves a specific governance structure for the entity, at which point decision-making authority is expected to transition to designated managers of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund operating under that structure. p1470: We face competition across multiple dimensions of our business. These competitors include:
p1471: We face direct competition from companies building frontier models for third-party software developers and enterprises, including OpenAI and Google, and large, well-capitalized technology companies investing to reach the frontier. p1472: We also face competition from a broader set of model providers. These include large companies, specialized AI labs and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights, training data, and code) models released by state actors and international and domestic research organizations. p1473: As a platform company, our primary focus is on building the foundation upon which other companies and software developers can create products and services driven by Powerful AI. p1474: Beyond direct competition, one obstacle to the diffusion of Claude is the natural resistance to change within organizations. Many enterprises operate with deeply entrenched legacy systems, established workflows, and institutional processes that have been refined over many years. Adopting frontier AI capabilities such as Claude often requires substantial change management, including workforce retraining, process redesign, internal policy development, and shifts in corporate culture. These can introduce friction, cost, and perceived risk that can delay or prevent adoption. Especially in highly regulated or risk-averse industries — where the perceived downside risk of major changes can often outweigh the potential benefits — decision-makers might default to maintaining the status quo.

p1495: We are subject to laws and regulations of various jurisdictions and government agencies affecting our operations and the provision of our models, platform, and applications, and we have been, and expect to continue to be, subject to inquiries, investigations, and subpoenas by governmental authorities relating to such laws and regulations. p1496: As an AI technology company, we are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental review across multiple jurisdictions. New laws, rules, regulations, and changes to existing laws and regulations are continuously being adopted, implemented, and interpreted as governments worldwide develop frameworks to address AI development, deployment, and safety. The primary areas of regulation that affect our business include AI-related regulations, data privacy and security, export controls and trade regulations, and other matters such as intellectual property, employment and labor, competition and antitrust, consumer protection, and tax.
p1497: The following discussion addresses the most significant regulatory areas affecting our business.
p1498: Various governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and other countries have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage, privacy, data protection, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, in the United States, AI regulation is developing at both federal and state levels. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has developed the AI Risk Management Framework, which is currently voluntary but could potentially inform or shape future mandatory requirements. The FTC and many state attorneys general are interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data. Various states have enacted or are considering enacting AI-related legislation. For example, on September 24, 2026, state attorneys general in New York and New Jersey, together with a coalition of other state and territorial attorneys general, sent a letter to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives leadership to urge Congress to establish comprehensive federal legislation and safety protocols for frontier AI. In the EU, the EU AI Act establishes a risk-based framework categorizing AI systems by potential risk level. General-purpose AI models face obligations including transparency requirements, technical documentation, EU copyright compliance, and publication of training data summaries, and those with systemic risk face additional obligations, including model evaluation, systemic risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection. High-risk systems must meet requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. Any actual or perceived non-compliance could result in regulatory investigations, enforcement actions and other actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of customer trust, and interruptions in the availability or performance of our products or services; require unfavorable changes to existing products or services; and delay the introduction of future products or services, which could have an adverse effect on our business.
p1499: We have called for regulation and oversight of frontier AI development, including standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that safety, alignment, and security practices advance in proportion with capabilities. We have also proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier AI developers to establish safety and evaluation standards. Certain of the approaches we support, if adopted, could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth.
p1500: We collect, store, transfer, and otherwise process various types of data, including personal information, and are subject to numerous federal, state, local, and foreign laws and regulations addressing privacy, data protection, security, data localization, and the collection, use, transfer, and other processing of data. p1512: In February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. p1513: Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose. In addition, a financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.
p1514: We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have generally aligned with our long-term commercial success and stockholders’ long-term monetary interests. However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’ balancing of these potentially competing interests. For a discussion of these risks, see “Risk Factors—Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock” and “Risk Factors—As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and our Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
p1515: In measuring our public benefit performance, our board of directors will consider the objectives set forth in our five mission pillars: that the technical problems of AI safety are solved, that AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law, that AI strengthens democracy and global stability, that AI expands prosperity and human flourishing, and that AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. We may also address the additional interests of our customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time. Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our public benefit performance against these objectives. We currently expect that our objectives and standards will be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public benefit impact develops.
p1516: As required by Section 366(b) of the DGCL, we will provide our stockholders no less than biennially with a statement assessing our promotion of the Company Purpose and of the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. p1517: We created the LTBT, which was designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose.
